cards.q: Why reproduce with a reduced configuration?
cards.a: To verify the pipeline and the protocol on your hardware. The absolute number scales with compute you can add later.
cards.n: Topic: Reading papers and reproducing benchmarks. Check yourself.

cards.q: What does a prior do when data are scarce?
cards.a: It dominates: the posterior stays near the prior until data accumulate, which is exactly the shrinkage that helps stations with few observations.
cards.n: Topic: Bayesian machine learning and Gaussian processes. Check yourself.

cards.q: Why do Gaussian processes suit hyperparameter tuning?
cards.a: They model a smooth unknown function with uncertainty from few evaluations, which is what Bayesian optimization needs to choose the next trial.
cards.n: Topic: Bayesian machine learning and Gaussian processes. Check yourself.

cards.q: A key takeaway from Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction (Murphy)?
cards.a: One vocabulary (likelihood, prior, posterior, predictive, decision) covers every model in the book, which is why the book is worth reading front to back.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I foundations: introduction; probability (univariate and multivariate models, Bayes' rule, exponential families, transformations, Monte Carlo);

cards.q: A key takeaway from The Elements of Statistical Learning (Hastie, Tibshirani, Friedman)?
cards.a: Chapter 7 (assessment) and chapter 10 (boosting) explain why LightGBM works and how to tune it; read those first.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters: introduction; overview of supervised learning (least squares and nearest neighbours, statistical decision theory, the curse of dimensionality, bias-variance);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms (Shalev-Shwartz, Ben-David)?
cards.a: Learnability requires a restricted class; generalisation bounds trade class richness (VC, Rademacher) against sample size.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I foundations: a gentle start (ERM, overfitting, finite hypothesis classes); a formal learning model (PAC, agnostic PAC, the realisability assumption);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Convex Optimization (Boyd, Vandenberghe)?
cards.a: Convexity is the property that makes a problem solvable exactly; learn to recognise and preserve it.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I theory: convex sets (affine and convex sets, operations that preserve convexity, generalised inequalities, separating and supporting hyperplanes, dual cones);

cards.q: A key takeaway from CS229 lecture notes (Stanford)?
cards.a: The GLM construction is the single most reusable derivation: it generates linear, logistic, Poisson and softmax regression from one recipe.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Main notes: supervised learning (linear regression, LMS, normal equations, probabilistic interpretation, locally weighted regression, logistic regression, Newton's method, GLMs and expon…

cards.q: A key takeaway from CS224W: Machine Learning with Graphs (Stanford)?
cards.a: A GNN layer is message, aggregate, update; every architecture is a choice of those three.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Lectures and slides: introduction (why graphs, applications, representations);

cards.q: A key takeaway from A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction (Angelopoulos, Bates)?
cards.a: Any model plus a calibration set gives valid prediction sets in three lines; the guarantee needs exchangeability, not correctness of the model.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Sections: conformal prediction (the recipe with a heuristic notion of uncertainty, a score function, a calibration set, the quantile, and prediction sets that contain the truth with the…

cards.q: A key takeaway from Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift (Gibbs, Candès, 2021)?
cards.a: Coverage under shift comes from feedback control, not from the model.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The paper: setting (online prediction with a model that may be arbitrarily wrong and data whose distribution shifts over time);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Statistical Rethinking lectures and course materials (McElreath)?
cards.a: Draw the DAG first; the elemental confounds tell you what to adjust for and what to leave alone.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Lecture series and course materials: science before statistics (models as golems, causal thinking, DAGs);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Probabilistic Programming and Bayesian Methods for Hackers (Davidson-Pilon)?
cards.a: Write the generative story, then let the sampler invert it; that is the whole workflow.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters (as notebooks): introduction (the Bayesian state of mind, Bayes' theorem, probability distributions, a text-message change-point example in PyMC);

cards.q: A key takeaway from A Visual Exploration of Gaussian Processes (Distill, 2019)?
cards.a: A kernel is a statement about function shape; choose it by what you know about the function.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: An interactive article: multivariate Gaussians (marginalisation and conditioning); Gaussian processes as distributions over functions defined by a mean and a kernel;

cards.q: A key takeaway from Foundations of Machine Learning (Mohri, Rostamizadeh, Talwalkar), 2nd edition?
cards.a: Rademacher complexity is the one tool that yields most bounds in the book, so learn its symmetrisation proof.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters: introduction; the PAC learning framework (guarantees for finite consistent and inconsistent hypothesis sets, generalities such as deterministic versus stochastic scenarios and…

cards.q: A key takeaway from PyTorch Geometric documentation?
cards.a: edge_index in COO plus a features matrix is the whole representation; get comfortable building it from a station adjacency table.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Get started (installation, introduction by example: data handling of graphs, common benchmark datasets, mini-batches, data transforms, learning methods on graphs);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition (Gelman, Carlin, Stern, Dunson, Vehtari, Rubin)?
cards.a: Model, condition, check, expand: the workflow matters more than any single model.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I fundamentals: probability and inference; single-parameter models (binomial, normal, Poisson, exponential, prior distributions, noninformative and weakly informative priors);

cards.q: A key takeaway from Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Rasmussen, Williams)?
cards.a: The marginal likelihood is the principled way to set kernel hyperparameters and it penalises complexity on its own.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Chapters: introduction; regression (weight-space view with Bayesian linear regression and feature projections, function-space view, varying the hyperparameters, decision theory for regre…

cards.q: A key takeaway from Deep Learning (Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville)?
cards.a: Chapters 6 to 8 (feedforward, regularisation, optimisation) are the durable core; read them fully.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: Part I applied math and ML basics: linear algebra; probability and information theory;

cards.q: A key takeaway from Graph WaveNet (Wu et al., IJCAI 2019)?
cards.a: Learning the graph (adaptive adjacency) beats trusting the road graph; the two together are best.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The paper: motivation (spatial dependencies in traffic are not fully captured by the road-distance graph, and RNN-based temporal models are slow);

cards.q: A key takeaway from METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN repository)?
cards.a: The METR-LA and PEMS-BAY format, split and masked metrics are the shared language of traffic forecasting; use the same format for Fremont so results are comparable.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The repository for Diffusion Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network: the two datasets (METR-LA, 207 loop detectors in Los Angeles County, four months of five-minute speeds in 2012;

cards.q: A key takeaway from ETA Prediction with Graph Neural Networks in Google Maps (Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021)?
cards.a: Multi-level supervision (segment, supersegment, route) makes the parts consistent with the whole.
cards.h: → one sentence, the resource's main lesson for this project
cards.n: Study guide: The paper: the problem (estimated time of arrival for a route as a sum over road segments, with a supersegment graph that groups segments);

cards.q: State the formula for loss (from The repo's own 00_CONCEPTS.md and…).
cards.a: loss = -mean(y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p))
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The repo's own 00_CONCEPTS.md and 05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md.

cards.q: State the formula for a·b (from Khan Academy: Linear algebra…).
cards.a: a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ = |a||b| cos θ
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Khan Academy: Linear algebra, Differential calculus, Statistics and probability.

cards.q: State the formula for x_{t+1} (from Mathematics for Machine Learning…).
cards.a: x_{t+1} = x_t − γ ∇f(x_t)ᵀ
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Mathematics for Machine Learning (Deisenroth, Faisal, Ong), chapters 2–7.

cards.q: State the formula for p-value (from OpenIntro Statistics).
cards.a: p-value = P(statistic at least as extreme | H₀)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for OpenIntro Statistics.

cards.q: State the formula for L (from Machine Learning Specialization…).
cards.a: L = −y log f(x) − (1 − y) log(1 − f(x))
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Machine Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng), courses 1 and 2.

cards.q: State the formula for F1 (from Machine Learning Specialization…).
cards.a: F1 = 2PR/(P + R)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Machine Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng), courses 1 and 2.

cards.q: State the formula for prediction bias (from Google's Machine Learning Crash Course).
cards.a: prediction bias = mean(predictions) − mean(labels)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Google's Machine Learning Crash Course.

cards.q: State the formula for w*_leaf (from The boosting papers: Friedman (2001)…).
cards.a: w*_leaf = −Σ_{i∈leaf} g_i / (Σ_{i∈leaf} h_i + λ)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The boosting papers: Friedman (2001), XGBoost (2016), LightGBM (2017).

cards.q: State the formula for MASE (from Forecasting: Principles and Practice…).
cards.a: MASE = MAE / MAE_naive_in-sample
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Forecasting: Principles and Practice, the Python edition (Hyndman, Athanasopoulos), chapters 1–5, 7, 9.

cards.q: State the formula for y_{t+h} (from Kaggle Learn: Time Series).
cards.a: y_{t+h} = f_h(y_t, y_{t−1}, …, x_t) (direct strategy, one model per h)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Kaggle Learn: Time Series.

cards.q: State the formula for wave speed w (from traffic-simulation.de and its model…).
cards.a: wave speed w = Δq/Δk between two traffic states
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for traffic-simulation.de and its model documentation (Treiber, Kesting).

cards.q: State the formula for RMSLE (from Kaggle: Store Sales, Time Series…).
cards.a: RMSLE = √( mean (log(1 + ŷ) − log(1 + y))² )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Kaggle: Store Sales, Time Series Forecasting competition.

cards.q: State the formula for RMSSE (from The M5 forecasting competition and its…).
cards.a: RMSSE = √( mean_h (y_{t+h} − ŷ_{t+h})² / mean_t (y_t − y_{t−1})² )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The M5 forecasting competition and its findings (Makridakis, Spiliotis, Assimakopoulos).

cards.q: State the formula for conv output size (from CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks…).
cards.a: conv output size = (W − F + 2P)/S + 1
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition, course notes.

cards.q: State the formula for softmax loss L_i (from CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks…).
cards.a: softmax loss L_i = −log( e^{f_{y_i}} / Σ_j e^{f_j} )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition, course notes.

cards.q: State the formula for lr (from Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et…).
cards.a: lr = d_model^{−0.5} · min(step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5})
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017).

cards.q: State the formula for perplexity (from Speech and Language Processing, 3rd…).
cards.a: perplexity = P(w₁…w_N)^{−1/N}
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft (Jurafsky, Martin).

cards.q: State the formula for L_DDPM (from The generative-model papers: VAE…).
cards.a: L_DDPM = E ‖ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t)‖²
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The generative-model papers: VAE (Kingma, Welling, 2013), GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014), DDPM (Ho, Jain, Abbeel, 2020).

cards.q: State the formula for L_simple (from What are Diffusion Models? (Weng…).
cards.a: L_simple = E_{t, x_0, ε} ‖ ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t) ‖²
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for What are Diffusion Models? (Weng, Lil'Log).

cards.q: State the formula for score (from The ML Test Score (Breck, Cai…).
cards.a: score = min over categories of Σ_tests {0, 0.5 manual, 1 automated}
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for The ML Test Score (Breck, Cai, Nielsen, Salib, Sculley, 2017).

cards.q: State the formula for cross-entropy (from Probabilistic Machine Learning: An…).
cards.a: cross-entropy = H(p) + KL(p || q)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction (Murphy).

cards.q: State the formula for alpha_{t+1} (from Adaptive Conformal Inference Under…).
cards.a: alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma (alpha - err_t), err_t = 1{ Y_t not in C_t }
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift (Gibbs, Candès, 2021).

cards.q: State the formula for WAIC (from Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition…).
cards.a: WAIC = -2 ( lppd - p_WAIC )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition (Gelman, Carlin, Stern, Dunson, Vehtari, Rubin).

cards.q: State the formula for Matérn nu (from Gaussian Processes for Machine…).
cards.a: Matérn nu = 3/2: k(r) = sigma^2 (1 + sqrt(3) r / l) exp( -sqrt(3) r / l )
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Rasmussen, Williams).

cards.q: State the formula for masked MAE (from METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN…).
cards.a: masked MAE = sum_{i: y_i != 0} |y_i - y_hat_i| / count(y_i != 0)
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN repository).

cards.q: State the formula for route ETA (from ETA Prediction with Graph Neural…).
cards.a: route ETA = sum over supersegments of predicted traversal time
cards.h: → the formula, then what each symbol means
cards.n: From the study guide for ETA Prediction with Graph Neural Networks in Google Maps (Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021).

cards.q: Define: Terminal
cards.a: The text window (the Terminal app on a Mac) where you type commands and press return instead of clicking. Every script in the course is started from it.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Shell
cards.a: The program inside the terminal that reads your commands; on a modern Mac it is zsh. Paths, pipes and environment variables are shell ideas.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Command
cards.a: One line typed into the shell: a program name followed by its arguments, such as python 02_collect_events.py.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Path
cards.a: The address of a file or folder. Absolute paths start at the root (/Users/you/Traffic1/data); relative paths start from the folder you are in (data/pems_raw). cd changes the current folder; ls lists it.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Pipe |
cards.a: Sends the output of one command into the next, so zcat file.gz | head -3 shows three lines of a compressed file without unpacking it.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Environment variable
cards.a: A named value the shell keeps and passes to programs, such as a password or an API key set with export PEMS_USERNAME=.... A .env file lists them so scripts can load them.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Python
cards.a: The programming language the course uses. It reads a text file of instructions and runs them one line at a time.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Script
cards.a: A file of Python code ending in .py, run with python name.py. The numbered files in Traffic1 (10_clean_pems.py and so on) are the pipeline's scripts.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Library (package)
cards.a: A bundle of ready-made code you load with import. pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, LightGBM and PyTorch are libraries.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: pip
cards.a: The tool that installs Python libraries: pip install pandas. requirements.txt lists everything the project needs so pip install -r requirements.txt installs it all.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Virtual environment (venv)
cards.a: A private copy of Python and its libraries for one project, so projects do not fight over versions. Create it once, activate it, install into it, and point VS Code and launchd at its Python.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: arm64 / Apple silicon
cards.a: The M-series chips in modern Macs. Python and its libraries must be the arm64 builds to use the chip well; platform.machine() must print arm64.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Jupyter notebook
cards.a: An app that runs Python one cell at a time and shows results, tables and plots under each cell. Good for looking at data; scripts are better for the pipeline.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: VS Code
cards.a: A free code editor. Point it at the venv's Python so it runs and checks code with the right libraries.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Git
cards.a: The version-control tool. It records snapshots (commits) of your files so you can see history, undo, and branch. GitHub hosts repositories online.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Repository (repo)
cards.a: A folder whose history git tracks. Traffic1 is one. .gitignore lists what git must never record, such as data/ and .env.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Commit, branch, push
cards.a: A commit is one saved snapshot with a message; a branch is a named line of commits; push copies your commits to GitHub.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: CSV
cards.a: Comma-separated values: a text table, one row per line, commas between fields. Easy to read, slow and large.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Parquet
cards.a: A compressed, column-by-column file format for tables. Small on disk, fast to load, keeps data types. The course stores every cleaned table this way.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: gzip (.gz)
cards.a: A compression format. PeMS files arrive gzipped; zcat prints them decompressed and pandas can read them directly.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: JSON
cards.a: A text format for lists and dictionaries ({"h": 30, "p": 0.42}) that every language can read. Used for thresholds, feature lists and the live predictions file.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: YAML / plist / XML
cards.a: Other text formats for settings. A launchd plist is XML: keys and values inside angle-bracket tags.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: launchd
cards.a: macOS's built-in scheduler. A plist in ~/Library/LaunchAgents tells it to run a program every N seconds or at boot, with logs to named files.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Log
cards.a: A text file a program appends lines to as it runs, so you can see what happened after the fact. Every stage in the course writes one line with its name, time and memory.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: API key / token
cards.a: A secret string that identifies you to a web service such as 511. Kept in .env, never in code or git.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: Polling
cards.a: Asking a server for its current data on a schedule, as the 511 collector does every few minutes.
cards.n: Glossary, tools and files.

cards.q: Define: PeMS
cards.a: Caltrans' Performance Measurement System: the archive of freeway detector readings for California, published as daily text files per district.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: 511
cards.a: The Bay Area traveller-information service; its API lists current incidents (crashes, stalls, closures) with times and locations.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Station (detector)
cards.a: One sensor site on the freeway, identified by a number. It reports flow, occupancy and speed every five minutes.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Mainline (ML)
cards.a: A detector on the through lanes, as opposed to an on-ramp, off-ramp or HOV lane. The course uses mainline stations only.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Postmile
cards.a: A station's distance along its freeway, used to put stations in driving order and find neighbors.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Upstream / downstream
cards.a: Upstream is where traffic comes from; downstream is where it is going. A jam downstream reaches you soon.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Registry
cards.a: The course's small curated table of the Fremont stations with their neighbors, built once from the PeMS meta file.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Flow
cards.a: Vehicles counted passing the detector in the interval.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Occupancy
cards.a: The fraction of the interval the sensor was covered by a vehicle; a stand-in for how densely packed the road is.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Speed
cards.a: Average speed in miles per hour over the interval.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: pct_obs
cards.a: The percentage of a five-minute row that came from real observations rather than PeMS's fill-in estimates. Below 50 the row is mostly guesswork.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Five-minute row / slot
cards.a: One reading per station per five minutes: 288 per day. The slot is the position in the day, 0 to 287.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Grid
cards.a: Every station × every slot, with no gaps. Missing readings are kept as NaN rows, never skipped, so shifts and windows stay aligned.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Timestamp
cards.a: A moment in time as a datetime value. Stored in UTC in the course; converted to Pacific time only to compute the hour of day.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Timezone, UTC, DST
cards.a: A timezone maps clock readings to moments. UTC is the single world clock. Daylight saving time makes one local hour vanish in spring and repeat in autumn, which the parsing code must handle.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: NaN / NaT
cards.a: Not a number / not a time: the markers for a missing value. Most pandas functions skip them; fillna replaces them.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Imputation
cards.a: Filling a missing value with an estimate. PeMS imputes; the course blanks heavily imputed rows and forward-fills short gaps.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Forward fill
cards.a: Copying the last known value into the following empty slots, up to a limit.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Incident
cards.a: A 511 event: crash, stall, closure, with created, updated and pulled-at times. Its reporting delay limits how much it can help.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: Schema
cards.a: The list of a table's columns and their types. Checked before every write.
cards.n: Glossary, data words.

cards.q: Define: pandas
cards.a: The Python library for tables. pd.read_csv, read_parquet, groupby, merge, shift, rolling are its verbs.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: DataFrame / Series
cards.a: A DataFrame is a table with named columns; a Series is one column. Selecting a column gives a Series.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: numpy
cards.a: The library for fast arithmetic on arrays. np.sin, np.mean, X @ w work on whole arrays at once.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Array / matrix / tensor
cards.a: A grid of numbers: one-dimensional (vector), two-dimensional (matrix), or more. PyTorch calls its arrays tensors.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Shape
cards.a: The size of each dimension of an array, such as (rows, columns) or (batch, time, channel, station). Most deep-learning bugs are shape bugs.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Index
cards.a: The row labels of a DataFrame. A MultiIndex has more than one level, such as (station, timestamp). reset_index turns levels back into columns.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Boolean mask
cards.a: A column of true/false, one per row, used to select rows: df[df.speed < 35].
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: .loc / .iloc
cards.a: Select by label (.loc[row, column]) or by position (.iloc[0]). Assigning to .loc[mask, col] changes only the masked rows.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: groupby
cards.a: Split a table into groups by a key, compute something per group, and combine. groupby("station_id").size() counts rows per station.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: transform
cards.a: A groupby method that returns a result the same length as the input, so it can be stored as a new column.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: merge (join)
cards.a: Line two tables up on shared key columns and combine their other columns. how="left" keeps every row of the left table.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: shift(k)
cards.a: Move a column down by k rows (a lag). A negative k moves it up, which looks into the future: allowed only for targets.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: rolling(n)
cards.a: A window of the last n rows; .mean(), .std(), .sum(), .max() summarize it. Rows must be in time order first.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: pivot
cards.a: Turn a long table (one row per station and time) into a wide one (one row per time, one column per station).
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Chunking / streaming
cards.a: Reading a file in pieces (chunksize) and keeping only what is needed from each, so memory stays small.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: float32 / int8
cards.a: Number types that use 4 bytes and 1 byte instead of 8. Halving or quartering memory with no real loss for speeds and flags.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: f-string
cards.a: Text with values filled in: f"speed_lag_{k}".
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: List comprehension
cards.a: A one-line loop that builds a list: [c for c in cols if c != "y"].
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Lambda
cards.a: A small unnamed function written inline: lambda s: s.rolling(3).sum().
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: assert
cards.a: A check that must be true or the program stops with an error. The cheapest safety net; put one before every write.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Seed (random_state, default_rng(0))
cards.a: A fixed starting point for random numbers, so a run can be repeated exactly.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: matplotlib
cards.a: Python's plotting library. plt.plot, plt.scatter, plt.show.
cards.n: Glossary, tables and code words.

cards.q: Define: Unit
cards.a: The thing a row describes: one station at one timestamp.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Inputs (features)
cards.a: The columns a model reads. Every one must be known at the row's moment.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Target (label)
cards.a: The column the model tries to predict. Here 1 if the station is inside a slow episode h minutes later, else 0.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Horizon
cards.a: How far ahead the prediction looks: 15, 30 or 60 minutes, one model each.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Slow episode
cards.a: Three consecutive five-minute rows with speed below 60 percent of the station's typical speed for that slot and day type.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Profile
cards.a: The typical speed per station, day type and slot, computed as the median over training rows only.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Prevalence
cards.a: The share of rows that are positive. Small here, which is why accuracy is useless and average precision is used.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Leakage
cards.a: Any information from after a row's moment getting into its inputs, or test data influencing training choices. The mistake that makes models look great and then fail.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Feature engineering
cards.a: Deciding and computing the input columns: lags, rolling statistics, time-of-day circle, holidays, neighbor readings.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Lag
cards.a: A value from k steps earlier in the same station's series.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Cyclic encoding
cards.a: Placing a time on a circle with sine and cosine so 23:55 and 00:05 are close.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Split (train / validation / test)
cards.a: Dividing the data by date. The model learns from training, choices are made on validation, and test is scored once at the end.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Baseline
cards.a: The simplest forecast without a model: persistence (the future equals now) and the profile rate (the historical average). Every model must beat them.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Metric
cards.a: How guesses are scored. Average precision, precision, recall, Brier score, lead time and false-alarm rate are the course's metrics.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Precision / recall
cards.a: Precision is the share of alarms that were right; recall is the share of real jams that were alarmed. Raising one usually lowers the other.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Average precision (AP)
cards.a: The area under the precision-recall curve: the prevalence for random guessing, 1.0 for perfect. Not fooled by rare positives.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Threshold (τ)
cards.a: The score above which an alert fires. Chosen on validation to meet a required precision.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Calibration
cards.a: Whether a score of 0.3 really means a 30 percent chance. Checked with a reliability diagram; fixed with isotonic regression.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Brier score
cards.a: Mean squared difference between predicted probability and outcome; lower is better.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Bootstrap
cards.a: Estimating uncertainty by resampling the data many times and recomputing the score. Resample whole days for time series.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Onset, lead time, false alarm
cards.a: An onset is the first row of an episode; lead time is minutes from the first alert to the onset; a false alarm is an alert with no episode in the next hour.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Drift
cards.a: The data slowly changing after training. Measured with the population stability index; confirmed by delayed scoring.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Population stability index (PSI)
cards.a: One number comparing a feature's distribution now with training. Below 0.1 stable, above 0.25 moved.
cards.n: Glossary, prediction words.

cards.q: Define: Model
cards.a: A function from inputs to a score, with parameters set by training.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Parameters (weights) / hyperparameters
cards.a: Parameters are learned from data; hyperparameters (learning rate, number of leaves) are chosen before training.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Logistic regression
cards.a: Weighted sum of features plus bias, squashed by the sigmoid into a probability. The simplest model that outputs a probability.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Sigmoid
cards.a: 1 / (1 + e^(−z)): turns any number into a value between 0 and 1.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Logit
cards.a: The number before the sigmoid. PyTorch's loss takes logits directly for numerical safety.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Loss
cards.a: A number measuring how wrong the model is. Cross-entropy (log loss) for probabilities; training makes it smaller.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Cross-entropy
cards.a: −log p for a true positive, −log(1 − p) for a true negative, averaged. Punishes confident wrong answers heavily.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient
cards.a: The direction in which the loss rises fastest, one number per parameter. Training steps against it.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient descent / mini-batch / epoch / learning rate
cards.a: Repeatedly step the parameters against the gradient. A mini-batch is a random slice of rows per step; an epoch is one pass over all rows; the learning rate is the step size.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient check
cards.a: Comparing the formula's gradient with a brute-force slope from nudging one parameter. Done once per new model.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Standardization
cards.a: Subtract the training mean and divide by the training standard deviation, per column, so features are on one scale.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Regularization
cards.a: Any penalty or constraint that keeps a model from fitting noise: weight decay, leaf limits, feature and row subsampling, early stopping.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Overfitting
cards.a: Fitting the training data's noise so that validation gets worse while training gets better.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Early stopping
cards.a: Stop training when the validation metric has not improved for a while, and keep the best point.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Decision tree
cards.a: A model that asks yes/no questions about features and gives a constant answer in each leaf.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Gradient boosting / LightGBM
cards.a: Hundreds of small trees, each fitted to the errors of the ones before; their sum is the score. LightGBM is the fast library used in production here.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Categorical feature
cards.a: A column of names rather than amounts (station id, direction). Declared so the trees can split on sets of values.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Feature importance / SHAP
cards.a: Importance by gain totals how much each feature reduced the loss; SHAP splits one prediction into per-feature contributions.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Neural network / MLP
cards.a: Layers of weighted sums with a nonlinearity (ReLU) between them. A multilayer perceptron is the plain version.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: ReLU
cards.a: max(z, 0): zeroes negatives. The nonlinearity that lets a network bend.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Backpropagation
cards.a: The chain rule applied layer by layer, backward from the loss, to get every gradient.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: PyTorch / autograd / MPS
cards.a: The deep-learning library; autograd derives gradients automatically; MPS is how it reaches the Mac's GPU.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Optimizer (AdamW)
cards.a: The rule that turns gradients into parameter updates; AdamW adapts the step per parameter and adds weight decay.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Recurrent network / GRU
cards.a: A model that reads a sequence step by step, keeping a hidden state; the GRU uses gates to decide what to remember.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Hidden state
cards.a: The vector a recurrent network carries from step to step: its summary of what it has read.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Adjacency matrix
cards.a: An N × N table of 0/1 saying which stations are neighbors. A @ h sums each station's neighbors' vectors.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Graph neural network / neighbor mixing
cards.a: A model that lets each station read transformed summaries of its neighbors, using the adjacency matrices.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Multi-task
cards.a: One model with several outputs, here the three horizons.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Residual connection
cards.a: Adding a layer's input to its output (h + f(h)), so the layer learns a correction.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Autocorrelation
cards.a: Correlation of a series with itself at a lag; how long the past stays informative.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Fundamental diagram
cards.a: Flow against occupancy: rising while the road is free, falling once it is saturated. Congestion is the falling branch.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Isotonic regression
cards.a: A step function that only goes up, fitted to map raw scores to observed frequencies. The calibration method used.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Atomic write
cards.a: Write to a temporary file, then rename it over the real one, so a reader never sees a half-written file.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

cards.q: Define: Resident memory (RSS)
cards.a: The RAM a process is actually using, logged per stage so a 16 GB machine never swaps.
cards.n: Glossary, model words.

items: **The project is the syllabus.** Every topic in the first seven phases is here because a stage of the traffic model needs it, and you learn it the week you build that stage. The later phases cover the rest of machine learning with the same discipline: each topic ends in something that runs.

**Build it twice.** First with the library, so it works. Then the core from scratch in numpy, the way `03_train_from_scratch.py` does, so you know what the library hides. Then back to the library, faster.
**Evaluate before you model.** Baselines, metrics and leakage come before any algorithm past logistic regression. A number without a baseline next to it is not a result.
**Math just in time.** Linear algebra, calculus and probability in the amounts the stage needs, derived once by hand. Depth comes in the final phase, when you know what it is for.
**Write it down.** A lab notebook every week, a README per stage, a write-up per phase. If you cannot explain it in plain words you do not have it yet.
**Checkpoints are things that run.** Each phase ends with code that produces a number or a file, not with a quiz.
**Framing.** Turn a fuzzy question into a unit, a target, a horizon and a metric, and say what the answer cannot mean.
**Data.** Build the pipeline from raw files or a database, know its failure modes, and measure its memory and time.

**Models.** Know the whole toolbox, from logistic regression to transformers and graph networks, well enough to say which wins on which data and why, and to implement the core of any of them from a paper.
**Evaluation.** Design a split that cannot leak, pick metrics the imbalance cannot fool, put a baseline next to every number, and calibrate what you ship.
**Engineering.** Ship one implementation used by training and serving, containerize it, schedule it, monitor it, retrain it, and roll it back.
**Acting.** Know what changes when a model's output is a decision: causal questions, feedback loops, fairness and privacy.
**Reading.** Read a new paper in an evening and say what it would change in your system and what it would not fix.
**Explaining.** Describe all of the above to a smart person outside the field without hiding behind jargon.

about.title: How to study so it sticks

items: **A weekly rhythm at ten hours.** Three hours of reading or lectures with notes. Five hours building. One hour rewriting the week's notes from memory. One hour explaining it to someone, or to a file if no one is around.
**The three passes.** Run it. Change it and predict what will happen before you run it. Rebuild it from a blank file. Only the third pass counts as knowing.
**A lab notebook.** `notebook/YYYY-WW.md`: what you tried, what broke, what you learned, the number. Numbers without the setup that produced them are noise a month later.
**A baseline next to every result.** Persistence, the profile rate, the previous version. No exceptions, including for plots.
**What would fool this metric?.** Ask it of every number. Accuracy under imbalance, AUC with persistence, F1 without a threshold rule, a shuffled split on a time series.
**Read in this order.** Code, then docs, then papers, then blog posts. Blog posts last because they are the easiest to write badly.
**The stuck rule.** Thirty minutes alone. Then write the question down precisely, which solves half of them. Then ask, with the exact error and what you already tried.
**One project.** The traffic model is enough for the first year. Later phases add small side projects only where the traffic data cannot carry the idea.
**Rest.** Two long sessions beat five short ones for building; five short ones beat two long ones for math. Sleep is when it consolidates.
Every link was checked in September 2026. Editions and chapter numbers drift; if a chapter does not match its description, find the topic in the index.
The hours assume a beginner. If a phase takes twice as long, take it. Reorder nothing before phase 8; the later phases can be taken in any order.
The math in phase 2 is the part people skip and the part that separates using ML from understanding it. Derive the gradient once by hand; everything in phases 7 and 8 is that derivation repeated.
Being good at ML is mostly being good at evaluation. Phases 4 to 6 are where that is learned; do not shorten them to reach the neural networks sooner.
The traffic project cannot carry vision, language or reinforcement learning; those topics use small public datasets and simulators, chosen to run on the Mac mini.

phases.title: Setup and habits

b.s: A working machine and a working routine.

items: The terminal: `cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `head`, pipes, environment variables.
Git: clone, branch, commit, push, diff, `.gitignore`; what a repository and a README are.
Native arm64 Python on Apple silicon (miniforge or python.org), virtual environments, `pip`, VS Code, Jupyter.
The shape of this repo: the numbered scripts, `data/`, `models/`, `.env`, and why secrets never get committed.
What the traffic model predicts, so every later week has a destination.

items.title: The terminal, git and a Python environment

b.s: Talk to the computer by typing, keep every version of your work, and give this project its own toolbox.
The computer has a secret room called the terminal where you talk to it by typing instead of clicking.
Git is a magic notebook that remembers every version of your work, so if you mess something up you can go back to yesterday's page.
A Python environment is a toybox where you keep the tools for one project, so they do not get mixed up with another project's tools.
Ask someone to open the terminal and type `ls`. It means 'list', and it shows what is in the folder you are standing in.
The terminal runs commands: `cd` moves between folders, `ls` lists files, `cat` shows one, and `python script.py` runs a program.
Git saves snapshots called commits, each with a message saying what changed. `git log` shows the history, and GitHub is where a copy lives online.
A virtual environment (`python -m venv .venv`) is a private folder of installed packages for this project, so upgrading something for one project cannot break another.

Make a folder, put a text file in it. Run `git init` (tells git to start watching this folder), then `git add .` (marks every file in it for the next snapshot), then `git commit -m 'first'` (takes the snapshot). Change the file and run `git diff`. Read what it shows you.
Shell essentials: absolute and relative paths, pipes with `|`, redirects with `>`, environment variables (`export PEMS_USERNAME=...`), `.env` files that scripts load, `which python`.
Git's model: working tree, staging area, repository. Branches are pointers to commits. `git status` before every commit; `.gitignore` keeps `data/` and `.env` out of history forever.

Python on Apple silicon: install a native arm64 Python (miniforge or python.org), check with `python -c 'import platform; print(platform.machine())'` which must print `arm64`, then `pip install -r requirements.txt` inside the venv. VS Code needs to be pointed at that interpreter.

Run the collector once with `python 02_collect_events.py`, then `git status`. The `data/` folder should not appear as untracked. If it does, fix `.gitignore`: open it in your editor (create the file in the Traffic1 folder if it doesn't exist yet), add a line that just says `data/`, save it, and run `git status` again to confirm `data/` disappears from the list.

These tools exist for reproducibility. A venv plus pinned requirements turns 'works on my machine' into 'works on any machine'; git makes every change attributable and reversible; the shell makes procedures scriptable, and a Makefile target is a shell script with declared dependencies.

Know the difference between `pip` and `conda`, between a shell variable and an exported one, and how `PATH` resolves the word `python`. Rosetta versus native is visible through `arch` and `platform.machine()`; native wheels exist for numpy, LightGBM and PyTorch.
Git workflow even when alone: feature branches, small commits, and a pull request you review yourself. Reading your own diff before merging catches most mistakes.
Write a Makefile with `setup`, `collect` and `test` targets, where `test` depends on `setup`. Run `make test` from a fresh clone.

Environments are dependency graphs: solver conflicts, lock files (pip-tools, uv, conda-lock), and the reason a lock file belongs in the experiment record. Numerical results can change with a BLAS backend or a compiler flag.

Git internals: content-addressed objects (blob, tree, commit), refs, the reflog as a safety net, and `bisect` for finding the commit that broke a metric. Shell as glue: `set -euo pipefail`, and knowing when a task has outgrown the shell and belongs in Python.
On macOS: launchd rather than cron, `caffeinate` for long jobs, and the permission system (Full Disk Access) that silently blocks scheduled jobs from reading files.
Break a metric deliberately in one commit among twenty, then find it with `git bisect` driven by a script. Afterward, delete a branch and recover it from the reflog.

At scale, environments become containers and hermetic builds (Nix, Bazel), because ML reproducibility depends on driver versions, BLAS backends and compiler flags that a requirements file does not capture. Git's model does not fit large data and model artifacts, which is why data versioning and model registries grew separate lineage systems.
Security hygiene is part of the craft: secrets in a credential manager, least-privilege tokens, and a scanner that fails the build if a key appears in a diff.
The reproducibility problem in research is mostly this stage done badly. A lock file, a data hash and a hardware note are the minimum for a claim to be checkable a year later.
Write the 'reproduce this result' section of a paper for this repository: exact commands, content hashes for data, versions, hardware, and expected runtime. Then have someone else follow it.

This is the one walkthrough where nothing is assumed: no Python, no git, no editor. Every command is typed into the Terminal app, one line at a time, pressing return after each. If a step fails, read the error out loud before doing anything else; the fix is nearly always in the last line of it.

The Terminal is an app that comes with macOS: press Command and the space bar, type `terminal`, press return. A window opens showing a prompt, a line ending in `%` (or `$`) that means the computer is waiting. You type one command, press return, it runs, and the prompt comes back. That is the entire loop.

Three commands cover ninety percent of moving around. `pwd` means print working directory: it answers 'which folder am I in right now?'. `ls` lists what is in that folder. `cd` means change directory: `cd Documents` goes into a folder named Documents, `cd ..` goes up one level, and `cd ~` goes to your home folder. The `~` character is shorthand for your home folder, `/Users/yourname`.

Two habits that save hours. Press the tab key halfway through a name and the shell completes it for you, which also proves the name exists. And if a command ever hangs or runs away, press Control and C together to stop it.
`mkdir` makes a directory. The `-p` flag means 'make parent folders as needed and do not complain if it already exists', which makes the command safe to run twice.
Open Terminal and make a folder to keep projects in, then go into it.

pwd
ls
mkdir -p ~/code
cd ~/code
pwd

items: `pwd` — prints the folder you are in; it will say /Users/yourname
`ls` — lists that folder's contents, so you can see Desktop, Documents and the rest
`mkdir -p ~/code` — creates a folder called code in your home folder, quietly succeeding if it is already there
`cd ~/code` — moves into it; the prompt now shows code
`pwd` — confirms the move: /Users/yourname/code

b.s: Git is the tool that records versions of your work, and on a Mac it arrives inside Apple's Command Line Tools, a free download that also includes the compiler some Python packages need. You do not need the full Xcode app, which is many gigabytes; the command line tools are a few hundred megabytes.
Running the install command opens a small dialog box asking you to agree and install. It takes a few minutes. If the tools are already present, the command says so and does nothing, which is fine.
After it finishes, `git --version` should print something like `git version 2.39.5`. Any version above 2.30 is fine for this course.
Install Apple's command line tools, then check that git is there.

xcode-select --install
git --version

items: `xcode-select --install` — opens the installer dialog; click Install and wait, or read the note that they are already installed
`git --version` — proves git now exists and is on your PATH, the list of folders the shell searches for commands

b.s: macOS ships with a Python, and you must not use it. It belongs to the system, it is often an old version, and installing packages into it can break parts of macOS. Every serious project installs its own Python.

There are two good ways to get one on Apple silicon. Miniforge is a small installer from the conda-forge community that gives you a native Python plus the conda tool; it is the smoothest path on an M-series Mac and is what this walkthrough uses. The other is the official installer from python.org, which is equally fine; if you take that route, download the macOS 64-bit universal2 installer, double-click it, and skip to the next step.

Native matters. Apple silicon runs two kinds of program: native arm64 code, and older Intel code translated on the fly by Rosetta, which runs at roughly half speed and cannot use the Mac's GPU from PyTorch. The check at the end of this step must print `arm64`. If it prints `x86_64`, you have an Intel Python and should uninstall it and start this step again.

The commands below download an installer script, run it, and then tell your shell about the new Python. `curl` fetches a file from the internet; `-L` follows redirects; `-O` saves it under its own name. `bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh -b -p ~/miniforge3` runs the installer in batch mode (`-b`, meaning do not ask questions) into the folder `~/miniforge3` (`-p` for prefix). `conda init zsh` edits your shell's startup file, `~/.zshrc`, so that new terminal windows can find this Python. Because that file is only read when a shell starts, you must close the Terminal window and open a new one before the last line will work.
Install a native arm64 Python, then open a new Terminal window and prove it is native.

cd ~/Downloads
curl -L -O https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh
bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh -b -p ~/miniforge3
~/miniforge3/bin/conda init zsh

# now quit Terminal (Command-Q), open it again, and run:
python -c "import platform, sys; print(platform.machine(), sys.version)"
which python

items: `curl -L -O https://...Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh` — downloads the installer script for Apple silicon into your Downloads folder
`bash Miniforge3-MacOSX-arm64.sh -b -p ~/miniforge3` — runs it without prompts, installing into a folder called miniforge3 in your home folder
`~/miniforge3/bin/conda init zsh` — adds a few lines to ~/.zshrc so future terminals find this Python first
`python -c "...print(platform.machine(), sys.version)"` — runs one line of Python; it must print arm64 followed by a version of 3.11 or newer

`which python` — shows which file the word python actually runs; it should be inside your miniforge3 folder, not /usr/bin. `which python3` prints the identical path: from here on the two names are the same interpreter, so instructions that say `python3` and instructions that say `python` mean exactly the same thing

b.s: A repository, or repo, is a folder whose history git tracks. The course's repo is Traffic1 on GitHub. Cloning it copies the whole folder and its history to your machine.

`git clone URL` creates a folder named after the repo and downloads it. If you have your own copy of Traffic1 on GitHub, use its URL instead. If you have no repo at all yet, take the second block: `git init -b main` turns an ordinary folder into a repo with a first branch called main, which is what GitHub expects.

After cloning, `ls` shows the files. Right now the repo holds the planning documents; the numbered scripts are what you will write during the course, starting with the collector in step 11 of this walkthrough.
Get the project folder onto your machine and go into it.

cd ~/code
git clone https://github.com/21AG21/Traffic1.git
cd Traffic1
ls

# no repo of your own yet? do this instead:
# mkdir -p ~/code/Traffic1 && cd ~/code/Traffic1 && git init -b main

items: `git clone https://github.com/21AG21/Traffic1.git` — downloads the repository and its history into a new folder called Traffic1
`cd Traffic1` — moves into the project; every command from here on assumes you are in this folder
`ls` — lists what came down: the plan and lesson documents
`git init -b main` — the alternative: start a fresh repository in the current folder with main as the first branch

b.s: A virtual environment, or venv, is a private copy of Python and its packages that belongs to one project. Without one, every project shares a single set of packages and they eventually conflict: one project needs an old pandas, another needs a new one, and installing for one breaks the other. With one, each project gets its own, and deleting the folder undoes everything cleanly.

`python -m venv .venv` runs Python's built-in venv tool and creates a folder called `.venv` inside your project. The leading dot means the Finder and `ls` hide it by default; `ls -a` shows hidden files. The name `.venv` is a convention that VS Code recognizes automatically.

Creating it is not enough; you must activate it. `source .venv/bin/activate` changes the current terminal so the word `python` means the one inside `.venv`. You will see `(.venv)` appear at the start of your prompt, which is how you know it is on. Activation lasts only for that terminal window: every new window, and every restart, needs the `source` line again. `deactivate` turns it off.
The `.venv` folder is large and is rebuilt from requirements.txt in one command, so it never goes into git. Step 9 adds it to `.gitignore`.
Create the project's virtual environment, turn it on, and confirm which Python is now in charge.

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
which python
python -V

items: `python -m venv .venv` — creates the private environment in a hidden folder called .venv
`source .venv/bin/activate` — switches this terminal into it; your prompt gains a (.venv) prefix

`which python` — must now print .../Traffic1/.venv/bin/python — inside the project, not miniforge3. `which python3` prints that same path; inside a venv both names run the one interpreter, so either spelling works
`python -V` — prints the version, which should match the Python you installed

b.s: `requirements.txt` is a plain text file listing the packages the project needs, one per line, so anyone (including you on a new machine) can install all of them with one command. This is the file you asked about, and here is exactly what to put in it.

Each line is a package name and a version rule. `pandas>=2.2` means 'at least 2.2, newer is fine'. Loose rules like that are right while you are setting up, because they always resolve. Once everything works, you freeze the exact versions with `pip freeze > requirements.lock.txt`, and that lock file is what makes a run reproducible months later. Text after `#` is a comment that pip ignores.

Why these packages: pandas and numpy are the table and array libraries; pyarrow lets pandas read and write Parquet; requests fetches the 511 feed; python-dotenv reads your `.env` file; scikit-learn provides the baselines, metrics and calibration; lightgbm is the production model; torch is PyTorch for the neural networks and is the only large download; matplotlib draws the plots; jupyterlab runs notebooks; pytest runs the tests; holidays marks public holidays; psutil measures memory; duckdb runs SQL over Parquet; tqdm draws progress bars; shap explains model predictions.

The command below writes the file using a here-document: `cat > requirements.txt << 'EOF'` means 'take everything up to a line containing EOF and write it into requirements.txt'. The quotes around 'EOF' stop the shell from interpreting anything inside. You can equally create the file in VS Code once step 8 is done, or in TextEdit as plain text; the content is what matters.
Create requirements.txt with exactly these lines.

cat > requirements.txt << 'EOF'
# data
pandas>=2.2            # tables: read, clean, group, join
numpy>=1.26            # arrays and the maths under pandas
pyarrow>=15.0          # lets pandas read and write Parquet files

# getting the data
requests>=2.31         # HTTP calls to the 511 traffic feed
python-dotenv>=1.0     # loads secrets from the .env file

# models
scikit-learn>=1.4      # baselines, metrics, calibration, splits
lightgbm>=4.3          # gradient boosted trees: the production model
torch>=2.2             # PyTorch, the neural networks (large download)
shap>=0.45             # explains which features drove a prediction

# looking at things
matplotlib>=3.8        # plots
jupyterlab>=4.1        # notebooks for exploring

# the rest
pytest>=8.0            # tests
holidays>=0.45         # public holiday calendar for the feature set
psutil>=5.9            # memory and timing for every pipeline stage
duckdb>=0.10           # SQL over Parquet without a database server
tqdm>=4.66             # progress bars for long loops
EOF

cat requirements.txt

items: `cat > requirements.txt << 'EOF'` — starts writing the file; everything until the EOF line goes into it
`pandas>=2.2` — one requirement: the package name, then the lowest version that will do
`# tables: read, clean, group, join` — a comment; pip ignores everything after the hash
`EOF` — ends the here-document and closes the file
`cat requirements.txt` — prints the file back so you can see it saved correctly

b.s: `pip` is Python's package installer. It reads requirements.txt and downloads each package from PyPI, the public package index. Because your venv is active, everything lands inside `.venv` and nothing touches the rest of your machine.

Upgrade pip itself first; old versions sometimes fail to find the right wheel. A wheel is a pre-built package: if one exists for your Mac, installation is a fast download, and if not, pip compiles from source, which is slow and is where the command line tools from step 2 earn their place. Expect the whole install to take a few minutes, most of it PyTorch.

Then verify by importing everything and asking PyTorch whether it can see the Mac's GPU. MPS stands for Metal Performance Shaders, Apple's GPU interface; `torch.backends.mps.is_available()` printing True means later lessons can train on the GPU. False is not fatal, it just means training runs on the processor.

One known failure on macOS: `import lightgbm` raising an error about `libomp` or OpenMP. LightGBM needs Apple's OpenMP runtime, which is not bundled. The fix is Homebrew, the package manager for macOS: install it from brew.sh with the one line on that page, then run `brew install libomp`, then open a new terminal and try again.
Install everything from the file, then prove each import works.

python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install -r requirements.txt

python - << 'EOF'
import platform, pandas as pd, numpy as np, sklearn, lightgbm as lgb, torch
print("machine      ", platform.machine())
print("pandas       ", pd.__version__)
print("numpy        ", np.__version__)
print("scikit-learn ", sklearn.__version__)
print("lightgbm     ", lgb.__version__)
print("torch        ", torch.__version__)
print("GPU (mps)    ", torch.backends.mps.is_available())
EOF

items: `python -m pip install --upgrade pip` — updates the installer itself before it does any real work
`pip install -r requirements.txt` — reads the file and installs every package into the active venv
`python - << 'EOF' ... EOF` — runs the block of Python between the markers without saving it to a file
`print("machine", platform.machine())` — arm64 again: this time it proves the venv's Python is native too
`torch.backends.mps.is_available()` — True means PyTorch can use the Mac's GPU in the neural network lessons

b.s: VS Code is a free editor from Microsoft and the one this course assumes. Download it from code.visualstudio.com, open the downloaded file, and drag the app into your Applications folder. Open it once from Applications so macOS allows it to run.

Connecting it to your project is two connections, not one. First the folder: File, then Open Folder, and choose `~/code/Traffic1`. Everything you do in VS Code from then on is relative to that folder. Second the interpreter: VS Code must be told to use the `.venv` Python rather than some other one, or your imports will be underlined in red and running a file will fail with 'no module named pandas'.

To do that, install the Python extension: click the Extensions icon in the left bar (four squares), search for `Python`, and install the one published by Microsoft. Then press Command, Shift and P together to open the command palette, type `Python: Select Interpreter`, press return, and choose the entry whose path ends in `Traffic1/.venv/bin/python`, usually labelled Recommended. The chosen interpreter then shows in the bottom status bar, and that is your proof it worked.

Two more things worth doing once. The command palette entry `Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH` lets you type `code .` in a terminal to open the current folder in VS Code. And a settings file inside the project makes the choice stick for every future window and makes VS Code's own terminal activate the venv automatically, so you do not have to `source` it there.

Running code: open a `.py` file and press the triangular Run button at the top right, or use VS Code's terminal, which is the panel you get with Control and the backtick key. The terminal is the honest way, because it is the same command you would type anywhere.
Open the project in VS Code, install the Python extension, select the .venv interpreter, and save the project settings.

mkdir -p .vscode
cat > .vscode/settings.json << 'EOF'
{
  "python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python",
  "python.terminal.activateEnvironment": true,
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "editor.rulers": [100]
}
EOF

code .   # opens this folder in VS Code, once the 'code' command is installed

items: `mkdir -p .vscode` — makes the folder VS Code keeps per-project settings in
`"python.defaultInterpreterPath": "${workspaceFolder}/.venv/bin/python"` — tells VS Code to use this project's venv without asking again
`"python.terminal.activateEnvironment": true` — makes VS Code's built-in terminal activate the venv for you
`"editor.rulers": [100]` — draws a faint line at 100 characters so lines stay readable
`code .` — opens the current folder in VS Code; the dot means 'here'

b.s: `.gitignore` is a list of things git must never record. It has to exist before your first commit, because git history is permanent: a secret committed once stays in the history even if you delete the file in the next commit, and public repositories are scanned by bots within minutes of a push.

Four kinds of thing belong in it. Secrets, meaning `.env`. Data, because the PeMS files are hundreds of megabytes a day and are re-downloadable. Anything rebuildable: `.venv`, trained models, outputs, logs, Python's `__pycache__` folders. And editor or operating system litter such as `.DS_Store`.

Patterns are simple. A name ending in `/` matches a folder, `*.pyc` matches by extension, and a line starting with `!` is an exception that keeps a file which an earlier pattern excluded. The `!.env.example` line below is exactly that: the real `.env` stays out, but a template with empty values stays in, so the next person knows which variables to set.
Write .gitignore before anything is committed.

cat > .gitignore << 'EOF'
# secrets
.env
!.env.example

# data and anything rebuilt from it
data/
models/
output/
logs/

# the environment
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc

# notebooks and macOS litter
.ipynb_checkpoints/
.DS_Store
EOF

git status --short

items: `.env` — the secrets file: never recorded
`!.env.example` — an exception: the template with blank values is recorded, so the file list is documented
`data/` — the trailing slash means a folder; everything inside it is ignored
`*.pyc` — ignores compiled Python files wherever they appear
`git status --short` — lists what git currently sees as new or changed; data and .venv must not appear

b.s: 511.org is the Bay Area's traveller information service, and its traffic events feed is one of the two data sources for the model. The key is free: go to 511.org/open-data/token, fill in your name and email, and the token arrives by email as a long string of letters, digits and dashes.

A token is a secret. It goes in a file called `.env`, one `NAME=value` per line, with no spaces around the equals sign and no quotes. Nothing else reads that file by magic: the `python-dotenv` package's `load_dotenv()` reads it and puts the values into `os.environ`, the dictionary of environment variables that Python programs can see.
Name the variable `TOKEN_511` rather than `511_TOKEN`, because shell variable names cannot start with a digit and you will eventually want to export it by hand.
Write `.env.example` alongside it with the same names and empty values. It is the documented list of what a newcomer must supply, and it is safe to commit because it contains no secret.
Get a free 511 token, put it in .env, and write the example file beside it.

cat > .env << 'EOF'
TOKEN_511=paste-your-token-here
EOF

cat > .env.example << 'EOF'
# copy this file to .env and fill in your own values
TOKEN_511=
EOF

python -c "from dotenv import load_dotenv; import os; load_dotenv(); print('token loaded:', bool(os.environ.get('TOKEN_511')))"

items: `TOKEN_511=paste-your-token-here` — replace the right-hand side with the token from your email; no quotes, no spaces
`.env.example with an empty value` — documents the variable without revealing it, and is safe to commit
`load_dotenv()` — reads .env from the current folder and adds its names to os.environ
`print('token loaded:', bool(os.environ.get('TOKEN_511')))` — prints True when the token was found; False means the file is misspelt or you are in the wrong folder

b.s: Now the first real script: it asks 511 for the current traffic events near Fremont and appends them to a CSV file, one row per event per poll. Run it every few minutes and you build the incident history the model later joins to the detector data.

What the code uses. `requests.get(url, params={...})` makes the web request and builds the query string for you. The 511 response carries a byte-order mark, an invisible marker at the start of the text that makes a plain `.json()` call fail with a confusing error, so the code decodes the bytes with `utf-8-sig`, which strips it. `.get('key')` on a dictionary returns `None` instead of crashing when a field is missing, which matters because not every event has every field. `csv.DictWriter` writes dictionaries as rows and can write the header line only when the file is new. `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` stamps each row with when we pulled it, in UTC. The `try` and `except` around the request means a network blip prints a message instead of killing the program. And `if __name__ == '__main__':` at the bottom means the file runs when you call it directly but stays importable from other scripts and tests.
Before trusting any of it, the script prints how many events came back and the keys of the first one, so you see the real shape of the data rather than assuming it.
Write 02_collect_events.py, run it once, and look at what it wrote.

# 02_collect_events.py
import csv, os, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from pathlib import Path

import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

URL = "https://api.511.org/traffic/events"
OUT = Path("data/fremont_events_log.csv")
FIELDS = ["pulled_at", "id", "event_type", "severity", "headline", "roads", "created", "updated"]


def fetch_events(token):
    r = requests.get(URL, params={"api_key": token, "format": "json"}, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json() if not r.content.startswith(b"\xef\xbb\xbf") else __import__("json").loads(r.content.decode("utf-8-sig"))


def flatten(event, pulled_at):
    roads = event.get("roads") or []
    return {
        "pulled_at": pulled_at,
        "id": event.get("id"),
        "event_type": event.get("event_type"),
        "severity": event.get("severity"),
        "headline": (event.get("headline") or "").replace("\n", " "),
        "roads": "; ".join(r.get("name", "") for r in roads),
        "created": event.get("created"),
        "updated": event.get("updated"),
    }


def main():
    load_dotenv()
    token = os.environ.get("TOKEN_511")
    if not token:
        sys.exit("No TOKEN_511 in .env — see step 10.")

    try:
        payload = fetch_events(token)
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        sys.exit(f"Could not reach 511: {e}")

    events = payload.get("events", [])
    print(f"{len(events)} events came back")
    if events:
        print("fields on the first one:", sorted(events[0].keys()))

    pulled_at = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
    OUT.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    new_file = not OUT.exists()
    with OUT.open("a", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        w = csv.DictWriter(fh, fieldnames=FIELDS)
        if new_file:
            w.writeheader()
        for e in events:
            w.writerow(flatten(e, pulled_at))
    print(f"wrote {len(events)} rows to {OUT}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items: `requests.get(URL, params={...}, timeout=30)` — asks 511 for the events; timeout stops it hanging forever
`r.raise_for_status()` — turns an HTTP error such as 401 (bad token) into a Python exception you can see
`decode("utf-8-sig")` — strips the invisible byte-order mark that would otherwise break JSON parsing
`event.get("severity")` — returns None for a missing field instead of crashing
`datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()` — the moment of this poll, in UTC, as text; the delay between created and pulled_at is the model's blind spot
`OUT.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` — creates the data folder the first time, and does nothing after that
`OUT.open("a", ...)` — opens the file in append mode so each run adds to the history
`if new_file: w.writeheader()` — writes the column names only when the file was just created
`if __name__ == "__main__": main()` — runs main() when you launch the file, but not when a test imports it

b.s: Now run it and read the output. Save the file in VS Code (Command and S), then run it from the terminal with the venv active. Three things should happen: a count of events, the field names of the first one, and a line saying rows were written.

Common failures and what they mean. `No TOKEN_511 in .env` means the file is missing, misspelt, or you are in the wrong folder. A 401 error means the token is wrong; copy it again without spaces. `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named requests` means the venv is not active in this terminal, so run `source .venv/bin/activate` and try again.

`head -2` prints the first two lines of a file: the header and one event. `wc -l` counts lines. Run the script twice, a minute apart, and the line count grows while the header stays single, which is the append working correctly.
Run the collector, then look at the CSV it produced.

python 02_collect_events.py
head -2 data/fremont_events_log.csv
wc -l data/fremont_events_log.csv

items: `python 02_collect_events.py` — runs the script; the venv must be active in this terminal
`head -2 ...csv` — shows the header line and the first event, so you can see the columns are what you declared
`wc -l ...csv` — counts the lines; run the script again and this number grows

b.s: Time to record the work. Git has three places: the working tree (your files), the staging area (what the next commit will contain), and the repository (the permanent history). `git add` moves changes into staging, `git commit` writes them into history with a message, `git push` sends them to GitHub.

Check before you commit, every time. `git status --short` lists what will go in: `??` means untracked, `A` means added, `M` means modified. If `data/` or `.env` appear here, stop and fix `.gitignore` first, because after a commit and push it is too late and the honest fix becomes rotating the token.
`git ls-files` lists what git is actually tracking, which is the strongest check available: piping it through `grep` and counting should give zero for both the environment file and the data folder.

If you cloned from GitHub, `git push` already knows where to send things. If you started with `git init`, create an empty repository on GitHub first, then add it as the remote named origin, as the commented lines show. `-u` on the first push links your local main to the remote one so later pushes are just `git push`.
Check what is staged, commit, and push, proving no secret went with it.

git status --short
git ls-files | grep -c -E '^\.env$|^data/' || echo "0 secrets tracked — good"

git add -A
git status --short
git commit -m "Set up the environment and the 511 collector"

# only if you started with git init:
# git remote add origin https://github.com/YOURNAME/Traffic1.git

git push -u origin main
git log --oneline -3

items: `git status --short` — the pre-commit check: two-letter codes beside every file that changed
`git ls-files | grep -c -E '^\.env$|^data/'` — counts tracked secrets and data files; anything but zero means fix .gitignore now
`git add -A` — stages every change in the folder, respecting .gitignore
`git commit -m "..."` — writes the staged changes into history with a message saying why
`git push -u origin main` — sends the commits to GitHub and remembers the destination
`git log --oneline -3` — shows the last three commits, newest first, one line each

b.s: The last habit is the notebook, and it is not optional. A weekly plain-text file where you write what you did, what broke, and what confused you turns a scattered course into something you can look back through. Name it by ISO week so the files sort themselves.

Jupyter is the other kind of notebook: an app that runs Python one cell at a time and shows tables and plots underneath. `jupyter lab` starts it and opens a browser tab; press Control and C twice in the terminal to stop it. Inside, when you create a notebook, choose the kernel whose name matches your project's Python; because Jupyter was installed inside `.venv`, that is the default.
Use notebooks to look at data and scripts to build the pipeline. Anything that must run the same way twice belongs in a `.py` file.
Start the lab notebook, and open Jupyter once to see it work.
