`notebook/2026-W37.md` — ISO week numbering, so the files sort in order by name
`## Confused by` — the most valuable heading in the file; fill it in honestly and revisit it a week later
`jupyter lab` — starts the notebook app in your browser; Control-C twice in the terminal shuts it down

b.s: One last thing to memorise, because it is what you will type at the start of every session from now on. A new terminal window knows nothing about your venv: it must be pointed at the project and switched on again.
If you forget, the symptom is always the same: `ModuleNotFoundError` for a package you know you installed. The cure is the second line below.
Learn the three commands that start every working session.

cd ~/code/Traffic1
source .venv/bin/activate

items: `cd ~/code/Traffic1` — go to the project
`source .venv/bin/activate` — turn the environment on; the prompt gains (.venv)
`code .` — open the editor on this folder, if you want it

b.q: Why must `.env` never be committed?

a.s: It holds credentials. Git history is permanent, and public repositories are scanned for keys within minutes of a push.

b.q: What does a virtual environment isolate?

a.s: Installed packages and the interpreter. Not your data, not the operating system's libraries, and not your git history.

items.title: The question: what are we predicting?

b.s: Turn 'will traffic be bad?' into a unit, a target, a horizon and a metric, and see why a probability is the right kind of answer.
Roads get slow sometimes, like when everyone leaves the park at the same time and the path gets crowded.
We are building a helper that looks at the road right now and guesses whether it will be slow in a little while, so people can pick a different road before they get stuck.
It is like looking at a dark sky and guessing it will rain soon. Sometimes the guess is wrong, and that is okay. A good helper is right more often than a coin.
Look out the window and guess whether it will rain in one hour. Check later. Were you right? What clue did you use?
Every half mile or so on the freeway there is a sensor in the pavement that counts cars and measures their speed, and it writes a row of numbers every five minutes.
Our program reads the last hour of those rows and answers, for every sensor, one question three times: will this spot be slow 15, 30 and 60 minutes from now?
The answer is not yes or no. It is a number between 0 and 1. A 0.8 means 'very likely slow'; a 0.1 means 'probably fine'. Later we decide how big the number must be before we warn anyone.

To find out whether the program is any good, we wait and see what actually happened. At 4:00 pm sensor 12 shows 65 mph and the program says 0.7 for 4:30. At 4:30 the sensor shows 22 mph. That guess was right.
Write down what 'slow' should mean. Under 30 mph? Slower than it usually is at this time? Both are reasonable, and they are different questions. Keep your answer; lesson 4 comes back to it.

A prediction problem has four parts. The unit: one station at one 5-minute timestamp. The inputs: everything known at that moment, and nothing after it. The target: a yes-or-no fact about the future, here 'the station is inside a slow episode h minutes later', with h in {15, 30, 60}. The metric: how guesses are scored.
A slow episode is three consecutive 5-minute steps in which speed is below 60 % of what is typical for that station at that time of day. Three steps, so a single noisy reading does not count.

The model outputs a probability rather than a verdict because a 0.55 and a 0.95 carry different information, and because the decision of when to warn depends on how costly a false alarm is compared with a missed jam. That threshold is chosen afterwards, not baked into the model.
One model per horizon, so the 15-minute question and the 60-minute question get their own answers.

Pick a station in your head. Write one row on paper: a few input columns (speed now, speed 5 minutes ago, speed at the next station downstream) and one target column (slow in 30 minutes?). Notice that at the moment you would use this row, the target column is blank. That blank is the whole point.

Formally this is supervised binary classification (fitting a model to labeled examples so it learns to sort new cases into one of two classes) on a panel indexed by (station s, time t). The feature vector x_{s,t} is a function of the information available at t, written F_t; the superscript in y^{(h)}_{s,t} just marks which horizon h the target belongs to, and 1[label(s, t+h) = 1] is an indicator, equal to 1 when the bracketed statement is true and 0 when it is false. We fit f_h(x) ≈ P(y^{(h)} = 1 | x), read 'the probability that y^{(h)} is 1, given x,' for each horizon, a direct multi-horizon strategy rather than a recursive one.

The distinction between nowcasting (h = 0) and forecasting (h > 0) is not cosmetic. With `speed_lag_1` in the features and a three-step label, h = 0 is almost solved by copying the last value, which is exactly what the reference plan would have measured.

Calibrated probabilities matter because the alert is a decision. With costs C_FA for a false alarm and C_miss for a missed episode, the Bayes decision rule warns when p > C_FA / (C_FA + C_miss). That is only valid if p is an honest probability.

The metric follows from prevalence: positives are a few percent of rows, so the natural summary is average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve, because the operational question is 'how good is the ranking near the top'.

Derive the threshold rule: write expected cost as a function of the decision for a row with probability p and show that warning is cheaper exactly when p exceeds C_FA / (C_FA + C_miss). Then compute it for a false alarm costing 1 and a miss costing 4.

The label is a function of a future path, three consecutive slow steps ending at t + h, not of a single future point, so the targets across horizons and across adjacent timestamps are strongly dependent. The panel is neither independent across t (autocorrelation) nor across s (propagation), so the effective sample size is orders of magnitude below the ten million rows, and every confidence interval must respect that.

The target is defined relative to a profile estimated from training data. Label noise therefore inherits the profile estimator's error, and the label's meaning shifts with the split. Two competing framings avoid part of this: regress the speed ratio with a quantile loss and threshold afterwards, keeping ordinal information; or model episode onset as a hazard and predict time-to-onset.

Direct multi-horizon classifiers ignore coherence: nothing forces the 60-minute probability to relate sensibly to the 30-minute one. Joint sequence outputs or monotone post-processing are the usual fixes.
Prevalence drifts across seasons and roadwork, so a single test window is one draw from a moving distribution. Report rolling-origin folds, not one number.
Show that if the profile were computed on the test period too, the positive rate on test would be pinned near a fixed quantile by construction, and explain why that hides real change.

At the scale of a phone maps product the unit is a road segment with probe data from devices, not a fixed detector, and the problem becomes travel-time and speed prediction over a graph of millions of segments under privacy constraints: on-device aggregation, differential privacy on aggregate speeds, and sparse coverage that varies by segment and hour. The binary 'slow episode' is a product simplification that trades information for interpretability; production systems keep a continuous target and threshold at the edge.

The literature that matters here is graph-based ETA prediction on supersegments (Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021) and the spatio-temporal forecasting benchmarks on PeMS data (DCRNN, STGCN, Graph WaveNet). Open questions worth a thesis chapter: multi-horizon coherence with monotone or joint outputs; non-stationarity handled online versus by periodic retraining; and performative prediction, since drivers who act on an alert change the very label the alert predicted.

The 16 GB Mac mini is a useful proxy for on-device budgets: model size, latency and energy are the constraints that decide what ships, and a model that only runs in a data center is a different product.
Define the label on probe data with heterogeneous sampling rates. State the estimator bias it introduces for low-coverage segments and propose a correction.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

You will run this code in Python, the programming language the whole course uses. Python is a program that reads a text file of instructions and carries them out one line at a time. You type the lines into a file such as `scratch.py` and run it from the terminal with `python scratch.py`, or you paste them into a Jupyter notebook cell and press shift-enter. The terminal is the text window (the Terminal app on a Mac) where you type commands instead of clicking; Jupyter is a notebook app that runs Python one cell at a time and shows the result under each cell. Either is fine; the notebook is friendlier for looking at data.

`pandas` is the library, meaning a bundle of ready-made code, that Python uses for tables. Its table type is called a DataFrame: rows and named columns, like a spreadsheet you drive with code. `numpy` is the library underneath it for fast arithmetic on arrays of numbers. `import pandas as pd` loads the library and gives it the short name `pd`, so later lines can say `pd.something`.

Parquet is a file format for tables. Unlike a CSV text file it stores each column separately and compressed, so a month of detector rows is small on disk and fast to load. `data/pems_processed/2026-03.parquet` is the cleaned table that lesson 3 produces; the path is relative to the Traffic1 folder, so run the code from there. If you have not built that file yet, make a fake one: a DataFrame with the columns `station_id`, `timestamp`, `speed` and `label`, 288 rows per day (one every five minutes), any plausible numbers.

A station is one detector site on the freeway, identified by a number in the `station_id` column. The line that picks a station reads in three parts: `df.station_id.iloc[0]` takes the first station number in the table; `df[df.station_id == that]` keeps only the rows for that station (a boolean mask: a true-or-false test per row, used to filter); `sort_values("timestamp")` puts those rows in time order; `reset_index(drop=True)` renumbers them 0, 1, 2, … so that row 100 really is the 101st reading. The result, `s`, is one station's month as a single time series: one row per five minutes.
Load one month of cleaned rows (or fake them) and pick a station.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np
df = pd.read_parquet("data/pems_processed/2026-03.parquet")
s = df[df.station_id == df.station_id.iloc[0]].sort_values("timestamp").reset_index(drop=True)

items: `import pandas as pd, numpy as np` — loads the table library and the numeric library under the short names used everywhere in the course
`pd.read_parquet(...)` — reads the Parquet file into a DataFrame called df, every station, every five-minute row of the month
`df[df.station_id == df.station_id.iloc[0]]` — keeps only rows belonging to the first station in the file
`.sort_values("timestamp").reset_index(drop=True)` — orders them by time and numbers them from zero, so row positions mean time positions

b.s: A row's inputs are what was known at that row's moment. The simplest inputs are the station's own recent speeds. A lag is a value from some steps earlier: lag 1 is the previous row (five minutes ago), lag 3 is three rows back (fifteen minutes ago), lag 0 is the row itself.

`s["speed"]` is one column of the table, a Series in pandas language. `.shift(k)` returns the same column moved down by k rows, so the value that was at row 99 now sits at row 100 when k is 1. The first k rows have nothing above them and become NaN, which is pandas' marker for a missing number (short for not a number). Assigning `s["speed_lag_1"] = ...` creates a new column with that name.

The `for k in (0, 1, 2, 3):` line is a loop: Python runs the indented line once with k set to 0, then 1, then 2, then 3. The `f"speed_lag_{k}"` is an f-string, a way of building text where whatever is inside the curly braces is filled in, so the four columns are named `speed_lag_0` to `speed_lag_3`.
Build the input side of one row: speed now and 5, 10, 15 minutes ago.

for k in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    s[f"speed_lag_{k}"] = s["speed"].shift(k)

items: `for k in (0, 1, 2, 3):` — repeat the next line for each of the four lag distances
`s[f"speed_lag_{k}"] = s["speed"].shift(k)` — make a column holding the speed from k rows earlier; the first k rows are NaN because there is no earlier reading

b.s: The target is the thing to predict: whether the station is inside a slow episode thirty minutes after the row's moment. The cleaned table already has a `label` column (lesson 4 shows how it is made) that says, for each row, whether that row is slow now. To know what happens thirty minutes later, look six rows further down, because each row is five minutes and 6 × 5 = 30.

`shift(-6)` is the same shift as before with a negative number, which moves the column up by six rows: the value that was at row 106 now sits at row 100. That is exactly the future label lined up next to the present inputs. The last six rows of the month have no future inside the file and become NaN.

`s.loc[100, [...]]` picks row 100 and a list of columns; `print` shows them. Printing rows 100 and 106 side by side is the check: the `y_30` at row 100 must equal the `label` at row 106, and the timestamps must be thirty minutes apart. The text after `#` on a line is a comment: Python ignores it; it is a note for the reader.
Build the target side: the label 30 minutes later is the label six rows down.

s["y_30"] = s["label"].shift(-6)      # negative shift looks forward
print(s.loc[100, ["timestamp", "speed_lag_0", "y_30"]])
print(s.loc[106, ["timestamp", "label"]])   # same value as y_30 at row 100

items: `s["y_30"] = s["label"].shift(-6)` — new column: the slow-or-not label from six rows (thirty minutes) later, the target
`print(s.loc[100, ["timestamp", "speed_lag_0", "y_30"]])` — show one row's time, its present speed and its future label
`print(s.loc[106, ["timestamp", "label"]])` — show the row thirty minutes later; its label must match y_30 above

b.s: Leakage is the mistake that makes traffic models look brilliant and then fail: letting information from after a row's moment into that row's inputs. A model trained with leaked columns learns to read the answer instead of predicting it. This step is a habit rather than code: every time you make an input column, ask where each value came from in time.

The rule you check here has two parts. Every lag column was made with `shift(k)` and k at least zero, so each input value is from the same moment or earlier. The only column made with a negative shift is the target. If you ever find yourself writing `shift(-something)` for an input, stop: that column is looking into the future.
Confirm there is nothing in the inputs from after the row's timestamp. Every lag has k ≥ 0 and the only forward shift is on the target.

A positive is a row whose target is 1 (slow in thirty minutes); a negative has target 0. The share of positives is called the prevalence. `.mean()` of a column of zeros and ones is exactly that share, because the sum of the ones divided by the count of rows is the fraction that are ones. NaN rows are skipped automatically.

The prevalence matters twice. It tells you how rare the event is, usually a few percent, which is why accuracy is a useless score: a model that always says no is right most of the time. And it is the score of a model that guesses at random under average precision, the metric lesson 6 introduces. Any real model must beat this number, so write it down.
Count the positives. That number is the prevalence and the baseline average precision.
print(s["y_30"].mean())

items: `print(s["y_30"].mean())` — the fraction of rows that are positive: the prevalence, and the average precision of random guessing

b.q: Why is the target column blank at the moment you would use the row?

a.s: Because the target is a fact about t + h, and at t it has not happened yet. Training rows are built from history where t + h is already known; serving rows never have it.

b.q: Why three separate models rather than one model with a 'horizon' column?

a.s: Simplicity and honest early stopping: each horizon stops training where its own validation score peaks, and the three thresholds are chosen independently. A single model is possible and slightly more coherent across horizons, at the cost of one more feature to get wrong.

b.q: Why not output yes or no?

a.s: The cost of a false alarm and of a miss are not equal and are not known when the model is trained. A probability defers that decision to a threshold chosen later, and can be evaluated for honesty (calibration).

items: 'The model predicts crashes.' It predicts slow episodes; most are propagation of a jam that already exists somewhere downstream, or the daily build-up.
'Accuracy is the score.' With 5 % positives, always saying 'not slow' is 95 % accurate. Average precision and recall at a threshold are the scores.
'More horizons are free.' Each horizon is a separate, harder problem; skill at 60 minutes is modest and must be shown against persistence.

items.lives: Lives in the plan's 'What is being predicted'; stages 6, 8 and 10.

resources.title: Software Carpentry: The Unix Shell, Version Control with Git

b.s: Two short lessons on the internet that teach you to talk to the computer by typing, and to use the magic notebook that remembers your work. You follow along and type every command yourself, and the lesson tells you what should happen after each one.

Free workshops written for scientists who have never programmed. Each takes about half a day. The Shell lesson teaches moving between folders, listing files, and joining small commands together with pipes. The Git lesson teaches saving snapshots of your work and pushing them to GitHub so a copy lives online. Do them in order with a terminal open, and do the exercises; watching is not the same as typing.

The Carpentries lessons are hands-on with checkpoints every few minutes. The shell lesson covers navigation, wildcards, pipes and filters, loops and simple shell scripts. The git lesson covers `init`, `add`, `commit`, `diff`, `log`, branches, remotes, and collaborating through GitHub, including how to resolve a conflict. That is exactly the set of commands this repository's workflow needs, and nothing you will not use. Budget one day for both and take notes on the commands you find yourself reaching for.

These lessons are the minimum viable toolkit for reproducible work: scripting a procedure rather than clicking through it, and versioning every change so any result can be traced to the code that produced it. Their pedagogy, live coding with frequent small exercises, is worth copying when you later teach someone else. After them, the man pages and `git help <command>` become readable, and Pro Git's chapters 1 to 3 will feel like a review with more depth.

Compact enough to finish in a day, they leave deliberate gaps you will fill later: shell robustness (`set -euo pipefail`, quoting, exit codes), git internals and history rewriting, and the difference between a merge and a rebase. Treat them as the vocabulary lesson before the grammar book. Their assessment data (they have been taught to tens of thousands of researchers and iterated on feedback) is a rare example of evidence-based technical teaching.

Written and maintained by The Carpentries community, these are the lessons to hand to a new hire from a domain science before they touch the pipeline. For a research lead the value is twofold: a shared baseline of tooling across a team, and a template for writing your own onboarding lesson for this repository in the same style, with exercises that run against real PeMS files.

Two half-day lessons. The shell lesson teaches you to navigate a file system, create and inspect files, combine small tools with pipes, and write loops and scripts. The git lesson teaches you to record versions of a project, inspect and undo changes, and share work through a remote repository.

items: The file system is a tree; you always stand somewhere in it (`pwd`), move with `cd`, and list with `ls`. Absolute paths start at the root `/`; relative paths start from where you stand; `..` is the parent, `~` is home.
Files and directories: `mkdir` creates, `touch` and editors create files, `mv` renames or moves, `cp` copies, `rm` deletes with no undo. Tab completion and the up arrow save most of your typing.

Pipes and filters: every tool reads text and writes text, so `wc -l`, `sort`, `head`, `tail`, `cut`, `uniq`, `grep` can be chained with `|`. `>` sends output to a file and `>>` appends. This is how you inspect a 200 MB PeMS file without opening it.

Loops: `for f in *.txt.gz; do echo $f; done` repeats a command over many files; variables are set with `name=value` and read with `$name`. A script is a file of such commands run with `bash script.sh`, with `$1` for its first argument.
Finding things: `grep pattern file` searches contents; `find . -name '*.parquet'` searches names; `man cmd` or `cmd --help` explains flags.

Git's model: a repository stores snapshots (commits) of a project; each commit records who, when, why, and points to its parent. `git init` starts one; `git status` shows what changed; `git add` stages; `git commit -m 'why'` records.

History and undo: `git log` lists commits; `git diff` shows changes since the last commit or between commits; `git checkout -- file` discards working changes; `git revert` makes a new commit that undoes an old one.
Ignoring: `.gitignore` lists patterns (`data/`, `.env`, `*.parquet`) that git should never track. Secrets and large data never go in.

Remotes: `git remote add origin URL`, `git push -u origin main` publishes; `git pull` fetches and merges; a clone is a full copy of the history. Conflicts happen when two people edit the same lines; git marks them with `<<<<<<<` and you resolve by editing and committing.
Collaboration: branches let work proceed in parallel; pull requests are reviewed merges; a README and a license make a repository usable by others.

b.s:
pwd; ls -la; cd data; cat file | head -3
zcat d04_text_station_5min_2026_03_02.txt.gz | head -1 | tr ',' '\n' | wc -l
git init; git add .; git commit -m 'first'; git diff; git log --oneline
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/Traffic1; git push -u origin main

items: Everything in the shell is text flowing between small tools; learn ten commands and pipes and you can inspect any file.
A commit is a snapshot with a message that says why; small commits with honest messages are the whole discipline.
Secrets and data never enter git; `.gitignore` is the first file you write.

b.s: Count the rows and columns of one PeMS file from the shell alone, then commit a script that does it and push it to GitHub.

resources.title: Pro Git, chapters 1–3

b.s: A book about a tool called git. Git is like a magic notebook that remembers every version of your drawing, so if you make a mess you can flip back to yesterday's page. The first three chapters teach you how to save a page, look back at old pages, and share the notebook with a friend.

Pro Git is the free official book for git, the tool programmers use to save snapshots of their work and share them on GitHub. Chapter 1 explains what git is and installs it, chapter 2 covers the everyday commands (making commits, seeing what changed, undoing mistakes, working with a remote copy), and chapter 3 covers branches, which are parallel copies you can experiment on and merge back. Read it with a terminal open and run each command on a practice folder.

The reference for git, free online, by Scott Chacon and Ben Straub. Chapter 1 explains the snapshot model: git stores whole snapshots, not differences, and a commit is a pointer to one. Chapter 2 is the daily toolkit: `init`, `clone`, `add`, `commit`, `status`, `diff`, `log`, `remote`, `push`, `pull`, plus tagging and aliases. Chapter 3 is branching and merging, including what a fast-forward is and how to handle a conflict. That is enough for a year of solo and small-team work; the later chapters (rebase, hooks, internals) can wait until you need them.

The value of the first three chapters is the mental model rather than the commands: the three areas (working tree, index, repository), commits as immutable objects in a graph, and branches as movable pointers to commits. Once that picture is in your head, every confusing git situation becomes a diagram you can draw, and `git log --graph --oneline --all` becomes your debugger. Read chapter 3 twice; branching is where most people's understanding is vague.

Chapter 10 on internals is the next read: the content-addressed object store (blobs, trees, commits named by hash) is the same idea as the manifest hashes in this pipeline and as data-versioning tools such as DVC and lakeFS. Git's model of history is what makes reproducible experiments possible: a commit hash plus a data hash names a result forever. Chapter 7's tools (stash, bisect, reflog, rewriting history) are what you reach for when an experiment goes wrong.

At scale git's limits show: monorepos, large binary artifacts (git LFS), and the mismatch between versioning code and versioning data or models, which is why model registries and data lakes grew their own lineage systems. Still, the discipline the book teaches, small atomic commits with messages that explain why rather than what, is what makes a research codebase reviewable and a production incident debuggable at 3 am. For a team, the book is also the reference for a written branching policy.

The reference for git. Chapter 1 explains what version control is and how git differs from older systems. Chapter 2 is the daily toolkit for a single repository. Chapter 3 is branching and merging, the feature that makes git what it is.

items: Git stores snapshots, not differences: each commit is a picture of every tracked file (unchanged files are shared by reference). Almost every operation is local and fast, and git only adds data, so committed work is nearly impossible to lose.

Three states: files are modified (in the working directory), staged (in the index, chosen for the next commit), or committed (in the repository). `git add` moves work into the index; `git commit` records the index.

Getting a repository: `git init` in an existing folder or `git clone URL`. Tracking: `git status` (with `-s` for short form), `git add`, `.gitignore` with glob patterns, `git diff` (working versus index) and `git diff --staged` (index versus last commit).

Committing and history: `git commit -m`, `git commit -a` to skip staging for tracked files, `git rm`, `git mv`, and `git log` with `--oneline`, `-p`, `--stat`, `--graph`, and filters by author, date and path.

Undoing: `git commit --amend` rewrites the last commit; `git restore --staged file` unstages; `git restore file` discards working changes (dangerous: unrecoverable). Anything committed can be recovered from the reflog.
Remotes: `git remote -v`, `git fetch` (download without merging), `git pull` (fetch and merge), `git push origin branch`; tags with `git tag -a v1.0 -m` mark releases; aliases shorten commands.

Branches are pointers: a branch is a movable name for a commit; `HEAD` points to the current branch. `git branch name` creates, `git switch name` moves HEAD, `git switch -c name` does both. Creating a branch costs nothing.

Merging: a fast-forward merge just moves the pointer when history is linear; a three-way merge creates a merge commit with two parents when branches diverged. Conflicts are marked in the files and resolved by editing, `git add`, `git commit`.

Workflows: long-running branches (main, develop) and short topic branches; remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`) record where the remote was at last fetch; `git push origin --delete branch` cleans up.
Rebasing (end of chapter 3): replays commits onto another base for a linear history; never rebase commits that others already have.

b.s:
git status -s; git diff --staged; git log --oneline --graph --all
git switch -c feature/clean-pems; ...; git switch main; git merge feature/clean-pems
git fetch origin; git log main..origin/main; git pull
git reflog   # find any commit you thought was lost

items: Commits are snapshots in a graph and branches are pointers into it; every confusing situation becomes a drawing.
The index is a staging area for composing a commit; use it to make commits small and coherent.
Merges are safe and rebases rewrite history; use rebases only on branches nobody else has.

b.s: Create a topic branch for the cleaning script, make three commits, merge it into main with a merge commit, then draw the resulting graph from `git log --graph` by hand.

resources.title: The repo's own `00_CONCEPTS.md` and `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md`

b.s: The project's own notes, written by the people who built it. They explain what the helper is for and how the pieces fit together, like the instruction sheet that comes in a toy box.

Two documents inside this repository. The concepts file explains the ideas behind the first model, including the math of the logistic regression, in plain language. The plan file describes how the PeMS sensor data and the 511 incident feed will be combined into one training table. Read them once now, even if half of it is unclear, and again after phase 4, when all of it will make sense.

Read them like a map of the project. `00_CONCEPTS.md` explains the sigmoid, cross-entropy and gradient descent that lesson 7 rebuilds. `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md` sets out the stages, the label definition, the join rules between incidents and stations, and the time-zone warning that lessons 3 to 5 elaborate. Write down every term you do not understand; that list is your study plan for the next three phases.

Project documentation is a primary source: it records decisions and their reasons, and it goes stale the moment code diverges from it. Compare the plan with the flowchart document (`21_PLAN_M1_TRAFFIC_MODEL.md`) and list what changed and why: the forward-shifted targets, the train-only profile, the second label, the missing real-time feed. That diff is a lesson in how plans evolve when they meet data.

Read them critically. The original plan paired features at t with the label at t, and computed the profile on all history; both are design errors that would have produced flattering numbers. Finding such issues in a design document before code exists is a core research and engineering skill; practice it by writing a one-page review of `05_PLAN_COMBINED_DATASETS.md` as if it were a submission.

Design documents are where most of the leverage in an ML project lives, and most teams write them badly. The exercise at your level is to write the version a team could execute: explicit interfaces between stages, success criteria with numbers, risks with owners, and what would make you stop. Use these two files as the before, and the flowchart plan as a partial after.

The project's own documents. The concepts file explains the first model: how events become a training table, what logistic regression computes, and how gradient descent fits it. The plan file specifies how PeMS detector data and 511 incidents are cleaned, labelled, joined, featurized, split and evaluated.

items: The v1 model: a grid of road × hour × weekend cells, each labelled 1 if any incident ever occurred there. Features are hour (scaled to 0–1), a weekend flag and one-hot road indicators; the model is a logistic regression trained by hand-written gradient descent.

Logistic regression in the concepts file: score z = w·x + b, probability p = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), loss = −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], gradient (p − y)·x, update w ← w − η·gradient. Lesson 7 rebuilds this.

The plan's pipeline: download PeMS 5-minute files and station metadata; clean (timezone to UTC, sanity bounds, short-gap fill, Fremont station filter); label slow episodes from a speed profile; join incidents by route, direction and distance; engineer lag, rolling, neighbor, calendar and incident features; split chronologically; train baselines, logistic regression, trees and an MLP; evaluate with standard metrics and lead time.

The plan's cautions: the timezone step is mandatory and easy to get wrong; PeMS column layout must be verified against a real file; the label threshold should be versioned in filenames; class weighting when positives are rare.

What the flowchart plan changed: targets shifted forward by the horizon, a train-only profile, a second absolute label, weather and static features, LightGBM as production, calibration and thresholds, a serving loop and monitoring, and the admission that no real-time speed feed exists yet.

b.s:
p = sigmoid(x @ weights + bias)
loss = -mean(y*log(p) + (1-y)*log(1-p))
weights -= lr * X.T @ (p - y) / n

items: Read a design document as a hypothesis about data you have not seen yet; the first real file will change it.
The v1 model is a lookup table shaped like a model; its value is teaching the mechanics.
The plan's later revisions are the record of what evaluation discipline caught.

b.s: List every difference between the plan file and the flowchart plan, and for each say what evidence or reasoning caused the change.

resources.title: The Missing Semester of Your CS Education (MIT)

b.s: A short free class about the tools programmers use every day but nobody teaches: the typing window, the magic notebook, and how to make the computer do boring jobs for you.

MIT students made a course about the things regular classes skip: the shell, editors, git, debugging, command-line tools, and automating tasks. Eleven lectures with notes and exercises, all free. Do the shell, editors and git lectures during phase 0.

The lectures on the shell and shell tools, on editors (Vim), on data wrangling (pipes, grep, sed, awk), on git, and on debugging and profiling are directly useful. The git lecture's model of commits as a graph is the best short explanation there is; the data-wrangling lecture teaches you to inspect a PeMS file without Python.

Its value is the mental models: the shell as a programming environment, git as a content-addressed graph, profiling before optimizing. The exercises are small and worth doing; the notes are good references for the flags you forget.
A compact syllabus of practitioner tooling that most graduate students still lack; its debugging and profiling lecture is a fair summary of how to approach a slow or wrong pipeline stage.

For onboarding engineers and researchers alike, this is the shortest path to shared tooling literacy; its lecture on metaprogramming (build systems, testing, continuous integration) is the bridge to the engineering phase.

Eleven one-hour lectures with notes and exercises on the tools around programming: the shell, shell scripting, editors, data wrangling with command-line tools, command-line environments, version control, debugging and profiling, metaprogramming (build systems, dependencies, testing), security, and a potpourri.

items: Shell basics: how the shell finds programs through `PATH`, quoting and expansion, redirection, and why permissions (`chmod`, `sudo`) block scripts silently.

Shell scripting: variables, functions, exit codes (`$?`), `&&` and `||`, command substitution `$(cmd)`, `for` loops, `find`, `xargs`, and shebangs. The lecture's advice: use the shell for glue, Python for logic.
Editors: the Vim lecture teaches modal editing and why an editor you can drive without the mouse pays off; whichever editor you use, learn its search, multi-cursor and integrated terminal.

Data wrangling: `sed` substitutions, regular expressions (character classes, anchors, groups), `awk` for columns, `sort | uniq -c | sort -nk1`, `paste`, `bc`, and building a one-line analysis of a log file. Directly applicable to a PeMS file.
Command-line environment: job control (`&`, `Ctrl-Z`, `fg`, `bg`), terminal multiplexers (tmux), aliases and dotfiles, SSH keys and port forwarding for remote machines.

Version control: git's data model as a directed acyclic graph of commits over trees of blobs; the staging area; branches as references; merging and conflicts; `git bisect` to find a bad commit; `git stash`.

Debugging and profiling: print debugging versus logging levels, debuggers (`pdb`), `strace`-style system tracing, static analysis (linters, type checkers), CPU profilers and flame graphs, memory profilers, and `time` versus wall-clock.
Metaprogramming: build systems (`make` with targets and dependencies), semantic versioning, lock files, continuous integration, and testing vocabulary (unit, integration, regression, mocking).
Security: hashes, key derivation, symmetric and asymmetric encryption at a user's level, SSH keys, password managers, and why secrets never go in repositories.

b.s:
cat log | grep 'Error' | sed -E 's/.*station=([0-9]+).*/\1/' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nk1 | tail
make all   # a Makefile target with dependencies runs only what changed
git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.0; # test, mark, repeat

items: The shell is a programming environment; learning to compose its tools removes a category of Python scripts.
A Makefile with dependencies is the simplest correct pipeline runner.
Profile before optimizing and bisect before guessing.

resources.title: Elements of AI (University of Helsinki)

b.s: A gentle online course that explains what artificial intelligence is and is not, with pictures and simple quizzes, made for everyone.

A free course from the University of Helsinki, no math required: what AI means, how problems are solved by search, how probability handles uncertainty, what machine learning is, how neural networks work, and what AI does to society. About thirty hours, spread over a couple of weeks. A good first map before the phases begin.

Do it in the first week for the vocabulary and the big picture: the difference between rules and learning, why probability matters, what a neural network does in outline, and why AI's effects are a social question. The chapter on machine learning is a preview of phase 4 with no code.
It is deliberately non-technical; use it to calibrate how you explain the course to others, and note where it simplifies (it treats learning as fitting without discussing evaluation).
A model of public education about a technical field: careful about hype, honest about uncertainty, and concrete about societal effects.
Worth knowing as the reference for what a general audience can be expected to understand about AI, which matters when you write for policy makers or the public.

A non-technical introduction in six chapters: what AI is, problem solving by search, real-world AI and probability, machine learning, neural networks, and the implications of AI. Each chapter has short readings and exercises.

items: Defining AI: it is not one thing; useful distinctions are narrow versus general, autonomy versus adaptivity, and the observation that once something works we stop calling it AI. The Turing test and the Chinese room as framing arguments.

Search and games: a problem as states and actions, breadth-first and depth-first search, and game trees with the minimax idea; why exhaustive search fails as branching grows and heuristics are needed.
Probability: odds and probabilities, Bayes' rule with a medical-test example (base rates matter), naive Bayes for spam filtering; the point that uncertainty is handled by arithmetic, not intuition.

Machine learning: supervised (labelled examples), unsupervised (structure without labels) and reinforcement (rewards) learning; nearest neighbors and linear regression as first models; overfitting as memorization; the need for held-out evaluation.
Neural networks: neurons as weighted sums with a squashing function, layers, the idea of training by adjusting weights, and what deep networks do with images.

Implications: prediction versus explanation, bias in data becoming bias in decisions, the limits of current systems (no common sense, brittle outside training data), and the questions society should ask.

b.s: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) P(disease) / P(positive)

items: AI is a set of methods with limits, not a mind; know which method is being used.
Base rates decide what a positive test means; the same logic runs through every alert this course builds.
Overfitting and biased data are the two failure modes a non-expert should be able to name.

b.s: Explain to someone outside the field, in five sentences, what the traffic model does, what it cannot do, and why its alerts need a threshold.
