resources.title: Kaggle Learn: Intro to SQL, Advanced SQL

b.s: Two short online lessons about asking questions of a giant table of data, with answers checked as you type.

Kaggle's SQL courses run against real public datasets in BigQuery, Google's cloud database service, from the browser, so there's nothing to install. Intro to SQL covers select, where, group by, order by, and joins; Advanced SQL covers joins in depth, analytic (window) functions and nested data. An afternoon each.

Do Intro to SQL after SQLBolt and Advanced SQL's window-functions lesson before rewriting the lag feature in DuckDB. The window-functions lesson is the same idea as `shift` and `rolling` in pandas, expressed in SQL.
The courses use a cloud warehouse, which shows what large-scale analytical SQL feels like (partitioning, cost of scans); the ideas transfer to DuckDB unchanged.
Their coverage of nested and repeated fields previews the semi-structured data you meet in event streams such as the 511 feed.
A free, practical introduction to warehouse SQL for a team that needs analysts and engineers to share feature definitions.

Intro: getting started with BigQuery and SQL, SELECT/FROM/WHERE, GROUP BY/HAVING/COUNT, ORDER BY, AS and WITH (common table expressions), and joining data. Advanced: JOINs and UNIONs in depth, analytic (window) functions, nested and repeated data, and writing efficient queries.

items: Warehouse basics: datasets and tables, schemas with types, previewing rows, estimating a query's scanned bytes before running it (cost awareness).
Core clauses: SELECT and WHERE with types and dates, aggregations with GROUP BY and HAVING, ORDER BY with dates, `EXTRACT` for parts of a timestamp, and aliases.
CTEs: `WITH name AS (SELECT ...)` to stage intermediate results, which keeps multi-step feature queries readable; joins on keys with table aliases.
Joins and unions: inner, left, right, full outer; UNION ALL versus UNION; joining more than two tables; self-joins.

Analytic functions: `OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN ...)`; `LAG`, `LEAD`, `FIRST_VALUE`, `RANK`, `ROW_NUMBER`, running totals and moving averages; the exact machinery of lag and rolling features.
Nested and repeated fields: STRUCT and ARRAY columns, `UNNEST` to flatten, which is how the 511 event's `roads` list would be stored in a warehouse.
Efficiency: select only needed columns, filter early, avoid `SELECT *`, use partitions, and read the query plan.
CTEs make feature queries readable; window functions make them possible.
Nested fields are unnested with UNNEST; event lists become rows.
Scan less; column pruning and partition filters decide cost.

resources.title: Select Star SQL

b.s: A free online book that teaches you to ask a database questions by working through one real story from start to finish.

An interactive SQL book, free and without sign-up, that uses one real dataset throughout and builds up to real questions. Four chapters, about half an hour each. Do it after SQLBolt for a project-shaped practice run.

Its single-dataset design mirrors how you will work with the traffic data for months; the chapters on aggregation and on joins are the operations of the profile computation and the incident join. Its final chapter asks questions that need several steps, which is where SQL fluency is tested.
The book is short and stops before window functions; pair with DuckDB's documentation for those. Its emphasis on reading the data before querying is the right habit.
Useful mostly as a teaching resource; its narrative approach is a good model for a project-specific SQL primer.
A small, well-made open resource; the kind of thing to fork and adapt to a team's own dataset for onboarding.

An interactive book in four chapters over one dataset (Texas death-row records): beazley (SELECT, WHERE, LIMIT, basic filters), hierarchy (aggregations, GROUP BY, HAVING, counting and averaging), harder (CASE, subqueries, joins, NULL handling), and the story (composing several steps to answer a real question), with exercises checked in the browser.

Filtering and projecting: SELECT chosen columns, WHERE on text and numbers, `LIKE` patterns, `LENGTH` and string functions, `LIMIT` for inspection.
Aggregation: `COUNT`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` over groups; `GROUP BY` one or several columns; `HAVING` on aggregates; `ORDER BY` an aggregate.
Conditional logic: `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` to bucket values (a severity code from text) or to count conditionally with `SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.
Subqueries and joins: a query in FROM or WHERE, joining a table to an aggregate of itself, and the reasoning about NULLs in comparisons and aggregates.
Composing a story: chaining steps, checking intermediate results, and stating the assumptions the query makes about the data.

Every aggregate query hides an assumption about NULLs; make it explicit.

phases.title: Classical machine learning, the core

b.s: Labels, the incident join, baselines, logistic regression, gradient boosted trees, calibration, and honest row-level evaluation.

items: The supervised setup: features, target, train, validation, test, and why three. Overfitting, bias and variance, regularization, early stopping.
Metrics: confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, the precision-recall curve and average precision, ROC-AUC, log loss, Brier score, reliability diagrams; why accuracy lies under imbalance.
Leakage in its three forms: target, temporal, group. Class weighting.
Linear and logistic regression with scikit-learn; decision trees; random forests; gradient boosting and what `num_leaves`, `learning_rate` and `min_data_in_leaf` do; categorical handling.
Feature engineering as hypothesis-making; feature importance and SHAP values.
Isotonic and Platt calibration; choosing a threshold from a curve.

items.title: Labels: what does 'slow' mean?

b.s: Define the target precisely, compute it without leaking, and understand that the definition decides what the model can mean.
How do we know a road is slow? We compare it with how it usually is.
If cars usually zoom at 65 and today they crawl at 30, that is slow. If they always crawl at five o'clock, that is just five o'clock.
So the helper first learns what 'usual' looks like for every road and every time of day, and then notices when today is different.
Is it cold today? Compared with what: yesterday, summer, or winter? Notice that the answer changes with what you compare to.

For every station and every 5-minute slot of the day, separately for weekdays and weekends, we find the typical speed by taking the median of all the days we have. The median is the middle value when you line the numbers up, so a couple of crazy days do not drag it around the way an average would.
Then 'slow' means today's speed is below 60 % of that typical speed. A slow episode is three slots in a row that are slow, fifteen minutes, so one odd reading does not count.
That definition has a surprise inside it: the evening rush hour, which is slow every day, is not 'slow' by this rule, because slow is normal then. The rule finds unusual slowness.
Line up these speeds: 62, 64, 65, 12, 66, 63, 65. Find the median and the mean. Which one is a better 'typical'? Why?

Three formulas. profile(s, slot, daytype) = median of speed over training days. ratio = speed / profile. is_slow = ratio < 0.6, and label = 1 when is_slow holds for three consecutive steps, the window ending at the row's own time.

Two design choices with consequences. Relative to profile: the label flags unusual slowness, so recurrent congestion is invisible to it. Absolute (speed below 35 mph for three steps): the label flags congestion itself, rush hour included. The plan computes both and makes you pick.

Details that matter: 5-minute slots instead of hours, because a 4 pm median mixes free flow at 4:00 with a jam at 4:55; and free-flow speed is better measured as the station's 85th percentile than as a median, which is why the plan adds `ratio_ff` too.
Make up one day of speeds for a station with a 5 pm rush hour. Compute both labels by hand. Where do they disagree, and which one would a driver want?

The label is a deterministic function of the series and an estimated profile, so the profile is part of the model. Estimating it on all data lets the test period influence training labels: target leakage through the label definition. The profile must be fit on training timestamps only and stored as an artifact.

Quantile estimation: the median has a 50 % breakdown point and, for n days per cell, a standard error near 1.25 σ/√n; with eight weeks of weekdays that is n ≈ 40, so smoothing across neighboring slots trades a little bias for a useful variance reduction, and cells below 20 samples fall back to the hourly median.

Consecutive-run labels: label_t = Π_{k=0..2} is_slow_{t−k}. For horizon h = 3 steps, the label at t + 3 depends on speeds at t + 1, t + 2, t + 3 and does not touch the features at t. Prevalence is a steep function of the 0.6 cutoff and the run length; sweep both once and freeze them in the filename.
Show that for a horizon of two steps the label window at t + 2 would include the row at t itself, overlapping the feature `speed_lag_0`, and explain what that does to a naive evaluation.

Label design is a modelling decision. The relative label approximates conditional anomaly detection; the absolute label approximates a level target. They induce different class balance, different predictability (recurrent congestion is calendar-predictable, non-recurrent is not), and different product semantics, and a model good at one can be useless at the other.

Alternatives keep more information: regress the speed ratio with a pinball loss and derive probabilities from quantiles; or model episode onset as a point process, a model of when events happen along a timeline, with covariates, the input features that shift how likely an event is, and predict hazard, the instantaneous risk of an episode starting right now given none has started yet. Both avoid the brittle 3-step run, and both make horizon coherence natural: a single underlying model of the continuous process, rather than three separately-trained 15/30/60-minute classifiers, cannot contradict itself across horizons the way three independent binary models sometimes do.

Errors-in-variables: detector noise near the 0.6 boundary is heteroscedastic (single-loop speed error grows at low flow), so label noise is concentrated exactly where the decision is made. And because the profile pins the training positive rate near a quantile by construction, real seasonal shifts in congestion are masked in the training window.

Derive how a 5 % multiplicative bias in speed estimation shifts the positive rate near the threshold, given a local density of the ratio around 0.6, and propose a check using stations with double loops.

Production traffic systems keep the modelled quantity continuous (speed, travel time) and push any binary definition into a presentation policy. One model then serves several products, and changing what 'slow' means does not trigger retraining or invalidate history.

Research angles: learning when the target itself depends on estimated quantities; semi-supervised regime detection on the fundamental diagram (hidden Markov or change-point models that find breakdown without a hand threshold); and measuring label quality through agreement across definitions and across detector types.
Operationally, version the label definition as you would a schema. A label change invalidates every logged metric and every comparison across model generations.
Propose an A/B design that compares two label definitions on a downstream user metric such as reroute acceptance, and state what confounds the comparison.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

The label for this course is relative: slow compared with what is typical for that station at that time of day. 'Typical' is a profile computed from data, and here is the leakage trap: if the profile is computed from every row, including the months used later to test the model, then the test rows helped define their own labels. So the very first act is to fix the split dates, and to compute the profile from training rows only.

A split divides the data by time into training (the model learns from it), validation (used to make choices such as when to stop) and test (touched once, at the end, to report a number). `pd.Timestamp("2026-08-31", tz="UTC")` builds one moment in UTC; `df[df.timestamp <= train_end]` keeps rows up to and including it; `.copy()` makes an independent table called `tr` for training.
Choose the split dates first; the profile uses training rows only.

train_end = pd.Timestamp("2026-08-31", tz="UTC")
tr = df[df.timestamp <= train_end].copy()

items: `train_end = pd.Timestamp("2026-08-31", tz="UTC")` — the last moment of the training period
`tr = df[df.timestamp <= train_end].copy()` — the training rows only, which is all the profile may see

b.s: The profile is the typical speed for each station, in each five-minute slot of the day, for each type of day. A slot is the position within the day, 0 to 287: hour × 12 plus minute ÷ 5. The day type separates weekdays (`wd`), Saturdays (`sat`) and Sundays (`sun`), because traffic on a Sunday morning has nothing to do with a Monday morning.

`def daytype(ts):` defines a function, a named block of code you can call with an argument. Inside it `ts.dt.dayofweek` gives 0 for Monday to 6 for Sunday; `np.where(condition, a, b)` chooses a where the condition holds and b elsewhere, nested twice to get three categories. The `for x in (df, tr):` loop adds the slot and day-type columns to both the full table and the training table, with the hour taken in Pacific time (`tz_convert("America/Los_Angeles")`) because rush hour is a local-time idea.

`groupby(["station_id", "daytype", "slot"]).speed.median()` computes the median speed inside every (station, day type, slot) group. The median, the middle value, is used rather than the mean because a few crawling readings would drag a mean down; the median ignores them. `rename` names the result column and `reset_index` turns the group keys back into columns; `to_parquet` saves the profile with the training period in its name, so a profile is never silently reused with the wrong split.
Compute the profile per station, 5-minute slot and day type.

items: `def daytype(ts): ...` — weekday, Saturday or Sunday from a datetime column
`x["slot"] = hour * 12 + minute // 5` — the five-minute position within the local day, 0 to 287
`x["daytype"] = daytype(...)` — the day-type column, from local time
`prof = tr.groupby([...]).speed.median()...` — typical speed per station, day type and slot, from training rows only
`prof.to_parquet("models/profile_train2026.parquet")` — save it under a name that says which split made it

b.s: A merge is a join: it lines up two tables on shared key columns and combines their other columns. `df.merge(prof, on=[...], how="left")` attaches each row's profile speed by matching station, day type and slot; `how="left"` keeps every row of `df` even if no profile exists for it (then the profile is NaN).

The ratio `speed / profile_speed` says how the current speed compares with typical: 1.0 is normal, 0.5 is half speed. `is_slow` is 1 where the ratio is below 0.6, and 0 otherwise (a row whose profile is missing also lands on 0, since a comparison against a missing value is never true); it is stored as `float32`, a number rather than a plain true/false, because the next line sums three of these values together, and summing needs numbers, not booleans. Then the run rule: a slow episode needs three consecutive slow rows, so that one noisy reading does not count. `rolling(3).sum()` adds each row's value to the two before it within each station (`groupby("station_id")` keeps the window from crossing stations); a sum of 3 means three slow rows in a row. `reset_index(level=0, drop=True)` strips the extra group level that rolling adds so the result lines up with `df` again; `== 3` makes the boolean; `astype("int8")` stores it as a one-byte integer. The sort before rolling matters: rolling reads rows in table order, so the table must be in time order within each station.
Join the profile back and compute the ratio and the run-based label.

df = df.merge(prof, on=["station_id", "daytype", "slot"], how="left")
df["speed_ratio"] = df.speed / df.profile_speed
df["is_slow"] = (df.speed_ratio < 0.6).astype("float32")
df = df.sort_values(["station_id", "timestamp"])
df["label"] = (df.groupby("station_id").is_slow.rolling(3).sum().reset_index(level=0, drop=True) == 3).astype("int8")

items: `df = df.merge(prof, on=["station_id", "daytype", "slot"], how="left")` — attach the typical speed to every row
`df["speed_ratio"] = df.speed / df.profile_speed` — current speed relative to typical
`df["is_slow"] = (df.speed_ratio < 0.6).astype("float32")` — 1 where the row is below sixty percent of typical
`df = df.sort_values(["station_id", "timestamp"])` — time order within each station, required before rolling
`df["label"] = (df.groupby("station_id").is_slow.rolling(3).sum()... == 3).astype("int8")` — 1 where this row and the two before it are all slow: the episode label

b.s: One label definition is a choice, and a good analyst keeps a second definition beside it to see what the choice did. The absolute label says slow means below 35 miles per hour, three rows running, with no profile at all. `transform(lambda s: ...)` applies a small unnamed function (a lambda) to each station's speed column and returns a result the same length as the input, so it can be compared and stored directly; inside, `(s < 35).rolling(3).sum()` is the same run rule as before.

The free-flow ratio is a third view: `quantile(0.85)` of a station's training speeds is a speed that is exceeded only 15 percent of the time, a fair estimate of the station's uncongested speed. Merging it on `station_id` and dividing gives `ratio_ff`, the speed relative to free flow rather than relative to the time-of-day profile.
Compute the absolute label and the free-flow ratio alongside.

df["label_abs"] = (df.groupby("station_id").speed.transform(lambda s: (s < 35).rolling(3).sum()) == 3).astype("int8")
ff = tr.groupby("station_id").speed.quantile(0.85).rename("free_flow_85")
df = df.merge(ff, on="station_id", how="left"); df["ratio_ff"] = df.speed / df.free_flow_85

items: `df["label_abs"] = (df.groupby("station_id").speed.transform(lambda s: (s < 35).rolling(3).sum()) == 3).astype("int8")` — three consecutive rows under 35 mph: the absolute label
`ff = tr.groupby("station_id").speed.quantile(0.85)` — each station's free-flow speed, from training rows
`df = df.merge(ff, ...); df["ratio_ff"] = df.speed / df.free_flow_85` — speed relative to free flow

b.s: Prevalence by hour is the sanity check that catches a wrong label definition. Group the rows by the local hour (`dt.tz_convert(...).dt.hour`), and take the mean of each label column, which is the share of rows that are positive in that hour. Because the relative label compares each slot with its own typical speed, it should be roughly equally common at 3 a.m. and 5 p.m.; the absolute label should pile up at rush hour, when speeds really are low.

If the relative label also peaks at rush hour, the profile is not doing its job: a wrong day type, a slot computed in UTC instead of local time, or a profile built from too little data. Fix that before training anything.
Look at prevalence by hour for both labels. The relative label should be flat across the day; the absolute label should peak at rush hour. If not, something is wrong.
print(df.groupby(df.timestamp.dt.tz_convert("America/Los_Angeles").dt.hour)[["label", "label_abs"]].mean())

items: `df.groupby(local_hour)[["label", "label_abs"]].mean()` — share of positive rows in each hour of the day, for both labels

b.q: Why does the relative label ignore the rush hour?

a.s: Because the profile is the typical speed at that slot, and at 5 pm the typical speed is already slow. A ratio near 1 is 'normal for now', whatever the absolute speed.

b.q: What happens to the label if the profile is computed on all data?

a.s: Test-period speeds shape the profile that defines training labels, a leak. The evaluation then overstates skill in a way that is very hard to see.

b.q: Why three consecutive steps?

a.s: To reject single noisy readings. It also shifts the label window: the label at t + h depends on speeds at t + h − 2 through t + h, which must not overlap the features at t.

items: 'The median profile is the free-flow speed.' It is the typical speed, which at rush hour is far below free flow. Free flow is the 85th percentile.
'Threshold 0.6 is a fact.' It is a choice that sets prevalence and difficulty; version it.
'A label is ground truth.' It is a derived quantity with its own estimation error, concentrated at the boundary.

items.title: Features: turning the past into columns

b.s: Build about sixty columns that a model can use, every one of them known at prediction time, and the targets shifted into the future.
To guess what the road will do, we look at clues: how fast it was a minute ago, how fast the road just ahead is, whether there was a crash, whether it is a school day, whether it is raining.
Each clue is a number we write in a row. Lots of rows make a table. The helper learns which clues matter by reading the table.
What clues tell you it is almost dinner time? A smell, the clock, your tummy. Which clue is the most reliable?

A feature is one column of clues. The row for a station at a time has about sixty of them: the speed now and 5, 10, 15, 30, 60 minutes ago (lags); the average of the last 30 minutes (a rolling mean); the speed at the next station downstream and upstream; whether an incident is active nearby and how far away; the time of day, the day of the week, holidays, and rain.
The one rule: every clue must be something you could actually know at that moment. Speed ten minutes from now is not a clue, it is the answer.
The target columns are the answers, copied from the future: the label 15, 30 and 60 minutes later.
Which of these is a legal clue at 4:00 pm for predicting 4:30? Speed at 3:55. Speed at 4:10. Tomorrow's weather. Today's date. Yesterday's speed at 4:30. Say why for each.

Lags come from a shift within each station on the full grid: `df.groupby('station_id')['speed'].shift(k)`. Rolling statistics from `.rolling(6).mean()` where 6 steps is 30 minutes. The slope is `speed_lag_0 − speed_lag_3`.

Time is a circle: 23:55 is next to 00:00, but the number 1435 is far from 0. So minute-of-day becomes two columns, sin(2π m / 1440) and cos(2π m / 1440), which put midnight next to itself. Weekday gets the same treatment.

Neighbors come from the registry: look up the upstream and downstream station ids and merge their speed at the same timestamp. Incidents come from lesson 7's join. Targets are `label.shift(−h)` per station, where a negative shift looks forward.
Before training, one assert: no feature column may use any row after t. If you cannot say how a column is computed from the past alone, delete it.
Draw the sine and cosine of the hour on a circle for hours 0, 6, 12, 18, 23. Why do you need both columns rather than just one?

Every feature must be F_t-measurable, a function of information available at t. That single principle rules out centered rolling windows, target encodings computed on the same rows, and profiles fit on the future.

Mechanics: `groupby` before every shift and rolling to prevent cross-station contamination; `min_periods` to control early-window NaNs; the full grid so a positional shift is a time shift. Trees consume NaN natively and learn a default direction; linear models and networks need imputation plus a missing indicator, and standardization with training-set statistics only.
Categorical station identity: native categorical for LightGBM, one-hot or embedding elsewhere. Interactions (rain × rush hour) can be hand-built for linear models; trees discover them.
Expect the correlation between `speed_lag_0` and the target to fall with the horizon. That decay is the shape of the problem: momentum dominates at 15 minutes, neighbors and calendar at 60.
Compute the Pearson correlation of `speed_lag_0` with `y_15`, `y_30`, `y_60` on one month and plot it. Then do the same for `down1_speed`. Which decays slower, and why?

Feature sets carry bias-variance trade-offs that depend on the learner: a dozen correlated lags inflate variance for a linear model through multicollinearity and cost nothing for trees. Rolling summaries plus a few lags are the robust compromise.

Neighbor features encode a hand-specified graph prior (one or two hops along the postmile line); the spatio-temporal network learns the graph instead. Both are legitimate; the hand prior is cheaper to monitor.

Leakage is subtle: a centered rolling mean uses t + 1 through t + k; a target encoding of `station_id` must be computed out-of-fold in time; weather joined on the realized hour is fine for training but the serving loop only has the forecast, so training should use the forecast issued at t too, or the model will over-trust weather.
Lag features are stationary by construction; calendar and static features drift with roadwork and detector replacement.
Construct a toy series, compute a centered 30-minute rolling mean, use it as a feature for a 15-minute target, and quantify the inflation in average precision compared with the trailing mean.

The industry problem this stage solves is point-in-time correctness: computing training features exactly as they would have been available at serving time. Feature stores with time-travel joins exist for this; the plan's answer at small scale is one feature module used by both paths and a golden-file test that compares them bit for bit.

Representation learning replaces hand features at scale (learned embeddings for segments, time and weather), yet hand features remain the strongest baseline for tabular pipelines and are far cheaper to monitor, explain and debug. Choosing which to ship is an engineering decision about maintenance, not only accuracy.

Research threads: causal feature selection under shift (incident features and congestion share a latent cause), invariance-based training, and the marginal value of exogenous streams such as roadwork feeds, event calendars and school schedules.

Specify the point-in-time join for the weather forecast: the feature at t is the forecast for hour t + 1 issued at or before t, not the realized weather. Say how you would store forecast vintages to make training match serving.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

A feature is one input column, and feature engineering is deciding which columns to compute from the raw data. The rule from lesson 1 applies to every one of them: computed only from rows at or before the current timestamp. `g = df.groupby("station_id")` is saved once, because every feature here must stay inside a station; a grouped object can be reused for many computations.

The double loop makes lags at 0, 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 steps (now, 5, 10, 15, 30 and 60 minutes ago) for each of speed, occupancy and flow: eighteen columns. Rolling statistics summarize a recent window: `rolling(6, min_periods=3).mean()` is the mean of the last six rows (thirty minutes), computed as long as at least three of them are present, and `.std()` is the standard deviation, how much the speed has been jumping around. `transform` applies the rolling calculation per station and returns a column that lines up with `df`. The slope is the simplest trend feature: speed now minus speed fifteen minutes ago; negative means slowing.
Lags and rolling statistics, grouped by station, on the full grid.

g = df.groupby("station_id")
for k in (0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 12):
    for c in ("speed", "occ", "flow"):
        df[f"{c}_lag_{k}"] = g[c].shift(k).astype("float32")
df["speed_roll_mean_30"] = g.speed.transform(lambda s: s.rolling(6, min_periods=3).mean()).astype("float32")
df["speed_roll_std_30"]  = g.speed.transform(lambda s: s.rolling(6, min_periods=3).std()).astype("float32")
df["speed_slope_15"] = df.speed_lag_0 - df.speed_lag_3

items: `g = df.groupby("station_id")` — a grouped view, reused so nothing crosses stations
`df[f"{c}_lag_{k}"] = g[c].shift(k).astype("float32")` — the value of speed, occ or flow k rows earlier
`df["speed_roll_mean_30"] = g.speed.transform(lambda s: s.rolling(6, min_periods=3).mean())` — average speed over the last thirty minutes
`df["speed_roll_std_30"] = ...std()` — how variable speed has been over the last thirty minutes
`df["speed_slope_15"] = df.speed_lag_0 - df.speed_lag_3` — change over the last fifteen minutes

b.s: Time of day matters, but the number of minutes since midnight has a flaw: 23:55 and 00:05 are ten minutes apart yet 1430 minutes apart as numbers. The fix is to place the time on a circle. Any point on a circle is described by its sine and cosine, so `sin(2π m / 1440)` and `cos(2π m / 1440)` (1440 minutes in a day) are two columns that are close for times that are close, including across midnight. The same trick with 7 handles the day of the week.

`loc` is the timestamp column converted to Pacific time, because rush hour is local. `np.sin` and `np.cos` work on whole columns at once; `np.pi` is π. `holidays` is a small library listing public holidays; `holidays.US(state="CA", years=[2026])` gives the California set, and `loc.dt.date.isin(us_ca)` marks rows that fall on one, stored as `int8`. Install it once with `pip install holidays` in the course's virtual environment (venv), the private copy of Python and its libraries that the project uses.
Cyclic time and calendar flags.

import holidays
loc = df.timestamp.dt.tz_convert("America/Los_Angeles")
m = loc.dt.hour * 60 + loc.dt.minute
df["min_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * m / 1440).astype("float32"); df["min_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * m / 1440).astype("float32")
df["dow_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * loc.dt.dayofweek / 7).astype("float32"); df["dow_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * loc.dt.dayofweek / 7).astype("float32")
us_ca = holidays.US(state="CA", years=[2026])
df["is_holiday"] = loc.dt.date.isin(us_ca).astype("int8")

items: `loc = df.timestamp.dt.tz_convert("America/Los_Angeles")` — local time for calendar features
`m = loc.dt.hour * 60 + loc.dt.minute` — minutes since local midnight
`df["min_sin"], df["min_cos"] = sin, cos of 2π m / 1440` — time of day as a point on a circle
`df["dow_sin"], df["dow_cos"] = sin, cos of 2π dayofweek / 7` — day of week on a circle
`df["is_holiday"] = loc.dt.date.isin(us_ca).astype("int8")` — 1 on a California public holiday

b.s: Jams travel backward along the road: a slowdown at the next station downstream reaches you a few minutes later. So the downstream station's current speed is one of the strongest features, and the upstream one helps too. The registry from lesson 3 knows each station's `upstream_id` and `downstream_id`.

The trick is a self-join: the same table of (station, timestamp, speed, occ) is merged back onto `df` under a different name. First `df` is merged with the registry to gain the neighbor id column; then `nb`, a renamed copy of the current readings, is merged on (neighbor id, timestamp), so each row picks up its neighbor's reading at the same moment. The `rename(columns=...)` calls give the new columns names such as `down1_speed` (first downstream neighbor's speed) and `up1_occ`. Inside that rename, `side[:2 if side=='upstream' else 4]` is a conditional expression tucked inside a slice: Python first works out `2 if side=='upstream' else 4`, which is `2` when `side` is `'upstream'` and `4` otherwise, and only then applies `side[:that number]` to cut the word short, giving `'up'` or `'down'`. Same timestamp, so nothing from the future is used. After running this, check `df.down1_speed.isna().mean()` and `df.up1_speed.isna().mean()`: most rows should have a real number, since most stations have a neighbor; a value near 1.0 means the merge keys do not match, usually a wrong id type or a registry that failed to load.
Neighbor features from the registry.

reg = pd.read_parquet("data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet")[["ID", "upstream_id", "downstream_id"]]
cur = df[["station_id", "timestamp", "speed", "occ"]]
for side in ("upstream", "downstream"):
    nb = cur.rename(columns={"station_id": f"{side}_id", "speed": f"{side[:2 if side=='upstream' else 4]}1_speed", "occ": f"{side[:2 if side=='upstream' else 4]}1_occ"})
    df = df.merge(reg[["ID", f"{side}_id"]].rename(columns={"ID": "station_id"}), on="station_id", how="left")
    df = df.merge(nb, on=[f"{side}_id", "timestamp"], how="left")

items: `reg = pd.read_parquet("data/pems_meta/fremont_stations.parquet")[["ID", "upstream_id", "downstream_id"]]` — the registry's neighbor columns
`cur = df[["station_id", "timestamp", "speed", "occ"]]` — the readings to be looked up as a neighbor
`nb = cur.rename(columns={...})` — the same readings, named as the neighbor's
`df = df.merge(reg[...].rename(...), on="station_id", how="left")` — add each row's neighbor id
`df = df.merge(nb, on=[f"{side}_id", "timestamp"], how="left")` — attach the neighbor's reading at the same timestamp

b.s: Three horizons, three targets: `y_15`, `y_30` and `y_60` are the label 3, 6 and 12 rows later, made with a negative shift inside each station, exactly as in lesson 1.3. These are the only columns that may look forward.

Near the end of the data the future is unknown, and those rows have NaN targets. `dropna(subset=[...])` removes rows where any of the three targets is missing, giving `train_table`, the table every model in the course trains on. The `for h, steps in ((15, 3), ...)` loop unpacks two values per iteration, the horizon in minutes and the number of rows it corresponds to.
Targets shifted forward, then drop rows whose target is unknown.

items: `df[f"y_{h}"] = g.label.shift(-steps)` — the label 3, 6 or 12 rows ahead, within each station
`train_table = df.dropna(subset=["y_15", "y_30", "y_60"])` — keep rows whose future is known

b.s: Trust nothing you have not checked by hand once. This assertion picks one random row, rebuilds one of its features from the raw table the slow way, and demands that the two agree. `sample(1, random_state=0)` draws one row, with a fixed random seed so the check is repeatable; `.iloc[0]` turns the one-row table into a row object `r`.

`past` selects that station's rows strictly before the row's timestamp and takes the last three with `tail(3)`; the first of those three, `past.speed.iloc[0]`, is the reading three rows back, which is what `speed_lag_3` claims to be. `np.isclose` compares two floating-point numbers allowing tiny rounding differences. If the assertion fails, the feature is wrong or the grid has a gap; either way, stop. Repeat this for a neighbor feature and a rolling feature.
The leakage assert: recompute one feature by hand for a random row and compare.

r = train_table.sample(1, random_state=0).iloc[0]
past = df[(df.station_id == r.station_id) & (df.timestamp < r.timestamp)].tail(3)
assert np.isclose(r.speed_lag_3, past.speed.iloc[0])   # three rows back

items: `r = train_table.sample(1, random_state=0).iloc[0]` — one random row
`past = df[(same station) & (df.timestamp < r.timestamp)].tail(3)` — its station's three rows before it
`assert np.isclose(r.speed_lag_3, past.speed.iloc[0])` — the lag-3 feature equals the speed three rows back

b.q: Why sin and cos of the minute rather than the minute itself?

a.s: The minute jumps from 1439 to 0 at midnight; a model would see a cliff. The pair (sin, cos) is continuous around the circle and two columns are needed because sin alone maps two different times to the same value.

b.q: Why does the target use a negative shift?

a.s: `shift(−6)` pulls the value six rows later into the current row: the label thirty minutes ahead, aligned with the features at t.

b.q: Why keep NaN for LightGBM but impute for the network?

a.s: Trees route missing values down a learned branch; a network multiplies NaN into every weight. Impute, and add an indicator so the network can still know the value was missing.

items: 'More features always help.' Correlated features hurt linear models and slow trees; every feature is another thing to monitor for drift.
'Realized weather is a fine training feature.' At serving time only the forecast exists. Train on what you will have.
'Rolling windows are safe.' Only trailing windows are; centered windows look ahead.

items.title: Baselines and honest evaluation

b.s: Score a forecast so that the number means something: against a baseline, on later data, with metrics that imbalance cannot fool.
Before we say our helper is smart, we compare it with a very simple guess: 'the road will be like it is right now'. If the helper cannot beat that, it is not helping.
We also test it on days it has never seen, like a real quiz, not on the days it practiced on.
For one week, guess tomorrow's weather as 'same as today'. Keep score. How often is the lazy guess right? That is the score a smart guesser has to beat.
Two simple guesses, called baselines. Persistence: whatever the road is doing now, it keeps doing. Profile rate: how often this station is slow at this time of day, on average.
Two measurements. Of all the times we shouted 'slow!', how often was it really slow? That is precision. Of all the real slow times, how many did we catch? That is recall.
Because slow times are rare, maybe 5 % of rows, a helper that always says 'not slow' is 95 % 'accurate' and completely useless. That is why accuracy is not the score.
And we test on later weeks than we trained on, never on the same days, because two rows five minutes apart look almost the same and would make the quiz too easy.
There are 100 rows and 5 are slow. A helper says 'slow' 10 times, and 4 of those are right. Compute precision and recall. Now compute accuracy for a helper that never says 'slow'.

The confusion matrix gives true and false positives and negatives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall = TP / (TP + FN); F1 is their harmonic mean. Sliding the threshold traces the precision-recall curve; its area is average precision (AP), the headline metric here. ROC-AUC exists too but looks flattering under imbalance because true negatives are cheap.

For probabilities: log loss and the Brier score punish confident wrong answers. Calibration asks whether, among rows predicted at about 0.7, about 70 % turn out positive; a reliability diagram shows it.

The split is chronological: train on months 1 to 8, validate on 9 to 10, test on 11 to 12, with a one-day gap so lags and horizons never straddle a boundary. Skill is reported relative to persistence at each horizon.
Rank ten predictions by probability with three positives among them, and compute average precision by hand as the mean of precision at each positive's rank.

Shuffled K-fold is wrong for a time series because autocorrelation places near-copies of every test row in the training fold, and because the estimand is future performance, which only forward validation approximates. Use blocked or rolling-origin validation with a gap of at least the longest lag plus the horizon.

AP equals the mean over positives of the precision at their rank, and its no-skill value equals the prevalence. Log loss and Brier are proper scoring rules: they are minimized in expectation only by the true probabilities, which is what makes them honest. The Brier score decomposes into calibration plus refinement, and the reliability diagram with expected calibration error shows the first term.
Uncertainty: rows are dependent, so bootstrap over blocks (days) rather than rows to get intervals for AP.
Implement rolling-origin evaluation with three folds on one station's data and compare the spread of AP across folds with the spread from shuffled 3-fold. Explain the difference.

Evaluation is the main scientific control in this project. Effective sample size under spatio-temporal dependence is small; threshold and label sweeps create multiple comparisons; and per-row metrics hide what a user experiences, which is per-episode: lead time from first alert to onset, share of episodes caught, and false alarms per station-day.

Forecasting practice reports skill scores against persistence and climatology (the profile rate); the Brier skill score can be negative while AP looks respectable, and both should be shown. Calibration drifts between validation and test months, so recalibration cadence is itself a design parameter.
A single test window is one draw from a non-stationary process. Rolling folds give a distribution of scores; report it.
Derive the Brier skill score against the profile-rate climatology and construct an example where AP improves over the baseline while the skill score is negative.

Offline metrics are proxies. The product metric is what drivers do (reroutes, realized travel time), and its correlation with AP is unknown until measured; A/B tests in traffic suffer interference because routing changes the traffic everyone else sees, a textbook case of performative prediction.

Evaluation infrastructure at scale: metric definitions versioned with the label, backtests reproducible from logged features, slicing by segment, time and weather to surface failure modes, and guardrails such as never regressing worst-slice recall.

Research threads: evaluating forecasts under intervention, distribution-free control of alert rates (risk-controlling prediction sets), and calibration under covariate and label shift using unlabeled target data.
Design an interleaving or switchback experiment that measures the usefulness of alerts without exposing every driver to a possibly bad model, and state the interference assumptions it needs.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

Never split time-series data at random. Rows five minutes apart are nearly identical, so a random split would put near-copies of test rows into training and the score would be a fantasy. Split by date instead: train on the earliest months, validate on the next, test on the last, and leave a gap of a day between them so that a lag or rolling feature cannot straddle the boundary.

`t = train_table.timestamp` saves the column; comparing it with a date string such as `"2026-08-30"` works because pandas parses the string. `tr`, `va` and `te` are the three tables. The validation set is for decisions (which model, how many trees, what threshold); the test set is opened once, at the very end, to report the number you will believe.
Chronological split with a one-day gap.

t = train_table.timestamp
tr = train_table[t <= "2026-08-30"]; va = train_table[(t >= "2026-09-01") & (t <= "2026-10-30")]; te = train_table[t >= "2026-11-01"]

items: `tr = train_table[t <= "2026-08-30"]` — training: everything up to the end of August
`va = train_table[(t >= "2026-09-01") & (t <= "2026-10-30")]` — validation: September and October, after a one-day gap
`te = train_table[t >= "2026-11-01"]` — test: November onward, touched once

b.s: A baseline is the simplest forecast you can make without a model, and every model is judged against it. Two baselines here. Persistence says the future equals the present: the label now (`va.label`) is the forecast for thirty minutes from now. The profile rate says the future equals the historical average: how often, in training, this station in this slot on this day type was slow thirty minutes later.

The metric is average precision, `ap`, imported from scikit-learn (`sklearn`), the standard Python machine-learning library. It takes the true labels and the scores and summarizes the precision-recall curve: precision is the share of alarms that were right, recall is the share of real jams that were alarmed, and the curve traces both as the alarm threshold moves. Average precision equals the prevalence for random scores and 1.0 for perfect ones, and it is not fooled by rare positives the way accuracy is. `groupby(...).y_30.mean()` computes the profile rate per (station, day type, slot); the merge attaches it to validation rows; `fillna(0)` gives zero where a group never appeared in training.
Baselines: persistence and profile rate.

from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score as ap
rate = tr.groupby(["station_id", "daytype", "slot"]).y_30.mean().rename("profile_rate").reset_index()
va = va.merge(rate, on=["station_id", "daytype", "slot"], how="left")
print("prevalence", va.y_30.mean())
print("persistence AP", ap(va.y_30, va.label))          # label now as the forecast
print("profile-rate AP", ap(va.y_30, va.profile_rate.fillna(0)))

items: `from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score as ap` — the metric, under a short name
`rate = tr.groupby([...]).y_30.mean()...` — historical share of slow-in-30-minutes per station, day type and slot
`va = va.merge(rate, on=[...], how="left")` — attach that rate to every validation row
`ap(va.y_30, va.label)` — score of the persistence baseline
`ap(va.y_30, va.profile_rate.fillna(0))` — score of the profile-rate baseline

b.s: A model gives each row a score, `p_30`, between 0 and 1. An alert fires when the score is above a threshold, written τ (tau). Choosing τ is a business decision expressed in precision: here, at least half of all alarms must be right. `precision_recall_curve` returns three arrays: precision and recall at every possible threshold, and the thresholds themselves, which has one fewer element (the last precision-recall point has no threshold, hence `p[:-1]`).

`np.where(p[:-1] >= 0.5)[0]` gives the positions where precision reaches 0.5; scikit-learn orders thresholds increasing, so the first such position is the lowest threshold that meets the requirement, which is also the one with the most recall. `thr[ok[0]] if len(ok) else 1.0` is a conditional expression: use that threshold, or 1.0 (never alert) if no threshold reaches the precision. Print the recall at τ too: that is the share of real jams you will catch at this alarm quality.
Precision-recall curve and a threshold at 0.5 precision.

from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve
p, r, thr = precision_recall_curve(va.y_30, va.p_30)          # p_30 from any model
ok = np.where(p[:-1] >= 0.5)[0]
tau = thr[ok[0]] if len(ok) else 1.0
print("tau", tau, "recall at tau", r[ok[0]] if len(ok) else 0)

items: `p, r, thr = precision_recall_curve(va.y_30, va.p_30)` — precision and recall at every threshold
`ok = np.where(p[:-1] >= 0.5)[0]` — thresholds at which at least half of alarms are correct
`tau = thr[ok[0]] if len(ok) else 1.0` — the lowest such threshold, or never alert
`print("tau", tau, "recall at tau", ...)` — the chosen threshold and how many jams it catches

b.s: Calibration asks whether a score of 0.3 means a 30 percent chance. A reliability diagram checks it: sort rows into bins by predicted score, and compare each bin's average prediction with the share of positives actually observed in it. `calibration_curve` from scikit-learn does the binning; `n_bins=10` makes ten bins and `strategy="quantile"` gives each bin the same number of rows rather than the same width, which matters when most scores are small.

It returns two arrays, the observed fraction of positives and the mean predicted score per bin; `zip` walks the two together and the f-string prints them with two decimals. A well calibrated model prints pairs that nearly match; a model that prints predicted 0.60, observed 0.30 is overconfident and needs the calibration step in lesson 11.
Reliability diagram numbers.

items: `frac_pos, mean_pred = calibration_curve(va.y_30, va.p_30, n_bins=10, strategy="quantile")` — ten equal-count bins: observed rate and mean prediction in each
`for a, b in zip(mean_pred, frac_pos): print(...)` — predicted versus observed, one line per bin

b.s: A single average precision number hides how much it would move with a different two months of data. The bootstrap estimates that by resampling: draw days at random with replacement (a day can be picked twice, another not at all), recompute the score, and repeat two hundred times; the spread of those scores is the uncertainty. Resampling whole days rather than rows is the block bootstrap, needed because rows within a day are not independent.

`va.timestamp.dt.floor("D").unique()` lists the validation days. `np.random.default_rng(0)` is a random number generator with a fixed seed so the run is repeatable; `rng.choice(days, size=len(days), replace=True)` draws the resample. The list comprehension inside `pd.concat` gathers each picked day's rows, and `ap` scores the resampled set. `np.percentile(scores, [2.5, 97.5])` gives the range that holds the middle 95 percent of the scores: report it beside the point estimate.
Block bootstrap over days for an interval on AP.

days = va.timestamp.dt.floor("D").unique()
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); scores = []
for _ in range(200):
    pick = rng.choice(days, size=len(days), replace=True)
    sub = pd.concat([va[va.timestamp.dt.floor("D") == d] for d in pick])
    scores.append(ap(sub.y_30, sub.p_30))
print(np.percentile(scores, [2.5, 97.5]))

items: `days = va.timestamp.dt.floor("D").unique()` — the validation days
`pick = rng.choice(days, size=len(days), replace=True)` — one resample of days, some repeated
`sub = pd.concat([va[va.timestamp.dt.floor("D") == d] for d in pick])` — the rows of those days
`scores.append(ap(sub.y_30, sub.p_30))` — the score on this resample
`np.percentile(scores, [2.5, 97.5])` — a 95 percent interval for average precision

b.q: Why is persistence such a strong baseline at 15 minutes?

a.s: Speed five minutes ago is highly autocorrelated with speed in fifteen; jams rarely appear from nothing inside one step. Skill over persistence grows with horizon.

b.q: Why bootstrap over days rather than rows?

a.s: Rows within a day are dependent; resampling rows pretends they are independent and gives intervals that are far too narrow.

b.q: What does a high ROC-AUC with a low AP tell you?

a.s: The model ranks negatives well below positives on average, but the top of the ranking, which is what alerts use, is still polluted with false positives. Under imbalance ROC-AUC is the flattering one.

items: 'Cross-validation is always better than a single split.' Shuffled CV on a time series leaks and reports fantasy scores; only forward splits are valid here.
'Beating the baseline once is enough.' Report it per horizon and per fold; a model can beat persistence at 60 minutes and lose at 15.
'Calibration is a detail.' It is the difference between a probability and a score, and the threshold rule assumes a probability.

items.title: Gradient boosted trees

b.s: Understand why hundreds of small trees, each fixing the last one's mistakes, are the production model for tabular data, and how to tune them without fooling yourself.
A decision tree is a game of twenty questions. Is the road ahead slower than 40? Is it raining? Is it five o'clock? Each answer takes you down a branch to a guess.
Boosting is playing many tiny question-games in a row. Each new game only tries to fix what the games before it got wrong, and at the end all the little answers are added up.
Play twenty questions to guess an animal. Notice that the best questions split the possibilities in half. A bad question ('is it a zebra?') wastes a turn.
One tree splits the rows by asking questions about the clues and ends in leaves, each with a score. One tree is rough and jumpy.

Boosting builds hundreds of small trees. Each is trained on the mistakes left over by the ones before, and its score is shrunk by a 'learning rate' before being added, so no single tree can dominate. The sum of all the shrunken trees is the model.
LightGBM is a fast program that does this. It bins each clue into 255 buckets so it can try splits quickly, and it can stop adding trees when the score on held-out data stops improving.
Write ten rows with a speed and whether the road was slow 30 minutes later. Try the split 'speed < 40' and count slow and not-slow on each side. Try 'speed < 55'. Which split separates them better?

A tree chooses the split that most reduces the mix of classes in its leaves (the gain). Depth and the number of leaves control how detailed it can be. Boosting: start with a constant F₀, then repeatedly fit a small tree h_m to the residuals (for logistic loss, y − p) and set F_m = F_{m−1} + η h_m.

The knobs that matter: `num_leaves` (63 here), `learning_rate` (0.05), `min_data_in_leaf` (200, so a leaf cannot fit noise), `feature_fraction` and `bagging_fraction` (randomness that reduces overfitting), and early stopping on validation average precision. `is_unbalance` reweights the rare positives. `station_id` is passed as a categorical, not one-hot.
Thousands of trees at a small learning rate usually beat hundreds at a large one, and early stopping picks the count for you.
Explain in your own words why 3000 trees at η = 0.05 can beat 300 trees at η = 0.5, and what early stopping is protecting against.

Gradient boosting is gradient descent in function space (Friedman, 2001). Modern libraries use the second-order expansion of the loss: with per-row gradient g and Hessian h, a leaf's optimal value is −Σg / (Σh + λ) and a split's gain is the increase in Σ(Σg)² / (Σh + λ) across the two children. For logistic loss g = p − y and h = p(1 − p).

Histogram-based split finding bins features to 255 values (one byte per cell), which sets memory at roughly rows × features bytes; LightGBM grows leaf-wise (best leaf first) rather than level-wise, and adds gradient-based one-side sampling and exclusive feature bundling for speed.
Regularization is λ, minimum child weight, shrinkage and subsampling. Importance by gain is biased toward high-cardinality features; TreeSHAP gives exact per-row attributions.
Derive the optimal leaf weight and the split gain from the second-order Taylor expansion of a general loss, then specialize to logistic loss.

Boosted trees win on tabular data for identifiable reasons (Grinsztajn et al., 2022): they are invariant to feature scaling and rotation-non-invariant in a way that suits heterogeneous columns, and they are robust to uninformative features. Their failure modes are just as identifiable: piecewise-constant extrapolation outside the training range, sensitivity of split thresholds to distribution shift, and poorly calibrated raw scores, hence the isotonic step.

Monotone constraints encode physics: the probability of a slow episode should not increase with downstream speed. Class weighting, threshold moving and focal loss are three ways to handle imbalance with different effects on calibration.
Hyperparameter search must use the chronological validation split, and choosing among many configurations on that split is itself a fit; nested rolling-origin evaluation is the honest cost.
Show that for a well-specified model class weighting is equivalent to shifting the decision threshold, then explain concretely why the equivalence fails for finite trees with early stopping.

In production, boosted ensembles are compiled to branch-free code or shipped on device through Core ML tree ensembles, quantized, and watched for drift through the histogram of values arriving at each split. Retraining at scale uses warm starts and careful control of tree count so that latency budgets hold.

Research threads: margin-based theory of boosting; hybrids with networks (differentiable trees, GBT-initialized MLPs, deep forests); uncertainty for ensembles (natural-gradient boosting, quantile boosting, conformal on top); and the persistent empirical finding that on ten-million-row engineered tabular data a boosted ensemble is the strongest and cheapest baseline.
The senior judgment is choosing when not to replace it: a model that is 0.01 AP better and ten times harder to monitor is a worse product.

Propose a set of monotone constraints for this problem, argue which are physically justified from kinematic wave theory and which are merely plausible, and describe how you would test that a constraint does not cost skill.
Every step first explains the tools, terms and commands it uses, then says what to do, then reads the code line by line.

A decision tree splits data with questions like 'is downstream speed below 40?' and gives a constant answer in each leaf. Gradient boosting builds hundreds of small trees in sequence, each one trained to correct the errors of the ones before it; the sum of their outputs is the score. LightGBM is a fast, memory-frugal library for this from Microsoft, installed with `pip install lightgbm` in the venv, imported as `lgb`.

The feature list is everything in the table except the columns that are not inputs: the timestamp, the two present-time labels, the three targets and any helper column. Building it by exclusion is convenient and dangerous — anything you forget to name is silently used as a feature, and the table still carries `ts`, the original timestamp text, along with `district` and `lane_type`, which hold the same value in every row here. LightGBM will not train on text at all: a column of Python strings stops it with `DataFrame.dtypes for data must be int, float or bool` before the first tree is built, so those three have to be named in `drop`. A categorical feature is one whose values are names rather than quantities (station id, freeway, direction, day type); declaring them lets LightGBM split on 'is the station one of these' instead of treating the id as a number. Declaring is not enough on its own: the column has to be pandas `category` dtype first, and the categories have to be the same list in every split, or the same code means a different station in training and in validation. `pd.CategoricalDtype(sorted(train_table[c].dropna().unique()))` builds one shared dtype per column from the whole table and `astype` applies it to all three splits. `lgb.Dataset` wraps a table and its targets in LightGBM's own binned format; `reference=dtr` makes the validation set use the same bins as training; `free_raw_data=False` keeps the original table available for later predictions. The `assert` is there because this is the mistake that costs an evening: it fails loudly, and here, if a text column is still in the list.
Drop the text columns, give the categoricals one shared dtype, then build the LightGBM datasets.

import lightgbm as lgb
drop = {"timestamp", "ts", "district", "lane_type", "label", "label_abs", "y_15", "y_30", "y_60", "speed_t30"}
cats = ["station_id", "fwy", "dir", "daytype"]
ctype = {c: pd.CategoricalDtype(sorted(train_table[c].dropna().unique())) for c in cats}
tr = tr.astype(ctype); va = va.astype(ctype); te = te.astype(ctype)
feats = [c for c in train_table.columns if c not in drop]
assert not [c for c in feats if tr[c].dtype == object], "a text column is still in feats"
dtr = lgb.Dataset(tr[feats], tr.y_30, categorical_feature=cats, free_raw_data=False)
dva = lgb.Dataset(va[feats], va.y_30, categorical_feature=cats, reference=dtr)

items: `drop = {"timestamp", "ts", "district", "lane_type", ...}` — the timestamp, the text columns and the label columns, none of which are inputs
`ctype = {c: pd.CategoricalDtype(sorted(train_table[c].dropna().unique())) for c in cats}` — one shared category list per column, so the codes mean the same thing in every split
`tr = tr.astype(ctype); va = va.astype(ctype); te = te.astype(ctype)` — apply it to all three splits
`feats = [c for c in train_table.columns if c not in drop]` — every column that is a legitimate input
`assert not [c for c in feats if tr[c].dtype == object]` — fail here if a text column slipped through, not deep inside LightGBM
`cats = ["station_id", "fwy", "dir"]` — the columns that are names, not amounts
`dtr = lgb.Dataset(tr[feats], tr.y_30, categorical_feature=cats, free_raw_data=False)` — training data in LightGBM's format
`dva = lgb.Dataset(va[feats], va.y_30, categorical_feature=cats, reference=dtr)` — validation data, binned the same way

b.s: Hyperparameters are the settings chosen before training. `objective="binary"` means a yes-or-no target with log loss; `is_unbalance=True` up-weights the rare positives; `num_leaves=63` limits each tree's size; `min_data_in_leaf=200` forbids leaves that fit a handful of rows; `learning_rate=0.05` scales each tree's contribution so that many trees are needed and each is a small correction; `feature_fraction` and `bagging_fraction` at 0.8 train each tree on a random 80 percent of features and rows, which reduces overfitting; `bagging_freq=1` re-draws that sample every tree; `lambda_l2` is a penalty on leaf values; `max_bin=255` is how finely each feature is bucketed; `num_threads=8` uses the M1's eight cores; `metric="average_precision"` is what the validation set is scored with; `verbose=-1` silences chatter.

`lgb.train` fits up to 3000 trees. Early stopping watches the validation metric and stops when it has not improved for 100 rounds, then remembers the best round as `m.best_iteration`; that is the number of trees to use at prediction time. `log_evaluation(100)` prints the metric every hundred rounds so you can watch it climb and flatten.
Train with early stopping on average precision.

params = dict(objective="binary", is_unbalance=True, num_leaves=63, min_data_in_leaf=200, learning_rate=0.05,
              feature_fraction=0.8, bagging_fraction=0.8, bagging_freq=1, lambda_l2=1.0, max_bin=255,
              num_threads=8, metric="average_precision", verbose=-1)
m = lgb.train(params, dtr, num_boost_round=3000, valid_sets=[dva], callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100), lgb.log_evaluation(100)])
print("best iteration", m.best_iteration)

items: `params = dict(...)` — the settings, each explained above
`m = lgb.train(params, dtr, num_boost_round=3000, valid_sets=[dva], callbacks=[early_stopping(100), log_evaluation(100)])` — train until validation average precision stops improving
`print("best iteration", m.best_iteration)` — how many trees the final model uses

b.s: `m.predict(table, num_iteration=m.best_iteration)` scores rows with the best number of trees, returning a probability per row; store it in the validation table as `p_30`. The comparison against persistence, the baseline from lesson 6, is the whole point: the boosted model should beat it clearly, typically by a wide margin at 30 minutes and by less at 60. If it does not, look for a feature bug before touching hyperparameters.
Score validation and compare with the baselines from lesson 6.

va["p_30"] = m.predict(va[feats], num_iteration=m.best_iteration)
print("LightGBM AP", ap(va.y_30, va.p_30), "persistence AP", ap(va.y_30, va.label))

items: `va["p_30"] = m.predict(va[feats], num_iteration=m.best_iteration)` — model scores on validation
`print("LightGBM AP", ap(va.y_30, va.p_30), "persistence AP", ap(va.y_30, va.label))` — the model against the baseline it must beat

b.s: Importance by gain totals, for each feature, how much the loss dropped at splits that used it; `feature_importance("gain")` returns those totals in feature order, and wrapping them in `pd.Series(..., index=feats)` names them so `sort_values` and `head(15)` show the top fifteen. Expect downstream speed, speed lags and the profile ratio near the top; a calendar flag at the very top would be suspicious.

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) goes further: for one row it splits the prediction into a contribution from each feature, positive or negative. `shap.TreeExplainer(m)` builds an explainer for a tree model, `shap_values` computes the contributions for a sample of twenty thousand rows (`sample(20_000, random_state=0)` draws the same rows both times), and `summary_plot` draws the distribution of contributions per feature. Install it with `pip install shap` in the venv, the same one every other library in this course goes into; it can take a few minutes on the M1, which is why a sample is used.
Importance by gain and a SHAP summary for one horizon.

imp = pd.Series(m.feature_importance("gain"), index=feats).sort_values(ascending=False)
print(imp.head(15))
import shap
ex = shap.TreeExplainer(m); sv = ex.shap_values(va[feats].sample(20_000, random_state=0))
shap.summary_plot(sv, va[feats].sample(20_000, random_state=0), max_display=15)

items: `imp = pd.Series(m.feature_importance("gain"), index=feats).sort_values(ascending=False)` — features ranked by how much they reduced the loss
`ex = shap.TreeExplainer(m); sv = ex.shap_values(sample)` — per-row, per-feature contributions on a sample
`shap.summary_plot(sv, sample, max_display=15)` — the picture: which features push predictions up or down, and how much

b.s: A saved model is only useful if you can tell, months later, exactly what it predicts. Put the label definition in the filename: horizon 30, threshold 0.6, window 3. `save_model` writes the trees as text; `num_iteration=m.best_iteration` saves only the useful trees. The feature list is saved beside it as JSON, a text format for lists and dictionaries that any language can read, because the live predictor must build its input columns in exactly this order. `json.dump(obj, open(path, "w"))` writes it.
Save with the label definition in the name, plus the feature list.

m.save_model("models/gbt_h30_thresh0.6_win3.txt", num_iteration=m.best_iteration)
import json; json.dump(feats, open("models/gbt_h30_features.json", "w"))

items: `m.save_model("models/gbt_h30_thresh0.6_win3.txt", num_iteration=m.best_iteration)` — the model, named by what it predicts
`json.dump(feats, open("models/gbt_h30_features.json", "w"))` — the exact feature order the model expects

b.q: What does `min_data_in_leaf = 200` protect against?

a.s: A leaf that isolates a handful of rows fits their noise; 200 forces every leaf to summarize a real population, which is regularization by construction.

b.q: Why pass `station_id` as a categorical rather than as an integer?

a.s: As an integer the tree would split on 'id < 4123', which is meaningless. As a categorical it can group stations by behavior.

b.q: Why is early stopping done on the validation split and not on training loss?

a.s: Training loss keeps falling as trees are added; validation AP peaks and then declines as the ensemble fits noise. The peak is the model you want.

items: 'More trees always help.' Past the validation peak they hurt, which is what early stopping finds.
'Feature importance shows causation.' It shows what the trees used; a proxy for the cause ranks as high as the cause.
'Tree scores are probabilities.' They are ranked well and calibrated badly; isotonic regression fixes that in lesson 11.

resources.title: Machine Learning Specialization (Andrew Ng), courses 1 and 2

b.s: Video classes by a famous teacher who explains how computers learn, slowly and kindly, with drawings on a screen.

A set of online courses on Coursera that you can watch for free. Course 1 covers linear and logistic regression and gradient descent, the same ideas as lesson 7. Course 2 covers neural networks and decision trees, plus practical advice on what to do when a model does badly. Do the labs; they are small Python notebooks where you fill in the missing pieces.

Course 1 is lesson 7's math in video form with numpy labs, and its explanation of the cost function's shape and of feature scaling is the clearest available. Course 2's sections on evaluation, bias versus variance, and error analysis are the practical heart of phase 4, and its decision-tree week is a preview of lesson 8. Watch at normal speed and pause to write the equations yourself.

Ng's strength is the practitioner's loop: diagnose whether the problem is bias or variance, then act (more data, more features, more regularization, a different model), and analyze the errors by hand. The treatment is light on theory and on modern tooling, so pair it with ISLP for depth and with the LightGBM documentation for the tools you will actually use.

The specialization's error-analysis method, look at the examples the model gets wrong, categorize them, and prioritize the largest category, is underused in research and is exactly how to improve the traffic model's worst stations: pull the episodes it missed, group them by cause (incident, rain, detector fault), and fix the largest group first.

Ng's courses shaped how a generation frames ML projects around iterative diagnosis, and his later data-centric argument, that data quality dominates model choice on most real problems, is the thesis of this entire pipeline. For a lead, the course is also the common vocabulary a mixed team can be assumed to share.

Course 1, supervised learning with regression and classification: what ML is, linear regression with one and many variables, the cost function, gradient descent, feature scaling, learning rate, polynomial features, logistic regression, decision boundaries, the logistic cost, overfitting and regularization. Course 2, advanced algorithms: neural networks (neurons, layers, forward propagation, TensorFlow, vectorization), training (activations, multiclass with softmax, Adam, layer types), advice for applying ML (evaluation, bias and variance, learning curves, error analysis, data augmentation, transfer learning, skewed data with precision and recall and F1), and decision trees (splits by entropy and information gain, one-hot, regression trees, random forests, XGBoost).

items: Linear regression: model f(x) = wx + b; squared-error cost J(w, b) = (1/2m) Σ (f(xᵢ) − yᵢ)²; gradient descent updates w ← w − α ∂J/∂w and b ← b − α ∂J/∂b simultaneously; the learning rate α too small is slow, too large diverges; plot J against iterations.

Multiple features: vectorized f(x) = w·x + b; feature scaling (mean normalization, z-score) so gradient descent converges; feature engineering (products, polynomials) lets a linear model fit curves; checking convergence.

Logistic regression: sigmoid g(z) = 1/(1 + e^{−z}); f(x) = g(w·x + b) read as P(y = 1 | x); decision boundary where w·x + b = 0; the logistic loss −y log f − (1 − y) log(1 − f) (convex, unlike squared error on a sigmoid); gradient descent has the same form as for linear regression.
Overfitting: high variance versus high bias; fixes are more data, fewer features, or regularization; the regularized cost adds (λ/2m) Σ wⱼ², shrinking weights; regularization for logistic regression.

Neural networks: a layer computes a = g(Wx + b) for several units; layers stack; forward propagation; matrix form; TensorFlow's `Sequential` and `Dense`; ReLU versus sigmoid and why ReLU trains better; softmax for multiclass with the categorical cross-entropy; numerically stable implementation with logits; Adam as adaptive learning rates.

Applying ML: evaluate on a test set; choose models on a cross-validation set; diagnose bias (high training error) versus variance (large gap to validation error); learning curves; regularization and model size trade-offs; the iterative loop of error analysis on misclassified examples; adding data, augmentation, synthesis, transfer learning.
Skewed classes: precision = TP/(TP + FP), recall = TP/(TP + FN), the F1 score as their harmonic mean, and choosing a threshold by the trade-off.

Decision trees: choose the split maximizing information gain (reduction in entropy H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1 − p) log₂(1 − p)); stopping criteria; continuous features by thresholds; regression trees by variance reduction; tree ensembles by bagging (random forests) and boosting (XGBoost); when to use trees (tabular) versus networks (unstructured).

b.s:
J(w,b) = (1/2m) Σ (w·xᵢ + b − yᵢ)²;  w ← w − α (1/m) Σ (f(xᵢ) − yᵢ) xᵢ
L = −y log f(x) − (1 − y) log(1 − f(x))
H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1 − p) log₂(1 − p);  gain = H(root) − (w_L H(L) + w_R H(R))
F1 = 2PR/(P + R)

items: Diagnose bias versus variance first; the fix is different for each.
Precision, recall and the threshold are the vocabulary of alerts.
Trees for tables, networks for unstructured data; information gain is how a tree chooses.

b.s: Reproduce the course's bias-variance diagnosis on the traffic features: plot training and validation AP against LightGBM's number of leaves and label the underfitting and overfitting regions.

resources.lives: course · free (audit) · six weeks · the classic; audit for free

resources.title: An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Python (ISLP), chapters 2–4 and 8

b.s: A famous textbook, free, that explains learning machines with pictures and real examples, written by teachers who invented some of the methods.

Written by statisticians, with Python labs. Chapter 2 explains what learning from data is and why a model can be too simple or too complicated. Chapter 3 is linear regression, chapter 4 is classification including logistic regression, and chapter 8 is trees, forests and boosting. Read a chapter, then do its lab in a notebook.

The clearest explanation anywhere of bias versus variance (chapter 2, with figures worth redrawing), of logistic regression as a model of probability (chapter 4), and of why boosting works by fitting small trees to what is left over (chapter 8). Its lab for chapter 8 uses the same scikit-learn calls you will make in stage 9.

ISLP is the practical face of The Elements of Statistical Learning. Add chapter 5 on cross-validation and the bootstrap, and chapter 6 on model selection and regularization; together with the core chapters they cover phase 4's theory. Its treatment of the bootstrap is the basis for lesson 6's block bootstrap, with the modification that blocks are days.

After ISLP, go to ESL for proofs and depth. ISLP's boosting section gives the additive-model view; combine it with Friedman's 2001 paper for the gradient view that LightGBM implements. Note where ISLP's examples assume independent rows and how each method's assumptions change under temporal dependence.

As a citation for standard methods and as a teaching text it is the reference, and its evolution from R to Python editions tracks the field's tooling. For research, its framing of methods as estimators with bias and variance you can reason about is the habit that distinguishes a careful ML engineer from a library user.

Chapter 2, statistical learning: what it is, prediction versus inference, parametric and nonparametric, the bias-variance trade-off, the classification setting and the Bayes classifier, k-nearest neighbors. Chapter 3, linear regression: simple and multiple, coefficient estimates and their accuracy, model fit, qualitative predictors, interactions, nonlinearity, potential problems, comparison with KNN. Chapter 4, classification: logistic regression, multinomial, generative models (LDA, QDA, naive Bayes), comparison, generalized linear models (Poisson regression). Chapter 8, tree-based methods: regression and classification trees, pruning, bagging, random forests, boosting, Bayesian additive regression trees.

items: The setup: Y = f(X) + ε; we estimate f for prediction or to understand which inputs matter; reducible versus irreducible error; parametric methods assume a form (linear), nonparametric do not (KNN) and need more data; flexibility versus interpretability.

Assessing accuracy: training MSE falls with flexibility but test MSE is U-shaped; expected test error = variance + bias² + irreducible noise; flexible methods have low bias and high variance; cross-validation estimates test error.

Classification: the error rate; the Bayes classifier assigns the most probable class and is the lower bound; KNN estimates conditional probabilities locally; small k is flexible (low bias, high variance).

Linear regression: least-squares estimates, standard errors and confidence intervals for coefficients, t-tests, R² and residual standard error; multiple regression and the F-test; qualitative predictors as dummies; interaction terms; polynomial terms; diagnostics for nonlinearity, correlated errors (time series!), heteroscedasticity, outliers, high leverage, and collinearity (VIF).

Logistic regression: the logit model log(p/(1 − p)) = β₀ + β₁x; maximum likelihood estimation; interpreting coefficients as changes in log odds; multiple logistic regression and confounding; multinomial for several classes.

Generative classifiers: model P(X | Y) and the prior, apply Bayes; LDA (shared covariance, linear boundary), QDA (separate covariances), naive Bayes (independent features); ROC curves and the trade-off between sensitivity and specificity; when each method wins.
Trees: recursive binary splitting to minimize RSS or Gini/entropy; cost-complexity pruning chosen by cross-validation; trees are interpretable but high variance.

Ensembles: bagging averages trees grown on bootstrap samples and out-of-bag error estimates test error; random forests decorrelate trees by sampling m of p predictors at each split; boosting grows trees sequentially on residuals with shrinkage λ, depth d and B trees chosen by cross-validation; variable importance; BART as a Bayesian ensemble.

b.s:
E[(y₀ − f̂(x₀))²] = Var(f̂(x₀)) + [Bias(f̂(x₀))]² + Var(ε)
log(p(X)/(1 − p(X))) = β₀ + β₁X
Boosting: f̂ ← f̂ + λ f̂ᵇ, where f̂ᵇ is a depth-d tree fit to the residuals r ← r − λ f̂ᵇ(x)

items: Test error is U-shaped in flexibility; the bias-variance decomposition says why.
Logistic coefficients are log odds ratios; generative classifiers model the inputs instead.
Boosting fits small trees to residuals slowly; shrinkage and the number of trees trade off.

b.s: Fit logistic regression, LDA and a random forest to the same traffic features on the chronological split; report AP and a ROC curve for each and explain the ordering using the chapter's arguments about bias and variance.

resources.lives: book · free · three weeks · free PDF; the clearest account of trees and boosting

resources.title: Google's Machine Learning Crash Course

b.s: A free class from Google with short videos and little exercises that teach how computers learn from examples.

Google's free course covers linear and logistic regression, classification metrics, overfitting and regularization, neural networks, embeddings, and fairness, with short videos, interactive exercises and quizzes. It covers what a practitioner's textbook would, in about fifteen hours.

The modules on linear regression, logistic regression, classification (precision, recall, ROC, and thresholds), data, and overfitting map onto phase 4; the fairness module previews phase 10. Its interactive exercises on learning rate and on thresholds are worth doing twice.

The course is practical and current, and its treatment of data quality, of feature crosses and of embeddings connects the classical and neural halves of the course. It is light on theory; ISLP supplies that.
Its production-oriented sections (data preparation, fairness, real-world ML) reflect Google's own practice; read them with the Rules of ML.
A free, maintained, vendor-flavored but sound curriculum; useful as a shared baseline for a mixed team.

Modules: introduction to ML; linear regression (loss, gradient descent, hyperparameters); logistic regression (sigmoid, log loss, regularization); classification (thresholds, confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, ROC and AUC, prediction bias); working with numerical data (scaling, clipping, binning, scrubbing, qualities of good features); categorical data (one-hot, hashing, feature crosses); datasets, generalization and overfitting (splits, imbalanced data, transformations); neural networks (nodes, layers, activations, backpropagation, multiclass); embeddings; large language models (tokens, transformers, fine-tuning); production ML systems; AutoML; and fairness (types of bias, identifying and mitigating).
