items.title: Convolutional networks and computer vision

b.s: Understand how networks see: convolutions, pooling, feature hierarchies, and the tasks built on them.
A picture is a grid of tiny colored dots. A computer can slide a small window over the grid looking for edges, then corners, then eyes and wheels, and finally decide 'that is a car'.
Look at a photo through a paper tube. Move it around. You see edges and small parts before you can tell what the whole thing is.

A convolution slides a small filter (say 3 × 3 numbers) across the image and computes a weighted sum at each spot, so one filter finds one pattern everywhere. Stacking layers of filters finds bigger patterns; pooling shrinks the image so later layers see more of it at once.
Convolutional networks classify images, find objects with boxes, and label every pixel. They can also read a traffic camera and count cars, which is another way to measure a road.
Draw a 5 × 5 grid of zeros with a vertical line of ones, and slide a 3 × 3 filter [−1, 0, 1] across each row. Where does the output light up?

Layers: convolution (filters, stride, padding), nonlinearity, pooling, batch normalization, then fully connected layers or global pooling. Why convolutions: weight sharing (the same filter is reused at every position) and locality make them data-efficient and translation-equivariant, meaning a pattern learned in one part of the image is recognized anywhere else it appears, without learning it separately for each spot. Classic architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, ResNet with skip connections) and what each added.

Tasks: classification, detection (boxes), segmentation (pixels); transfer learning from ImageNet-pretrained models; data augmentation. A 1-D convolution over time is the same idea and is what temporal convolutions in traffic models do.
Train a small convolutional network on a public digits dataset in PyTorch on MPS, then replace the classifier head and fine-tune a pretrained ResNet on a tiny dataset of your own photos.

Convolution as a linear operator with structure (Toeplitz), receptive fields, dilations, depthwise separable convolutions and their cost, normalization variants, and residual connections as a fix for optimization depth. Detection pipelines (region proposals, anchor-free methods), segmentation with encoder-decoders, and the metrics (mAP, IoU).
Vision transformers as an alternative inductive bias, and when convolutions still win (small data, efficiency). Self-supervised pretraining for vision.
Implement a 2-D convolution in numpy with padding and stride, verify against PyTorch, and count the multiplications for a 3 × 3 convolution on a 224 × 224 × 64 tensor.

Equivariance and invariance as design principles (group-equivariant networks); the interplay of architecture and data scale (ConvNets versus ViTs as data grows); efficient architectures for edge devices (MobileNet, quantization); robustness to distribution shift and adversarial examples; explaining vision models (saliency, concept methods). For transport: camera-based traffic counting and incident detection as complementary sensors.
Design a camera-based vehicle counter for one Fremont on-ramp: architecture, training data, evaluation, and how you would fuse it with loop-detector counts.

Vision on device (phones, cameras, cars) is an engineering discipline of its own: latency and energy budgets, hardware-aware architecture search, quantization-aware training, and privacy (on-device processing of imagery). Research threads: multimodal models linking vision and language, 3-D and video understanding, and foundation models for perception.
Sketch a privacy-preserving on-device pipeline that turns roadside camera video into aggregate counts without storing images, and list the failure modes you would monitor.

b.q: Why share the same filter across the whole image?

a.s: A pattern is a pattern wherever it appears; sharing makes the network data-efficient and lets it recognize a car in any corner.

b.q: What does pooling buy?

a.s: A larger receptive field for later layers and some tolerance to small shifts, at the cost of resolution.

items.title: Language: tokens, embeddings, attention and transformers

b.s: Understand how text becomes numbers and how attention lets a model relate every word to every other.
A computer cannot read letters, so it turns words into lists of numbers. Words that mean similar things get similar numbers.
Then, to understand a sentence, it lets each word look at the other words and decide which ones matter for it. That looking is called attention.
In the sentence 'the road near the school was slow because of a crash', which words tell you why it was slow? Point at them. That is attention.

Tokens are pieces of text (words or word parts); each token gets an embedding, a vector learned so that related tokens sit near each other. Attention computes, for each token, how much to weigh every other token, then mixes their vectors accordingly. A transformer stacks attention and small networks many times.
The same machinery reads 511 incident headlines: 'Injury collision on I-880 N' can be turned into features, or classified by severity, by a small language model.
Take three incident headlines and list which words in each would help decide whether it is serious. Then guess which words a model would attend to.

Tokenization (byte-pair encoding), embeddings (word2vec's idea: predict neighbors), positional information, self-attention as softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V, multi-head attention, feed-forward blocks, residuals and layer normalization. Encoder models (BERT) for understanding, decoder models (GPT) for generation.

Older sequence models (RNNs, LSTMs) processed words in order and struggled with long range; attention sees everything at once, which is why transformers won. Evaluation: perplexity for language modelling, accuracy or F1 for classification.
Implement single-head self-attention in numpy for a sentence of six tokens with random embeddings, print the attention matrix, and explain what a row means.

The transformer in full: scaled dot-product attention and its quadratic cost, causal masking, positional encodings (sinusoidal, learned, rotary), training with teacher forcing, and the compute and memory of a layer. Pretraining objectives (masked language modelling, next-token prediction), fine-tuning for classification, and embeddings from encoders for retrieval.
Practical NLP: text preprocessing pitfalls, class imbalance in text classification, and using a small pretrained encoder on the 511 headlines for severity when the field is missing.
Fine-tune a small pretrained encoder to predict incident severity from headlines and compare with a bag-of-words logistic regression; report macro F1 and calibration.

Efficient attention (linear, sparse, flash), long-context methods, mixture of experts, and the interpretability of attention (attention is not explanation). Multilingual and multimodal models. Sequence models for non-text data: transformers over time steps and over stations in spatio-temporal forecasting, and their inductive-bias trade-offs against graph convolutions.
Replace the GRU in the spatio-temporal net with a small temporal transformer and the neighbor mixing with spatial attention; compare validation AP and training time on the M1.

Language models are now general-purpose components: embeddings for retrieval, classifiers with no labels, and interfaces to systems. The research frontier spans scaling, alignment, efficiency, and evaluation. For a transport product the relevant questions are extracting structured facts from free-text reports reliably and cheaply, and doing it on device where privacy demands.
Design an evaluation for a model that extracts route, direction and severity from free-text incident reports, including how you would build a labelled set and measure calibration of its confidence.

b.q: What is an embedding?

a.s: A learned vector for a token, arranged so that tokens used in similar ways end up near each other.

b.q: Why did attention replace recurrence?

a.s: It relates every position to every other in one step, trains in parallel, and handles long-range dependencies that recurrent models forget.

items.title: Large language models: pretraining, fine-tuning, prompting, retrieval and evaluation

b.s: Know what a large language model is, how it is trained and adapted, how to use one responsibly in a system, and how to evaluate it.
A large language model has read a huge amount of writing and learned to guess the next word so well that it can answer questions and write stories.
It is not always right, so people check its answers, and they give it the right documents to read when they want facts.
Ask an adult to ask a chatbot what time it is. It probably cannot know. Why not? Because it has no clock unless someone gives it one.

Pretraining: the model reads billions of words and learns to predict the next token. Fine-tuning: it is trained a little more on examples of the behavior you want. Prompting: you write instructions and examples in the input. Retrieval-augmented generation: you search your documents and put the relevant ones in the prompt so the model answers from them.
Models can be confidently wrong (hallucinate), so evaluation matters: test on questions with known answers and measure how often the model is right.
Write a prompt asking a model to turn 'Injury collision on I-880 N at Mission Blvd' into route, direction and location fields. Try three headlines. Where does it guess?

The training pipeline: pretraining on web-scale text, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations people wrote, and preference tuning, adjusting the model using which of two answers people preferred (reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization are two ways to do this). Scaling laws: loss falls predictably with model size, data and compute. Inference: sampling (picking words from the model's predicted probabilities rather than always the top one), temperature (a knob for how much randomness that sampling uses), context windows (how much text the model can read at once), and cost per token.

Adaptation: prompting (instructions, few-shot examples, structured output), parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), retrieval (embeddings, a vector index, chunking), and tool use. Evaluation: held-out benchmarks, task-specific test sets, and human review. On a 16 GB Mac mini, a quantized model, one whose weights are stored in fewer bits than usual (say 4 or 8 instead of 32) specifically to shrink it enough to fit in memory, runs locally at 3 to 8 billion parameters but competes with training for memory.
Run a small quantized open model locally, ask it to extract structured fields from 50 incident headlines, and measure exact-match accuracy against fields you labelled by hand.

Architecture and training at scale: decoder-only transformers, tokenizer design, data curation and deduplication, mixed precision, distributed training. Alignment methods and their failure modes; hallucination as a calibration problem; retrieval as grounding. Evaluation science: contamination, benchmark saturation, LLM-as-judge and its biases, and why task-specific evaluation sets beat leaderboards.

Systems: latency and cost, caching, batching, structured decoding, guardrails, and observability for model calls. For this project: an LLM could parse free-text reports or draft the weekly monitoring summary, never decide alerts.
Build a small retrieval-augmented question answerer over the repository's documentation with a local embedding model, and write a 30-question evaluation set with exact answers to score it.

Research threads: scaling and data efficiency, reasoning and tool use, long context, interpretability (probing, circuits), safety and alignment, efficient inference (quantization, speculative decoding, distillation), and evaluation methodology. The open scientific question of what capabilities emerge from next-token prediction and why.

Design an experiment measuring whether an LLM's extracted incident severity improves the traffic model's average precision over the raw feed's field, controlling for the cases where the feed's field is missing.

Deploying LLMs in products is a discipline of evaluation, cost and risk: task-specific evals with regression tests, human review loops, privacy of prompts, on-device versus server inference, and clear boundaries on what the model may decide. The research frontier includes reliable structured extraction, calibrated abstention, and agents that act through tools with verifiable behavior.
Write the evaluation and safety plan for using an on-device language model to summarize the weekly monitoring report for a traffic operations team, including what it must never assert.

b.q: What is retrieval-augmented generation for?

a.s: Grounding answers in your documents so the model reads facts instead of recalling them, which cuts hallucination and keeps knowledge current.

b.q: Why evaluate on your own test set rather than a public benchmark?

a.s: Public benchmarks may be in the training data and rarely match your task; a held-out set of your own questions measures what you will ship.

items.title: Generative models: autoencoders, variational autoencoders, GANs and diffusion

b.s: Understand models that learn to produce data, the ideas behind each family, and what they are for beyond pictures.
Some learning machines do not sort things; they make new things, like drawing a car that has never existed, by learning what cars usually look like.
Draw a car from memory. You are using what you learned about cars to make a new one. A generative model does the same with numbers.

An autoencoder squeezes data through a narrow middle and learns to rebuild it; the middle becomes a compact summary. A variational autoencoder makes that middle a probability so you can sample new data. A GAN trains a forger against a detective until the forgeries look real. A diffusion model learns to remove noise step by step, so starting from pure noise it can produce a realistic sample.
For traffic, generative models can produce realistic fake days for testing or fill in missing sensor data.
Take a daily speed profile, add random noise to it, and try to guess the original. That guessing, repeated many times, is what a diffusion model learns.

Autoencoders and reconstruction error as an anomaly score; VAEs with a latent Gaussian and a loss of reconstruction plus a KL term; GANs with a generator and discriminator and their training instability; diffusion models as learned denoising over many steps with a simple noise-prediction loss. Evaluation is hard: likelihood is not quality; sample-quality scores exist for images.
Uses: synthetic data, imputation, compression, and learning representations that transfer.
Train a small autoencoder on daily speed profiles in PyTorch; use reconstruction error to rank days by strangeness and inspect the top five.

The ELBO and amortized variational inference behind VAEs; the reparameterization trick; posterior collapse. GANs as a minimax game, mode collapse, Wasserstein formulations. Diffusion: forward noising process, reverse process, score matching, the connection to stochastic differential equations, classifier-free guidance. Normalizing flows as exact-likelihood models.
Time-series generation and imputation with these families; conditional generation (a day given weather and calendar) as a simulator for evaluation.
Derive the VAE loss from the ELBO and implement a conditional VAE that generates daily profiles given weekday and rain; compare generated and real distributions of the 5 pm speed.

Diffusion models' dominance in images and their extension to audio, video, molecules and time series; latent diffusion for efficiency; evaluation via distribution metrics and downstream utility. Generative models for scientific simulation and for data augmentation under distribution shift. Privacy risks (memorization) and the synthetic-data trade-offs.
Train a small diffusion model on daily station profiles and test whether augmenting training with its samples improves the classifier's average precision on rare rainy-day episodes.

Generative modelling is now infrastructure for media, science and simulation. The research frontier includes fast sampling, controllability, evaluation, and world models that couple generation with dynamics. For transport, generative simulators of traffic conditioned on interventions are a path to counterfactual evaluation of alerts and routing.
Propose a generative traffic simulator conditioned on incidents and weather, trained on PeMS history, and the validation that would let you trust its counterfactuals.

b.q: What does the KL term in a VAE do?

a.s: It keeps the learned latent distribution close to a simple prior so that sampling from the prior produces sensible outputs.

b.q: Why is likelihood a poor measure of sample quality?

a.s: A model can assign high likelihood to data while producing blurry or degenerate samples; likelihood and perceptual quality measure different things.

items.title: Transfer learning, self-supervision and foundation models

b.s: Reuse what a model learned elsewhere, learn from unlabeled data, and know when a pretrained model beats training from scratch.
If you already know how to ride a bicycle, learning a scooter is faster. Learning machines can also start from something they already learned instead of starting from zero.
Name one thing you learned that made a new thing easier. That is transfer.

Transfer learning takes a model trained on a big dataset and adapts it to a small one: keep the early layers, retrain the last part. Self-supervised learning makes its own labels from unlabeled data, like predicting a hidden word or a missing patch, so it can learn from everything. Foundation models are big models pretrained this way that many tasks reuse.
For traffic, a model pretrained on all of California's PeMS could be fine-tuned for Fremont with less data.
Cover part of a sentence with your hand and guess the missing word. You just made a label with no teacher.

Feature extraction versus fine-tuning; learning rates for pretrained layers; catastrophic forgetting, losing an old skill while learning a new one because the same weights get overwritten. Self-supervised objectives: masked prediction, contrastive learning (pull similar views together), next-step prediction. Foundation models in vision, language and now time series; zero-shot use (doing the new task with no examples of it) and few-shot use (with just a handful).

Practical rule: with little labelled data, start pretrained; with lots of in-domain data and a narrow task, training from scratch on tabular features still wins, which is why LightGBM is this project's production model.

Pretrain a small network on all Fremont stations with a masked-step objective, then fine-tune it on one station's classification task and compare with training that station's model from scratch on the same data.

Why transfer works (shared low-level features, representations as inductive bias), negative transfer, domain adaptation and domain shift; contrastive learning theory (InfoNCE as a mutual-information bound); masked autoencoders; scaling behavior of pretraining. Time-series foundation models and their mixed evidence against tuned task-specific models.
Evaluating transfer honestly: matched compute and data budgets, and the leakage risk when pretraining data overlaps the test period.

Implement a contrastive pretraining on station-day windows (two augmented views of the same window as positives), then a linear probe for the slow-episode label; report linear-probe AP against raw features.

Representation quality and its measurement (probes, transfer suites), the role of data curation in pretraining, parameter-efficient adaptation (adapters, LoRA), continual pretraining, and model merging. Foundation models for spatio-temporal data and the open question of whether traffic dynamics transfer across cities.
Design an experiment testing whether pretraining on PeMS District 4 improves 60-minute skill in Fremont, with a leakage-safe split in time and space.

The economics of pretraining (one large cost amortized over many tasks) reshaped ML organizations; the research frontier includes what pretraining learns, how to adapt safely, and how to evaluate foundation models on tasks they were not built for. For transport, a state-wide pretrained traffic model served to many cities is a plausible product and a research program.
Write the research plan for a California-wide traffic foundation model: data, objective, evaluation across cities, and the failure modes you would expect.

b.q: When does training from scratch beat a pretrained model?

a.s: With plenty of in-domain data and a narrow task, especially tabular problems where boosted trees on engineered features remain strongest.

b.q: What makes self-supervision possible?

a.s: The data contain their own supervision: hide part of an input and predict it from the rest.

resources.title: Understanding Deep Learning (Prince)

b.s: A newer big book about deep learning, free to read, with lots of clear pictures that show what each part of a network does.

Simon Prince's textbook (2023), free as a PDF with notebooks. It covers supervised learning, networks, training, measuring performance, regularization, convolutional and recurrent and transformer networks, graph networks, and generative models. It is more modern and more visual than the older Deep Learning book. Read the early chapters after phase 6.

Chapters 1 to 9 are the modern version of lesson 9: networks, loss functions, fitting, gradients and initialization, measuring performance, and regularization, each with figures that make the idea visible. Chapter 13 on graph neural networks covers the neighbor mixing of the spatio-temporal net. The notebooks let you run every figure.

Prince's treatment of why deep networks generalize, of the loss landscape, and of the transformer architecture is the clearest current textbook account, and it includes the recent empirical findings (double descent, scaling) that Goodfellow predates. Chapter 12 on transformers is the reading before lesson 8's attention material.

The chapters on generative models (VAEs, GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion) are a compact, correct introduction with the math intact, and the chapter on ethics is unusually careful for a technical text. Use it as the reference when reading current papers.

A free, modern, rigorous textbook is a public good; it is the one to recommend to a new graduate student and the one to cite for standard architectures in the current idiom. Its figures are also the model for how to draw a network in a paper.

Chapters: introduction; supervised learning; shallow networks; deep networks; loss functions; fitting models; gradients and initialization; measuring performance; regularization; convolutional networks; residual networks; transformers; graph neural networks; unsupervised learning; generative adversarial networks; normalizing flows; variational autoencoders; diffusion models; reinforcement learning; why does deep learning work; deep learning and ethics.

items: Shallow and deep networks: a shallow network is a linear combination of ReLU-transformed linear functions, producing piecewise linear maps with regions; depth composes such maps and creates exponentially many regions per parameter; universal approximation with width, efficiency with depth.

Losses from maximum likelihood: choose a distribution over outputs (Gaussian gives least squares, Bernoulli gives binary cross-entropy, categorical gives softmax cross-entropy, others give robust or heteroscedastic losses); the network predicts the distribution's parameters.

Fitting: gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, momentum, Adam; learning-rate schedules and warmup; backpropagation derived for the general case with the forward pass storing activations; initialization that preserves variance (He), and the analysis of exploding and vanishing signals.

Measuring performance: noise, bias and variance; the double-descent curve; hyperparameter search; the importance of test sets; the curse of dimensionality and how real data lie on lower-dimensional manifolds.

Regularization: explicit (L2, early stopping), implicit (SGD's noise, larger learning rates), heuristic (ensembling, dropout, augmentation, transfer learning, multi-task, self-supervision), and the general picture of why regularized deep networks generalize.

Architectures: convolutions (invariance, equivariance, pooling, receptive fields, classic networks), residual connections (why depth trained poorly before them, batch and layer norm), transformers (dot-product attention, positional information, encoder and decoder, scaling, vision transformers), graph networks (adjacency, node embeddings, message passing, graph-level and node-level tasks, spectral and spatial views).

Generative models: GANs (minimax, mode collapse, Wasserstein), normalizing flows (invertible transformations and exact likelihoods), VAEs (the ELBO, reparameterization, posterior collapse), diffusion (forward noising, reverse denoising, the training objective, conditioning and guidance).

Reinforcement learning basics, the chapter on why deep learning works (loss landscapes, overparameterization, lottery tickets, adversarial examples) and the ethics chapter (bias, explainability, misuse, environmental cost).

b.s:
deep network: y = φ_K ∘ … ∘ φ_1(x), each φ = ReLU(W h + b)
ELBO = E_q[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z))
attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d) V

items: Every loss is a negative log-likelihood of some output distribution.
Depth buys expressive piecewise-linear maps; normalization and residuals make depth trainable.
Generative families differ in how they make likelihood tractable: flows exactly, VAEs by bounds, diffusion by denoising, GANs not at all.

b.s: Implement a two-layer ReLU network on one input and plot its output to count linear regions as you add hidden units, then read the chapter's argument about depth and regions and relate it to your plot.

resources.lives: book · free · reference, chapters as needed · now chapters 10 to 18: convolutions, transformers, graphs, generative models

resources.title: Dive into Deep Learning (d2l.ai), chapters 3–5 and 9–10

b.s: A free online textbook where every idea comes with code you can run, about teaching computers using layers of simple math.

Chapters 3 to 5 cover linear and softmax regression and multilayer perceptrons with PyTorch code you can execute. Chapters 9 and 10 cover recurrent networks (RNN, GRU, LSTM) and how to train them well. Run the notebooks; each section ends with exercises that are worth doing.

Chapter 5's multilayer perceptron from scratch mirrors lesson 9's numpy network; chapter 9 explains why GRUs can remember and forget, which is the sequence half of the spatio-temporal network. The exercises about changing hidden size and learning rate are the experiments to actually run on the traffic data.

d2l's coverage of optimization (chapter 12), attention (chapter 11) and computational performance (chapter 13) is deeper than most books and free. Its consistent code style makes it easy to lift components, and its treatment of truncated backpropagation through time explains what a recurrent model can and cannot learn from a 12-step window.

Its graph-neural-network coverage is thin; use CS224W for that. Its attention chapters are the bridge to spatio-temporal transformers, and its chapter on computational performance (asynchrony, memory, multi-device) is the right background before profiling on unified memory.

A living, open textbook with code in several frameworks is itself a research-infrastructure achievement. Cite it for standard architectures, use its implementations as reference points when reproducing papers, and note its authors' choice to include the messy practical chapters most textbooks omit.

Chapter 3, linear neural networks for regression (linear regression, its implementation from scratch and concisely, generalization, weight decay). Chapter 4, linear networks for classification (softmax regression, the image classification dataset, implementations, generalization in classification, environment and distribution shift). Chapter 5, multilayer perceptrons (MLPs, implementation, forward and backward propagation, numerical stability and initialization, generalization, dropout, a Kaggle house-price example). Chapter 9, recurrent neural networks (sequences, text to sequence, language models, RNNs, implementation, backpropagation through time). Chapter 10, modern RNNs (LSTM, GRU, deep and bidirectional RNNs, machine translation data, encoder-decoder, sequence-to-sequence, beam search).

items: Linear regression as a network: the model, squared loss, minibatch stochastic gradient descent with learning rate and batch size, vectorization, the normal-distribution view of squared loss; from-scratch implementation with manual gradients, then `nn.Linear` and `MSELoss`.

Generalization and weight decay: training versus generalization error, model selection with validation, underfitting and overfitting versus capacity and data; L2 penalty as weight decay in the optimizer.

Softmax regression: one-hot targets, softmax outputs, cross-entropy loss and its gradient (softmax minus one-hot), the log-sum-exp trick for stability, accuracy as a metric; distribution shift (covariate, label, concept) and why test data may not match.

MLPs: hidden layers with nonlinear activations (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh) give universal approximation; forward propagation, the computational graph, backpropagation through it, and memory for stored activations.

Numerical stability: vanishing and exploding gradients from products of Jacobians, symmetry breaking by random initialization, Xavier initialization derived from keeping variances constant across layers; dropout as noise injection (zero units with probability p, scale by 1/(1 − p), off at test time).

Sequences: autoregressive models, the Markov assumption, tokenization and vocabularies, language modelling as next-token prediction, perplexity; RNNs with a hidden state h_t = φ(x_t W_xh + h_{t−1} W_hh + b), the character-level RNN from scratch, gradient clipping, truncated backpropagation through time and its analysis.

Gated RNNs: LSTM's input, forget and output gates with a memory cell; GRU's reset and update gates; why gates mitigate vanishing gradients; deep and bidirectional RNNs (bidirectional only when the whole sequence is available, never for forecasting).
Encoder-decoder: encoding a sequence to a state, decoding a sequence from it, teacher forcing during training, greedy versus beam search decoding, BLEU for evaluation.

b.s:
softmax(o)_j = exp(o_j)/Σ_k exp(o_k);  ∂L/∂o = softmax(o) − y
Xavier: Var(w) = 2/(n_in + n_out)
GRU: r = σ(x W_xr + h W_hr + b_r); z = σ(x W_xz + h W_hz + b_z); h̃ = tanh(x W_xh + (r ⊙ h) W_hh + b_h); h_new = z ⊙ h + (1 − z) ⊙ h̃

items: Cross-entropy's gradient is prediction minus target; that pattern runs from logistic regression to language models.
Initialization keeps variances constant across layers; dropout injects noise; both are about stability and generalization.
A GRU's gates decide what to keep and what to overwrite; that is the memory the traffic net uses.

b.s: Implement the GRU cell from the chapter's equations in PyTorch, verify it matches `nn.GRUCell` on random inputs, and use it as the sequence encoder in the spatio-temporal net.

resources.lives: book · free · reference, chapters as needed · now chapters 7, 8 and 11: convolutions and attention

resources.title: CS231n: Convolutional Neural Networks for Visual Recognition, course notes

b.s: The notes from a famous class that taught computers to see, with drawings of how a picture becomes numbers and then a label.

Stanford's computer vision course notes are free online: image classification, linear classifiers, optimization, backpropagation, neural networks, convolutional networks, and how to train them. The notes are written for beginners with some Python, and the assignments build a network from scratch.

Read the convolutional networks module: filters, stride, padding, pooling, and the famous architectures, with the parameter and computation counts worked out. The backpropagation and neural-network modules are a good second pass over the traffic course's lesson 9.

The notes' treatment of initialization, batch normalization, dropout and learning-rate schedules is compact and correct, and the assignment code (numpy implementations of layers) is the vision analogue of the from-scratch rule. The lecture videos add transfer learning, detection and segmentation.

The course predates vision transformers and self-supervised vision; read it for the convolutional foundations, then the recent literature for the rest. Its assignment design is a model for teaching by implementation.

CS231n shaped how a generation learned deep learning; knowing it tells you what practitioners take for granted. For a lead, its assignments are a fair calibration of what 'can implement a network from scratch' means.

Modules: image classification (data-driven approach, k-nearest neighbor, validation, the curse of dimensionality); linear classification (score function, SVM and softmax losses, regularization); optimization (loss landscapes, gradient computation, gradient descent, mini-batches); backpropagation (chain rule, staged computation, gradients of vector operations); neural networks part 1 (architectures, activations, representational power), part 2 (data preprocessing, weight initialization, batch normalization, regularization, loss functions), part 3 (gradient checks, sanity checks, monitoring training, hyperparameter optimization, ensembles); convolutional networks (architecture, layers, patterns, case studies, computational considerations); understanding and visualizing; transfer learning and fine-tuning.

items: Linear classification: a score function f(x) = Wx + b maps pixels to class scores; the multiclass SVM loss wants the correct score to exceed others by a margin; the softmax loss interprets scores as unnormalized log probabilities and minimizes cross-entropy; L2 regularization on W; the bias trick appends a constant feature.

Optimization: numerical versus analytic gradients; gradient checking with centered differences and relative error; step size; mini-batch gradient descent; the loss as a function of parameters, with the geometric picture of the SVM loss as a piecewise-linear bowl.

Backpropagation: any expression is a graph of gates; each gate computes its local gradient; the chain rule multiplies backward; sigmoid, max and multiply gates as examples; gradients of matrix-matrix multiplications by dimension analysis (dW = dOut · Xᵀ shapes must match); staged computation for readability.

Neural networks: layers of neurons with activations (sigmoid's saturation and non-zero-centered issues, tanh, ReLU's speed and dying units, Leaky ReLU, Maxout); fully connected architectures; universal approximation; why larger networks with proper regularization beat smaller ones.

Setting up: mean subtraction and normalization; initialization pitfalls (all zeros fails; small random numbers shrink activations; calibrate variance with 1/√n and Kaiming's 2/n for ReLU); batch normalization; regularization by L2, L1, max norm, dropout, and data augmentation; loss choices for classification, attribute prediction and regression.

Learning and evaluation: gradient checks with care (double precision, kinks, few points); sanity checks (initial loss value, overfit a tiny subset); monitoring loss curves, train/validation accuracy gap, update-to-weight ratios (about 1e-3), activation and gradient histograms; parameter updates (SGD, momentum, Nesterov, per-parameter methods such as Adagrad, RMSprop, Adam); learning-rate decay; hyperparameter search by random search on log scales in stages; model ensembles.

Convolutional networks: the convolution layer's filters, receptive field, depth, stride, zero-padding, and the output size formula (W − F + 2P)/S + 1; parameter sharing; pooling; normalization layers; the standard pattern (conv-ReLU repeated, pool, fully connected); case studies (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet) and their memory and compute budgets.
Transfer learning: use a pretrained network as a fixed feature extractor or fine-tune some layers; rules by dataset size and similarity; smaller learning rates for pretrained layers.

b.s:
conv output size = (W − F + 2P)/S + 1
softmax loss L_i = −log( e^{f_{y_i}} / Σ_j e^{f_j} )
relative error = |f′_a − f′_n| / max(|f′_a|, |f′_n|)  (gradient check; < 1e-7 good)

items: Every deep model is gates plus the chain rule; learn to compute gradients by shape.
Sanity checks (initial loss, overfit a subset, update ratios) catch most bugs.
Convolutions buy parameter sharing and locality; the output-size formula is the arithmetic of architecture.

b.s: Implement a 2-D convolution and max pooling forward and backward in numpy, verify with the course's gradient check recipe, and count parameters and multiply-adds for a three-layer network on 32×32 images.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; the convolutional foundations with worked counts

resources.title: The Illustrated Transformer (Alammar)

b.s: A web page with drawings that shows how a computer reads a sentence by paying attention to the words that matter, a bit like how you look at the important parts of a picture.

Jay Alammar's blog post explains the transformer, the model behind modern language models, with step-by-step pictures: how words become numbers, how attention lets each word look at the others, and how layers stack. Free, and readable without much math. Read it before any paper on transformers.

Follow the pictures of self-attention: queries, keys and values, the dot-product scores, the softmax, and the weighted sum. Then multi-head attention and the encoder-decoder structure. When you can redraw the attention diagram from memory, read Attention Is All You Need with the post open beside it.

The post is the intuition layer for the attention equation softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V; pair it with a from-scratch implementation (Karpathy's GPT lesson) so the pictures become code. Its companion posts on GPT-2 and on BERT extend the same method to decoder-only and encoder-only models.

It omits positional encodings' subtleties, training dynamics and scaling; those come from the papers and from Prince's chapter 12. For spatio-temporal traffic models, the relevant transfer is attention over stations (spatial attention) and over time steps, which later traffic transformers use.

Alammar's posts are the standard first explanation across the industry; for briefing non-specialists on what a language model does, they remain the reference, and their visual grammar is worth adopting in talks.

A visual walk through the transformer for translation: the encoder-decoder stack, embeddings, self-attention at a high level and in detail (queries, keys, values, scores, softmax, weighted sum), matrix form, multi-head attention, positional encoding, residuals and layer normalization, the decoder's masked attention and encoder-decoder attention, the final linear and softmax layer, training with cross-entropy and label smoothing, and greedy versus beam decoding.

items: Overall structure: an encoder stack (six identical layers of self-attention plus feed-forward) and a decoder stack (self-attention, encoder-decoder attention, feed-forward); inputs are word embeddings plus positional encodings; all positions are processed in parallel.

Self-attention step by step: for each input vector, compute a query, a key and a value by three learned matrices; score each position against every other by dot product of query and key; divide by the square root of the key dimension; softmax; multiply each value by its softmax weight and sum; the result is a context-aware vector for the position.
Matrix form: Q = XW_Q, K = XW_K, V = XW_V; Z = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V; the attention matrix is positions × positions.

Multi-head attention: several sets of Q, K, V matrices give several attention 'perspectives'; concatenate the heads' outputs and project with W_O; heads attend to different relations (the illustrated 'it' attending to 'animal' and to 'tired').

Positional encoding: a vector added to each embedding encoding position with sinusoids of different frequencies, so the model can use order and relative distances; the illustrated pattern of interleaved sines and cosines.
Residuals and normalization: each sub-layer's output is added to its input and layer-normalized, which stabilizes training and lets information bypass a layer.

Decoder: masked self-attention (future positions set to −∞ before softmax) so predictions depend only on earlier outputs; encoder-decoder attention uses queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder's output; the final linear layer maps to vocabulary logits and softmax to probabilities; generation is step by step.
Training: the target distribution is one-hot (or smoothed); the loss is cross-entropy summed over positions; decoding greedily or with beam search.

b.s:
Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) V
PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^{2i/d});  PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^{2i/d})
LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))

items: Attention is a softmax-weighted average of values, with weights from query-key similarity.
Multiple heads and stacked layers let different relations be captured in parallel.
Masking is what makes a decoder autoregressive.

b.s: Implement single-head and then multi-head self-attention in numpy for six tokens with random embeddings, print the attention matrices, then add a causal mask and confirm the upper triangle is zero.

resources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)

b.s: The paper that introduced the transformer, the design inside today's language models, by showing that paying attention to all words at once works better than reading them one by one.

A research paper from 2017 that proposed the transformer for translating languages. Its main idea is self-attention, where every word looks at every other word and decides what matters. It replaced the older recurrent networks and became the base of modern language models. Read the introduction and look at the architecture figure after the Illustrated Transformer.

Read it with the Illustrated Transformer open: the attention equation, multi-head attention, positional encodings, the encoder-decoder layout and the training setup. The results table compares with the recurrent baselines; note the compute cost column.

Work through the model dimensions and parameter counts, the reason for scaling by the square root of the key size, the role of residuals and layer normalization, and the label smoothing and learning-rate warmup in training. Then implement a single encoder layer from the paper in PyTorch.

The paper's details (sinusoidal positions, dropout placement) have been revised by later work; understand what survived (attention, residual stacks) and what changed (pre-norm, rotary positions, decoder-only). Its influence is the case study in how an architecture spreads.
A canonical citation; for research, the interesting questions are the ones it opened (efficiency of attention, positional information, what attention learns) rather than what it settled.

The paper: motivation (recurrence limits parallelism; attention allows constant path length between positions), the model architecture (encoder-decoder stacks, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, position-wise feed-forward networks, embeddings and softmax, positional encoding), why self-attention (complexity per layer, parallelizable operations, path length), training (data, hardware, schedule with warmup, regularization by residual dropout and label smoothing), results on translation with BLEU and cost, model variations (heads, key size, model size, dropout, positional encoding), and English constituency parsing.

items: Architecture: N = 6 layers each side; d_model = 512; each encoder layer has multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward network with residual connections and layer normalization; the decoder adds masked self-attention and attention over encoder outputs.

Scaled dot-product attention: softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V; scaling prevents large dot products from pushing softmax into regions with tiny gradients when d_k is large; compared with additive attention, it is faster in practice.
Multi-head attention: h = 8 heads with d_k = d_v = 64; project Q, K, V to lower dimensions per head, attend in parallel, concatenate and project; total cost similar to one full-dimensional head.
Feed-forward: two linear layers with ReLU applied identically at each position (inner dimension 2048); embeddings shared between input, output and the pre-softmax linear layer, scaled by √d_model.
Positional encoding: sinusoids at geometric frequencies so relative positions are linear functions; learned positions performed similarly; sinusoids may extrapolate to longer sequences.

Why self-attention: per-layer complexity O(n²·d) versus O(n·d²) for recurrence; sequential operations O(1) versus O(n); maximum path length O(1) versus O(n); restricted attention for very long sequences.

Training details: byte-pair or word-piece vocabularies; batches by approximate length; Adam with β₂ = 0.98 and a learning rate that warms up linearly for 4000 steps then decays as the inverse square root of the step; dropout 0.1 on residuals and embeddings; label smoothing 0.1 hurts perplexity but helps accuracy and BLEU; checkpoint averaging; beam search with size 4 and length penalty.

Results and ablations: state of the art on English-German and English-French at a fraction of prior training cost; single-head attention is worse than multi-head but too many heads also hurt; reducing key size hurts; bigger models help; dropout is needed.

b.s:
lr = d_model^{−0.5} · min(step^{−0.5}, step · warmup^{−1.5})
MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, …, head_h) W^O,  head_i = Attention(QW_i^Q, KW_i^K, VW_i^V)
FFN(x) = max(0, xW₁ + b₁)W₂ + b₂

items: Constant path length between any two positions is the reason attention beat recurrence on long-range structure.
The scaling by √d_k and the warmup schedule are small details that decide whether it trains.
The ablation table is the model for how to report architecture choices.

b.s: Implement one encoder layer from the paper's equations in PyTorch (multi-head attention, feed-forward, residuals, layer norm, sinusoidal positions), and train it as a temporal encoder over 12 traffic steps in place of the GRU.

resources.title: Hugging Face LLM course

b.s: A free online class that shows how to use ready-made language models, like borrowing a very well-read robot and teaching it your job.

A free course from Hugging Face, the company behind the most-used library for language models. Chapters 1 to 4 explain how transformer models work and how to download, run and fine-tune one; later chapters cover datasets, tokenizers and common language tasks. Everything runs in notebooks.

Do chapters 1 to 3 (transformers, using pretrained models, fine-tuning a classifier) and apply chapter 3 to the 511 headlines: fine-tune a small encoder to predict severity. Chapter 6 on tokenizers explains why 'I-880' may split oddly and how to handle it.

The course teaches the practical stack (models, datasets, tokenizers, training loops with the accelerate library) that most applied NLP uses; understand what the abstractions hide (padding, attention masks, learning-rate schedules) by reading the code of one training step.

Later chapters and the companion courses (agents, reinforcement learning from human feedback) track current practice; the course is a good index of what the ecosystem considers standard at any moment.

The Hugging Face ecosystem is where much of applied NLP lives; its course is also a reference for how open model sharing and evaluation are organized, which matters for reproducibility and licensing decisions in a product.

Chapters: transformer models (NLP and LLMs, what transformers can do, how they work, architectures, bias and limitations); using transformers (pipelines, models, tokenizers, handling multiple sequences, putting it together); fine-tuning a pretrained model (processing data, training with the Trainer API, a full training loop, learning curves); sharing models and tokenizers; the datasets library; the tokenizers library (byte-pair encoding, WordPiece, Unigram, training a tokenizer); classical NLP tasks (token classification, masked language modelling, translation, summarization, causal language modelling, question answering); building and sharing demos; reasoning models and fine-tuning with reinforcement learning (later chapters).

items: Pipelines: `pipeline('text-classification')` and others wrap preprocessing, model and postprocessing; the model hub; the three stages inside a pipeline (tokenizer, model, head).

Transformer families: encoder (BERT-like, bidirectional, for classification and token tasks), decoder (GPT-like, causal, for generation), encoder-decoder (T5, BART, for sequence-to-sequence); pretraining then fine-tuning as transfer learning; attention masks; biases inherited from data.

Tokenizers: word, character and subword tokenization; BPE merges, WordPiece scoring, Unigram pruning; special tokens, attention masks, padding and truncation, offsets; training a tokenizer on your own corpus (incident headlines have their own vocabulary).

Fine-tuning: load a dataset, tokenize with dynamic padding, `AutoModelForSequenceClassification` with a fresh head, `TrainingArguments` and `Trainer`, or a manual loop with `accelerate`; evaluation with metrics; learning rates around 2e-5 for fine-tuning; a few epochs.
Datasets: loading, mapping, filtering, streaming large data, saving; combining with pandas.

Tasks: token classification (named entities such as route names), masked language modelling for domain adaptation, causal language modelling for generation, summarization and translation with encoder-decoders, question answering with span prediction.
Demos: Gradio apps for sharing a model; the model card as documentation.

b.s:
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name); model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=3)
Trainer(model, TrainingArguments(output_dir, learning_rate=2e-5, num_train_epochs=3, per_device_train_batch_size=16), train_dataset=..., eval_dataset=..., compute_metrics=...).train()

items: Encoders classify, decoders generate, encoder-decoders transform; pick by task.
Fine-tuning is a small learning rate, a fresh head and a few epochs.
Tokenization decides what the model sees; train one on your domain if the vocabulary is odd.

b.s: Fine-tune a small encoder on incident headlines for severity with the Trainer API, log macro F1 per epoch, and compare with a bag-of-words logistic regression and with a version whose tokenizer was trained on the headlines.

resources.lives: course · free · two weeks · free; the practical stack for language models

resources.title: Speech and Language Processing, 3rd edition draft (Jurafsky, Martin)

b.s: A big free book about how computers handle language, from letters and words to whole conversations.

The standard textbook on natural language processing, free online as a draft that the authors update. It covers text processing, n-gram models, embeddings, neural networks for text, transformers and large language models, and speech. Read chapters as references when a topic comes up.

The chapters on tokenization and regular expressions, on vector semantics and embeddings, on transformers and on large language models are the textbook version of the language topic. Each ends with exercises; the embeddings chapter's exercises can be done on the incident headlines.

Jurafsky and Martin give the linguistic and statistical background (n-gram language models, smoothing, evaluation with perplexity) that makes modern models intelligible as a continuation rather than a break. The chapters on fine-tuning and on alignment (including direct preference optimization) are current.
Its breadth (parsing, semantics, dialogue, speech) is the map of the field beyond language modelling, useful when a product needs structured extraction or dialogue rather than generation.
A free, continuously revised textbook by leading researchers is the field's reference; its revision history is itself a record of how fast the field moved.

Part I, fundamental algorithms: words, tokens and unicode; n-gram language models; naive Bayes and sentiment; logistic regression; vector semantics and embeddings; neural networks; large language models; transformers; masked language models; model alignment, prompting and in-context learning. Part II, NLP applications: information retrieval and RAG; machine translation; question answering; chatbots; annotation; speech recognition and synthesis. Part III, linguistic structure: sequence labelling, parsing, semantics, discourse.

items: Text normalization: tokenization (including byte-pair encoding's learn-and-apply algorithm), normalization, lemmatization and stemming, sentence segmentation, edit distance.

N-gram models: the chain rule and the Markov approximation; maximum likelihood estimates; perplexity as the inverse probability per word; smoothing (Laplace, interpolation, backoff, Kneser-Ney) to handle unseen n-grams; the same ideas underlie neural language models' evaluation.

Classification: naive Bayes for text with bag-of-words counts, its assumptions, and sentiment features; logistic regression with features, cross-entropy loss, gradient descent, regularization and multinomial (softmax) classification; evaluation with precision, recall, F1, cross-validation and statistical significance tests (bootstrap).

Vector semantics: distributional hypothesis; term-document and term-term matrices; TF-IDF; PMI; word2vec's skip-gram with negative sampling and its objective; properties of embeddings (similarity, analogies, bias); visualization; evaluation.

Neural networks and neural language models: feed-forward networks, the feed-forward language model with embeddings and a context window, training with cross-entropy; the transformer chapter derives attention, multi-head, positional embeddings, the language modelling head and training; masked language models (BERT) with masked and span objectives, fine-tuning for classification and sequence labelling; large language models: decoding (greedy, beam, top-k, top-p, temperature), pretraining data, scaling laws, evaluation.
Alignment and prompting: instruction tuning, preference alignment (RLHF and direct preference optimization), prompting, in-context learning, chain of thought, and evaluation of LLMs.

Applications: information retrieval with vector models and dense retrieval; retrieval-augmented generation; question answering; machine translation with encoder-decoders and BLEU; dialogue systems and their evaluation; speech features, CTC and attention-based ASR, TTS.
Structure: part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition with HMMs and CRFs and with neural sequence labelling; constituency and dependency parsing; semantic roles; coreference.
Perplexity is cross-entropy exponentiated; language models are evaluated by surprise.
Embeddings come from predicting context; similarity is what the objective rewards.
Decoding choices (temperature, top-p) change outputs as much as the model does.

b.s: Train word2vec-style embeddings on the incident headlines with a small implementation, inspect nearest neighbors of 'collision' and 'I-880', then compute the perplexity of a bigram model on held-out headlines.

resources.lives: book · free · reference · free; the textbook for the language chapters

resources.title: LLMs-from-scratch repository (Raschka)

b.s: A free set of notebooks that build a small language model step by step in code, so you can see every part instead of trusting a magic box.

Sebastian Raschka's public repository walks through implementing a GPT-style model in PyTorch: the tokenizer, attention, transformer blocks, pretraining on text, and fine-tuning for classification and instruction following. The notebooks are free and complete; the companion book adds prose but is not required.

Work through the notebooks in order and keep the model tiny so training takes minutes on the Mac mini. Type the code rather than copying it. When you finish, the Hugging Face abstractions will be transparent.

The value is completeness: every tensor shape is shown, attention is built stepwise, and the training loop is explicit. Pair with the original papers and with Karpathy's GPT lesson for a second perspective on the same architecture.

It stops at small scale; the scaling questions (data curation, distributed training, evaluation) are in the ultra-scale playbook and CS336. The instruction-tuning notebook is a compact account of supervised fine-tuning.

A from-scratch implementation is the fastest route to reading language-model papers critically; for a lead, assigning the repository to an engineer is a reliable way to build a real mental model before they touch a production model.

Chapter notebooks: understanding large language models; working with text data (tokenization, byte-pair encoding, data sampling with a sliding window, token and positional embeddings); coding attention mechanisms (simplified attention, trainable weights, causal masking, dropout, multi-head); implementing a GPT model (layer normalization, GELU, feed-forward, shortcut connections, the transformer block, the full GPT, generating text); pretraining on unlabeled data (loss, training loop, decoding strategies, loading pretrained weights); fine-tuning for classification; fine-tuning to follow instructions; plus appendices on PyTorch, LoRA and more.

items: Data pipeline: a tokenizer (implementing simple tokenization, then using BPE via tiktoken), a dataset of sliding windows of context length with inputs and targets shifted by one, embeddings of dimension d_model plus learned positional embeddings.

Attention from scratch: dot products between token vectors as scores, softmax to weights, weighted sums; adding trainable W_q, W_k, W_v; scaling by √d_k; causal masking with an upper-triangular mask before softmax; dropout on weights; multi-head as a batched computation with reshapes.

GPT block: layer norm (implemented), GELU (implemented), feed-forward (expand by 4, GELU, project back), shortcut connections around attention and feed-forward, and the stacked block; the full model with an output head tied to the vocabulary; parameter counting (the 124 M configuration).

Pretraining: cross-entropy over next-token logits, training and validation loss, a training loop with evaluation, text generation with temperature and top-k, saving and loading, and loading OpenAI's GPT-2 weights into the implementation to verify it.
Classification fine-tuning: replace the output head with a class head, fine-tune selected layers, use the last token's representation, evaluate accuracy on a spam dataset.

Instruction fine-tuning: format instruction-input-response prompts, mask the prompt in the loss, batch with padding, train, generate responses, and evaluate with another model as a judge; the appendix on LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T), diagonal=1).bool(); scores.masked_fill_(mask, -inf)
x = x + attn(norm1(x)); x = x + ff(norm2(x))   # pre-norm transformer block
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), targets.flatten())

items: A GPT is embeddings, N pre-norm blocks of masked attention and feed-forward, and a tied output head.
Loading public weights into your own implementation is the proof it is right.
Fine-tuning replaces or adapts the head and trains a few layers with a small learning rate.

b.s: Build the model at a tiny scale (d_model 128, 4 layers), pretrain on the concatenated incident headlines and the repository's markdown for a few minutes on MPS, generate text, then fine-tune it for headline severity and compare with the encoder classifier.

resources.lives: code · free · two weeks · free notebooks; a GPT you built yourself

resources.title: Intro to Large Language Models (Karpathy, video)

b.s: A one-hour talk that explains, with simple drawings, what a large language model is, how it is trained, and what it can and cannot do.

Andrej Karpathy's free talk for a general audience: a model is two files (weights and code), pretraining compresses the internet into weights, fine-tuning teaches an assistant style, and scaling makes it better in predictable ways. It ends with what is coming and with security concerns. Watch it before the language-model topic.

The talk's framing (base model, assistant model, the training stages, scaling laws, tool use, and the jailbreak and injection risks) is the outline of the language-model topic; watch it, then read the topic's high-school level and notice what the talk simplified.

It is a survey, not a course; its value is the clear separation of pretraining, fine-tuning and preference tuning, and the honest treatment of security. Follow with the from-scratch repository for the mechanics.
Karpathy's later talks and his from-scratch series are the technical continuation; this one is the shared vocabulary for a mixed audience.
The talk to send to a stakeholder before a discussion about using a language model in a product; its security section is the part most people skip and should not.

A one-hour talk: what an LLM is (two files: parameters and code), how the parameters are obtained (pretraining as lossy compression of internet text), what next-token prediction learns, how a base model becomes an assistant (fine-tuning on conversations, comparison labels and reinforcement learning from human feedback), the leaderboard and open versus closed models, scaling laws, tool use and multimodality, the 'system 1 versus system 2' aspiration, self-improvement, customization, the LLM as an operating system, and security (jailbreaks, prompt injection, data poisoning).

items: The artifact: a large language model is a file of billions of parameters and a few hundred lines of code to run them; running it is easy, obtaining the parameters is the expensive part.

Pretraining: take a large chunk of the internet's text, train a transformer to predict the next token, at a cost of thousands of GPUs for weeks; the result compresses knowledge into weights, imperfectly, which is why it can produce plausible but wrong facts.
What is learned: predicting the next token well forces learning grammar, facts, reasoning patterns and styles; sampling produces text that resembles the training distribution.

From base model to assistant: fine-tune on a smaller, high-quality set of question-answer conversations written by people following guidelines; then improve with comparison labels (people rank responses) used to train a reward model and optimize the assistant with reinforcement learning; the stages have different data scales.
Scaling: performance improves predictably with parameters and data; capabilities appear as models grow; the reason for the compute race.
Tool use and modalities: models call a calculator, run code, search the web, view and generate images, and process speech; the picture of an LLM as a kernel orchestrating tools.
Directions: deliberate 'system 2' thinking through tree search and self-checking, self-improvement in verifiable domains, customization with documents and fine-tuning.

Security: jailbreaks (role-play, encodings), prompt injection through documents and web pages, backdoors from poisoned training data; the model executes instructions in its input, which is why untrusted text must be treated as data.

b.s: p(next token | context) → sample → append → repeat

items: An LLM is compressed text plus a sampler; its facts are reconstructions.
The assistant is a base model plus supervised and preference fine-tuning.
Prompt injection means any text the model reads can try to command it; design accordingly.

b.s: Write a one-page explanation of the talk's three training stages for a colleague, then design a prompt-injection test for the headline-extraction task and show whether a local model follows injected instructions.

resources.lives: video · free · one hour · free; one hour, the whole picture

resources.title: Stanford CS224N: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning

b.s: A university class, free to watch, about teaching computers to read and write, from single words to whole documents.

Stanford's course, with free lecture videos and notes: word vectors, neural networks for text, recurrent models, attention and transformers, pretraining, and the current state of language models. Watch the lectures on word vectors and on transformers during the language topic.

Lectures 1 and 2 (word vectors) explain embeddings from first principles; the lectures on transformers and on pretraining are the theory behind the Hugging Face course's practice. The assignments (word2vec from scratch, a dependency parser, a translation model) are demanding and worth one.

The course's treatment of word2vec's objective, of attention's derivation, and of pretraining objectives is rigorous; its later lectures on evaluation, on multilingual models and on ethics broaden the language topic.
CS224N's evolution across years is a record of the field; its final lectures on current research are a fair map of open problems.
The standard graduate NLP course; knowing it lets you calibrate what a new hire in language modelling can be assumed to know.

Lectures: word vectors (word2vec, GloVe, evaluation); neural classifiers and backpropagation; dependency parsing; recurrent networks and language models; sequence-to-sequence, attention and machine translation; transformers; pretraining (BERT, GPT, T5); prompting, instruction finetuning and RLHF; efficient adaptation; natural language generation; question answering; interpretability and analysis; model analysis and explanation; multimodal models; and ethics and the future. Assignments: word2vec from scratch, a dependency parser, a neural machine translation system, and a transformer-based final project.

items: Word vectors: the distributional idea; word2vec's skip-gram objective maximizing the probability of context words with a softmax over the vocabulary, made tractable by negative sampling; gradient derivations; GloVe as weighted least squares on co-occurrence logs; intrinsic evaluation (analogies, similarity) and extrinsic evaluation (downstream tasks).

Classification and backpropagation: a window-based classifier, softmax and cross-entropy, matrix calculus for gradients, and computation graphs; regularization, dropout, vectorization, and nonlinearities.

Language models and RNNs: n-gram models and sparsity, fixed-window neural models, RNNs applying the same weights at each step, training with teacher forcing, perplexity, vanishing and exploding gradients, LSTMs, bidirectional and multi-layer RNNs.

Sequence to sequence and attention: encoder-decoder translation, beam search, BLEU, and attention as a solution to the bottleneck (a weighted sum of encoder states per decoder step, with dot-product, multiplicative and additive variants).

Transformers: self-attention's advantages, the barriers (order, nonlinearity, future leakage) and their fixes (positions, feed-forward layers, masking), multi-head attention, scaling, residuals and layer norm, and the encoder-decoder variants.

Pretraining: the pretrain-finetune paradigm; decoders (GPT), encoders (BERT's masked language modelling and its variants), encoder-decoders (T5's span corruption); what pretraining teaches; scaling and emergent abilities.

Adaptation: prompting and in-context learning, chain of thought, instruction finetuning, RLHF (reward models from human comparisons, policy optimization) and its limits; parameter-efficient finetuning (adapters, LoRA, prefix tuning).

Generation and analysis: decoding methods and their failure modes, evaluation of generated text (automatic metrics, human evaluation), probing and behavioral analysis of what models learn, and the ethical issues of bias and misuse.

b.s:
skip-gram: J = −(1/T) Σ_t Σ_{−m≤j≤m, j≠0} log P(w_{t+j} | w_t),  P(o | c) = exp(u_oᵀ v_c)/Σ_w exp(u_wᵀ v_c)
attention scores e_i = s_tᵀ h_i;  α = softmax(e);  a_t = Σ α_i h_i

items: Word vectors come from predicting context; attention generalizes 'which context matters' to a learned weighting.
Pretrain then finetune is the paradigm; the objectives differ by architecture.
RLHF and preference optimization are how models become helpful; their reward models are learned from comparisons.

b.s: Do the word2vec assignment's gradient derivations for skip-gram with negative sampling, implement it in numpy on the incident headlines, and evaluate embeddings by nearest neighbors of route names.

resources.lives: course · free · a quarter · free lectures; embeddings to transformers, rigorously

resources.title: Hugging Face Computer Vision course

b.s: A free online class about teaching computers to see, with code you can run and pictures to try it on.

A community-written free course from Hugging Face covering image basics, convolutional networks, vision transformers, object detection, segmentation, video, and multimodal models, with notebooks. Do the units on convolutional networks and on transfer learning during the vision topic.

Units on the fundamentals of computer vision, on convolutional networks, on vision transformers and on transfer learning give working code for the vision exercises; the unit on model optimization for deployment previews on-device constraints.

It complements CS231n (foundations) with current practice (pretrained backbones, the transformers library for vision, evaluation on standard benchmarks); its multimodal units are a bridge to vision-language models.
Community courses vary in depth; this one is strongest on practice and on the current model zoo, weakest on theory. Use it accordingly.
A free, maintained map of practical vision tooling; useful for calibrating what a modern vision baseline is before proposing anything custom.

Units: fundamentals of computer vision (images as arrays, preprocessing, augmentation, feature extraction); convolutional networks (architectures, transfer learning); vision transformers (patches, attention, variants, fine-tuning); multimodal models (vision-language, CLIP, captioning, VQA); generative models (GANs, diffusion, evaluation); basic CV tasks (classification, detection, segmentation with the transformers library); video and video processing; 3-D vision and scene reconstruction; model optimization for deployment (quantization, pruning, distillation, ONNX); synthetic data; zero-shot and few-shot vision; ethics and biases; outlook.

items: Fundamentals: image representations (channels, dtypes, color spaces), classical preprocessing (resizing, normalization), augmentation (flips, crops, color jitter) and why it regularizes, and the shift from hand features to learned ones.
Convolutional networks: LeNet to ResNet to ConvNeXt, transfer learning with the transformers library's image classification models, feature extractors, and fine-tuning with the Trainer.

Vision transformers: split an image into patches, embed them linearly, add positions and a class token, run a transformer encoder; ViT needs pretraining at scale; DeiT, Swin and hierarchical variants; fine-tuning on small datasets.
Multimodal: CLIP's contrastive alignment of image and text embeddings enabling zero-shot classification; captioning and visual question answering with vision-language models; retrieval.
Generative: GAN basics and diffusion pipelines from the diffusers library; evaluation with FID and human judgment.
Tasks: object detection (DETR-style transformers, YOLO-style detectors, boxes, non-maximum suppression, mAP), semantic and instance segmentation (masks, IoU), and the pipelines to run them.
Deployment: quantization to int8, pruning, distillation into small students, export to ONNX, latency and memory on edge devices; the same constraints as on-device traffic counting.
Ethics: dataset bias, surveillance, consent, and evaluation across groups.

b.s:
ViT: patches (P×P) → linear embed → + position → transformer encoder → class token → head
CLIP: maximize cosine similarity of matched image-text pairs, minimize for mismatched (symmetric cross-entropy over a batch)

items: Pretrained backbones plus fine-tuning cover most vision tasks; ViTs and ConvNets are both viable.
CLIP-style alignment gives zero-shot classification from text labels.
Deployment is quantization, pruning and distillation; measure on the device.

b.s: Fine-tune a small pretrained vision model on a folder of your own photos with the transformers library, export it to ONNX, quantize it, and compare accuracy and inference time before and after.

resources.lives: course · free · weeks · free; current vision practice with notebooks

resources.title: The generative-model papers: VAE (Kingma, Welling, 2013), GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014), DDPM (Ho, Jain, Abbeel, 2020)

b.s: Three papers, years apart, each a new way for a computer to make new pictures: one squeezes and rebuilds, one plays forger against detective, one cleans up noise step by step.

The three papers that defined generative modelling: the variational autoencoder, the generative adversarial network, and denoising diffusion. All free. Read the introductions and look at the sample figures; then read Lilian Weng's diffusion post for the connections.

For each: the model, the training objective, and the samples. The VAE's loss has two parts (reconstruction and a KL term); the GAN is a two-player game; the diffusion model learns to predict noise. Compare their samples and note the years.

Work through the derivations: the evidence lower bound and the reparameterization trick; the minimax objective and its optimum; the diffusion forward process and the simplified noise-prediction loss. Each paper's experiments show the evaluation problem of generative models.
The later literature (Wasserstein GANs, hierarchical VAEs, score-based models, latent diffusion) builds directly on these; reading the originals shows what each solved and what it left.
Canonical citations; the interesting research questions are those they opened: evaluation, controllability, and the unification of the three families through score matching.

Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes: variational inference with a recognition network, the evidence lower bound, the reparameterization trick, and the VAE with Gaussian latent variables. Generative Adversarial Nets: a generator and a discriminator trained as a minimax game, the theoretical optimum, and the practical alternating training with a non-saturating generator loss. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models: a Markov chain of Gaussian noising, its reverse learned by a network, the simplified noise-prediction objective, and high-quality image samples.

items: VAE setup: latent variable z with prior p(z) = N(0, I), a decoder p_θ(x | z) and an encoder q_φ(z | x) approximating the intractable posterior; maximize the ELBO log p(x) ≥ E_q[log p_θ(x | z)] − KL(q_φ(z | x) ‖ p(z)).

Reparameterization: sample z = μ_φ(x) + σ_φ(x) ⊙ ε with ε ~ N(0, I) so gradients flow to the encoder; the KL term between diagonal Gaussians has a closed form; minibatch estimates make it stochastic gradient variational Bayes.

VAE behavior: the reconstruction term wants informative latents, the KL term wants them close to the prior; sampling z from the prior generates new data; blurry samples with Gaussian likelihoods; posterior collapse when the decoder is too strong.

GAN game: the discriminator D maximizes log D(x) + log(1 − D(G(z))); the generator G minimizes log(1 − D(G(z))) (or maximizes log D(G(z)) for better gradients early); at the optimum D(x) = p_data/(p_data + p_g) and the game's value relates to the Jensen-Shannon divergence; alternating gradient steps in practice.
GAN behavior: sharp samples, no likelihood, unstable training, mode collapse; later fixes (Wasserstein loss, gradient penalties, spectral normalization, progressive growing) address the instability.

DDPM setup: forward noising with a linear β schedule over T = 1000 steps; the reverse Gaussian with learned mean; the variational bound rewritten as KLs between Gaussians; the noise-prediction parameterization; the simplified unweighted objective works better than the exact bound.

DDPM behavior: slow sampling (T network passes), excellent sample quality and diversity, a connection to denoising score matching and Langevin dynamics, and progressive lossy decompression as a view of the process.

Comparing the three: VAEs optimize a likelihood bound and give an encoder; GANs optimize a two-player game and give sharp samples without likelihoods; diffusion models optimize a bound that reduces to denoising regression, are stable to train, and dominate quality at the cost of sampling time.

b.s:
ELBO = E_{q(z|x)}[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z));  z = μ + σ ⊙ ε
min_G max_D E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1 − D(G(z)))]
L_DDPM = E ‖ε − ε_θ(√ᾱ_t x_0 + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε, t)‖²

items: The three families differ in what they optimize: a likelihood bound, a game, or a denoising regression.
The reparameterization trick is what makes stochastic layers trainable.
Stability and sample quality explain diffusion's dominance; sampling cost is its price.

b.s: Train a VAE and a DDPM on daily speed profiles with the same small MLP budget; compare sample sharpness, training stability (loss curves over seeds) and the distribution of the 8 am speed against the real data.
