Boosting as forward stagewise additive modelling: AdaBoost minimises exponential loss stagewise; gradient boosting generalises to any differentiable loss by fitting trees to negative gradients; shrinkage and subsampling regularise; tree depth sets interaction order; partial dependence and relative importance interpret the ensemble.
Random forests decorrelate bagged trees by random feature subsets at each split; out-of-bag error is a free cross-validation; variable importance by permutation.
SVMs maximise margin with a kernel; the hinge loss puts them in the same family as logistic regression with a different loss; flexible discriminants generalise LDA.

Unsupervised: clustering as prototype fitting, PCA as the best rank-k reconstruction, spectral clustering from the graph Laplacian; high-dimensional chapter covers regularised discriminants, feature screening and multiple testing.

b.s:
bias-variance: E[(y - f_hat(x))^2] = sigma^2 + Bias^2(f_hat(x)) + Var(f_hat(x))
ridge: beta = (X^T X + lambda I)^{-1} X^T y;  df(lambda) = trace(X (X^T X + lambda I)^{-1} X^T)
gradient boosting step: fit tree to r_i = -dL(y_i, f(x_i))/df(x_i), then f <- f + nu sum_j gamma_j 1(x in R_j)
optimism: E[Err_in] - E[err_train] = (2/N) sum_i Cov(y_hat_i, y_i)

items: Chapter 7 (assessment) and chapter 10 (boosting) explain why LightGBM works and how to tune it; read those first.
Effective degrees of freedom is the concept that unifies ridge, splines, trees and boosting.
Every method is a bias-variance position; knowing where a method sits tells you what to try next.

b.s: Read chapters 7 and 10, then reproduce figure 10.2 style experiments on the Fremont data: AP versus number of boosting rounds for tree depths 1, 2, 4 and 6, with and without shrinkage 0.1, and identify the interaction order the problem needs.

resources.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms (Shalev-Shwartz, Ben-David)

b.s: A free math book that asks: why can a machine that learned from old examples be right about new ones? And it proves the answers.

A university textbook, free as a PDF, about the theory of learning: what it means to learn, when it is possible, and how much data you need. It is hard, and it is the right book when you want proofs rather than pictures. For the final phase.

The first part (the PAC learning framework, VC dimension, bias-complexity trade-off) is the formal version of the theory ladder. Read chapters 2 to 6 slowly, doing the exercises; they make the words overfitting and generalization precise.

Its coverage of uniform convergence, Rademacher complexity, regularization and stability, and convex learning gives the tools to read generalization bounds in papers. The chapters on boosting and on stochastic gradient descent connect the theory to the algorithms of phases 4 and 6.

It is the standard reference for classical learning theory; modern questions (overparameterization, implicit bias) build on it and are covered in recent lecture notes and papers rather than textbooks. Read it with Boyd's convex optimization for the optimization side.
The base layer for theoretical work; its exercises are qualifying-exam material, and its treatment of stability is the entry point to the generalization theory of SGD.

Part I foundations: a gentle start (ERM, overfitting, finite hypothesis classes); a formal learning model (PAC, agnostic PAC, the realisability assumption); learning via uniform convergence; the bias-complexity trade-off (no free lunch, error decomposition); the VC dimension (shattering, the fundamental theorem of statistical learning, Sauer's lemma); nonuniform learnability (structural risk minimisation, MDL, Occam's razor); the runtime of learning (computational complexity, hardness). Part II from theory to algorithms: linear predictors (halfspaces, perceptron, linear regression, logistic regression); boosting (weak learnability, AdaBoost, its VC dimension); model selection and validation; convex learning problems; regularisation and stability; stochastic gradient descent; support vector machines; kernel methods; multiclass, ranking and complex prediction; decision trees; nearest neighbour; neural networks. Part III additional models: online learning, clustering, dimensionality reduction, generative models, feature selection. Part IV advanced theory: Rademacher complexities, covering numbers, proof of the fundamental theorem, multiclass learnability, compression bounds, PAC-Bayes.

items: PAC learning formalises 'learning from examples': a class is learnable if some algorithm, with enough samples, outputs a hypothesis whose error is within epsilon of the best in the class with probability 1 - delta; the sample complexity of finite classes is log|H| / epsilon^2.
Uniform convergence: if empirical risks are close to true risks for all hypotheses simultaneously, ERM works; finite classes and finite VC dimension classes have uniform convergence.

The fundamental theorem: for binary classification, PAC learnability, agnostic PAC learnability, uniform convergence and finite VC dimension are equivalent; the sample complexity is proportional to VC dimension over epsilon squared.

No free lunch: without restricting the hypothesis class, no learner beats chance on all distributions; prior knowledge (inductive bias) is necessary; the error decomposition into approximation and estimation error.
Structural risk minimisation and MDL: choose among nested classes by penalising complexity; this justifies regularisation and Occam's razor in a formal sense.

Convex learning problems (convex, Lipschitz or smooth losses over bounded domains) are learnable by SGD with rates 1/sqrt(m); stability of the learning algorithm (regularisation) implies generalisation, an alternative to uniform convergence.

Algorithm chapters derive perceptron, SVM (hard and soft margin, the dual), kernels and the representer theorem, AdaBoost's training-error bound, decision trees, nearest neighbour's curse of dimensionality, and the expressiveness and hardness of neural networks.
Advanced chapters: Rademacher complexity as a data-dependent measure of class richness; covering numbers; compression schemes; PAC-Bayes bounds that depend on a prior over hypotheses.

b.s:
finite class sample complexity: m >= (log(|H|/delta)) / (2 eps^2)  (agnostic)
VC bound: m_H(eps, delta) ~ (d + log(1/delta)) / eps^2
Rademacher generalisation: L_D(h) <= L_S(h) + 2 R_m(H) + sqrt(2 log(2/delta) / m)
SGD for convex Lipschitz: E[L(w_bar)] - L(w*) <= B rho / sqrt(T)

items: Learnability requires a restricted class; generalisation bounds trade class richness (VC, Rademacher) against sample size.
Stability and regularisation are a second route to generalisation that explains why SGD on convex losses works.
The book's proofs are short enough to read; do at least the finite-class and VC chapters in full.

b.s: Prove the finite-class agnostic bound from Hoeffding plus a union bound, then compute an empirical Rademacher complexity for depth-limited trees on the Fremont features by fitting to random labels, and compare the resulting bound to the observed validation gap.

resources.title: Convex Optimization (Boyd, Vandenberghe)

b.s: A free math book about finding the lowest point of a bowl-shaped hill, which is what a learning machine does when it learns.

The standard textbook on convex optimization, free as a PDF, with lecture videos. It explains what makes a problem convex (a single lowest point), the methods that find it, and duality, a way of looking at the same problem from the other side. It is a graduate book; use it as a reference in the final phase.

Chapters 2 to 5 (convex sets, convex functions, convex problems, duality) are the language behind why logistic regression has a global optimum and why regularization works. Chapter 9 on unconstrained minimization covers gradient descent and Newton's method with convergence proofs.

Its treatment of gradient descent convergence, of conditioning, and of Newton and quasi-Newton methods gives the tools to reason about learning rates and about why second-order methods do not scale. The course's problem sets and the CVXPY library make it practical.

Convexity is the regime where theory is complete; deep learning is the regime where it is not. Reading Boyd is how you know exactly what guarantees you give up, and its duality chapters are the background for support vector machines and for constrained learning (fairness constraints, monotonicity).
A canonical reference; its lecture videos are the fastest way for a strong engineer to acquire the optimization vocabulary that research papers assume.

Part I theory: convex sets (affine and convex sets, operations that preserve convexity, generalised inequalities, separating and supporting hyperplanes, dual cones); convex functions (basic properties, operations that preserve convexity, the conjugate function, quasiconvex and log-concave functions); convex optimisation problems (standard form, equivalent problems, linear programs, quadratic programs, geometric programs, semidefinite programs, vector optimisation); duality (the Lagrange dual, weak and strong duality, Slater's condition, KKT conditions, perturbation and sensitivity analysis). Part II applications: approximation and fitting (norm approximation, regularised approximation, robust approximation, function fitting); statistical estimation (maximum likelihood, MAP, experiment design); geometric problems. Part III algorithms: unconstrained minimisation (descent methods, gradient descent, steepest descent, Newton's method, self-concordance); equality-constrained minimisation; interior-point methods (barrier method, primal-dual methods).

items: Recognising convexity is the skill: a problem that is convex can be solved reliably to global optimality; the calculus of convex sets and functions (compositions, maxima, perspective, conjugates) lets you prove it.
Standard problem classes nest: LP inside QP inside SOCP inside SDP; each has mature solvers; modelling languages (CVXPY) check convexity by disciplined convex programming rules.

Duality: the Lagrangian introduces multipliers; the dual function is always concave and lower-bounds the primal; strong duality holds under Slater's condition; the KKT conditions (stationarity, primal and dual feasibility, complementary slackness) characterise optimality and are the basis of SVM duals, LASSO analysis and interior-point methods.
Sensitivity: dual variables measure how the optimal value changes with constraint perturbations (shadow prices), which is the meaning of the multipliers in regularised learning.

Fitting as optimisation: least squares, L1 and Huber losses as norm approximation; regularisation as a trade-off curve (Pareto); robust approximation for uncertain data; maximum likelihood for exponential families is convex.

Newton's method converges quadratically near the optimum and, for self-concordant functions, in a bounded number of steps independent of the problem constants; gradient descent's rate depends on the condition number.
Interior-point methods solve constrained problems by a sequence of Newton steps on a barrier-augmented objective; polynomial time in practice and in theory.

b.s:
Lagrangian: L(x, lam, nu) = f0(x) + sum lam_i f_i(x) + sum nu_i h_i(x);  g(lam, nu) = inf_x L
KKT: grad f0 + sum lam_i grad f_i + sum nu_i grad h_i = 0; f_i <= 0; h_i = 0; lam_i >= 0; lam_i f_i = 0
gradient descent rate (strongly convex, smooth): f(x_k) - p* <= c^k (f(x_0) - p*), c = 1 - m/M
Newton step: dx = -grad^2 f(x)^{-1} grad f(x)

items: Convexity is the property that makes a problem solvable exactly; learn to recognise and preserve it.
KKT conditions and duality explain SVMs, LASSO paths, and the meaning of regularisation weights.
Condition number governs gradient descent; Newton's method removes it at the cost of a linear solve.

b.s: Read chapters 2 to 5 and 9, then formulate the isotonic calibration step as a convex QP (monotone least squares), solve it with CVXPY, and verify KKT complementary slackness on the solution; compare to scikit-learn's IsotonicRegression.

resources.lives: book · free · a semester, selectively · free PDF and lectures

resources.title: CS229 lecture notes (Stanford)

b.s: The notes from a famous university class about learning machines, free for anyone to read.

Stanford's machine learning course notes: linear regression, logistic regression, a family of related models called generalized linear models, models that describe how data is generated, support vector machines, and learning theory. Dense but clear. Read the first sections after phase 4, one section per sitting.

The logistic regression and generalized-linear-model sections give lesson 7's math in the standard notation, including the derivation of the gradient that this course rebuilds by hand. The learning-theory notes on bias, variance and uniform convergence are the source material for the theory ladder in phase 8.

The notes are the compact graduate treatment: exponential families unify linear, logistic and Poisson regression as one construction; the learning theory section introduces PAC-style bounds; the notes on regularization and model selection are practical. The public problem sets are worth doing for the theory sections.

Compare CS229's derivations with ESL's, then read the newer notes on deep learning and on generalization. The course's treatment of the EM algorithm and of factor analysis is the background for latent-variable models of traffic regimes, which lesson 4's higher levels gesture at.

CS229 is what most ML researchers learned from, so knowing it lets you calibrate what a reviewer or a new hire assumes as background, and what they will not have seen (dependent data, forecasting protocols, calibration under shift) and will need explained.

Main notes: supervised learning (linear regression, LMS, normal equations, probabilistic interpretation, locally weighted regression, logistic regression, Newton's method, GLMs and exponential families, softmax regression); generative learning (Gaussian discriminant analysis, naive Bayes, Laplace smoothing); kernel methods (feature maps, the kernel trick, properties); support vector machines (margins, optimal margin classifier, Lagrange duality, kernels, regularisation, SMO); deep learning (neural networks, backpropagation, vectorisation); generalisation (bias-variance, double descent, sample complexity bounds); regularisation and model selection (cross-validation, Bayesian statistics); unsupervised learning (k-means, mixtures of Gaussians, EM, factor analysis, PCA, ICA); self-supervised and foundation models; reinforcement learning (MDPs, value iteration, policy iteration, continuous states, LQR); with supplementary notes (Hoeffding, convex optimisation overview, the representer theorem).

items: Linear regression from three angles (least squares, gradient descent, maximum likelihood with Gaussian noise) and the normal equations; locally weighted regression as a nonparametric variant.

Logistic regression and Newton's method; then the generalised linear model construction: choose an exponential family for y, set its natural parameter to a linear function of x, and derive the model, the link and the learning rule; softmax falls out for the multinomial.

Generative versus discriminative: GDA models p(x|y) as Gaussians and derives a logistic posterior; naive Bayes for text; when the generative assumption holds it is more sample-efficient, when it does not the discriminative model wins asymptotically.
Kernels and SVMs: functional margin, geometric margin, the primal and dual optimisation problems, the kernel trick, soft margin with slack, and the SMO algorithm for the dual.
Deep learning notes: forward pass, backprop as the chain rule with cached activations, vectorisation over a batch, common layers and initialisation.

Generalisation notes: the bias-variance decomposition, the double-descent phenomenon in modern overparameterised models, and the classical finite-class and VC-based sample complexity bounds (with proofs in the supplement).

EM: the evidence lower bound, E-step as computing posteriors over latents, M-step as maximising the expected complete log-likelihood; mixtures of Gaussians and factor analysis as instances; PCA and ICA as dimensionality reduction.
RL notes: MDPs, Bellman equations, value and policy iteration, model learning, discretisation, fitted value iteration and linear quadratic regulation for continuous control.

b.s:
normal equations: theta = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y
GLM: p(y; eta) = b(y) exp(eta^T T(y) - a(eta)), eta = theta^T x
SVM dual: max sum alpha_i - (1/2) sum alpha_i alpha_j y_i y_j K(x_i, x_j) s.t. 0 <= alpha_i <= C, sum alpha_i y_i = 0
EM: log p(x) >= sum_z Q(z) log( p(x, z) / Q(z) )

items: The GLM construction is the single most reusable derivation: it generates linear, logistic, Poisson and softmax regression from one recipe.
EM is coordinate ascent on a lower bound; once seen that way, every latent-variable algorithm is familiar.
The notes are compact and rigorous; use them as the reference to re-derive whatever you use.

b.s: Derive Poisson regression for five-minute vehicle counts from the GLM recipe, implement its Newton updates in NumPy, fit it on one station, and compare its deviance to a Gaussian model on the same data.

resources.title: CS224W: Machine Learning with Graphs (Stanford)

b.s: A university class, free to watch, about learning from things that are connected to each other, like roads that join.

Jure Leskovec's course: how to represent a network of connected things, how to summarize each node with numbers, graph neural networks (where each node learns from its neighbors), and applications. The lectures are free on YouTube. Watch the graph-neural-network lectures after phase 6.

The lectures on message passing (graph convolutional networks, GraphSAGE, graph attention) explain what neighbor mixing in the spatio-temporal net is doing and how to generalize it: attention over neighbors, more hops, learned edge weights. The lecture on spatio-temporal graphs connects directly to DCRNN.

Understand graph convolutions as generalizations of image convolutions, the role of degree normalization, over-smoothing with depth, and the expressiveness limits given by the Weisfeiler-Leman test. A road is a directed graph, so the operators must be asymmetric, which is what DCRNN's forward and backward diffusion provides.

The course's coverage of heterogeneous graphs, knowledge graphs and scalable training (neighbor sampling) is the toolkit for city-scale models, and its assignments in PyTorch Geometric are a practical route to implementing Graph WaveNet without writing every operator by hand.

CS224W and the PyTorch Geometric ecosystem are the standard entry to graph machine-learning research. Its open problems (expressiveness, scalability, dynamic graphs, transfer across graphs) overlap with traffic forecasting's own, and the course's reading list is a good map of the field.

Lectures and slides: introduction (why graphs, applications, representations); traditional methods (node, link and graph-level features: degree, centrality, clustering coefficient, graphlets, Katz, Weisfeiler-Lehman kernel); node embeddings (random walks, DeepWalk, node2vec, embedding whole graphs); PageRank and matrix factorisation views; message passing and node classification (relational and iterative classification, belief propagation); graph neural networks (the GNN framework, GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT, design space: layers, aggregation, skip connections, normalisation, dropout); GNN augmentation and training (graph manipulation, prediction heads, splitting, training pipeline); theory of GNNs (expressive power, WL test, GIN); heterogeneous graphs and knowledge graphs (RGCN, TransE, DistMult, ComplEx); reasoning over knowledge graphs; frequent subgraph mining; community detection; generative models for graphs (GraphRNN); advanced topics (limitations, position-aware GNNs, identity-aware GNNs, robustness); scaling up (GraphSAGE neighbour sampling, cluster-GCN, simplified GCN); graph transformers; temporal graphs; and applications including traffic and recommender systems.

items: Graphs represent relational data; tasks are at node, edge and graph level; the traditional pipeline hand-designs features (centrality, clustering, graphlets) and feeds them to a classifier.

Node embeddings by random walks: co-occurrence of nodes on short walks defines similarity; node2vec's biased walks interpolate between BFS-like (structural) and DFS-like (community) neighbourhoods; embeddings are learned by a skip-gram objective with negative sampling.

GNNs: each layer aggregates messages from neighbours and updates the node representation; GCN uses normalised mean aggregation, GraphSAGE concatenates and allows other aggregators, GAT learns attention weights per edge; stacking k layers gives a k-hop receptive field; over-smoothing limits depth.

The design space: message computation, aggregation, layer connectivity (skip connections), and graph augmentation (virtual nodes and edges, feature augmentation for featureless nodes); prediction heads for node, edge and graph tasks; transductive versus inductive splits.

Expressive power: message-passing GNNs are at most as powerful as the 1-WL isomorphism test; sum aggregation with injective updates (GIN) reaches that bound; mean and max aggregation lose information.

Heterogeneous graphs need relation-specific weights (RGCN); knowledge-graph embeddings score triples with translation (TransE) or bilinear (DistMult, ComplEx) functions and differ in which relation patterns they can model.
Scaling: full-batch GCN needs the whole graph; neighbour sampling (GraphSAGE), subgraph sampling (cluster-GCN) and precomputed propagation (SGC) make training feasible on large graphs.

Temporal and spatio-temporal graphs: representations that evolve, and the specific pattern of graph convolution combined with temporal modelling that traffic forecasting uses (DCRNN, STGCN, Graph WaveNet appear as case studies).

b.s:
GCN layer: H^{(l+1)} = sigma( D~^{-1/2} A~ D~^{-1/2} H^{(l)} W^{(l)} ), A~ = A + I
GraphSAGE: h_v <- sigma( W [ h_v ; AGG({h_u : u in N(v)}) ] )
GAT attention: alpha_vu = softmax_u( LeakyReLU( a^T [W h_v ; W h_u] ) )
GIN: h_v <- MLP( (1 + eps) h_v + sum_{u in N(v)} h_u )

items: A GNN layer is message, aggregate, update; every architecture is a choice of those three.
Sum aggregation is strictly more expressive than mean or max; the 1-WL bound is the ceiling for message passing.
The traffic network is a small heterogeneous graph (stations, ramps, direction); a two-layer GCN over the station adjacency is the natural first spatial model.

b.s: Build the Fremont station graph (nodes are stations, edges connect consecutive stations per direction and ramp connections), implement a two-layer GCN in PyTorch that takes the last hour of speeds per node, and compare its 15-minute AP with the tabular model's per-station scores.
