resources.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction (Angelopoulos, Bates)

b.s: A short guide about how to make a learning machine say 'I am 90 % sure the answer is in this range' and actually be right 90 % of the time.

A tutorial paper, free, with code. It explains conformal prediction: measure how wrong your model is on data it has not seen, and use that to make ranges or sets of answers that hit the truth a guaranteed share of the time, no matter what model produced the predictions.

Section 1 gives the recipe in a page: compute a score on calibration data, take a quantile of the scores, build the set. Later sections cover intervals for regression (conformalized quantile regression), sets for classification, and the assumptions. Apply the recipe to the 30-minute speed prediction and check coverage on the test split.

The coverage guarantee follows from exchangeability in a few lines, which the tutorial proves. Understand why the guarantee is marginal rather than conditional, and what breaks under time-series dependence. The risk-control extension applies to controlling the false-alarm rate of a binary alert, which is lesson 11's problem.

Follow with the authors' work on conformal risk control and with adaptive conformal inference for time series (Gibbs and Candès), and think about how to obtain guarantees for the episode-level false-alarm rate rather than the row-level one, which is what a driver experiences.

Conformal methods are the practical route to distribution-free guarantees in products. The research frontier, conditional coverage, dependence, and feedback between predictions and outcomes, is where the traffic alert problem sits, and the tutorial's clarity makes it the right document to hand to a product or legal partner.

Sections: conformal prediction (the recipe with a heuristic notion of uncertainty, a score function, a calibration set, the quantile, and prediction sets that contain the truth with the target probability); examples (classification with softmax scores, adaptive prediction sets, regression with conformalised quantile regression, uncertainty on images, outlier detection, group-balanced and class-conditional coverage, distribution shift with weighted conformal, time series with adaptive conformal inference); evaluating conformal prediction (coverage, set size, conditional coverage checks); how to choose a score (the score determines everything); and the full theory in the appendix (exchangeability, the coverage proof, the upper bound, and the distribution of coverage over calibration sets).

items: The recipe: pick any model, define a nonconformity score s(x, y) that is large when y is implausible under the model, compute scores on a held-out calibration set of size n, take the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n empirical quantile q, and predict the set {y : s(x, y) <= q}; under exchangeability the set contains the true y with probability at least 1 - alpha.

The guarantee is marginal (averaged over test points and calibration sets), distribution-free and model-agnostic; it is not conditional on x, and adaptivity across inputs comes only from a well-designed score.
Classification: the simplest score is 1 minus the softmax of the true class; adaptive prediction sets use the cumulative sorted softmax mass, which gives sets that grow when the model is unsure.

Regression: conformalised quantile regression fits lower and upper quantile models and uses the score max(q_lo - y, y - q_hi), producing intervals with local width; naive absolute-residual scores give constant width.

Beyond exchangeability: covariate shift can be handled with likelihood-ratio weights on the calibration scores; time series break exchangeability, and adaptive conformal inference updates alpha online to track a coverage target.
Evaluation: check empirical coverage over many random calibration splits, look at set sizes (smaller is more informative), and check coverage across groups or bins to see conditional behaviour.
Group-balanced and class-conditional variants calibrate per group to give coverage within each group at the price of more calibration data.

b.s:
q_hat = Quantile( s_1, ..., s_n ; ceil((n+1)(1 - alpha)) / n )
C(x) = { y : s(x, y) <= q_hat };  P( Y in C(X) ) >= 1 - alpha
coverage upper bound: P( Y in C(X) ) <= 1 - alpha + 1/(n+1)
CQR score: s = max( q_lo(x) - y, y - q_hi(x) )

items: Any model plus a calibration set gives valid prediction sets in three lines; the guarantee needs exchangeability, not correctness of the model.
The score function decides how informative the sets are; validity is free, sharpness is design.
Traffic data are not exchangeable over time, so use weighted or adaptive conformal and check coverage by week.

b.s: Take the calibrated LightGBM probability, define the score 1 - p_true, calibrate on one month, and produce prediction sets ({no}, {yes}, or {no, yes}) for the next month; report coverage and the fraction of uninformative two-element sets by hour.

resources.lives: paper · free · an evening or two · free; intervals you can defend

resources.title: Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift (Gibbs, Candès, 2021)

b.s: A paper about keeping the 'I am 90 % sure' promise even when the world keeps changing, by adjusting how wide the range is as you go.

Conformal prediction promises a hit rate, but the promise assumes the future looks like the past. This paper adjusts the range online: if recent ranges missed too often, widen; if they hit too often, narrow. The result keeps the long-run hit rate even as the data shift, which is what traffic does across seasons.

The method is a few lines: track whether each interval covered the truth, and update a single number that sets the next interval's width. Implement it on the rolling 30-minute speed predictions and plot the realized coverage week by week; compare with a fixed conformal interval.

The guarantee is about long-run average coverage under arbitrary shift, achieved by an online update resembling gradient descent on the miscoverage rate; understand what it gives up (no per-period guarantee) and how the step size trades adaptivity for stability.
Follow with later work on conformal methods for time series and on risk control; the connection to online learning (regret bounds) explains why the method works without distributional assumptions.
The practical entry point to valid uncertainty in non-stationary deployed systems; for an alerting product, this line of work is how you keep a false-alarm promise honest over months.

The paper: setting (online prediction with a model that may be arbitrarily wrong and data whose distribution shifts over time); the method (maintain a running miscoverage level alpha_t and update it after each observation by a step gamma toward the target, raising the level after a miss and lowering it after a cover); the main result (the long-run empirical coverage converges to 1 - alpha regardless of the data distribution, with a bound on the deviation that depends only on gamma and the horizon); the relation to the fixed conformal quantile; practical guidance on the step size and on tracking when the shift is gradual or abrupt; experiments on stock-market volatility forecasting and on election-night predictions.

items: Fixed conformal quantiles lose validity under shift; the fix is feedback: treat the miscoverage level as a control variable and adjust it online from the observed hits and misses.

The update: alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma (alpha - err_t), where err_t is 1 if the interval missed and 0 otherwise; when the model misses too often, alpha_t falls and intervals widen; when it covers too often, alpha_t rises and intervals shrink.

The guarantee is on long-run frequency: the average error over T steps is within (max(alpha_1, 1 - alpha_1) + gamma) / (gamma T) of alpha, for any sequence, adversarial included; there is no distributional assumption.
The trade-off: larger gamma reacts faster to shift but oscillates more; smaller gamma is smoother but slow; the paper suggests values around 0.005 and shows sensitivity.
Local coverage is not guaranteed; the method can alternate between long stretches of over- and under-coverage that average out, which later work (aggregation over gammas, conformal PID) addresses.
The examples show ACI restoring coverage when a volatility model's residual distribution changes after market events, and adjusting on election night as returns arrive.

b.s:
alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma (alpha - err_t),  err_t = 1{ Y_t not in C_t }
bound: | (1/T) sum_t err_t - alpha | <= ( max(alpha_1, 1 - alpha_1) + gamma ) / (gamma T)

items: Coverage under shift comes from feedback control, not from the model.
One parameter, gamma, trades responsiveness for stability; tune it on a held-out period of shift.
For a traffic predictor that runs every five minutes, ACI is the cheapest way to keep interval coverage honest across seasons and incidents.

b.s: Implement ACI on top of the conformal sets from the previous guide with gamma = 0.005 and 0.02; simulate a shift by evaluating across a month that includes a holiday week, and plot rolling coverage for fixed conformal versus ACI.

resources.lives: paper · free · an evening or two · free; coverage that survives seasons

resources.title: Statistical Rethinking lectures and course materials (McElreath)

b.s: Free video lessons that teach how to think carefully about chance and evidence, using stories, drawings and small models.

Richard McElreath's Bayesian statistics course: the full lecture series is free on YouTube, and the course repository on GitHub has slides, homework and solutions, with code in several languages including Python ports. You build models by writing down what you believe, then update them with data.

Watch the lectures on Bayesian inference, on causal diagrams and on multilevel models, and do the homework with the Python code. Then apply partial pooling to per-station slow rates, which is the topic's exercise.

The lectures present hierarchical models with partial pooling (the answer to noisy per-station estimates) and causal thinking with DAGs in plain language; the homework, with solutions, is enough to learn the material without the book.
The course's emphasis on generative models and posterior predictive checks is a different evaluation culture worth adopting; pair with Bayesian Data Analysis for depth.
McElreath's causal-first framing is influential in applied statistics; the free lectures make it accessible to a whole team.

Lecture series and course materials: science before statistics (models as golems, causal thinking, DAGs); the garden of forking data (Bayesian updating from first principles, grid approximation); geocentric models (linear regression as a descriptive model, priors, prior predictive simulation, posterior predictive checks); categories and curves (indicator variables, polynomials, splines); elemental confounds (the fork, the pipe, the collider, the descendant; backdoor adjustment; simulation of each); good and bad controls; overfitting and regularisation (information criteria, cross-validation, PSIS-LOO, regularising priors); MCMC (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, diagnostics, Stan); modelling events (binomial and logistic regression, poisson); ordered categories; multilevel models (varying intercepts, partial pooling, shrinkage); multilevel adventures (varying slopes, covariance among effects); correlated varying effects and Gaussian processes (spatial and phylogenetic); measurement error and missing data; generalised linear madness (scientific models to statistical models); horoscopes (scientific practice).

items: Statistics is downstream of a causal model: draw the DAG, decide the estimand, then choose a statistical model; regression coefficients have no causal meaning without that step.
Bayesian updating from counting: the garden of forking data shows the posterior as the count of ways each hypothesis could produce the data; grid approximation makes it concrete before any sampler.

Priors are assumptions to be simulated: prior predictive simulation shows what the model believes before data, and catches absurd priors; posterior predictive checks show what the model got wrong after.
The four elemental confounds and their remedies: adjust for a fork, do not adjust for a pipe (mediator) when you want the total effect, never adjust for a collider, and beware descendants of these.

Overfitting is controlled by regularising priors and assessed by out-of-sample prediction estimated with PSIS-LOO or WAIC; the two goals (prediction and causal inference) can disagree on which variables to include.
MCMC with HMC: the physics analogy, why it scales, and the diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size, divergent transitions) that must be checked; Stan and its front ends.

Multilevel models: partial pooling shrinks group estimates toward the population according to how much data each has; varying slopes and correlated effects share strength across parameters; this is the default model for stations, hours and days.

Gaussian processes as continuous-category varying effects (distance between stations as the kernel input); measurement error and missing data as parts of the generative model rather than preprocessing.

b.s:
posterior ∝ likelihood × prior;  grid: p(theta_i | y) = L(y|theta_i) p(theta_i) / sum_j L(y|theta_j) p(theta_j)
varying intercepts: y_ij ~ Normal(a_j + b x_ij, sigma), a_j ~ Normal(a_bar, sigma_a)
PSIS-LOO: elpd_loo = sum_i log p(y_i | y_{-i}) estimated by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling

items: Draw the DAG first; the elemental confounds tell you what to adjust for and what to leave alone.
Simulate priors and posteriors; a model you cannot simulate from is one you do not understand.
Partial pooling across stations and hours is the natural Bayesian model of a corridor and gives honest uncertainty for stations with little data.

b.s: Fit a varying-intercept logistic model for bottleneck-in-15 with intercepts per station and per hour in PyMC or Stan, check R-hat and divergences, plot the shrinkage of station intercepts against station sample size, and compare calibration to LightGBM.

resources.lives: course · free · ten weeks · free lectures, slides and homework; the Bayesian track

resources.title: Probabilistic Programming and Bayesian Methods for Hackers (Davidson-Pilon)

b.s: A free online book that teaches Bayesian thinking with code first and math second, so you can see beliefs update on a screen.

Cameron Davidson-Pilon's book, free as notebooks, introduces Bayesian methods through probabilistic programming (PyMC): you describe a model in code, the library samples from the posterior, and you plot what you learned. Chapters cover Bayesian inference, sampling, priors, and practical examples.

Chapters 1 to 3 (introduction, a little more on PyMC, opening the black box of MCMC) are enough to build the Beta-Binomial model of station slow rates and to see the posterior update as data arrive. The examples are small and fast.

The book is intuition-first and light on theory; use it to become fluent with a probabilistic programming library before Bayesian Data Analysis makes the theory rigorous. Its chapter on priors and on loss functions connects to decision theory.

Probabilistic programming is how applied Bayesian work is done now; the book is the fastest way to a working model, and its limits (no hierarchical depth, dated library versions in places) are easy to work around with the library's current docs.
A free, code-first introduction; useful for getting a team from Bayesian ideas to running models in a week.

Chapters (as notebooks): introduction (the Bayesian state of mind, Bayes' theorem, probability distributions, a text-message change-point example in PyMC); a little more on PyMC (model building, stochastic and deterministic variables, modelling approaches, the Challenger disaster example, separation plots); opening the black box of MCMC (what it does, the landscape, the algorithms, convergence, autocorrelation, thinning, diagnostics); the greatest theorem never told (the law of large numbers, small-sample bias, ordering Reddit comments by lower bound); would you rather lose an arm or a leg (loss functions, Bayesian decisions, financial prediction, the Price is Right showcase); getting our priorities straight (priors: objective and subjective, empirical Bayes, the Wishart and conjugate priors, examples with bandits and stock returns); Bayesian A/B testing.

items: Bayesian inference as updating beliefs; the posterior over a change point in daily counts is the running example, with PyMC code that declares the generative model and lets the sampler do the work.
Building models in PyMC: prior distributions, deterministic transformations, observed variables; think generatively (how would this data be produced) and write that down.
MCMC intuition: the posterior is a landscape, the sampler wanders it in proportion to height; burn-in, autocorrelation and trace plots; convergence is checked, never assumed.
The law of large numbers and its failure at small n: ranking by posterior mean overrates small samples; use a lower quantile of the posterior for conservative ranking.
Loss functions turn posteriors into decisions: the expected loss under the posterior is minimised, and different losses give different optimal actions; the showcase example makes it concrete.
Priors: flat versus informative, empirical Bayes as a compromise, conjugacy for closed forms; Bayesian bandits as a demonstration of Thompson sampling.
Bayesian A/B testing: posteriors for two conversion rates and the probability that one exceeds the other, replacing p-values with direct statements.
Write the generative story, then let the sampler invert it; that is the whole workflow.
Small samples are overconfident under naive ranking; use posterior quantiles.
Decisions need a loss function, and the posterior makes expected loss computable.

b.s: Fit a change-point model to daily bottleneck counts at one station over a year to find when a signal timing or construction change happened; then run a Bayesian A/B comparison of bottleneck rate before and after.

resources.lives: book · free · weeks · free; Bayesian models in code first

resources.title: A Visual Exploration of Gaussian Processes (Distill, 2019)

b.s: A web page with pictures that move, showing a kind of model that draws a smooth curve through points and a band showing how unsure it is.

A free interactive article on Distill: what a Gaussian process is, how the kernel controls the shape of the curves, how observing data narrows the band, and what the hyperparameters do. Play with the figures before reading the Gaussian-process textbook.

Use the interactive figures to see how the kernel's length scale and the noise level change the fit, then reproduce the picture on one station's daily profile with a periodic kernel. The article's explanation of the prior over functions is the idea to keep.
The article's treatment of conditioning a multivariate Gaussian is the whole computation behind a Gaussian process; with it, the textbook's chapter 2 reads as a formalization of what you saw.
Distill's interactive format is the reference for explaining Bayesian nonparametrics; the article stops before sparse approximations and classification.
An exemplary explanation; the model for how to present a Bayesian method to an engineering audience.

An interactive article: multivariate Gaussians (marginalisation and conditioning); Gaussian processes as distributions over functions defined by a mean and a kernel; kernels (RBF, periodic, linear, and combinations by addition and multiplication, with interactive sliders for length scale, variance and period); prior and posterior with interactive sampling; the influence of noise; conditioning on training points to get the posterior mean and variance; and a short discussion of applications and complexity.

items: A GP is a prior over functions such that any finite set of function values is jointly Gaussian; the kernel defines the covariance between f(x) and f(x') and therefore the smoothness, periodicity and scale of the functions.

Conditioning a multivariate Gaussian on observed components gives a Gaussian over the rest; applied to function values, this is GP regression: the posterior mean interpolates the data, the posterior variance shrinks near data and grows away from it.
Kernel algebra: adding kernels adds behaviours (trend plus periodic), multiplying kernels gates one by the other (locally periodic); the article's sliders make each parameter's effect visible.
Noise enters as a diagonal term on the training covariance, which stops the posterior from interpolating exactly and widens the uncertainty.
Cost is cubic in the number of training points because of the matrix inverse, which motivates sparse and inducing-point approximations for large data.

b.s:
prior: f ~ GP(m(x), k(x, x'))
posterior mean: mu_* = K_*^T (K + sigma^2 I)^{-1} y
posterior covariance: Sigma_* = K_** - K_*^T (K + sigma^2 I)^{-1} K_*
RBF: k(x, x') = sigma_f^2 exp( -|x - x'|^2 / (2 l^2) )

items: A kernel is a statement about function shape; choose it by what you know about the function.
GP regression is Gaussian conditioning; uncertainty is a by-product, not an add-on.
Daily speed profiles are a natural GP target with a periodic-times-RBF kernel.

b.s: Fit a GP with a periodic (24 h) times RBF kernel to one week of five-minute speeds at one station using scikit-learn's GaussianProcessRegressor on a subsample, plot the posterior mean and two-sigma band, and compare interval coverage on the next day to the conformal sets.

resources.lives: interactive · free · an hour · free, interactive; the kernel's effect, seen

resources.title: Foundations of Machine Learning (Mohri, Rostamizadeh, Talwalkar), 2nd edition

b.s: A free math book that proves why learning from examples works and how many examples you need.

A graduate textbook on learning theory, free as a PDF from the authors: PAC learning, Rademacher complexity, support vector machines, kernels, boosting, online learning, and more, with proofs. Read it in the final phase alongside Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David.

Chapters 2 and 3 (the PAC framework, Rademacher complexity and VC dimension) are the theory topic's formal version; chapter 7 on boosting gives the margin theory behind lesson 8. Expect slow reading and do the exercises.

Its treatment of online learning and of ranking (chapters 8 and 10) connects to the bandit and recommender topics; its proofs are complete and its notation consistent, which makes it a good reference for reading theory papers.
Compare with Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David: Mohri is stronger on kernels, boosting and online learning; the other on stability and convex learning. Together they cover classical learning theory.
A standard reference; its exercises are qualifying-exam material and its later chapters are entry points to research areas.

Chapters: introduction; the PAC learning framework (guarantees for finite consistent and inconsistent hypothesis sets, generalities such as deterministic versus stochastic scenarios and Bayes error, agnostic PAC); Rademacher complexity and VC dimension (generalisation bounds, growth function, Sauer's lemma, lower bounds); model selection (estimation and approximation errors, empirical risk minimisation, structural risk minimisation, cross-validation, n-fold, regularisation-based algorithms, convex surrogate losses); support vector machines (margin theory, primal and dual, soft margin, margin-based generalisation bounds); kernel methods (PDS kernels, kernel SVMs, negative definite kernels, sequence kernels, approximate kernel feature maps); boosting (AdaBoost, margin bounds, game-theoretic interpretation, L1 regularisation, discussion); online learning (mistake bounds, halving, weighted majority, perceptron and winnow, online-to-batch conversion, game-theoretic connection); multiclass classification (uniform margin bounds, one-versus-all, structured prediction); ranking (bipartite ranking, AUC, RankBoost, margin bounds); regression (generalisation bounds, linear, kernel ridge, SVR, lasso, group norm); maximum entropy models (density estimation, conditional maxent, logistic regression as conditional maxent, L1 and L2 regularised maxent); conditional maximum entropy; algorithmic stability; dimensionality reduction (PCA, KPCA, KCCA, Johnson-Lindenstrauss); learning automata and languages; reinforcement learning; with appendices on linear algebra, convex optimisation, probability, concentration inequalities and information theory.

items: PAC framework with careful proofs: consistent finite hypothesis sets get a log|H| / epsilon rate, inconsistent ones (via Hoeffding) a 1/epsilon squared rate; the Bayes error and the noise setting.

Rademacher complexity as the central tool: generalisation bounds for any bounded loss class via symmetrisation; the growth function and VC dimension bound Rademacher complexity by Massart's lemma; lower bounds show these are tight in the worst case.

Margin theory: SVM generalisation bounds depend on the margin and the radius of the data, not on the dimension; the same margin bounds apply to boosting's ensemble, explaining why boosting resists overfitting after training error reaches zero.

Kernels: positive definite symmetric kernels define feature maps into an RKHS; closure properties; normalised kernels; kernel ridge regression and SVR with their duals; approximation of kernels by random features.

Online learning: mistake bounds for perceptron (in terms of margin), weighted majority and exponentiated weights (regret bounds), and the online-to-batch conversion that turns online algorithms into batch learners with guarantees.
Ranking and regression chapters give bounds and algorithms in the same style, including AUC as the bipartite ranking loss and RankBoost.

Maximum entropy: the dual of maximising entropy subject to feature-expectation constraints is a Gibbs distribution; conditional maxent is logistic regression; regularised maxent has generalisation bounds in terms of feature norms.

Stability: an algorithm whose output changes little when one training point changes generalises; regularised kernel algorithms are stable; this gives bounds for kernel ridge and SVM without VC dimension.

b.s:
Rademacher: R_m(G) = E[ sup_{g in G} (1/m) sum_i sigma_i g(z_i) ]
generalisation: E[g] <= E_hat[g] + 2 R_m(G) + sqrt( log(1/delta) / (2m) )
margin bound: R(h) <= R_hat_rho(h) + (2/rho) R_m(H) + sqrt( log(1/delta) / (2m) )
perceptron mistakes <= (r / rho)^2

items: Rademacher complexity is the one tool that yields most bounds in the book, so learn its symmetrisation proof.
Margin bounds explain both SVMs and boosting and are dimension-free.
Stability gives generalisation for regularised algorithms with no combinatorial argument.

b.s: Prove the Rademacher generalisation bound (chapter 3) and the perceptron mistake bound (chapter 8), then compute the margin distribution of the LightGBM score on training data and check whether the fraction below a margin rho tracks validation error as the margin bound suggests.

resources.lives: book · free · reference · free PDF; learning theory with proofs, a second view

resources.title: PyTorch Geometric documentation

b.s: The manual for a tool that lets a learning machine work on networks of connected things, like roads that join.

PyTorch Geometric is a free library for graph neural networks: graph data structures, message-passing layers, standard datasets and models. Its introduction and tutorials show how to build a graph model in a few lines. Use it to implement the road-graph models after CS224W.

Read the introduction by example and the tutorial on creating message-passing networks; then rebuild the two-hop neighbor mixing from lesson 10 as a PyG layer and compare with the hand-written version.

Understand the library's data model (edge index, batching of graphs), its implementations of the standard layers, and its handling of directed graphs, which the road network needs; the temporal extension covers spatio-temporal models.
PyG's model zoo includes the graph models from the traffic papers or their components, which makes reproduction faster and fairer; read the implementations to check them against the papers.
The standard toolkit for graph learning research; for a lead, it is the argument for not writing graph operators by hand past the learning stage.

Get started (installation, introduction by example: data handling of graphs, common benchmark datasets, mini-batches, data transforms, learning methods on graphs); tutorials (creating message-passing networks, creating your own datasets, heterogeneous graph learning, loading graphs from CSV, GNN explainability, compiled GNNs, scaling with neighbour sampling, point-cloud and multi-GPU training); advanced concepts (sparse tensor support, memory-efficient aggregations, TorchScript, remote backends); the package reference (torch_geometric.nn layers such as GCNConv, SAGEConv, GATConv, GINConv, ChebConv, models, pooling, normalisation; torch_geometric.data; torch_geometric.loader; torch_geometric.datasets; torch_geometric.transforms; torch_geometric.utils; torch_geometric.explain); and the cheat sheets for GNN layers and pooling.

items: The Data object holds node features x, an edge_index in COO format of shape (2, num_edges), optional edge attributes, labels and masks; graphs are batched by concatenating them into one disconnected graph with a batch vector.

Layers implement message passing: the MessagePassing base class separates message, aggregate and update; writing a custom layer is overriding those; the built-in layers cover the standard architectures.

Datasets and loaders: in-memory datasets for small graphs, NeighborLoader for sampling subgraphs of large graphs, DataLoader for batches of many small graphs; transforms add positional features or normalise.
Heterogeneous graphs: HeteroData with typed nodes and edges, and to_hetero to convert a homogeneous model into one with per-type parameters.
Explainability tools attribute predictions to edges and features; compiled GNNs and sparse-tensor formats speed up training; multi-GPU support via distributed sampling.

The traffic-relevant pieces: static graph with time-varying node features is handled by feeding each time step's feature matrix with the same edge_index, or by using the temporal extension library for recurrent graph layers.

b.s:
data = Data(x=[N, F], edge_index=[2, E], y=[N]);  loader = NeighborLoader(data, num_neighbors=[10, 10], batch_size=256)
class MyConv(MessagePassing): def forward(self, x, edge_index): return self.propagate(edge_index, x=x); def message(self, x_j): return x_j

items: edge_index in COO plus a features matrix is the whole representation; get comfortable building it from a station adjacency table.
MessagePassing's three methods are the implementation of the message, aggregate, update view from CS224W.
For a fixed road graph, batch over time windows, not over graphs.

b.s: Build the Fremont station graph as a Data object, implement a GCNConv-based model over one hour of speed features per node, train it on the M1 with MPS for the 15-minute bottleneck label, and compare to the hand-built GCN from the CS224W guide.

resources.lives: docs · free · an afternoon · free; graph networks without hand-written operators

resources.title: Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd edition (Gelman, Carlin, Stern, Dunson, Vehtari, Rubin)

b.s: A big free book about learning from data by keeping track of what you believed before and how the data changed it.

The standard graduate textbook on Bayesian statistics, free as a PDF from the authors. Part 1 covers the basics, part 2 the computation (sampling methods), part 3 regression and hierarchical models. It is demanding; use it as the reference after Statistical Rethinking.

Read the chapters on single-parameter models and on hierarchical models, and reproduce the classic eight-schools example in a probabilistic programming library. Then apply the same hierarchical model to per-station slow-episode rates.

Its treatment of hierarchical models, of model checking (posterior predictive checks), and of Markov chain Monte Carlo diagnostics is the rigorous base for applied Bayesian work; the chapters on decision analysis and on model comparison connect to calibration and to model selection.
Together with the authors' later work (Stan, workflow papers) it defines current Bayesian practice; its chapter on nonparametric models and on missing data are advanced references.
The canonical applied Bayesian text; for research, its emphasis on model checking and workflow is the counterweight to treating inference as a black box.

Part I fundamentals: probability and inference; single-parameter models (binomial, normal, Poisson, exponential, prior distributions, noninformative and weakly informative priors); multiparameter models (nuisance parameters, normal with unknown mean and variance, multinomial, multivariate normal); asymptotics and connections to non-Bayesian approaches; hierarchical models (exchangeability, the rat tumour and eight-schools examples, hierarchical normal model). Part II fundamentals of Bayesian data analysis: model checking (posterior predictive checks, graphical checks, p-values); evaluating, comparing and expanding models (predictive accuracy, information criteria, cross-validation, model averaging); modelling accounting for data collection (ignorability, sampling, experiments, observational studies, censoring); decision analysis. Part III advanced computation: posterior simulation (rejection, importance sampling), Markov chain simulation (Gibbs, Metropolis, convergence, effective sample size), computationally efficient MCMC (HMC, NUTS, Stan), modal and distributional approximations (Laplace, EM, variational inference, expectation propagation). Part IV regression models: linear regression, hierarchical linear models, generalised linear models, models for robust inference, models for missing data. Part V nonlinear and nonparametric models: parametric nonlinear models, basis functions, Gaussian process models, finite mixtures, Dirichlet process models.

items: The three steps: set up a full probability model, condition on data to get the posterior, evaluate the fit and the implications and expand the model; this loop is the practice of Bayesian data analysis.
Single and multiparameter models with conjugate and noninformative priors give closed-form posteriors and build intuition; nuisance parameters are integrated out.

Hierarchical models: exchangeable units share a population distribution; the eight-schools example shows partial pooling and the importance of the between-group variance parameter; the hierarchical model is the default structure for grouped data.

Model checking: posterior predictive checks compare replicated data to observed data on chosen statistics; graphical checks find misfit that summary statistics miss; posterior predictive p-values are diagnostics, not tests.

Model comparison by predictive accuracy: expected log predictive density estimated by WAIC or leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO); the discussion of why marginal likelihoods and Bayes factors are fragile.
Data collection matters: the sampling and treatment-assignment mechanisms must be included in the model unless ignorable; censoring, truncation and missing data are modelled, not dropped.

Computation: Gibbs and Metropolis, convergence with multiple chains and R-hat, effective sample size, HMC and NUTS as the modern default; Laplace approximation, EM and variational inference when sampling is too slow.

Regression chapters: Bayesian linear regression with weakly informative priors, hierarchical regressions with varying coefficients, GLMs, robust models with t distributions, and missing-data models with multiple imputation.
Nonparametric chapters: basis expansions, Gaussian processes as priors over functions, mixture models, and Dirichlet processes for an unknown number of components.

b.s:
posterior predictive: p(y_rep | y) = ∫ p(y_rep | theta) p(theta | y) dtheta
hierarchical normal: y_j ~ N(theta_j, sigma_j^2), theta_j ~ N(mu, tau^2)
R-hat = sqrt( (W (n-1)/n + B/n) / W ) for within (W) and between (B) chain variances
WAIC = -2 ( lppd - p_WAIC )

items: Model, condition, check, expand: the workflow matters more than any single model.
Hierarchical models are the answer to grouped data with unequal group sizes, which is what a corridor of stations is.
Check posteriors predictively and computationally (R-hat, ESS, divergences) before reporting anything.

b.s: Fit a hierarchical logistic regression for the 15-minute bottleneck with station-level and hour-level effects in Stan or PyMC, run four chains, check R-hat and ESS, do a posterior predictive check on the hourly bottleneck rate, and compute PSIS-LOO against a pooled model.

resources.lives: book · free · reference · free PDF; the applied Bayesian reference

resources.title: Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning (Rasmussen, Williams)

b.s: A free book about a kind of model that draws a smooth curve through data and also draws a band that shows how unsure it is.

The standard textbook on Gaussian processes, free online. Chapters 2 and 3 explain regression and classification with Gaussian processes, chapter 4 the kernels that define what 'similar' means, and chapter 5 how to choose them. It is mathematical but self-contained.

Read chapters 2 and 4 and implement Gaussian process regression on one station's daily profile with a periodic kernel. The predictive band is the picture to keep in mind whenever someone asks how sure the model is.

The book's treatment of the marginal likelihood for hyperparameter selection, of the connection to kernel methods and to Bayesian linear regression, and of approximations for classification is the foundation for Bayesian optimization and for modern probabilistic models.

Its coverage predates scalable approximations (inducing points, variational methods) and deep kernels; read those from the recent literature. The chapter on model selection and the appendix on Gaussian identities are lasting references.

The canonical reference; Gaussian processes remain the tool of choice for expensive-function optimization and for small-data science, and their theory underlies much of modern uncertainty quantification.

Chapters: introduction; regression (weight-space view with Bayesian linear regression and feature projections, function-space view, varying the hyperparameters, decision theory for regression, an example, smoothing and splines); classification (the Laplace approximation, expectation propagation, experiments); covariance functions (stationary, dot-product, other, making new kernels from old, the Matérn class, periodic and composite kernels); model selection and adaptation of hyperparameters (marginal likelihood, cross-validation, examples for regression and classification); relationships between GPs and other models (RKHS, regularisation, splines, SVMs, least-squares classification, neural networks and the infinite-width limit); theoretical perspectives (equivalent kernels, asymptotics, PAC-Bayes); approximation methods for large datasets (reduced-rank, subset of regressors, Nyström, subset of datapoints, projected process, Bayesian committee machine, iterative solutions); further issues and conclusions; with appendices on mathematics, Gaussian identities and datasets.

items: Two views of GP regression: the weight-space view (Bayesian linear regression in a feature space, with the kernel trick) and the function-space view (a prior over functions with mean and covariance); they coincide, and the function-space view generalises.

The predictive distribution is Gaussian with a closed-form mean and variance; noise appears as a diagonal added to the training covariance; hyperparameters (length scale, signal variance, noise variance) change the fit qualitatively.
Classification is not conjugate: the Laplace approximation and expectation propagation approximate the non-Gaussian posterior over latent functions; EP is generally more accurate.

Covariance functions encode assumptions: the squared exponential is infinitely smooth, the Matérn class controls smoothness by nu, periodic kernels for cycles, ARD length scales per input dimension for relevance; sums and products build structured kernels.

Model selection by the marginal likelihood (evidence), which trades data fit against complexity automatically; its gradients are available in closed form, so hyperparameters are optimised by gradient ascent; cross-validation is the alternative.

Connections: GP regression equals kernel ridge regression with a specific regulariser, splines are GPs with particular kernels, SVMs use the same RKHS with a different loss, and infinitely wide neural networks with Gaussian priors are GPs.

Approximations for large n: low-rank kernel approximations (Nyström, subset of regressors), inducing-point methods (projected process), and iterative linear solvers; these are what make GPs run on tens of thousands of points.

b.s:
predictive mean: f_bar_* = k_*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} y
predictive variance: V[f_*] = k(x_*, x_*) - k_*^T (K + sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} k_*
log marginal likelihood: log p(y|X) = -(1/2) y^T K_y^{-1} y - (1/2) log|K_y| - (n/2) log 2 pi
Matérn nu=3/2: k(r) = sigma^2 (1 + sqrt(3) r / l) exp( -sqrt(3) r / l )

items: The marginal likelihood is the principled way to set kernel hyperparameters and it penalises complexity on its own.
Kernel design is model design; ARD length scales tell you which inputs matter.
GPs and kernel ridge, splines and wide networks are one family; the GP adds calibrated uncertainty.

b.s: Implement GP regression from the formulas in NumPy with a Matérn 3/2 kernel plus a periodic kernel, optimise the log marginal likelihood with scipy on one station-day of speeds, and print the learned length scales and noise; then repeat with sparse inducing points on a week of data.

resources.lives: book · free · two chapters, a week · free; models with their own error bars

resources.title: Deep Learning (Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville)

b.s: The big classic book about deep neural networks, free online, by three of the people who built the field.

Three parts: the math background, practical deep networks (feedforward nets, regularization, optimization, convolutional and recurrent networks), and research topics. Read chapters from the second part as references after phase 6, when the words will already be familiar.

Chapter 6 on feedforward networks and backpropagation and chapter 8 on optimization are the rigorous versions of lesson 9; chapter 10 on sequence modelling covers recurrent networks and gated units; chapter 7 on regularization explains early stopping, dropout and weight decay and why they work.

It is the theory reference: backpropagation as a general algorithm on computation graphs, the difficulties of optimization (saddle points, ill-conditioning), and the regularization view of generalization. It predates transformers and modern training recipes, so supplement with Dive into Deep Learning and recent papers.

Part three (representation learning, structured probabilistic models, generative models) frames later research. Some material is dated, but the conceptual chapters remain the shared vocabulary of the field, and its chapter on practical methodology is a good checklist before any training run.

A canonical citation and a snapshot of the field as of 2016. Knowing what it lacks (attention, scaling laws, modern generative models, the empirical understanding of generalization) is as important as knowing what it contains, and reading it against Murphy's second volume shows how the field's framing has shifted.

Part I applied math and ML basics: linear algebra; probability and information theory; numerical computation (overflow, conditioning, gradient-based optimisation, constrained optimisation); machine learning basics (learning algorithms, capacity, overfitting, hyperparameters and validation, estimators, bias and variance, MLE, Bayesian statistics, supervised and unsupervised algorithms, SGD, building an ML algorithm, challenges motivating deep learning). Part II deep networks: deep feedforward networks (XOR, gradient-based learning, hidden units, architecture design, backpropagation); regularisation (parameter norm penalties, constrained optimisation, dataset augmentation, noise robustness, semi-supervised, multitask, early stopping, parameter tying, sparse representations, bagging, dropout, adversarial training, tangent methods); optimisation for training (how learning differs from pure optimisation, challenges, basic algorithms, initialisation, adaptive learning rates, second-order methods, strategies and meta-algorithms); convolutional networks; sequence modelling with RNNs (unfolding, teacher forcing, bidirectional, encoder-decoder, deep recurrent, recursive, long-term dependencies, LSTM and GRU, optimisation, explicit memory); practical methodology (performance metrics, default baselines, more data, hyperparameters, debugging); applications. Part III research: linear factor models, autoencoders, representation learning, structured probabilistic models, Monte Carlo methods, the partition function, approximate inference, deep generative models.

items: Deep learning as representation learning: compose simple functions to learn features rather than engineer them; the universal approximation theorem says depth is not needed for expressiveness, but depth helps statistically and computationally.

Feedforward networks: output units paired with losses (linear with squared error, sigmoid with Bernoulli cross-entropy, softmax with categorical cross-entropy), hidden units (ReLU and variants), and backpropagation as reverse-mode differentiation through the computational graph.

Regularisation is any modification that reduces generalisation error but not training error: weight decay as a Gaussian prior, early stopping as L2 in disguise, dropout as an ensemble of subnetworks, data augmentation, noise injection, multitask learning.

Optimisation for training differs from pure optimisation (surrogate losses, minibatches, non-convexity, saddle points and cliffs, long-term dependencies); SGD with momentum, adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam), initialisation scale, batch normalisation, curriculum learning.
Convolution as sparse interactions, parameter sharing and equivariance to translation; pooling for invariance; the variants (strides, dilation, tiled convolution) and efficient implementations.
RNNs unfold a recurrence; backpropagation through time; teacher forcing; the vanishing and exploding gradient problem; gated units (LSTM, GRU) as the remedy; encoder-decoder for sequence to sequence.

Practical methodology chapter: choose metrics, start with a default baseline, decide whether to gather more data, tune hyperparameters manually or by random search, and debug with unit tests of gradients and by fitting tiny datasets.

Part III: autoencoders and representation learning, structured probabilistic models, Monte Carlo and the partition function, variational inference, and the generative models of 2016 (VAEs, GANs, autoregressive models).

b.s:
weight decay: J~ = J + (alpha/2) w^T w
dropout inference: scale weights by keep probability p
BPTT gradient: dL/dh_t = dL_t/dh_t + (dh_{t+1}/dh_t)^T dL/dh_{t+1}
LSTM cell: c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * c~_t;  h_t = o_t * tanh(c_t)

items: Chapters 6 to 8 (feedforward, regularisation, optimisation) are the durable core; read them fully.
Regularisation methods are one idea with many faces; recognise which face each trick is.
The practical methodology chapter is a checklist worth rereading before every deep learning project.

b.s: Read chapters 6, 7, 8 and 11; then implement dropout, weight decay and early stopping as three separate switches on the GRU challenger, run a small random search over them on the M1, and write a one-page methodology note in the style of chapter 11.

resources.lives: book · free · reference · free online

resources.title: Graph WaveNet (Wu et al., IJCAI 2019)

b.s: A paper where scientists let the computer figure out for itself which roads affect which, instead of telling it.

The third traffic paper. Instead of a fixed map of neighbors, Graph WaveNet learns which sensors influence which from the data (an adaptive adjacency), and it uses stacked convolutions over time instead of a recurrent network. It improved on DCRNN and STGCN on the same benchmarks.

Read it after DCRNN and STGCN: what changes is the graph (learned from node embeddings) and the temporal model (dilated causal convolutions, cheaper to train than recurrence). Its ablation shows the learned graph helps even when a physical graph is available, which is a hint that the postmile line misses some dependencies.

The adaptive adjacency, a softmax over the product of two learned embedding matrices, is a learned low-rank graph; combined with the diffusion operators it captures dependencies the road line misses, such as interchanges and parallel routes. Dilated convolutions give a long receptive field with few layers, which is why it trains fast.

Later work (MTGNN, spatio-temporal transformers) generalizes the learned-graph idea. Evaluate whether learned graphs are interpretable and stable across retrains, which is a practical concern for monitoring: a graph that changes every month is hard to trust and hard to explain.

For Fremont the learned graph could reveal cross-freeway coupling (I-880 to I-680 through SR-84 and Mission), and testing whether that improves 60-minute skill is a concrete, publishable experiment that fits on the M1. The paper is also a good example of an ablation done properly.

The paper: motivation (spatial dependencies in traffic are not fully captured by the road-distance graph, and RNN-based temporal models are slow); the model (an adaptive adjacency matrix learned from node embeddings, combined with the given graph in a diffusion convolution layer; stacked dilated causal convolutions for temporal modelling, WaveNet-style, with gated activations and skip connections); the training setup (METR-LA and PEMS-BAY, twelve steps in, twelve out, MAE, RMSE, MAPE at 15, 30 and 60 minutes); results that beat DCRNN and STGCN with much faster training; and ablations showing that the adaptive adjacency helps even without any given graph.

items: Spatial modelling: diffusion convolution treats traffic flow as a random walk on the graph in both directions (forward and backward transition matrices) with K steps; the paper adds a learned adaptive adjacency, the softmax of ReLU(E1 E2^T) for node embeddings E1 and E2, which discovers dependencies the road graph misses.

Temporal modelling: dilated causal convolutions with exponentially growing dilation give a receptive field that grows exponentially with depth, so twelve steps are covered by a shallow stack, and the whole model is parallel over time (no recurrence).

Architecture: blocks of gated temporal convolution followed by graph convolution, residual and skip connections, with the skip outputs summed and passed through output layers that produce all twelve horizons at once.
Training: MAE loss with masking of missing values, Adam, dropout, and a curriculum that is not needed because there is no autoregressive decoding.

Results: on METR-LA at 60 minutes, MAE around 3.5 versus DCRNN's 3.6 and STGCN's 4.6, and training several times faster; on PEMS-BAY MAE around 1.95 at 60 minutes; the adaptive-only variant is competitive, meaning the learned graph carries most of the information.
Limitations noted: fixed sensor set (the adaptive adjacency is per-node and does not transfer), and the twelve-step horizon.

b.s:
adaptive adjacency: A_adp = softmax( ReLU( E1 E2^T ) ), E1, E2 in R^{N x c}
diffusion conv: Z = sum_{k=0}^{K} P_f^k X W_k1 + P_b^k X W_k2 + A_adp^k X W_k3
gated TCN: h = tanh(Theta1 * x) ⊙ sigmoid(Theta2 * x)
receptive field with dilations 1, 2, 4, 8: 1 + (k-1)(1+2+4+8)

items: Learning the graph (adaptive adjacency) beats trusting the road graph; the two together are best.
Dilated causal convolutions replace RNNs for short horizons with a large speed gain and no exposure bias.
This is the reference architecture for the spatio-temporal challenger on the Fremont corridor, at a size that fits the M1.

b.s: Implement Graph WaveNet's core (adaptive adjacency, one diffusion layer, two gated TCN blocks) in PyTorch for the Fremont stations with a 12-in, 12-out speed target, train on MPS with masked MAE, and compare 15-, 30- and 60-minute MAE with the GRU challenger and with persistence.

resources.lives: paper · free · an evening or two · free; the third traffic paper

resources.title: METR-LA and PEMS-BAY datasets (DCRNN repository)

b.s: Two ready-made piles of road sensor data that scientists all use to test their traffic guessers, so everyone can compare fairly.

The DCRNN paper's authors published their code and two datasets on GitHub: METR-LA (207 sensors in Los Angeles) and PEMS-BAY (325 sensors in the Bay Area, from PeMS like our data). Everyone since has tested on them. Download them in the final phase to reproduce a paper on the Mac mini.

The repository contains the data files, the adjacency matrices built from road distances, and scripts to create the 12-step windows and the train, validation and test splits. Study how the splits are made and how missing values are masked; that protocol is what every paper's table assumes.

Use the datasets to reproduce DCRNN and STGCN at reduced scale and to test your own spatio-temporal net under the standard protocol, so your numbers are comparable with the literature. Note the differences from Fremont: no incidents, no weather, a fixed sensor set, and speed only.

The benchmark's known issues (data leakage through normalization statistics in some codebases, sensitivity to the graph construction) are documented in later papers; reading those is part of using the benchmark responsibly.
Shared benchmarks made the field comparable and also narrowed it; extending the protocol with incidents and weather, and evaluating episode-level metrics, is a contribution in itself.

The repository for Diffusion Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network: the two datasets (METR-LA, 207 loop detectors in Los Angeles County, four months of five-minute speeds in 2012; PEMS-BAY, 325 sensors in the Bay Area, six months of five-minute speeds in 2017) as HDF5 speed matrices, sensor-location CSVs, and precomputed adjacency matrices from road-network distances with a Gaussian kernel threshold; the data-preparation script that builds sliding windows (twelve steps in, twelve steps out) with time-of-day features and the train/validation/test split by time (70/10/20); the DCRNN model (diffusion convolution inside a GRU cell, encoder-decoder with scheduled sampling); training scripts and configs; evaluation with masked MAE, RMSE and MAPE at 15, 30 and 60 minutes; and the published results tables that every later traffic paper compares against.

items: The data format that became the benchmark standard: a dense (time, sensor) speed matrix with zeros for missing values, sensor coordinates, and a distance-based adjacency; understanding this format lets you read every traffic-forecasting paper's setup.
Adjacency from distances: W_ij = exp(-d_ij^2 / sigma^2) if d_ij <= kappa else 0, with sigma the standard deviation of distances; road-network distance, not Euclidean, and directional.
Windowing: for each time t, input is speeds at t-11 to t plus time-of-day, target is speeds at t+1 to t+12; splits are contiguous in time to avoid leakage.

DCRNN: replaces the matrix multiplications in a GRU with diffusion convolutions over the graph, so the hidden state mixes information from neighbours each step; the decoder generates the twelve outputs autoregressively with scheduled sampling to reduce exposure bias.
Masked metrics: sensors reporting zero (missing) are excluded from both loss and evaluation; the choice of masking affects numbers and must be matched when comparing.
The results table (METR-LA 60-minute MAE 3.60 for DCRNN, 4.59 for STGCN's setting, higher for historical average and ARIMA) is the baseline for the field; PEMS-BAY is easier, with DCRNN at 2.07.

b.s:
adjacency: W_ij = exp( -dist(v_i, v_j)^2 / sigma^2 ) if dist <= kappa else 0
DCRNN gate: r = sigma( Theta_r *_G [X, H] + b_r ), where *_G is diffusion convolution
masked MAE = sum_{i: y_i != 0} |y_i - y_hat_i| / count(y_i != 0)

items: The METR-LA and PEMS-BAY format, split and masked metrics are the shared language of traffic forecasting; use the same format for Fremont so results are comparable.
Graph construction from road distances with a Gaussian threshold is a standard, and it is also a modelling choice that adaptive adjacency later questioned.
PEMS-BAY is Caltrans District 4 data of the same kind as the Fremont PeMS feed, so the pipeline transfers directly.

b.s: Convert the Fremont PeMS speeds to the DCRNN HDF5 format with a distance-based adjacency for the local stations, run the repository's data generation script to produce twelve-in twelve-out windows, and train the repository's DCRNN for a few epochs on the M1 to get a comparable 15-minute MAE.

resources.title: ETA Prediction with Graph Neural Networks in Google Maps (Derrow-Pinion et al., 2021)

b.s: A paper about how a maps app guesses how long a drive will take, by looking at the roads as a connected network and learning from millions of trips.

A research paper describing the graph neural network behind travel-time estimates in Google Maps. Roads are grouped into segments and supersegments, a network learns how traffic on connected pieces relates, and the model runs at enormous scale. It is the industrial version of what the spatio-temporal net does for Fremont.

Read the system description: the supersegment graph, the features (segment attributes, real-time speeds, time), the graph network with message passing, and the training tricks (MetaGradients, ensembling). Compare its evaluation (travel-time error across cities) with the row-level metrics of this project.

The paper is a case study in making graph learning work in production: stability across retrains, latency, and the engineering around a model that is a small part of a larger system. Its ablations show which components mattered, which is the discipline to copy.

Contrast the probe-data setting (trip-based, sparse, privacy-constrained) with fixed-detector data; the modelling choices differ accordingly. Its treatment of training stability is relevant to any graph model retrained monthly.

One of few public accounts of a deployed spatio-temporal graph model at scale; it frames the open problems (transfer across regions, non-stationarity, coupling with routing) that a research agenda in this area would address.

The paper: the problem (estimated time of arrival for a route as a sum over road segments, with a supersegment graph that groups segments); the data (segment features such as length, speed limit, road class, real-time and historical speeds and traversal times); the model (a graph network over supersegments with node, edge and graph-level features and outputs, message passing with an edge model, node model and global model; multi-horizon outputs for departure times in the future); the training details that mattered in production (MetaGradients for learning-rate schedules, a combination of losses with Huber terms at node, edge and graph levels, and ensembling via exponential moving averages to reduce serving-time variance); the deployment (regional models, caching of predictions per supersegment, latency constraints); and results showing large reductions in negative ETA outcomes across cities such as Sydney, Tokyo and Taichung.

items: Framing ETA as a graph problem: a route is a path of segments; segments are nodes, adjacencies are edges, and the whole supersegment has a graph-level output (its traversal time); predictions at all three levels are trained jointly so the model learns consistent parts and wholes.

The graph network block: update edges from their endpoints and the global, update nodes from aggregated incident edges and the global, update the global from aggregated nodes and edges; a few rounds of this give each segment context from its neighbourhood.
Features combine static road attributes with real-time and historical speeds over time-of-week buckets; multiple horizons (now, in 10 minutes, in 20 minutes) share the trunk.

Production lessons: training instability across regions was solved with MetaGradients to adapt learning rates online; variance between checkpoints was reduced by averaging parameters (EMA), which mattered more than architecture changes; auxiliary losses on segment-level traversal times regularised the model.
Serving: models per region, predictions cached per supersegment and refreshed on a schedule so that route queries are sums of cached predictions, meeting latency constraints with modest compute.

Evaluation: RMSE on traversal time and the fraction of routes with large negative errors (arrivals later than predicted), by city; improvements of 16 to 51 percent in the negative-outcome metric over the prior production model.

b.s:
graph network: e' = phi_e(e, v_s, v_r, u);  v' = phi_v(v, agg(e' incoming), u);  u' = phi_u(u, agg(v'), agg(e'))
route ETA = sum over supersegments of predicted traversal time
EMA of parameters: theta_ema <- beta theta_ema + (1 - beta) theta

items: Multi-level supervision (segment, supersegment, route) makes the parts consistent with the whole.
In production, stability and variance reduction (EMA, adaptive learning rates) delivered more than architecture novelty.
Cache predictions per graph piece and compose at query time; the same pattern serves a corridor model that predicts per station.

b.s: Reframe the Fremont corridor as a supersegment graph (station-to-station segments as nodes), predict segment traversal times with a small graph network with node and graph outputs, train with a Huber loss at both levels, and evaluate corridor travel-time RMSE and the fraction of underestimates by more than five minutes.

phases.lives: Everything this asks for has been explained above: the lessons and topics for the ideas, the walkthroughs for the code, the books and courses for depth. The glossary at the end defines any word that is still new.

terms.def: The text window (the Terminal app on a Mac) where you type commands and press return instead of clicking. Every script in the course is started from it.
levels: The terminal is a secret room inside the computer where you talk to it by typing words instead of clicking pictures. It is like whispering instructions to a very literal genie who does exactly what you say, letter for letter. Type `ls` and the genie shows you what is inside the room you are standing in.

The terminal is a program that lets you run other programs by typing their names instead of clicking icons. You type a command, press return, and the computer does it and prints the result right below what you typed. `cd` moves you into a folder, `ls` lists what is inside it, and `python script.py` runs a program called script.py. Every tool in this course, from downloading traffic data to training a model, starts with a command typed here.

The terminal runs a shell, a program that reads a line of text, splits it into a command and its arguments, and executes it. `pwd` prints the folder you are in, `cd data` moves into a folder named data, `ls -la` lists every file including hidden ones with details, and `cat file.csv` prints a file's contents. Commands can be chained: `python 02_collect_events.py && git status` runs the second command only if the first succeeds.

The shell is itself a small programming language: it has variables, conditionals, loops, and a way to combine programs by piping one's output into another's input with `|`. Every command runs as a separate process with its own exit code, 0 for success and nonzero for failure, which is how shells decide whether `&&` chains continue. `PATH` is a list of folders the shell searches to find the program behind a bare word like `python`, and `which python` shows which one it found. Redirection (`>` to overwrite a file, `>>` to append, `<` to feed a file in as input) lets a command read or write files without any code written for the purpose, which is why so much data plumbing in this course is a one-line shell command rather than a script.

Shells differ in scripting semantics that matter once a pipeline has more than a few lines: bash and zsh handle word splitting, globbing and quoting slightly differently, which is why portable scripts pin a shell with a shebang line and set `set -euo pipefail` to stop on the first error instead of silently continuing with bad data. A pipeline's exit status by default is the exit status of its last command, which can hide a failure earlier in the chain unless `pipefail` is set. People overuse the shell for logic that belongs in Python once there are more than a few conditionals, because shell error handling and data structures are much weaker than a real language's.

In production ML systems the terminal is mostly a human interface; the actual work runs through orchestrators, container entrypoints and CI runners that execute shell commands non-interactively, so scripts written for a person typing at a prompt often break in a machine context that has no TTY, no interactive password prompt and different default shells. Apple's internal tooling, like most large companies', wraps common shell invocations in typed command-line tools with structured output, because free-text terminal output is hard to parse reliably at scale. The open question engineers still argue about is how much of a build or data pipeline should live as raw shell versus a proper workflow engine, since shell is fast to write and fragile to maintain.

terms.def: The program inside the terminal that reads your commands; on a modern Mac it is zsh. Paths, pipes and environment variables are shell ideas.
levels: The shell is the little helper inside the terminal that listens to what you type and does it. You type 'make a sandwich' in shell-speak and it goes and makes it. It only understands its own special words, so you have to learn its language first.

The shell is the program that runs inside the terminal and reads the commands you type, like `cd` and `ls`, and carries them out. On a Mac the shell is usually zsh, though some computers use bash instead. It can chain commands together, sending the output of one into the input of another, and it remembers settings called environment variables. Typing `echo $SHELL` prints which one you are using.

The shell parses each line you type into a command, its arguments, and any special symbols such as `|` (pipe), `>` (redirect), and `$VAR` (variable expansion), then runs the result. `export PEMS_USERNAME=you` sets an environment variable that child processes inherit; `which python` asks the shell which file on `PATH` will run when you type `python`. Example: `cat 02_collect_events.py | grep def | wc -l` runs three programs and pipes each one's output into the next.

The shell is a full programming language with variables, conditionals, loops and functions, layered under an interactive read-eval-print loop; `.zshrc` configures it at startup, and `.env` files are loaded by scripts rather than by the shell itself. Everything the shell manipulates is text, arguments, output, environment variables, which is powerful and also the source of quoting bugs when a filename has a space in it. It fails silently by default: a failing command in the middle of a pipeline does not stop the ones after it unless you opt in with `set -e` and `pipefail`. Scripts written for interactive use often break when run non-interactively, in cron or a CI job, because aliases and functions from `.zshrc` are not loaded there.

The shell sits at the boundary between the OS's process model, fork and exec, file descriptors, signals, and human convenience, and that boundary explains most of its rough edges: a pipeline is several processes running concurrently connected by kernel pipes, so `set -o pipefail` is required to catch a failure anywhere but the last stage. Practitioners get bitten by unquoted variable expansion, `rm -rf $DIR/*` when `$DIR` is empty can delete far more than intended, by relying on shell aliases inside scripts, which are not expanded non-interactively, and by assuming `cd` in a subshell persists in the parent shell. The tradeoff in a data pipeline is expressiveness versus auditability: a one-line shell pipeline is fast to write and fragile to review, while the same logic in Python is longer but testable. `set -euo pipefail` at the top of every script is the cheapest fix for most of these failure modes.

At production scale the shell mostly recedes into thin glue, a Makefile target, a launchd plist, a CI step, while the real logic moves to a typed language, because shell has no type system and its error handling composes badly across large scripts. What survives is its role as the universal debugging interface: ssh into a machine, and the shell is still there when everything else is broken. An open practical question in ML infrastructure is how much of that surface, piping, redirection, environment inheritance, should move to structured tools like typed task runners without losing the low ceremony that makes the shell fast for one-off investigation.

terms.def: One line typed into the shell: a program name followed by its arguments, such as `python 02_collect_events.py`.
levels: A command is like telling a robot exactly one instruction, such as "bring me the red block." You type the words and press a key, and the computer does exactly that one thing, nothing more and nothing less.

A command is one line you type into the terminal: the name of a program, then whatever it needs to know, separated by spaces. `python 02_collect_events.py` means "run the program `python`, and use `02_collect_events.py` as the file to run." The terminal reads the line, finds the program, hands it the rest of the words, and waits for it to finish before showing you a new prompt.

A command has the shape `program arg1 arg2 ...`, where each argument is separated by whitespace and quotes group words that contain spaces. Flags like `-r` or `--verbose` are arguments that change behavior rather than naming a file. Running `python 02_collect_events.py --hours 24` calls the `python` interpreter, passes it the script name, and passes the script the flag `--hours` with value `24`; the script itself decides what to do with that flag. The shell exits with a status code, 0 for success and nonzero for failure, which scripts and Makefiles check.

Under the hood, the shell parses the line, expands variables and globs (`*.csv`), then calls `fork` and `exec` to start the named program as a new process, handing it the parsed argument list (`argv`) and the current environment. Standard input, output and error are three file descriptors the shell can redirect (`>`, `<`, `2>`) or connect between commands with a pipe (`|`), which is why `cat data.csv | head` works. Which program actually runs is resolved by searching `PATH` in order for an executable matching the name, so two different `python`s can shadow each other depending on which environment is active. A command fails silently more often than beginners expect, since forgetting to check the exit code, or piping into something that swallows errors, hides a crash you needed to see.

In scripts, `set -euo pipefail` changes the failure behavior: `-e` stops the script on the first nonzero exit, `-u` treats an unset variable as an error, and `pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails, not just the last one, without which a crashed data-collection step earlier in a pipe can be masked by a successful `head` at the end. Command substitution (`$(...)`) and here-documents let a command's own output feed later commands, which is how Makefiles and CI systems compose pipelines out of otherwise independent programs. A practitioner mistake is treating a command as atomic when it is not: `python 02_collect_events.py` can be interrupted mid-write, leaving a partial file, which is why production pipelines write to a temp path and rename on success. Argument parsing itself is a small design problem, since `argparse` versus a config file versus environment variables trade discoverability against scriptability, and most real pipelines end up using all three.

At scale, a "command" is rarely typed by a person; it is generated by an orchestrator (a workflow scheduler, a CI runner, a Makefile) that must serialize arguments correctly across shells with different quoting rules, which is a persistent source of subtle bugs. Reproducibility work treats the exact command line, environment and working directory as part of the experiment record, not just the code, because two runs of the "same" command with different environment variables can silently produce different numbers. An open practical question is how much of this should move from shell strings to typed, structured command objects, as some workflow engines do, to eliminate an entire class of quoting and escaping bugs.

terms.def: The address of a file or folder. Absolute paths start at the root (`/Users/you/Traffic1/data`); relative paths start from the folder you are in (`data/pems_raw`). `cd` changes the current folder; `ls` lists it.
levels: A path is the directions to find something, like telling a friend 'go to the kitchen, then open the second drawer.' On a computer, a path tells it exactly which folder and which file to look inside. If you say the wrong path, the computer looks in the wrong drawer and finds nothing.

A path is the address of a file or folder on a computer, written as a chain of folder names separated by slashes. An absolute path starts from the very top, the root, like `/Users/you/Traffic1/data`. A relative path starts from wherever you already are, like `data/pems_raw` if you are standing in the project folder. Typing `cd data` moves you into a folder, and `ls` shows you what is inside it.

An absolute path always begins at the filesystem root (`/` on Mac and Linux) and names every folder down to the target, so it works no matter what folder you are currently in. A relative path is resolved against the current working directory, so `data/pems_raw` means different things depending on where you run the command from. `cd path/to/folder` changes the current directory, `pwd` prints it, and `ls` lists what a path points to. `..` means the parent folder and `.` means the current one, so `cd ..` steps up one level. A script that hardcodes an absolute path breaks the moment it runs on someone else's machine.

Paths are how every layer of a system — the shell, Python's `open()`, `pandas.read_csv`, a config file — locates a resource, and they come in exactly two flavors, absolute and relative, resolved against a working directory that a process carries with it. Because the working directory can differ between an interactive terminal, a cron job, and a Docker container, code that assumes a fixed relative path is a common source of 'works on my machine' bugs. The standard fix is to compute paths relative to the script's own location, for example with Python's `pathlib.Path(__file__).parent`, rather than relative to wherever the script happens to be launched from. Path separators also differ by operating system (`/` versus `\\`), which is another reason to use a library like `pathlib` instead of string concatenation. Symlinks add a further wrinkle: a path can point through one or more redirections before reaching the real file, and tools differ in whether they follow them. In this course, the PeMS data pipeline reads and writes paths under a `data/` folder that is deliberately kept out of git.

Path handling is a recurring source of subtle bugs and security holes: path traversal attacks exploit `../` sequences to escape an intended directory, so any path built from user input needs to be normalized and checked against an allowed root before use. Case sensitivity differs by filesystem — macOS is case-insensitive by default even though its underlying Unix tools look case-sensitive, which can hide a bug that only appears on a case-sensitive Linux server. Long paths, spaces, and non-ASCII characters each break naive string handling differently across operating systems, which is why `pathlib` and `os.path` exist rather than manual slash-joining. In data pipelines, mixing absolute paths (baked into a script) with relative ones (passed as arguments) is a common source of the 'file not found' bug that only shows up when a job is scheduled or containerized rather than run by hand. A practitioner's habit worth building: log the resolved absolute path (`Path(...).resolve()`) at the start of a job, so a failure a day later is diagnosable from the log alone.

At scale, 'a path' often stops meaning a local filesystem location at all: it becomes a URI into cloud object storage (`s3://`, `gs://`) or a distributed filesystem, and code has to abstract over both so the same pipeline runs on a laptop and on a cluster. Systems like fsspec exist precisely to give paths a uniform interface across local disks, S3, and other backends. Reproducibility work increasingly hashes the content a path points to, not the path itself, because paths change between environments while content should not. An open practical problem in large ML systems is path drift: configs, notebooks and scripts accumulate hardcoded paths from whoever wrote them first, and cleaning that up is unglamorous but necessary work before a pipeline can move between environments reliably.

terms.def: Sends the output of one command into the next, so `zcat file.gz | head -3` shows three lines of a compressed file without unpacking it.
levels: Imagine a line of toy trucks passing buckets of blocks to each other. A pipe in the terminal does that with words: whatever one command hands out, the next command catches and uses right away.

The pipe symbol `|` connects two terminal commands so the output of the first becomes the input of the second, without saving anything to a file in between. `ls | head -3` lists the files in a folder and only keeps the first three lines. This lets you chain small tools into one line instead of writing a program.

A pipe connects one process's standard output to the next process's standard input, so `command1 | command2` runs both at once, streaming data between them. `zcat file.gz | head -3` decompresses a gzipped file and immediately shows the first three lines, without ever writing an unzipped copy to disk. You can chain more than two: `cat log.txt | grep ERROR | wc -l` counts error lines in one line.

A pipe is built on the same file-descriptor mechanism as redirection, but instead of connecting a process to a file, the shell connects one process's stdout directly to another's stdin through an in-memory buffer, so both processes run concurrently rather than one waiting to finish before the next starts. Because the buffer is bounded, a slow consumer can block a fast producer, which is why streaming tools that read incrementally, like `head` or `grep`, can short-circuit a huge upstream computation, as `zcat file.gz | head -3` does: `zcat` stops decompressing once `head` has what it needs and closes the pipe. Pipes only carry bytes, so structured data crossing a pipe, JSON lines, CSV, needs both ends to agree on a text format.
