Failures are silent by default: an error in the first command of a pipeline does not stop the second from running on empty or partial input, unless `set -o pipefail` is set.

The concurrency that makes pipes fast also makes them a common source of subtle bugs: a pipeline's exit status is normally that of its last command, so a failure early in the chain, `grep` finds nothing, a command segfaults, can be masked unless `pipefail` is on, which is why production shell scripts set `set -euo pipefail` as a matter of course. Buffering behavior differs by program and by whether stdout is a terminal or a pipe: many tools switch from line-buffered to block-buffered output when piped, which can make `tail -f log | grep pattern` appear to hang even though data is flowing, a classic surprise fixed with `stdbuf` or a tool's own line-buffered flag. Pipes fit Unix's small-tools philosophy well for text streams, but they are a poor fit for anything needing random access or two-way communication, where a named pipe or a socket is the right tool instead. Practitioners sometimes reach for a pipeline where a single script would be clearer and more testable; the discipline is to pipe when each stage is a genuine, reusable filter, not just to avoid writing Python.

At production scale, the pipe's idea generalizes far past the shell: a batch pipeline of Parquet-to-Parquet stages, a stream processor's operator graph, and a Unix pipe are all the same pattern of composable, backpressured stages, and the same failure modes reappear, a silently swallowed error in an early stage, an unbuffered stage stalling the whole chain under load. The open engineering question at that scale is less about the pipe itself and more about observability: knowing, for a multi-stage pipeline processing millions of rows an hour, exactly which stage is slow or wrong without re-running the whole thing, which is why production systems replace bare shell pipes with orchestrators that log per-stage metrics, the way this project's own scripts print one structured line per stage.

terms.def: A named value the shell keeps and passes to programs, such as a password or an API key set with `export PEMS_USERNAME=...`. A `.env` file lists them so scripts can load them.
levels: An environment variable is like a sticky note the computer keeps nearby with a secret written on it, like your login name. Any program you run can peek at the sticky note without you having to say the secret out loud every time.

An environment variable is a named piece of information the shell remembers and hands to any program that runs, like a password or a username. You set one with a command such as `export PEMS_USERNAME=kunal`, and after that any script can read `PEMS_USERNAME` without you typing it again. A `.env` file is just a text file listing several of these so a script can load them all at once. They keep secrets out of the code itself.

`export NAME=value` creates an environment variable in the current shell session, and every program launched from that shell inherits it. In the Fremont traffic project, `PEMS_USERNAME` and `PEMS_PASSWORD` are set this way so the collector script can log in to PeMS without the credentials being written in the code. A `.env` file stores these as `NAME=value` lines, and a library like `python-dotenv` reads it into the process's environment at startup. Because `export` only affects the current shell and its children, closing the terminal loses the variable unless it is saved in a startup file or a `.env`.

Environment variables are a key-value store attached to a process, inherited from its parent shell at the moment it is launched, and invisible to processes that start independently, such as ones started by launchd. This makes them the standard way to inject configuration and secrets into a program without hardcoding them, since the same code can read `PEMS_USERNAME` in development, in CI, and in production, each with a different value supplied by the environment. They fail when a value is exported after a long-running process has already started, since that process keeps the environment it was launched with; they also fail silently when a name is misspelled, since an unset variable usually just reads as empty or `None` rather than raising an error. `.env` files solve the reproducibility problem of remembering many exports by hand, but they are not a secrets vault: anyone who can read the file can read the secret, so `.env` belongs in `.gitignore`, never in the repository.

The security tradeoff is real: environment variables are visible to any process running as the same user, readable from `/proc/<pid>/environ` on Linux, and often captured whole in crash reports, container image layers and CI logs, so treating them as a secure secrets channel is a common and costly mistake. The alternative — a credential manager or secret-injection service that hands out short-lived tokens at runtime — avoids leaving a long-lived password sitting in plaintext, at the cost of more moving parts. A subtler bug is precedence: a variable set in the shell, one loaded from `.env`, and one baked into a launchd plist can disagree, and whichever loads last silently wins, which is a frequent source of 'it works in my terminal but not when scheduled' failures. Practitioners also conflate 'exported in this shell' with 'set for this program forever'; a background job launched by cron or launchd does not inherit an interactive shell's exports at all, which is exactly why scheduled jobs need their own explicit environment block.

In production ML systems environment variables scale into whole configuration layers — feature flags, per-region endpoints, model version pins — managed by tools like Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets or a credential vault, which add rotation, auditing and access control that a flat `.env` file cannot. The open problem is provenance: when a training run's result depends on an environment variable's value, that value has to be captured in the experiment record, or the run is not reproducible even with identical code and data. At scale, teams increasingly push toward config-as-code — typed, validated configuration objects checked into version control — precisely to get away from untyped, silently overridable environment state.

terms.def: The programming language the course uses. It reads a text file of instructions and runs them one line at a time.
levels: Python is a language for talking to the computer, like a very picky friend who only understands exact words and gets confused by typos. You write a list of instructions in a file, and the computer follows them in order, one at a time, like a recipe. If you tell it to mix the eggs before cracking them, it will try anyway and something will go wrong.

Python is a programming language: a set of words and punctuation rules for writing instructions that a computer can run. You save the instructions in a file ending in `.py`, and running `python script.py` makes the computer read that file top to bottom and do what it says. It is popular because the rules are close to plain English, and there are ready-made toolkits (libraries) for almost anything, including reading traffic data and building models.

Python is an interpreted language: `python script.py` reads the file and executes it line by line, rather than compiling it into a separate program first. Variables are created by assignment (`x = 5`), functions by `def`, and indentation, not braces, marks which lines belong to a loop, function, or if-statement. A single misplaced indent changes what the code means, which is unusual compared to languages like C or Java. Errors show as a traceback: the last few lines usually name the file, the line number, and what went wrong.

Python is dynamically typed, meaning a variable's type is checked at run time, not in advance, and garbage-collected, which trades some raw speed for fast, readable code, a fair trade for data science, where the real cost is usually reading files and calling into fast libraries such as numpy and pandas that are themselves written in C. The reference implementation, CPython, has a Global Interpreter Lock that prevents true multi-threaded parallelism for Python code, though numeric libraries route around it by releasing the lock during their own C code. Its ecosystem, pandas for tables, scikit-learn for classical models, PyTorch for neural networks, is why it dominates ML, not raw language speed. It fails or frustrates when a task needs real parallel CPU work in pure Python, or when a project's dependency versions drift and code that worked last year no longer runs.

The GIL forces a choice: use multiple processes instead of threads for CPU-bound parallelism, or lean on libraries that release it, which is why `multiprocessing`, joblib, and vectorized numpy or pandas calls matter more than Python's own loops for performance. Type hints (`def f(x: int) -> float`) do not change what runs; they only let tools like mypy catch mistakes before execution, so they are documentation with teeth, not real static typing. A common mistake is writing row-by-row Python loops over a pandas DataFrame instead of vectorized operations, which can be a hundred times slower for the same result. Packaging and environments, the actual versions of Python and its libraries, matter as much as the code itself, because the same script can give different numeric results on different machines.

At production scale, Python is usually the orchestration and modeling layer, while the inner loops that matter for speed are compiled: numpy and PyTorch call into C, C++, and CUDA or Metal kernels. Projects like Cython, Numba, and a no-GIL build of CPython (PEP 703) are ongoing attempts to close the gap without leaving the language. The open question in industry is less whether Python is fast enough and more whether a huge, dynamically typed codebase can stay correct as it grows, which is why large Python codebases invest heavily in type checking and testing infrastructure the language itself does not require.

terms.def: A file of Python code ending in `.py`, run with `python name.py`. The numbered files in Traffic1 (`10_clean_pems.py` and so on) are the pipeline's scripts.
levels: A script is like a recipe card that tells the computer exactly what to do, step by step, in order. You do not have to do the steps yourself, you just say go and the computer follows the card. In this project, one card cleans the traffic data and another card trains the guesser.

A script is a text file full of Python instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom. It ends in `.py`, and you run it by typing `python name.py` in the terminal. The Traffic1 project is built from numbered scripts like `10_clean_pems.py` and `20_train_model.py`, each doing one job in the pipeline. Running them in order turns raw traffic files into a trained model.

A script is a `.py` file executed by the Python interpreter with `python script.py`, running each line in order unless a loop or function redirects the flow. Scripts can take command-line arguments (`python 10_clean_pems.py --since 2024-01-01`) and can be imported as modules if they define functions instead of only top-level code. In Traffic1, the numbered prefix (`10_`, `20_`, `30_`) signals pipeline order: `10_clean_pems.py` must finish before `20_build_features.py` can read its output. A script that raises an uncaught exception stops immediately and prints a traceback to the terminal.

A script differs from a reusable module mainly by intent: a module defines functions and classes meant to be imported, while a script is meant to be run directly, often guarded by `if __name__ == "__main__":` so its top-level code does not execute on import. Good scripts are idempotent where possible, rerunning `10_clean_pems.py` on the same input should produce the same output, which matters for a pipeline rerun after every new day of PeMS data. They read configuration from arguments or environment variables rather than hardcoded paths, so the same script works in development and in a scheduled job. A script touching disk should fail loudly and early, checking inputs and schemas, because a silent partial write corrupts the next stage. In production, the same file is often invoked identically by a human at a terminal and by a scheduler like cron or launchd.

The line between a script and a pipeline component blurs once scripts need retries, logging, and dependency tracking, at which point teams often move the same logic into a workflow orchestrator or a Makefile with explicit targets so failures are visible and reruns are scoped to what actually changed. A common mistake is a script that silently reuses global state across runs, a cached file it forgot to delete, a random seed it forgot to set, which makes results nondeterministic in ways that are hard to trace back. Scripts run from a scheduler differ subtly from scripts run at a terminal: the working directory, PATH, and environment variables may not be the same, the classic cause of it works when I run it but not when the schedule runs it. Testing scripts is undervalued because they look like glue code, but a bug in `10_clean_pems.py` silently corrupts every downstream stage, so a small test target that runs each script on a tiny fixture is worth more than its size suggests.

At scale, a numbered script pipeline becomes a DAG-based workflow system with lineage tracking, so a bad label or a schema change can be traced back to the exact script version and input snapshot that produced it. Scripts that once ran on a laptop become containerized jobs with resource requests, retries, and alerting, and the informal contract that one script's output is another script's input becomes an explicit, versioned schema. The open problem is less about running scripts reliably, that is largely solved, and more about making the dependency graph between hundreds of such scripts legible enough that an engineer six months later can trust what depends on what.

terms.def: A bundle of ready-made code you load with `import`. pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, LightGBM and PyTorch are libraries.
levels: A library is a box of tools someone else already built, so you do not have to build a hammer before you can hang a picture. In code you say `import` and the whole toolbox appears in your program. pandas is the toolbox for tables, and numpy is the toolbox for fast number crunching.

A library is a collection of code, written and tested by other people, that you load into your own program with an `import` statement instead of writing it yourself. Once imported, its functions and classes behave as if you had written them, so `import pandas as pd` gives you `pd.read_csv` and every other tool inside pandas. This course uses pandas for tables, numpy for arrays, scikit-learn for baseline models, LightGBM for gradient boosting, and PyTorch for neural networks. Using a library means trusting its authors' choices about how something is computed, which is usually a good trade since the code is more tested than anything written from scratch in an afternoon.

In Python, `import numpy as np` runs the numpy package's initialization code once and binds the name `np` to it in the current namespace; `from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression` pulls one class out of a package instead of the whole thing. Libraries are installed with `pip install numpy` (or listed in `requirements.txt` and installed all at once with `pip install -r requirements.txt`) into the current Python environment, and Python finds them by searching the folders listed in `sys.path`. A library has a version, and code written against one version can break against another, which is why this course pins exact versions in `requirements.txt`.

Under an import lies a package: a folder with an `__init__.py` file and possibly submodules, distributed as a wheel or source archive on PyPI and installed by a resolver that reads its declared dependencies. Choosing a library is a real design decision with tradeoffs: scikit-learn favors a simple, uniform `.fit()`/`.predict()` interface at the cost of speed on large data, LightGBM trades that uniformity for speed and accuracy on tabular data through histogram-based tree building, and PyTorch trades ease of use for full control over the computation graph. Libraries built on top of a fast compiled core, like numpy's C and Fortran routines or LightGBM's C++ engine, run orders of magnitude faster than equivalent pure-Python loops because the loop itself executes in compiled code, not the Python interpreter. When two libraries pin incompatible versions of a shared dependency, installation fails or, worse, silently installs an unintended version, which is why a lock file is the safer way to record what was actually used.

Library boundaries are also API contracts: a well-designed library exposes stable functions and hides its internal representation, so its authors can rewrite the internals (say, swap numpy's BLAS backend) without breaking code that calls it, but a library that leaks its internals, or one you monkey-patch, couples your code to an implementation detail that can change on any release. Semantic versioning is a promise, not a law, and real libraries occasionally break it, which is why serious projects pin exact versions and re-test before upgrading rather than trusting a caret range. A common mistake is treating a library's convenience defaults, like scikit-learn's default regularization strength, as if they were neutral choices instead of themselves a modeling decision. Reading a library's source when its documented behavior does not match your data is a normal part of debugging, not a sign that something is broken.

At Apple's and similar companies' scale, the biggest library-related risk is the software supply chain: a compromised or accidentally-broken release of a widely used package can hit thousands of internal services at once, so production pipelines mirror approved packages through an internal index and pin hashes, not just version numbers. Performance work increasingly means choosing between libraries that use the same algorithm but target different hardware, such as a CPU-optimized LightGBM versus a GPU-accelerated boosted-tree library, and the right choice depends on where the bottleneck actually is, which requires profiling rather than assumption. An open problem across the industry is how to keep the convenience of high-level libraries while getting real visibility into what they do under the hood when something silently goes wrong, since a library's abstraction is exactly what makes debugging it hard.

terms.def: The tool that installs Python libraries: `pip install pandas`. `requirements.txt` lists everything the project needs so `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs it all.
levels: pip is like a delivery truck for your computer. You tell it the name of a toy you want, like 'pandas', and it goes and fetches it and puts it in your toybox. You never have to build the toy yourself.

pip is the command that installs Python libraries, the packages of code other people wrote so you do not have to write it yourself. `pip install pandas` downloads pandas and everything it needs. A `requirements.txt` file lists every package a project needs, one per line, so `pip install -r requirements.txt` installs them all at once.

pip downloads a package from the Python Package Index, resolves its declared dependencies, and installs it into whichever Python environment is currently active. `pip install pandas==2.2.2` pins an exact version; `pip freeze > requirements.txt` writes down every installed package and its version so the environment can be rebuilt. Running pip outside a virtual environment installs into the system Python, which is the mistake `python -m venv .venv` exists to prevent.

pip's job is dependency resolution: given a set of requested packages, find versions that satisfy every package's declared constraints, a hard problem that pip's modern resolver, since 2020, solves by backtracking properly rather than guessing. It installs prebuilt wheels when one matches your platform and Python version, and falls back to building from source when it does not, which is where compiler and BLAS mismatches on Apple silicon show up. `requirements.txt` pins top-level packages but not always their transitive dependencies unless it was generated by `pip freeze`, which is why two 'identical' installs can still drift apart. pip has no environment concept of its own; it always installs into whatever `python` currently resolves to, which is why the venv matters at least as much as pip itself.

The unpinned-transitive-dependency problem is real: a `requirements.txt` with only top-level packages can resolve to different versions months apart as upstream packages release, silently changing numerical results, which is why reproducible pipelines use a lock file, pip-tools, uv, or conda-lock, that pins every package in the graph, direct and transitive. Practitioners get bitten by mixing pip and conda in the same environment, which can corrupt binary compatibility for packages like numpy that ship compiled extensions. The tradeoff pip embodies is speed and simplicity of the tool versus correctness of the result: it will happily install a set of versions that satisfy the stated constraints but conflict at runtime in ways it cannot detect, because Python has no strict ABI enforcement across packages.

At scale, teams stop calling pip directly and instead build and publish internal wheels through an artifact repository, so a training job's dependency set is fixed at build time rather than resolved fresh on every machine, removing pip's resolution step from the hot path entirely. Reproducibility audits increasingly require a full lock file plus a hash of each wheel, since a supply-chain compromise of a single transitive dependency on PyPI is a realistic attack surface. The open tooling question is whether Python's ecosystem converges on one fast, correct resolver, uv is the current leading contender, the way other languages did with Cargo or npm, since pip's resolver, while now correct, remains slow on large dependency graphs.

terms.def: A private copy of Python and its libraries for one project, so projects do not fight over versions. Create it once, activate it, install into it, and point VS Code and launchd at its Python.
levels: Imagine every toy project gets its own toy box, so the blocks from your spaceship set never get mixed up with the blocks from your castle set. A virtual environment is a toy box just for one project's Python tools.

A virtual environment is a private folder that holds one project's own copy of Python's installed libraries, kept separate from every other project's. You make one with `python -m venv .venv`, turn it on with `source .venv/bin/activate`, and then anything you `pip install` goes into that folder instead of your whole computer. That way, upgrading a library for one project cannot quietly break a different, older project that needed an older version.

Creating an environment (`python -m venv .venv`) copies a small Python interpreter and an empty `site-packages` folder into `.venv`; activating it (`source .venv/bin/activate`) changes your shell's `PATH` so that typing `python` and `pip` finds this copy first. `pip install -r requirements.txt` then installs exactly the pinned versions the project needs, isolated from any other project's environment. Running `which python` after activating should print a path inside `.venv`, and forgetting to activate before installing is the most common way people end up with two conflicting copies of a library.

A venv works by giving each project its own `site-packages` directory and rewriting `sys.path` so the interpreter looks there before the system location; it does not copy the interpreter binary itself, only reference it, which is why the base Python version still matters. This solves the "works on my machine" problem for library versions, but it does not solve interpreter-version drift, differing operating systems, or non-Python system dependencies like a BLAS library, which is why a requirements file is necessary but not sufficient for reproducibility. `conda` environments solve a broader version of the same problem, since they can also pin non-Python binaries, at the cost of a heavier, slower solver. A common failure mode is a stray global `pip install`, run without activating the venv first, that silently pollutes the system Python instead of the project's copy.

Environments are really dependency graphs, and `pip`'s resolver can accept a set of version constraints that is technically satisfiable but numerically different depending on resolution order and what was already cached, which is why plain `requirements.txt` pinning is weaker than a proper lock file (pip-tools, uv, conda-lock) that records every transitive version and hash. On Apple silicon specifically, an environment can silently run under Rosetta instead of natively, producing a working but much slower environment where `platform.machine()` still reports the wrong architecture until you rebuild the interpreter itself as arm64. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming an environment fixes numerical reproducibility: the same pinned versions of numpy or LightGBM can still produce different floating-point results across a different BLAS backend, chip, or thread count. Nested or shadowed environments, such as a venv activated inside a conda environment, or a Jupyter kernel pointed at the wrong interpreter, are a frequent source of "but I installed it" confusion.

At production scale, per-project venvs give way to containers and hermetic build systems (Docker, Nix, Bazel), because reproducibility has to span operating system libraries, drivers and compilers that a venv cannot capture at all. Model registries and experiment trackers increasingly snapshot the resolved environment, a lock file plus a container digest, alongside the model weights, treating the environment as part of the artifact rather than an assumption about the world. An open engineering problem is that hermetic environments are heavier and slower to iterate in than a venv, so most teams live with a tradeoff between the fast, leaky venv workflow for development and a slow, sealed container for anything that has to be reproduced later.

terms.def: The M-series chips in modern Macs. Python and its libraries must be the arm64 builds to use the chip well; `platform.machine()` must print `arm64`.
levels: Apple silicon is the brain inside a new Mac, and it speaks a different language than older Mac brains did. Programs have to be written in that new language to run at their fastest, the same way you run faster in shoes that actually fit you. arm64 is just the name of that language.

arm64 is the name of the chip family (the M1, M2, M3 chips and so on) that Apple puts in modern Macs, replacing the older Intel chips. Software written for the old Intel chips can still run through a translator called Rosetta, but it runs slower than software built natively for arm64. You can check which one you are running with `platform.machine()` in Python, which should print `arm64` on these Macs. Getting a native arm64 Python, rather than an Intel one running in translation, matters for speed.

arm64 (also called Apple silicon or M-series) is the chip architecture Apple switched Macs to starting in 2020, replacing x86-64 Intel chips. Software compiled for one architecture cannot run directly on the other; Rosetta 2 translates x86-64 code to run on arm64, but at a real speed cost, especially for numeric code. `python -c 'import platform; print(platform.machine())'` prints `arm64` for a native install and `x86_64` for one running under Rosetta. The fix is to install a Python distribution built for arm64, such as miniforge or the arm64 installer from python.org, so that `pip install`-ed packages like numpy come as native arm64 wheels rather than translated ones.

Apple silicon (arm64) is Apple's own ARM-based system-on-chip design, and the switch from x86-64 broke binary compatibility for any package that ships compiled code — essentially all numeric Python libraries. Rosetta 2 provides emulation so old binaries still run, but emulated numeric code, particularly anything using vectorized instructions, can be meaningfully slower than native arm64 code. The practical fix is ensuring the whole toolchain is native: an arm64 Python interpreter, and arm64 wheels for numpy, pandas, LightGBM and PyTorch, all of which now publish native builds. A common failure mode is a mixed environment — an Intel-installed Python found first on `PATH`, with an arm64 one installed alongside it — which silently runs everything under emulation without any error. `arch` at the shell and `platform.machine()` in Python are the two commands used to check which architecture is actually active. Apple silicon also has a unified memory architecture and dedicated matrix/ML accelerators (the Neural Engine), which some frameworks can target directly.

The arm64 transition exposed how much of the scientific Python stack depends on precompiled binary wheels linked against specific BLAS/LAPACK implementations, and for a period after the M1 launch, some packages had no arm64 wheel at all, forcing users to compile from source or stay on Rosetta. Numerical results can differ slightly between an Intel build (often linked against MKL) and an Apple silicon build (typically linked against Apple's Accelerate framework or OpenBLAS), because floating-point summation order and vectorized instruction sets are not bit-identical — a subtlety that matters for reproducibility claims. Conda's channel ecosystem was slower to catch up than pip's for arm64, which is part of why miniforge (which defaults to conda-forge, an early adopter of arm64 builds) became the recommended installer over the standard Anaconda distribution. A mistake practitioners make is trusting `python --version` or `which python` alone; neither tells you the binary's architecture, only `platform.machine()` or `file $(which python)` does. Apple's Metal Performance Shaders backend for PyTorch (`mps`) is arm64-specific and has its own gaps in operator coverage relative to CUDA, so code that runs unmodified on a Linux GPU box can silently fall back to CPU on a Mac.

At Apple's own scale, arm64 is not just the laptop story — the same architecture family, extended, underlies the Neural Engine and custom silicon used in on-device inference, so code paths optimized for arm64 on a MacBook and code paths for shipping models to iPhones share real lineage, even though the deployment targets (macOS ML training versus on-device Core ML inference) are different systems. Cross-compiling and testing for both x86-64 (still dominant in cloud training clusters) and arm64 (dominant on-device and increasingly in Apple's own server hardware) is a standing tax on any team that develops locally on a Mac and deploys to Linux. An open, ongoing problem is bit-for-bit numerical reproducibility across BLAS backends and hardware — a model trained identically on Accelerate versus MKL versus a GPU can diverge slightly, which complicates any claim of exact reproducibility and pushes serious work toward hashing outputs within a tolerance rather than expecting exact equality.

terms.def: An app that runs Python one cell at a time and shows results, tables and plots under each cell. Good for looking at data; scripts are better for the pipeline.
levels: A Jupyter notebook is like a picture book where each page has a little bit of computer code, and when you tap the page, the computer does that bit and draws the answer right underneath.

A Jupyter notebook is an app that runs Python code one chunk, called a cell, at a time, instead of running a whole file at once. You type code into a cell and press shift-enter, and the result, a number, a table, or a plot, appears right under it. It is great for poking at data, but for a program that should run the same way every time, a plain `.py` script is better.

A notebook file (`.ipynb`) stores a sequence of cells, each either code or explanatory text, along with the saved output from the last time each cell ran. Running cells out of order is easy and dangerous: a variable defined in cell 5 and used in cell 2 will work in the notebook's current session but fail if you restart and run top to bottom, so 'Restart and run all' before trusting a notebook's results. For example, you might load a month of PeMS data in one cell, then run `df.describe().T` in the next to see each column's range, with the table appearing immediately below.

A notebook is a JSON file wrapping a persistent Python kernel: state, variables, imports, lives in that running kernel process, not in the file, so displayed outputs can silently drift out of sync with the code as cells are edited and rerun in a different order than they appear on the page. This makes notebooks excellent for exploratory data analysis, where you want to see a table or a plot after every small step and keep looking at real numbers rather than staring at code, but poor for anything that must be reproducible, tested, or run unattended, because hidden state and out-of-order execution are invisible in the saved file. The standard discipline is to prototype in a notebook, then move working logic into functions in a `.py` module that both the notebook and a production script import, so the two never diverge. Version control is also awkward: notebooks store output alongside code, so diffs are noisy unless outputs are stripped before committing.

The tension between notebooks and scripts is really a tension between exploratory and confirmatory analysis, and treating a notebook as a pipeline stage conflates the two: a data scientist tweaking a threshold cell by cell is doing exploration, and a scheduled job producing tomorrow's predictions needs a deterministic script with no hidden kernel state. Tools like `nbconvert`, `papermill`, and `jupytext`, which pairs a notebook with a plain-text `.py` mirror, exist precisely because teams want the interactivity during development and the reproducibility of a script in production, and getting the boundary wrong, shipping notebooks as production code, is a common and expensive mistake. A subtler failure practitioners hit constantly: a notebook that looks correct top to bottom because cells were run in a convenient order during debugging, not the order printed on the page, so a colleague's 'Restart and run all' produces a different, sometimes wrong, result. Extensions like autoreload and interactive widgets add further hidden state that can make a notebook's behavior depend on invisible history.

In research and applied teams, notebooks remain the default surface for first-look data analysis and model debugging because switching to a script for every quick question costs too much, but any result meant to be trusted, a claim in a paper, a number that drives a launch decision, gets re-derived in a script or test that runs clean from a fresh kernel before anyone relies on it. Newer tools, reactive notebooks that automatically rerun downstream cells when an upstream one changes, try to fix the hidden-state problem at the tool level rather than through discipline, and it remains an open question whether reactive execution can keep the fast, ad hoc feel that makes notebooks useful while removing their central reproducibility failure.

terms.def: A free code editor. Point it at the venv's Python so it runs and checks code with the right libraries.
levels: VS Code is like a big coloring book for writing computer instructions, where the computer helps you see mistakes by underlining them. You open a project's folder in it and it shows you all your files in one place.

VS Code (Visual Studio Code) is a free program for writing and editing code, with color-coded text and built-in error checking. For Python projects it needs to know which Python to use, so you point it at the project's virtual environment (the venv) instead of some other Python on the computer. It can run scripts, show file changes tracked by git, and open a terminal inside the same window. Most people in the course write every script in it.

VS Code is an editor, not a compiler: it highlights syntax, shows inline errors from a linter, and lets you run or debug a script with a keyboard shortcut, but the actual Python still comes from wherever its interpreter setting points. Command Palette then 'Python: Select Interpreter' picks which Python VS Code uses to run and check code; picking the project's `.venv` instead of a system Python is what makes autocomplete and error-checking match the packages actually installed for this project. Its Source Control panel shows the same staged and unstaged changes as `git status`, just clickable. Extensions add most of the useful behavior: the Python extension for linting and debugging, GitLens for blame and history.

VS Code separates 'editing' from 'running': the editor process renders and lint-checks your code using whatever interpreter and language server you configured, while a run or debug session launches a separate Python process, and a mismatch between the two — editor pointed at system Python, terminal running the venv's Python — produces the confusing symptom of code that runs fine in the terminal but shows phantom import errors in the editor. Its integrated terminal is a real shell, so activating a venv there (`source .venv/bin/activate`) affects only that terminal pane, not the interpreter the editor uses for linting, unless the interpreter setting is separately pointed at the same venv. Workspace settings (`.vscode/settings.json`) can pin the interpreter path per project so the whole team gets the same setup from a fresh clone. Extensions run in their own sandboxed process and can be slow or resource-heavy on large repos, which is the usual cause of a 'VS Code feels laggy' complaint that has nothing to do with the code itself.

The core design tradeoff is VS Code's language-server-protocol architecture: intelligence like autocomplete, go-to-definition and type checking comes from a separate long-running server process (Pylance, for Python) that indexes the project, which gives rich, near-IDE features in a lightweight editor shell but means that a stale or confused index — after a large refactor, or a `.venv` swapped out from under it — silently degrades suggestions rather than erroring, and the fix is usually reloading the window or restarting the language server. Remote development (SSH, containers) runs the whole extension host on the remote machine while the UI stays local, which practitioners get wrong by assuming an extension installed locally is available remotely — extensions install per host. For notebooks, VS Code's Jupyter extension executes cells against a real kernel process, which means kernel state (variables from a previous cell) persists independent of what the editor displays, a common source of 'it works when I re-run everything but not from a fresh restart' bugs.

At scale, teams standardize editor configuration itself — shared `.vscode/settings.json`, devcontainer definitions, recommended-extensions lists — as part of reproducibility, so that 'works in my editor' does not silently depend on personal setup the way an unpinned interpreter or a missing linter config would. The frontier is AI-assisted editing built into the same surface, inline completion and chat against the open files, which raises a genuinely open question for research and production code alike: how much of the editor's suggestion should be trusted without the same review a human-written diff gets. None of this changes the basic contract from the age-5 explanation, it is still an editor pointed at an interpreter, but at scale the pointing has to be declared in a file, not remembered by each engineer.

terms.def: The version-control tool. It records snapshots (commits) of your files so you can see history, undo, and branch. GitHub hosts repositories online.
levels: Git is a magic notebook for your project that remembers every version of your work. Every time you save a snapshot, called a commit, the notebook writes down what changed and lets you flip back to any earlier page. GitHub is like a shelf in the cloud where you can keep a copy of the notebook so it does not get lost.

Git is a tool that tracks changes to your files over time. You take a snapshot with `git commit -m "message"`, and `git log` shows every snapshot you have ever taken, in order. If you break something, you can look back through the history and see exactly what changed and when. GitHub is a website that stores a copy of your Git history online, so you can share it or work on it from another computer.

Git has three areas: the working tree, your files as you see them, the staging area, what `git add` has queued for the next snapshot, and the repository, the committed history. `git status` shows which files are staged, unstaged, or untracked; `git diff` shows exact line changes before you commit. Branches are just movable pointers to a commit, so `git branch` and `git checkout -b` let you try something without touching the main line of work. A `.gitignore` file lists patterns, like `data/` or `.env`, that Git should never track, which keeps large data files and secrets out of history.

Git commits form a directed acyclic graph, each commit pointing to its parent, or parents, for a merge, which is what makes history browsable and branches mergeable. A branch name is only a label on a commit; merging combines two histories, and rebasing rewrites one branch's commits to sit on top of another instead. Git tracks content, not files by name, so renaming a file is detected by comparing content, not recorded as a special operation. Workflow habits, small commits, clear messages, reviewing your own diff before committing, matter more for solo reproducibility than any single Git feature, because the log is only useful if it is honest about what changed and why.

Internally, Git stores every version as a content-addressed object, blobs for file contents, trees for directory structure, commits for snapshots, each named by the hash of its content, so two identical files anywhere in history are stored once. The reflog records where branch tips have pointed, even after a rebase, reset, or deleted branch, which makes almost anything recoverable for a while even when the visible history looks gone. `git bisect` does binary search over commits to find which one introduced a bug or, in ML work, changed a metric, far faster than checking commits one by one. A common mistake is committing large binary data or model checkpoints directly, which bloats the repository forever, since Git's history is append-only and rewriting it after the fact is disruptive.

At scale, plain Git strains under huge monorepos and large binary artifacts, which is why organizations add Git LFS, partial clones, or move data and model files to separate versioning systems that store lineage without bloating the Git object store. Code review at scale is built on top of Git, not inside it; pull requests, required checks, and blame tooling all sit outside Git's own model of commits and branches. An open practical problem is tying together the two histories that matter for a reproducible ML result, the code history in Git and the data and model history in whatever system tracks those, so that a commit hash alone is not enough to reproduce a claim.

terms.def: A folder whose history git tracks. Traffic1 is one. `.gitignore` lists what git must never record, such as `data/` and `.env`.
levels: A repository is like a treasure chest that keeps every old drawing you ever made of your project, not just the newest one. You can always open the chest and find yesterday's drawing again. Traffic1 lives in a chest like that.

A repository, or repo, is a folder whose entire history git keeps track of, one saved snapshot at a time. Each snapshot is called a commit, and together the commits form the project's timeline. Traffic1 is one repository, and a file called `.gitignore` tells git which things to never save, like the raw `data/` folder or a `.env` file of secrets. GitHub is a website that hosts a copy of a repository online so others can see it or copy it.

A repository is a directory containing a hidden `.git` folder that stores every committed snapshot as content-addressed objects, plus branches, tags, and the commit history's graph. `git init` creates a new repository, `git clone <url>` copies an existing one, and `git remote -v` shows where it syncs to, typically GitHub. `.gitignore` uses patterns, `data/`, `*.env`, `__pycache__/`, to keep files out of every future commit, but it does not remove files already tracked; those need `git rm --cached`. In Traffic1, `data/` and `.env` are gitignored because raw traffic data is large and credentials must never enter history.

A repository's real unit is not the file but the commit, an immutable snapshot of the entire tree, addressed by a hash of its contents, so two commits with identical trees are literally the same object. This content-addressing is what makes git's history tamper-evident: changing any past commit changes its hash and every descendant's hash. A repository can have multiple remotes, and the repository as a mental model usually means the local `.git` plus whichever remote, `origin`, is treated as the source of truth. Because `.gitignore` only prevents future tracking, secrets committed once remain in history forever unless the history itself is rewritten, which is why scanning for accidental secret commits before pushing matters more than a `.gitignore` entry added after the fact.

The tradeoff a repository forces is between what belongs in version control and what does not: code and small config belong; multi-gigabyte PeMS extracts and trained model binaries generally do not, because git was designed for text diffs, not binary blobs, and a large repository degrades clone and diff performance for everyone. Git LFS, DVC, or an external artifact store are the usual fixes, each trading some git-native ergonomics for scalability. A subtlety practitioners miss: a monorepo versus many small repositories is not just a style choice, it changes how atomic a cross-project change can be, and how coarse or fine the access control and CI triggers are. Reflog and content-addressing mean almost nothing committed is ever truly lost, but an accidentally force-pushed history on a shared branch can still cause real damage to collaborators' local clones.

At scale, the repository for a production ML system is rarely one git repo, it is git for code plus a separate, often internally built system for data and model lineage, because git's object model does not scale to petabyte datasets or to tracking which exact data snapshot trained which model checkpoint. Monorepos at large companies solve cross-team coordination but require custom tooling, sparse checkouts, virtual file systems, to keep git usable at that size. The open problem is unifying code lineage and data or model lineage into one queryable graph, so that what changed and why a metric moved can be answered by tracing a repository-like history spanning code, data, and model artifacts together.

terms.def: A commit is one saved snapshot with a message; a branch is a named line of commits; push copies your commits to GitHub.
levels: A commit is like taking a photograph of your entire project at one moment, with a little note describing what changed. A branch is like starting a new comic strip page so you can try something new without messing up the original story. Push means mailing copies of your photographs to a faraway library called GitHub so they are safe even if your computer breaks.

A commit saves a snapshot of every tracked file in your project along with a short message describing the change, and `git log` shows the list of commits in order. A branch is a separate line of commits that starts from some point in history, so you can make changes on a branch named `feature` without touching the `main` branch until you are ready. Push sends your local commits up to a remote copy of the repository, usually on GitHub, so other people (or other computers) can see them. `git add`, `git commit -m 'message'`, and `git push` are the three commands that do this in order.

`git commit -m 'message'` takes everything staged with `git add` and records it as a new commit object, pointing at the previous commit as its parent, which is what makes history a chain. `git branch feature` creates a new pointer named `feature` at the current commit, and `git checkout feature` (or `git switch feature`) moves you onto it, so commits made afterward extend that branch instead of `main`. `git push origin feature` uploads the commits on `feature` that the remote does not yet have, creating the branch on GitHub if it does not exist there. `git diff` before committing shows exactly what changed since the last commit, and running it is good practice before every `git commit`.

A commit is not literally a full copy of the project; git stores content-addressed objects and a commit points to a tree of files, so unchanged files are shared between commits and only new or changed content takes new space. Branches are cheap because a branch is just a movable pointer (a 40-character hash reference) to a commit, not a copy of the repository, which is why git encourages making a new branch for almost any change. Pushing fails if the remote branch has commits your local branch does not, because git refuses to silently overwrite history; the fix is `git pull` (fetch and merge) or `git fetch` plus a manual merge or rebase before pushing again. A commit message convention, such as a short imperative summary line plus a blank line and details, makes `git log` and `git blame` far more useful months later, which is a discipline most beginners skip and later regret.

The real subtlety is what belongs in one commit: an atomic commit does one logical thing, so a bug can be isolated with `git bisect` and a bad change can be reverted with `git revert` without undoing unrelated work, but many teams commit far too coarsely, mixing a feature, a formatting pass and an unrelated fix in one commit that is then impossible to review or revert cleanly. Rewriting history with `git rebase -i` before pushing to squash or reorder commits is safe on a private branch but dangerous on a branch others have already pulled, since it changes commit hashes and orphans anyone who based work on the old ones — the rule of thumb is never rewrite history that has been pushed to a shared branch. Force-pushing (`git push --force`) after a rebase is sometimes necessary and sometimes a way to destroy a colleague's work, which is why many teams require `--force-with-lease` instead, a safer variant that refuses to overwrite commits it has not seen. A common misconception is that a branch 'contains' its own commits exclusively; in fact commits belong to the shared object graph and can be reachable from multiple branches at once.

At Apple's scale, commits and branches are the substrate that CI, code review and release engineering are built on: a pull request is a proposed set of commits on a branch, gated by required reviews and automated checks before it can merge, and a monorepo can have millions of commits across branches that a naive `git log` cannot render, pushing teams toward tools like sparse checkouts and virtual file systems. Commit provenance also matters for security and compliance — signed commits and verified authorship let a build system prove which engineer's change introduced a given line, which is part of how supply-chain integrity is enforced internally. An open problem in large-scale version control is that git's model, designed for source code, strains under very large binary or generated artifacts (models, datasets), which is why such organizations increasingly pair git with separate artifact and data versioning systems rather than committing large files directly.

terms.def: Comma-separated values: a text table, one row per line, commas between fields. Easy to read, slow and large.
levels: A CSV is like a shopping list written on lined paper, one item per line, with commas splitting the name from the price. Anyone can open it and read it, even without a fancy program.

A CSV file stores a table as plain text: each line is a row, and commas separate the columns within that row. You can open one in a text editor, in Excel, or read it into Python with `pandas.read_csv`. A PeMS detector file might have columns for the time, the station number, and the speed, all comma-separated on one line per five-minute reading.

A CSV has no built-in types: every value is text until something parses it, so a date column reads in as a string and must be converted with `pd.to_datetime`. `pd.read_csv('file.csv', header=None, names=[...])` reads a file with no header row and assigns column names explicitly, which the PeMS files require. CSV also has no schema enforcement, so a stray comma inside an unquoted field, or a column that is sometimes an integer and sometimes empty, can silently corrupt the table unless it is checked.

CSV's assumptions are minimal by design, no types, no compression, no indexing, which makes it universally readable but expensive: parsing text into typed values takes real CPU time, and a month of five-minute detector rows across hundreds of stations can be hundreds of megabytes as text versus a fraction of that as compressed columnar Parquet. It fails on data with commas or newlines inside a field unless the writer quotes correctly, and different tools disagree at the edges, quoting, encoding, line endings, which is the source of most 'my CSV won't parse' bugs. `pd.read_csv` accepts a gzipped file directly and infers most of this, but explicit `dtype` and `parse_dates` arguments make loading both faster and less error-prone than letting pandas guess.

CSV is text, so it stores no data type, no null-versus-empty-string distinction beyond convention, and no per-column encoding, which pushes correctness work downstream into every reader's parsing code; a known failure mode is a numeric ID like a station code getting silently reinterpreted, dropping a leading zero, when a spreadsheet program round-trips the file. At scale, row-oriented text has poor compression and forces reading whole rows even when only one column is needed, which is exactly what columnar formats fix; the tradeoff practitioners weigh is CSV's universal compatibility against Parquet's speed, size and type safety for anything beyond a one-off inspection. A common mistake is treating a CSV export as a stable interface when the producing system silently changes column order or adds a column, which breaks a `names=[...]` argument written for the old schema.

In production data platforms, CSV survives mainly as an ingestion and interchange format at the edges, the format a third-party vendor or public agency like PeMS actually ships, while everything internal moves to columnar formats within minutes of arrival, precisely because CSV's lack of schema makes it unsafe to depend on directly at scale. Schema-on-read tooling and data-quality frameworks exist largely to catch the failure modes CSV allows silently. The frontier problem is less about the format itself than about provenance: knowing, for every row in a warehouse, which CSV export it came from and whether that export's schema changed underneath you.

terms.def: A compressed, column-by-column file format for tables. Small on disk, fast to load, keeps data types. The course stores every cleaned table this way.
levels: Imagine a big box of crayons sorted by color instead of thrown in all mixed up, since it is easier and faster to grab "all the reds" that way. Parquet stores a table sorted like that, by column instead of by row, so the computer can grab just what it needs quickly.

Parquet is a file format for saving tables, like a fancier version of a CSV file. Instead of saving row by row, it saves column by column, and it compresses each column, so the file on disk is much smaller and loads much faster. It also remembers each column's type, that a speed column is a number and a station name is text, so you never have to re-guess it after loading, the way you sometimes do with CSV.

A Parquet file stores each column contiguously and compressed, with metadata describing the schema (column names and types) and statistics per chunk, so a query that only needs `speed` and `station_id` can skip reading every other column entirely. In pandas, `df.to_parquet('data.parquet')` writes it (through the `pyarrow` engine) and `pd.read_parquet('data.parquet')` reads it back with the same dtypes it was saved with, unlike `read_csv`, which has to re-infer types like dates and doesn't preserve categoricals. For a table of 5-minute PeMS rows with many repeated station IDs, Parquet's compression and columnar layout typically make the file five to ten times smaller than the equivalent CSV.

Parquet is a columnar, compressed, self-describing binary format built for analytical workloads: data is organized into row groups, each column within a row group stored contiguously with its own encoding (dictionary encoding for low-cardinality columns like station ID, run-length encoding for repeated values) and per-column min/max statistics that let a reader skip entire row groups without decompressing them. This is why tools like DuckDB can run `SELECT AVG(speed) WHERE station_id = 400001` over a Parquet file far faster than over CSV, without an index, since predicate pushdown uses the statistics to prune, and it only decodes the one column the query touches. Parquet fails to help, and can even hurt, for workloads that need every column of every row, a full table scan with no column pruning, or that mutate data in place, since Parquet files are written once and read many times, not updated incrementally. Choosing a compression codec (snappy for speed, zstd for ratio) and a row-group size are real tuning decisions that trade write time, read time and file size against each other.

The subtlety practitioners get wrong is schema evolution: adding, removing or widening a column across many Parquet files written over time can produce a dataset where different files disagree on schema, and readers that assume a single fixed schema will fail or silently coerce types inconsistently unless the pipeline enforces a schema explicitly. Partitioning a dataset into many small Parquet files by date or station, a common pattern for streaming ingestion, trades query pruning, skipping whole partitions cheaply, against the overhead of opening thousands of small files, and the right partition granularity depends on typical query patterns more than on any general rule. Parquet's compression is also not free at read time, since decompression is real CPU work, so a codec chosen for the smallest file is not always the fastest to read for downstream training. Dictionary encoding, which is a major source of Parquet's advantage on categorical columns like station ID, degrades badly if the column has very high cardinality, at which point it can end up larger than a naive encoding.

At scale, Parquet is the substrate under most data-lake formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi), which layer transactional guarantees, schema versioning and time travel on top of plain Parquet files because Parquet itself has no notion of "this table changed" beyond the files present in a directory. Feature stores for production ML lean on Parquet's columnar pruning to serve wide feature tables efficiently, but they must solve a problem Parquet does not: keeping training-time and serving-time reads of the same features consistent when the underlying files are being rewritten concurrently. An open question in these systems is how to preserve Parquet's read efficiency while getting closer to database-style point updates, which is most of what the newer lakehouse formats are trying to do.

terms.def: A compression format. PeMS files arrive gzipped; `zcat` prints them decompressed and pandas can read them directly.
levels: gzip is like squishing a big pillow into a small bag so it takes up less room, and then someone can un-squish it later to get the same pillow back. PeMS sends its files squished this way to save space. A file ending in `.gz` is a squished file.

gzip is a way of compressing a file so it takes up less disk space and downloads faster, and a compressed file usually ends in `.gz`. The command `zcat` prints a gzipped file's contents to the screen without you having to un-compress it into a separate file first. Because gzipped files are so common for data downloads, pandas can read a `.gz` file directly with `read_csv`, decompressing it automatically. PeMS, the traffic sensor data source in this course, ships its files gzipped.

gzip is a lossless compression algorithm (based on DEFLATE) that shrinks text files, especially repetitive ones like CSVs, often to a fifth of their original size or smaller. A compressed file conventionally has a `.gz` suffix appended to its original name, so `d07_text_station_5min.txt.gz` decompresses to `d07_text_station_5min.txt`. `zcat file.gz` prints the decompressed contents to standard output without writing a new file, and `gunzip file.gz` decompresses it in place. `pandas.read_csv('file.csv.gz')` detects the `.gz` extension and decompresses on the fly, so there is usually no need to decompress PeMS files by hand before loading them.

gzip implements DEFLATE, a combination of LZ77 dictionary compression and Huffman coding, and it works well on PeMS-style data because sensor CSVs are highly repetitive: the same column structure and many similar numeric values recur every five minutes. Reading a large gzip file entirely into memory before processing defeats much of the benefit of compression in the first place, so the standard pattern for a big file is to stream it in chunks — `pandas.read_csv(path, compression='gzip', chunksize=...)` — decompressing and processing a slice at a time rather than materializing the whole decompressed table at once. gzip decompresses sequentially, so unlike some other formats it does not support random access to the middle of a file without reading everything before it. This is one reason columnar formats like Parquet, which support predicate and column pushdown, are preferred over gzipped CSV for large repeated analytical reads, even though gzip remains the standard way raw data is shipped in the first place. Compression level is a speed-versus-size tradeoff; the default level is usually a reasonable middle ground for pipeline work.

gzip's lack of random access, and DEFLATE's relatively modest compression ratio and speed compared to newer codecs (zstd, lz4), are why it has been displaced as a data-warehouse format even as it remains the near-universal choice for one-off file distribution — it is simple, has essentially unconditional support, and its slower decompression rarely matters for a file read once. A subtlety practitioners miss: gzip files can be concatenated (multiple gzip streams back to back form a valid gzip file that decompresses to the concatenation of the parts), which some tools handle correctly and some silently truncate after the first stream — a source of quietly-wrong row counts in a pipeline that appends compressed log files. Verifying integrity matters at scale: a truncated or corrupted `.gz` file can decompress partially without an error in some readers, producing a silently incomplete DataFrame rather than a crash, which argues for checking expected row counts or file hashes rather than trusting that a read succeeded.

At production scale, gzip is increasingly a legacy interchange format rather than a storage format: pipelines land raw gzipped files as they arrive from a source system, then immediately convert to a columnar, splittable, often zstd- or snappy-compressed format (Parquet) for anything that will be queried repeatedly, because gzip's lack of splittability makes it a poor fit for parallel processing across a cluster. An open practical question for any ingestion pipeline is how much validation to do at decompression time — checking a stored checksum, expected row count, or schema against the file — versus trusting the source, since silent partial reads from a truncated gzip are a real and hard-to-catch failure mode in long-running automated collectors.

terms.def: A text format for lists and dictionaries (`{"h": 30, "p": 0.42}`) that every language can read. Used for thresholds, feature lists and the live predictions file.
levels: JSON is a way of writing down a list of facts, like the ball is red and the ball is round, using curly braces and colons, so any computer in the world can read it and understand which fact is which.

JSON is a text format for storing structured data: numbers, strings, lists, and dictionaries, which are lookup tables from a name to a value. It looks like `{"h": 30, "p": 0.42}`, meaning h is 30 and p is 0.42. Almost every programming language can read and write JSON, which is why it is used to pass data between very different programs.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) nests four building blocks: numbers, strings in double quotes, lists in square brackets, and objects (dictionaries) in curly braces mapping string keys to values. Python's `json` module converts between JSON text and native objects: `json.dump(obj, f)` writes a dict or list to a file, and `json.load(f)` reads it back. In this course, `models/calibration.json` stores the alert threshold τ per horizon, for example `{"15": 0.62, "30": 0.51, "60": 0.44}`, so changing the required precision later means rerunning one small step, not retraining.

JSON's four data types, number, string, boolean or null, and the two containers, array and object, form a strict grammar with no comments and no trailing commas, which is what makes it unambiguous to parse in any language but also unforgiving to hand-edit. It has no native representation for dates, sets, or NaN, so a Python `datetime` or `numpy.nan` must be converted, typically to an ISO string and `null` respectively, before serialization, and `float()` is the usual fix for numpy scalars that otherwise raise a type error on serialization. It is a good format for small, structured configuration and output, thresholds, feature lists, one row of live predictions, but a poor one for millions of numeric rows, where its per-value text overhead and lack of columnar structure make Parquet far smaller and faster to read. JSON Lines, one JSON object per line, is the common middle ground for streaming many records without loading a giant array into memory at once.

JSON's simplicity is also its limitation as a schema-less format: nothing in the file itself enforces that every prediction record has the same keys or that `p` is always a float between 0 and 1, so validation has to happen in code, with libraries like `pydantic` or JSON Schema filling that gap when a service's contract must be enforced. A subtlety practitioners hit often: JSON numbers have no fixed precision, and different parsers round large integers or long floats differently, which matters for anything like a hash or a high-precision timestamp passed through JSON. In a serving system, JSON is usually the wire format for an API's request and response, readable and debuggable with `curl`, while the storage format underneath is something denser, Parquet, Avro, or a database, precisely because JSON's human-readability trades away compactness and typed schema enforcement.

At scale, JSON stays the lingua franca at system boundaries, an API response, a config file, a log line, because every tool speaks it, but internal high-throughput paths move to binary, schema'd formats, Protocol Buffers, Avro, Arrow, once record count and the need for backward-compatible schema evolution outgrow what a schema-less text format can enforce safely. The open craft problem is less about JSON itself and more about contract discipline: keeping producers and consumers of a JSON API in sync as fields are added, renamed, or deprecated, which is why schema registries and strict validation at the boundary, rather than JSON's own grammar, are what actually keep large systems from breaking on silent format drift.

terms.def: Other text formats for settings. A launchd plist is XML: keys and values inside angle-bracket tags.
levels: YAML, plist and XML are different ways grown-up computers write down lists of settings, like different handwriting styles for the same shopping list. XML writes each item inside little angle-bracket tags, like `<name>eggs</name>`.

YAML, plist and XML are text formats for storing settings and configuration, not code. YAML uses indentation and colons, like `name: value`, and is common for tools like Docker Compose. A plist ('property list') is Apple's format for settings, and on the Mac it is actually written in XML: every key and value sits inside angle-bracket tags, such as `<key>Label</key><string>traffic-predictor</string>`. All three are just structured text a program reads back in.

YAML represents nested data with indentation and `key: value` pairs, and lists with a leading dash, which makes it readable but sensitive to exact spacing — a tab where a space was expected breaks the file. XML wraps every value in an opening and closing tag, `<key>...</key>`, which is more verbose but unambiguous about where each value starts and ends; a launchd job description is written this way, for example `<key>StartInterval</key><integer>300</integer>` to run something every 300 seconds. A plist can also be stored in a binary form, but the human-edited version is the XML one. Docker Compose files use YAML to describe services, networks and volumes.

These are three serialization formats for the same underlying idea, nested key-value data, with different tradeoffs. YAML is terse and human-friendly but has a notoriously large and ambiguous specification (unquoted `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off` parse as booleans in some parsers), so production tooling increasingly restricts itself to a 'safe' subset. XML is verbose but has strict, well-specified parsing and schema validation, which is why Apple standardized on it for plists: a launchd job file that a system daemon parses benefits from XML's unambiguity more than from YAML's brevity. Malformed indentation in YAML fails at parse time with an error whose line number often points at the wrong place, which is the most common practical complaint from people used to XML's tag-matching or JSON's braces.

The historical throughline is that each format traded human-readability against parsing safety in a different place: JSON kept a small, unambiguous grammar at the cost of no comments and stricter syntax; YAML added human conveniences (comments, anchors and aliases for reuse) that also expanded its attack surface — YAML deserialization vulnerabilities, where a parser turns tagged text into arbitrary objects, have caused real security incidents, which is why libraries expose a `safe_load` that restricts parsing to plain data. XML's schema languages (XSD) let a consumer validate a document's shape before trusting it, a discipline YAML and JSON only get via separate tools such as JSON Schema. Practitioners often get bitten by YAML's type coercion, like a version string `1.0` parsing as a float and losing the trailing zero, and by plist binary-to-XML round-tripping silently reordering keys, both of which argue for treating any of these formats as data to be validated, not trusted by inspection.

At scale, hand-written configuration in any of these formats becomes a liability, so large systems generate it from a typed source of truth (a Python or Starlark config object, a Kubernetes custom resource) and treat the YAML, plist or XML file as a compiled artifact rather than something engineers edit directly, closing the class of bugs where a manually edited config drifts from what the code actually expects. On Apple platforms specifically, most engineers now edit plists through Xcode's property list editor or generate them from build settings rather than hand-writing XML, for the same reason. The open tooling question across the industry is whether a stricter, still human-editable format like TOML or CUE can replace YAML's role without losing its readability advantage.

terms.def: macOS's built-in scheduler. A plist in `~/Library/LaunchAgents` tells it to run a program every N seconds or at boot, with logs to named files.
levels: launchd is like an alarm clock built into a Mac that can wake up a program instead of a person. You tell it when to run something, every so often, or the moment the computer turns on, and it remembers, even while you are asleep.

launchd is the part of macOS that starts programs on a schedule or at login, instead of you having to remember to run them yourself. You describe the job in a small settings file called a plist, saved in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, which says what program to run and how often. Loading it with `launchctl load` tells macOS to start watching the clock; from then on the job runs automatically, even if you never open a terminal.

A launchd plist is an XML file with keys like `ProgramArguments`, the command to run, `StartInterval`, seconds between runs, and `StandardOutPath`/`StandardErrorPath`, where logs go. You load it with `launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.you.job.plist` and check it is running with `launchctl list | grep job`. Unlike cron, launchd can also run a job at login, at wake, or whenever a file changes, not just on a fixed clock.

launchd is macOS's single service manager for both user jobs, LaunchAgents, running as you, with access to your desktop session, and system jobs, LaunchDaemons, running as root, without a session, which replaced the older cron and init on macOS. Because agents run only while a user is logged in, a job that must run overnight on a laptop also needs `caffeinate` to stop the machine sleeping, or it silently never fires. Errors typically show up not as a crash but as a missing log file, an empty output file, or a job listed with a nonzero last exit code in `launchctl list`. It fails quietly when the plist has a syntax error, a wrong path, or when macOS's permission system blocks the job from reading files it needs.

A recurring silent failure on macOS is Full Disk Access: a launchd job runs, but the script it calls cannot read files in protected locations unless the terminal or Python binary that launchd invokes has been explicitly granted access in System Settings, and the job fails with a permissions error deep in its own log rather than a launchd error. `StartInterval` fires roughly every N seconds from load time, not on the wall-clock schedule a `StartCalendarInterval` gives you, so the two are easy to confuse when precise timing matters. Because agents only run in a login session, unattended data-collection jobs on a personal Mac are more fragile than the same job on a server, and practitioners often discover this only when a week of expected data is missing. A `KeepAlive` key can restart a crashing job forever, which turns a silent bug into a fast, repeated failure that fills logs rather than showing an obvious crash.

In production, cron-like scheduling on a single machine does not scale to the retraining and monitoring jobs a real pipeline needs; the equivalent problems are solved by workflow schedulers with retries, alerting, and dependency graphs between jobs, none of which launchd provides. launchd remains useful for exactly the case this course uses it for, a personal machine collecting data unattended, where the tradeoffs of sleep, permissions, and no dependency graph are acceptable. The open, unglamorous problem in real deployments is the same one at any scale: knowing when a scheduled job silently stopped working, not just when it crashed loudly.

terms.def: A text file a program appends lines to as it runs, so you can see what happened after the fact. Every stage in the course writes one line with its name, time and memory.
levels: A log is like a diary the computer writes for itself while it works, one line at a time. If something goes wrong, you can read the diary to see what it was doing right before. Grown-ups read logs the way you might read a diary to figure out what happened.

A log is a text file a program keeps adding lines to as it runs, recording what happened and when. Each stage of the traffic pipeline writes a line with its own name, the time it ran, and how much memory it used. Reading the log after a run tells you whether a stage succeeded, failed, or is taking longer than usual. Logs are usually plain text, so you can open them with `cat` or search them with `grep`.

A log is produced by calling something like Python's `logging` module, which writes timestamped lines at levels such as DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, and ERROR, letting you filter noise later by level. A typical line includes a timestamp, the stage name, and a message, for example `2024-06-01T08:05:00Z clean_pems INFO rows=105234 memory_mb=412`. `grep ERROR pipeline.log` finds only the failures; `tail -f pipeline.log` follows a log while a job is still running. Logs differ from print statements mainly in that they are structured, leveled, and usually kept even after the program exits.

Well-designed logs are structured, JSON lines or key equals value pairs, rather than free text, because structured logs can be parsed and queried at scale, you can ask which runs of clean_pems used over 1 GB without regex-scraping sentences. Log levels exist to separate what an operator needs during normal operation, INFO, from what a developer needs while debugging, DEBUG, and setting the wrong default level either drowns the log in noise or hides the detail needed to diagnose a failure. Logs should include enough context, a run ID, the input file's hash, the git commit, to reconstruct exactly what happened, which is the same instinct behind reproducibility more generally. A common failure is logging so much that the log itself becomes a storage and cost problem, or so little that a 3am failure is undiagnosable.

At the scale of a real pipeline, logs, metrics, and traces are treated as three related but distinct signals: logs are discrete events, metrics are aggregated numbers over time, and traces follow one request or run across stages, conflating them, using logs to compute a metric by grepping and counting, is a well-known anti-pattern that does not scale and is fragile to log format changes. Centralized log aggregation trades local simplicity for queryability across the whole pipeline, but introduces its own failure mode: if the logging pipeline itself breaks silently, you lose visibility exactly when you need it most. Practitioners often under-invest in log retention policy, either paying to keep everything forever or deleting logs needed for a postmortem six months later. Sampling matters at high volume, logging every row is wasteful, but logging only aggregates can hide the one malformed row that broke everything downstream.

At production scale, logs feed observability platforms that correlate them automatically with metrics and distributed traces, and the frontier work is in making that correlation automatic rather than something an engineer reconstructs by hand during an incident. Structured logging schemas become a contract across teams, versioned like an API, because a silent field rename breaks every downstream dashboard and alert built on it.
