Imputation methods range from simple (forward-fill, mean-fill) to model-based (regression on neighboring stations and recent history, k-nearest-neighbors, or a full probabilistic model of the missingness), and the right choice depends on the missingness mechanism: data missing completely at random can be imputed with less bias than data missing because of the very condition you're trying to predict, such as a detector that tends to fail during severe congestion. Naive imputation systematically underestimates variance, since a filled-in value has none of the noise a real measurement would have, which can make a model overconfident if imputed and measured rows are not distinguished. The standard defensive move is to keep an "is imputed" indicator as a feature alongside the filled value, so a downstream model can learn to trust it less. Imputation fails badly when gaps are long or occur at exactly the informative moments, and a detector going dark right as a jam begins is the worst case, since the imputed value likely just repeats the pre-jam pattern.

The rigorous way to think about imputation is as a measurement model: observed value equals true value plus detector noise plus imputation error, where the imputation error is itself the output of another model, often built from neighboring stations and recent history, so any uncertainty estimate that ignores this second source of error is too confident. Multiple imputation, generating several plausible filled datasets and pooling results across them, propagates that uncertainty properly but is rarely used in practice for pipelines at this scale because of the added compute and complexity. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is correlating imputation quality with the label: if detector health itself predicts the outcome, a detector more likely to go dark during a jam, then treating the imputation mask as noise rather than as a feature throws away real signal, and PeMS-scale reality, a fifth to a third of detectors unhealthy at any time in a typical district, makes this a first-order rather than a marginal effect. Downstream, a model that has learned to lean on the smoothness of imputed segments can look artificially accurate offline and then fail in exactly the situations, real, fast-changing congestion, that matter operationally.

At production scale, imputation and detector-health modeling become a system in their own right, a component that estimates per-station reliability continuously and feeds that estimate both into the imputation itself and into every downstream model as a feature, rather than a one-off cleaning step. Modern approaches lean on spatiotemporal models (graph neural networks that treat a station's neighbors and recent history jointly) to impute, which blurs the line between "cleaning the data" and "part of the forecasting model," raising a genuine methodological question about where imputation should stop and prediction should begin. An open research question is how to certify the uncertainty of an imputed value well enough that downstream models and human operators can calibrate their trust in a specific reading, rather than treating all reported values as equally real.

terms.def: Copying the last known value into the following empty slots, up to a limit.
levels: Sometimes a sensor forgets to write down a number, leaving a blank spot. Forward fill just copies the last number it did see into the blank spots, like writing yesterday's weather into today's box if you forgot to check. It only does this for a little while, not forever.

Forward fill is a way to handle missing data by copying the most recent known value forward into the empty rows that follow it, up to some limit so it does not go on forever. In pandas this is `.ffill()`, or `.ffill(limit=3)` to only fill up to three rows in a row. It is a reasonable guess for short gaps because traffic speed usually does not change drastically in five or ten minutes, but a bad guess for long gaps.

Forward fill (`.ffill()` in pandas) replaces a missing value with the last valid value that came before it in the same column, and `limit=3` caps how many consecutive missing rows it will fill before giving up and leaving the rest as missing. It matters that this is done per group: `df.groupby('station_id').ffill(limit=3)` ensures a station's last known speed is never carried across into a different station's rows just because they happen to be adjacent in the table. Forward filling makes sense for a slow-changing signal like traffic speed over a few missing minutes, but it silently invents data, so filling too far assumes something that may not be true.

Forward fill is a simple imputation method that assumes the last observed value is the best available guess for a missing one, which is a reasonable assumption for a slowly-varying, autocorrelated time series like traffic speed over short gaps, but a poor one across a real outage — filling ten missing minutes with a five-minute-old reading can make an actual slowdown look like normal flow, or vice versa. The `limit` parameter exists precisely to bound how much is invented: beyond the limit, the value stays missing (`NaN`) and is handled downstream, either dropped or flagged with a separate 'was this imputed' indicator feature. Grouping by station before filling (`groupby('station_id').ffill(...)`) is essential and easy to forget; without it, pandas will happily carry the last row of one station into the first row of the next station in a sorted, concatenated table, producing a subtly wrong value that no error will flag. Forward fill is a form of leakage-adjacent risk too if applied carelessly across a train/test boundary in time: filling a training row using a value that is only available because of future test data would leak information, though within-station, causally-ordered forward fill (only ever looking backward in time) does not have this problem by construction.

Forward fill has a subtle interaction with model evaluation: if missingness itself is informative (a sensor tends to go quiet exactly during severe congestion, because heavy traffic can affect detector reliability), then forward-filling erases a signal that a model could otherwise have used, and adding a binary 'was imputed' feature recovers some of that lost information. The choice of fill limit is a bias-variance tradeoff dressed up as a data-cleaning decision: a short limit produces more missing rows (which then get dropped, shrinking the training set and possibly biasing it toward well-instrumented stations), while a long limit produces more confidently-wrong imputed values during real gaps. A mistake practitioners make is applying forward fill before splitting by station and by time, rather than after — the operation must respect both boundaries simultaneously, which is exactly what `groupby(...).ffill(limit=...)` gets right and a naive `sort_values` plus `.ffill()` on the whole DataFrame gets wrong. For longer or more consequential gaps, model-based imputation (interpolation using neighboring stations, or a small predictive model for the gap) is worth the extra complexity.

In production pipelines running at real-time or near-real-time scale, forward fill is often the first line of defense against sensor dropout, but it is deliberately kept simple and heavily monitored rather than trusted blindly: a station that has been forward-filled for an extended period is usually flagged and excluded from serving rather than silently fed to a live model, because a model making decisions on stale data can be worse than a model that abstains. The open engineering question at scale is less about the imputation method itself and more about observability — knowing, in real time, which fraction of current inputs are genuinely fresh versus filled, since a quiet increase in sensor dropout can degrade a live system's accuracy without any single component actually failing.

terms.def: A 511 event: crash, stall, closure, with created, updated and pulled-at times. Its reporting delay limits how much it can help.
levels: An incident is when something happens on the road, like a crash or a stall, and a helper called 511 writes it down with the time it happened, kind of like a hall monitor reporting that there was a spill by the door.

An incident is an event from the 511 traffic feed: a crash, a stall, a closure, or roadwork, each with a location and a time. The 511 service is polled every 15 minutes, and each incident is logged with `created` (first reported), `updated` (details changed), and `pulled_at` (when this project's own collector fetched it). Incidents are one of the two main data sources for the traffic project, alongside the five-minute detector rows from PeMS.

An incident record comes from 511.org and includes a road name, a map point, and three timestamps: `created`, `updated`, and `pulled_at`, logged by `02_collect_events.py` every time it polls the feed. Because 511 is sampled every 15 minutes rather than continuously, an incident's start and end times are interval-censored: the true crash time is somewhere before `created`, not exactly at it. An `incident_active` flag built from this feed can be joined to the five-minute detector rows as one input feature, marking every row within some distance and time window of a live incident.

Incident data carries its own measurement error layered on top of the freeway's real state: reporting delay, the gap between the physical event and CHP logging it, missing or approximate geography, unrecorded severity, and a selection effect, since incidents tend to get reported more readily once congestion from them is already visible, which quietly links the incident feature to the very slowdown it is meant to help predict. This reporting delay is exactly why incidents help less than intuition suggests for a short-horizon prediction: by the time an incident is logged, the traffic model's own speed and flow features may already reflect the slowdown it caused, making the incident feature partially redundant rather than an early warning. Treating `created` as ground truth for when something happened without accounting for that lag is a common mistake, since it can make an incident look like it precedes a slowdown it actually follows.

The incident feed exposes several subtleties easy to get wrong: because reports are event-driven and irregularly spaced against the regular five-minute detector grid, joining incidents to that grid requires an explicit windowing decision, how far in space, how far in time counts as near, and the choice materially changes what an incident feature captures. Interval censoring on start and end times means the feed cannot cleanly answer whether there was an incident at exactly this station at exactly this minute, only whether one was reported nearby around this time, so any binary incident flag is a noisy proxy rather than ground truth. There is also a subtler leakage risk: `updated` can move forward in time as an incident's details are corrected, so using the latest known state of an incident record for a point-in-time feature, rather than what was known as of the prediction moment, leaks future information about the incident's own resolution.

At larger scale, incident-style event data is where the project touches an open research area: representing sparse, irregularly reported events, a marked point process, jointly with a dense, regular sensor grid, rather than crudely converting one into a flag on the other, is an active line of work in spatio-temporal modeling. The production question this raises is about latency versus completeness: a system that waits for 511's polled, human-reported incidents is always behind connected-vehicle or camera-based detection, so teams operating at scale increasingly fuse multiple asynchronous sources with different delay and coverage profiles, a harder sensor-fusion problem than joining one clean feed to one clean grid.

terms.def: The list of a table's columns and their types. Checked before every write.
levels: A schema is like a rulebook for a toy box that says exactly what kinds of toys go in each bin, blocks in this one, cars in that one, so nothing gets put in the wrong place.

A schema is the definition of what columns a table has and what type each one is, for example, `station_id` is a whole number, `speed` is a decimal, `timestamp` is a date and time. Before the traffic pipeline writes new rows to a table, it checks the schema to make sure the new data has the right columns and types. If a column is missing or a number shows up where text was expected, the write should fail loudly instead of silently corrupting the table.

A schema can be enforced by a database (a `CREATE TABLE` statement with typed columns) or checked in code with a library like pandera or pydantic, which validates a DataFrame against a set of rules, column names, types, allowed ranges, before it is trusted downstream. In the traffic project, a schema check might assert that `speed` is a positive float, `station_id` matches a known station, and `timestamp` falls within the expected day, catching a malformed PeMS download before it silently pollutes a month of training data. `df.dtypes` shows pandas's inferred schema for a loaded table, which is worth comparing against what you expected.

Schema checking is the first and cheapest layer of data validation, catching structural problems, wrong column, wrong type, unexpected nulls, before any statistical check runs, and it is cheap precisely because it does not need to know anything about what 'correct' traffic data looks like statistically, only what shape it must have. A rigid schema fails loudly and immediately on a source format change, which is a feature: silent schema drift, a new PeMS export renaming a column, is far more dangerous than a crash, because it can pass silently into training and degrade a model without any error ever being raised. The tradeoff is between a strict schema, which is safer but brittle to legitimate upstream changes, and a loose one, which tolerates change but pushes the burden of catching errors onto later, harder-to-diagnose stages. Nullable columns need explicit schema decisions: is a missing `speed` an error, or an expected and handled case?

Schema evolution, the fact that a schema legitimately changes over time as new fields are added, deprecated or renamed, is a genuinely hard versioning problem: a schema check that is too strict breaks every time the upstream source adds a harmless new column, while one that is too loose, ignoring unknown columns, can hide a real breaking change. Systems like Avro and Protobuf solve this for streaming pipelines with explicit forward- and backward-compatibility rules, a new field must have a default, a removed field must not be reused for something else, a discipline most pandas-based research pipelines skip entirely, which is why schema bugs are disproportionately common in ML code compared to traditional software. Practitioners often check schema once at ingestion and then trust the data through every subsequent transformation, but a join, a reshape, or a type coercion partway through a pipeline can silently violate the original schema's assumptions, a merge introducing unexpected nulls, without tripping any check placed only at the start.

At scale, schema becomes part of a data contract between teams, the table's producer and its consumers agree on a schema and version it explicitly, with automated tests that fail a deploy if a producer's change would break a downstream consumer's schema expectations, which is the industrial answer to the evolution problem above. Streaming systems add the further complication of late and out-of-order data arriving under an old schema after a new one has already shipped, requiring the pipeline to handle multiple schema versions simultaneously rather than assume a clean cutover. The open engineering challenge is making schema contracts cheap enough to write and maintain that teams actually keep them current, rather than letting them rot into documentation nobody trusts, which is the practical failure mode research prototypes rarely encounter but every production pipeline eventually does.

terms.def: The Python library for tables. `pd.read_csv`, `read_parquet`, `groupby`, `merge`, `shift`, `rolling` are its verbs.
levels: pandas is a toolkit for working with big lists that look like a spreadsheet, with rows and columns. It can read a table from a file, sort it, and let you look at just the rows you care about, much faster than doing it by hand.

pandas is a Python library, a bundle of ready-made code, for working with tables of data. You load it with `import pandas as pd`, then read a file with `pd.read_csv("file.csv")`, which gives you a DataFrame, rows and named columns, like a spreadsheet you can control with code. From there you can filter rows, add new columns, or compute summaries like an average, all with one line of code instead of writing a loop yourself.

A pandas DataFrame is a 2-D table with a row index and named columns, each column its own array of a single data type, int, float, string, datetime. Core operations include `df["speed"] > 30`, a boolean mask for filtering, `df.groupby("station_id").mean()`, aggregate per group, `df.merge(other, on="station_id")`, join two tables, and `df["speed"].shift(3)`, shift a column down by 3 rows, useful for value 15 minutes ago at 5-minute steps. `df.dtypes` shows each column's type, and mismatched types are a frequent source of bugs, such as a timestamp column that loaded as text instead of a datetime.

pandas is built on numpy, so its speed comes from vectorized operations, applying a function to a whole column at once in compiled code, rather than Python loops over rows, which are typically 10 to 100 times slower for the same computation. Its object model has real subtleties: a slice of a DataFrame can be a view or a copy of the underlying data depending on how it was produced, which is the source of the notorious SettingWithCopyWarning. Time-series operations like `shift` and `rolling` assume the rows are already sorted and evenly spaced in time; applied to unsorted or gappy data, they silently produce wrong answers rather than raising an error. It fails, or at least misleads, on large data primarily through memory: a DataFrame typically uses several times the raw file size in RAM, and naive code that keeps multiple intermediate copies during a groupby-shift can exceed available memory well before the raw data would suggest.

`groupby` followed by `shift` or `rolling` should be applied within each group, `df.groupby("station_id")["speed"].shift(3)`, not on the whole table at once, or values leak across station boundaries, a classic and easy mistake that produces a plausible-looking but wrong lag feature. pandas 2.x's optional Arrow-backed dtypes and nullable integer types change some of these performance and correctness tradeoffs, proper NA handling for integers, less memory for strings, but are not yet the default, so most code still lives with float64-only NaN semantics, where an integer column touched by any missing value silently becomes float. Method chaining versus intermediate variables is a real style tradeoff: chains are compact but harder to debug, since inserting a print or breakpoint mid-chain requires restructuring the code. A frequent practitioner mistake is comparing floats for exact equality after a groupby or merge, when floating-point aggregation can introduce tiny differences that make equality comparisons fail unpredictably.

At production data-pipeline scale, pandas's single-machine, in-memory model is the limiting factor, which is why teams move to Arrow-native tools or distributed systems once a table stops fitting comfortably in RAM or a job needs to run in parallel across machines. pandas remains dominant for the get-from-a-few-files-to-a-clean-feature-table phase of a project because of its ecosystem, nearly every ML and visualization library expects a DataFrame-shaped input, even as faster engines take over the heavy transforms underneath it. The open practical tension in real ML pipelines is keeping the same feature logic correct and identical between an interactive pandas prototype and whatever faster or distributed engine eventually replaces it in production, since subtle semantic differences, NaN handling, join behavior, sort stability, between engines are a common source of train and serve skew.

terms.def: A DataFrame is a table with named columns; a Series is one column. Selecting a column gives a Series.
levels: A DataFrame is like a big table you'd draw on paper, with rows for each thing and columns for each fact about it, except the computer can read and change it super fast. If you point at just one column, like everyone's age, that column alone is called a Series. Think of a DataFrame as a whole spreadsheet and a Series as one column of it.

A DataFrame is pandas's table: rows of data with named columns, similar to a spreadsheet but controlled entirely by code. In Traffic1, a DataFrame might have columns `station_id`, `timestamp`, `speed`, and `label`, with one row for every station at every five-minute interval. Picking a single column, like `df['speed']`, gives back a Series, a one-dimensional list of values with an index attached. You can filter rows, add new columns, and compute summaries on a DataFrame using pandas methods.

A DataFrame is a two-dimensional pandas object with an index, row labels, and columns, each column being a Series with its own dtype, int, float, string, datetime, and so on. `df.head()`, `df.shape`, and `df.dtypes` are the standard first checks after loading data. Selecting one column with `df['speed']` or `df.speed` returns a Series; selecting several columns with `df[['speed', 'station_id']]` returns a DataFrame. Operations broadcast across a Series the way they do across a numpy array, so `df['speed'] * 1.60934` converts an entire column from miles per hour to kilometers per hour in one line without a loop.

A DataFrame is backed by columnar storage, historically numpy arrays per column, increasingly Arrow-backed, which makes column-wise operations fast because each column is contiguous and typed, but makes row-wise operations comparatively slow, which is why idiomatic pandas code favors vectorized column operations over `.iterrows()`. The index is not just row numbers, it can be a meaningful key, like a timestamp, that operations like joins and groupby use for alignment, and misunderstanding this is a frequent source of subtle bugs when two DataFrames with different indices are combined and rows silently fail to match. groupby followed by transform versus agg versus apply differ in output shape and are a common point of confusion: transform returns something the same length as the input, so it can become a new column, while agg collapses each group to one row. Memory for a DataFrame is roughly rows times columns times bytes-per-value, so dtype choices, float32 versus float64, category versus object for strings, materially affect whether a multi-year PeMS extract fits in memory.

pandas's traditional numpy-backed DataFrame has real limitations at scale, no zero-copy interop with other tools, weak native support for missing values in integer columns, and single-machine, mostly single-threaded execution, which is why the ecosystem has grown Arrow-backed pandas 2.x, Polars, and distributed frameworks that expose similar mental models with different performance characteristics. A subtlety many practitioners get wrong is chained indexing, `df[df.speed < 20]['label'] = 1`, which can silently write to a copy rather than the original DataFrame, pandas will sometimes warn about this, and the fix is `.loc` with a single indexing operation. Another common mistake is treating groupby operations as free; grouping a large DataFrame by a high-cardinality key like `station_id` and calling `.apply()` with a Python function forfeits vectorization and can be orders of magnitude slower than an equivalent transform or a vectorized groupby method. Time-series-specific gotchas, a DataFrame not sorted by timestamp before a lag or rolling computation, or an index with duplicate timestamps after a resample, produce wrong numbers without an error, which is why validating the index's monotonicity and uniqueness is a standard first step.

At production scale, DataFrame-shaped computation runs on distributed engines, Spark, Ray, or internal systems, where the DataFrame API is preserved as an interface but the execution model, lazy evaluation, query planning, columnar shuffle, is entirely different from single-machine pandas, and code that works correctly on a pandas DataFrame can behave subtly differently, different NaN handling, different join semantics, when ported to a distributed one. Feature engineering pipelines increasingly compile a DataFrame-like specification to both a batch engine, for training, and a streaming engine, for serving, because keeping training and serving feature computation in sync by hand is a major source of production bugs, training-serving skew. The open problem is unifying the ergonomics of pandas-style exploratory analysis with the correctness guarantees and performance of a distributed, typed, lazily-evaluated engine, without forcing every data scientist to learn a fundamentally different programming model.

terms.def: The library for fast arithmetic on arrays. `np.sin`, `np.mean`, `X @ w` work on whole arrays at once.
levels: numpy is a toolbox that lets the computer do math on a whole list of numbers at once, instead of one at a time. It is like having a magic calculator that can add a hundred pairs of numbers together in one button press instead of a hundred button presses. `np.mean` is one of its buttons, and pressing it finds the average of a whole list instantly.

numpy is a Python library for working with arrays, which are grids of numbers, and for doing arithmetic on the whole grid at once instead of writing a loop. `np.array([1, 2, 3]) * 2` gives `[2, 4, 6]` without a single explicit loop in your own code, because numpy does the looping internally, in fast compiled code. `np.mean(x)` gives the average of an array, and `np.sin(x)` applies sine to every element at once. This course uses numpy both directly and underneath pandas, since a pandas column is really a numpy array with row labels attached.

A numpy array (`ndarray`) has a fixed shape and a single data type for all its elements, unlike a Python list, which lets numpy store it compactly and process it with vectorized, compiled loops instead of the slow Python interpreter loop. `X @ w` computes a matrix-vector product (equivalent to `np.dot(X, w)`), which is exactly the score computation `w·x` behind logistic regression, done for every row of `X` at once. Broadcasting lets numpy combine arrays of different but compatible shapes, so `x - x.mean()` subtracts a single number from every element of an array without writing a loop. `np.random.default_rng(seed)` gives a reproducible source of randomness, important for splitting data or initializing weights the same way every run.

numpy's speed comes from storing arrays as contiguous blocks of memory of a single dtype and delegating the actual arithmetic to compiled C and Fortran routines (via BLAS/LAPACK for linear algebra), so a vectorized operation like `X @ w` runs orders of magnitude faster than an equivalent pure-Python loop over rows. Broadcasting rules are precise but easy to misuse: two shapes are compatible if, comparing from the trailing dimension, sizes match or one of them is 1, and getting this wrong silently produces a differently-shaped result rather than an error, which is a common source of subtle bugs. numpy assumes dense, rectangular data with a known dtype; it is a poor fit for ragged data (rows of different lengths) or heterogeneous columns, which is exactly why pandas exists as a labeled, mixed-type layer on top of it. Integer overflow is a real risk with numpy's fixed-width integer types (`int32` silently wraps around on overflow rather than raising an error the way Python's arbitrary-precision integers do), which matters for anything that sums a lot of counts.

The performance ceiling of pure numpy is the memory bandwidth of moving whole arrays through intermediate temporaries; an expression like `a * b + c` on large arrays allocates a temporary for `a * b` before adding `c`, and libraries like `numexpr` or writing the loop in a compiled extension exist precisely to avoid that overhead when arrays are large enough for it to matter, a distinction most practitioners never need to think about until a memory profile forces the question. The BLAS backend numpy is linked against (OpenBLAS, MKL, Apple's Accelerate framework) changes both speed and, in floating point, the exact bit-for-bit result of operations like matrix multiplication, because summation order differs across backends, which is why 'the same' numpy code can give a result that differs in the last few decimal digits on different machines. A common misconception is that numpy operations are always faster than a Python loop; for very small arrays the fixed overhead of dispatching into compiled code can make numpy slower than a tight Python loop, and vectorizing an operation that is inherently sequential (like a recursive filter) can require real cleverness or simply is not possible. `np.float64` versus `np.float32` is a real precision-versus-memory tradeoff that matters once arrays reach the scale of this course's ten-million-row PeMS panel.

In production ML systems, numpy is rarely the final compute engine; it is the reference implementation and the interchange format that faster systems (compiled kernels, GPU arrays via frameworks that mimic its API, Arrow-backed columnar engines) are validated against, precisely because its semantics are well specified and widely trusted. Apple's on-device and server ML stacks run the equivalent arithmetic through Accelerate, Metal Performance Shaders or custom kernels for real workloads, keeping numpy mainly for prototyping, testing and small-scale feature engineering, since numpy's single-threaded, CPU-only default execution does not scale to production inference volumes. An open engineering problem is numerical reproducibility across this stack: a model trained with numpy-based features on one BLAS backend and served with a different backend or precision downstream can drift in ways too small to catch in ordinary testing but large enough to matter for a threshold-sensitive decision, which is why serious ML infrastructure pins BLAS versions and precision explicitly rather than trusting defaults.

terms.def: A grid of numbers: one-dimensional (vector), two-dimensional (matrix), or more. PyTorch calls its arrays tensors.
levels: An array is a row of number boxes lined up like an egg carton. A matrix is a grid of them, like a chessboard of numbers. A tensor is what grown-ups call it once the grid has more dimensions than you can draw.

A one-dimensional array, also called a vector, is a list of numbers, like the speeds at one station over an hour. A two-dimensional array, a matrix, is a table of numbers with rows and columns, like every station's speed at every five-minute slot. In PyTorch, arrays of any number of dimensions are called tensors, and `torch.tensor([1,2,3])` makes one.

NumPy stores an array's numbers as one flat block of memory plus a shape describing how to read it as rows and columns, which is why operations like `np.exp(arr)` run fast, they act on the whole block at once instead of looping in Python. `X.shape` for a feature table might be `(50000, 20)`, 50000 rows, 20 columns. A PyTorch tensor adds two things an array doesn't have by default: it can live on a GPU, and it can track gradients for backpropagation.

The core assumption behind array-based computing is that most numerical work is naturally expressed as elementwise or broadcasted operations over whole arrays rather than explicit loops, and the underlying implementation exploits that to avoid Python's per-element overhead, often a hundredfold speedup. Broadcasting rules, aligning shapes from the right, stretching size-1 dimensions, let arrays of shapes like `(1000, 5)` and `(5,)` combine without an explicit loop, but silently produce wrong results when shapes accidentally broadcast in an unintended way rather than raising an error. A matrix multiply, `@`, versus an elementwise multiply, `*`, is a common source of shape-mismatch bugs for anyone moving from scalar to array thinking. Tensors extend this to GPUs by mapping the same elementwise and matrix operations onto thousands of parallel cores.

Memory layout, row-major versus column-major order, determines which axis is contiguous in memory, and operations that traverse the non-contiguous axis are slower than they look, a subtlety that shows up in profiling but rarely in tutorials. Practitioners get bitten by implicit dtype upcasting, mixing int32 and float64 silently promotes everything to float64, doubling memory, and by views versus copies, a sliced array can share memory with the original, so mutating it mutates the original unexpectedly. The tradeoff tensors add over plain arrays, autograd bookkeeping and device placement, costs memory and adds a class of bugs, a tensor accidentally left on CPU when the model is on GPU, that arrays never had.

At production scale, array and tensor computation is inseparable from hardware: compilers like XLA and MLIR fuse chains of elementwise and matrix operations into single kernels tuned for the target accelerator, GPU, TPU, or a neural engine, because the naive sequence of separate calls each round-trips through memory and leaves most of the hardware's throughput unused. Quantization, storing a tensor's values in int8 or lower instead of float32, trades numerical precision for memory bandwidth and is now standard for on-device inference. Open research continues on sparse and structured tensor representations that skip storing and computing over the often-majority of near-zero values in large models, since dense array assumptions increasingly overstate the compute actually needed.

terms.def: The size of each dimension of an array, such as (rows, columns) or (batch, time, channel, station). Most deep-learning bugs are shape bugs.
levels: If you stack blocks into a rectangle, the shape is how many rows tall and how many blocks wide it is. A table of numbers has a shape too: how many rows and how many columns.

The shape of an array tells you its size along each dimension. A table with 1,000 rows and 5 columns has shape `(1000, 5)`; in pandas, `df.shape` gives you exactly that as a pair of numbers. For a deep learning model, arrays can have more dimensions, so a batch of 32 examples, each with 10 time steps and 4 sensor readings, has shape `(32, 10, 4)`, and every layer of the model expects its input to arrive in a particular shape.

`array.shape` returns a tuple, one number per dimension, in order; `numpy` and `pandas` both use this, and PyTorch tensors use `.shape` or `.size()` the same way. A common real shape in this course is `(batch, time, station)` for a window of recent readings across several detector stations feeding a recurrent model, versus `(rows, features)` for the flat table logistic regression and LightGBM expect. Mismatched shapes are the single most common runtime error in model code, since `matmul` fails immediately if the inner dimensions don't agree, so printing `.shape` after each transformation is standard practice for debugging.

Shape mismatches surface at very different points depending on the operation: some (matrix multiplication, concatenation along a fixed axis) fail loudly and immediately, while broadcasting rules in numpy and PyTorch will silently "fix" a shape mismatch by expanding a smaller array, which is convenient when intended and a serious silent bug when not, since a `(100,)` array broadcasting against a `(100, 1)` array instead of raising an error is a classic trap. Reshaping (`.reshape`, `.view`, `.transpose`) changes how the same underlying data is interpreted, and confusing `.reshape` with `.transpose`, since the first reinterprets memory layout and the second actually permutes axes, is a common source of models that train without error but learn nothing useful, because the data reaching each parameter is scrambled relative to what the architecture assumes. For sequence and graph models specifically, getting the batch, time and feature or node axes in the order a layer expects (`batch_first=True` or not, for instance) is exactly the kind of shape detail that has no visible symptom besides poor accuracy until you print shapes at every step.

Shape bugs are insidious specifically because many operations degrade gracefully rather than crashing: broadcasting, implicit type promotion, and squeeze or unsqueeze mismatches can all produce a tensor of a plausible-looking shape that is nonetheless semantically wrong, so a model can train, converge, and even report a reasonable loss while learning from corrupted or misaligned data. A related subtlety is that shape correctness is necessary but not sufficient: two tensors can have identical shape while their axes carry different meaning, such as station-major versus time-major ordering, which no shape check catches and which only a semantic assertion or a unit test on known input can catch. Practitioners commonly under-invest in shape assertions (`assert x.shape == (batch, T, S)`) at module boundaries, treating them as clutter, right up until a refactor silently swaps two axes and a week of training runs on scrambled data before anyone notices. In graph and spatiotemporal models specifically, the number of axes that matter grows (batch, time, node, channel, and sometimes edge), and the einsum-style explicit notation (`'btnc,cd->btnd'`) is often worth the verbosity precisely because it makes every axis's role unambiguous.

At production scale, shape contracts between components, a data pipeline, a feature store, a model, a serving layer, are often enforced with typed schemas and shape-checked interfaces (via tools like `jaxtyping`, `torchtyping`, or protocol buffers with fixed dimensions) precisely because a silent shape or axis-order mismatch between two independently deployed services is one of the more common causes of an ML incident that produces plausible-looking but wrong outputs rather than a visible crash. Dynamic and variable shapes, such as a variable number of active stations on a graph or ragged sequence lengths, push teams toward padding-and-masking schemes or sparse tensor formats, each with real performance tradeoffs on accelerator hardware that favor fixed, regular shapes. An open engineering problem is verifying shape and semantic axis-order correctness automatically across a pipeline of independently versioned components, rather than relying on runtime asserts that only catch a mismatch after it has already reached production.

terms.def: The row labels of a DataFrame. A MultiIndex has more than one level, such as (station, timestamp). `reset_index` turns levels back into columns.
levels: An index is like the name tags on a row of lockers, so you can find locker number 7 without opening every single one. In a table of numbers, the index tells you which row is which. It is the label, not the stuff inside.

The index of a DataFrame is the set of labels for its rows, similar to how a spreadsheet has row numbers down the left side, except an index can be more meaningful, like a date or a station name. A MultiIndex uses more than one label per row at once, for example a station id together with a timestamp, so you can find one station's one time slot directly. `reset_index()` turns those labels back into ordinary columns if you want to work with them as regular data.

A DataFrame's index is a separate structure from its columns: it labels each row and is used for fast lookups and alignment, for example `df.loc['station_5']` finds rows by label rather than by position. A `MultiIndex` stacks more than one level of labels, like `(station_id, timestamp)`, so `df.loc[(5, '2024-01-01 08:00')]` finds one specific row directly rather than filtering. `set_index(['station_id', 'timestamp'])` builds this structure from existing columns, and `reset_index()` reverses it, moving the index levels back into ordinary columns. Sorting the index (`sort_index()`) matters for performance and for operations like forward fill that depend on row order being meaningful.

The index exists to make row alignment explicit and fast: operations between two DataFrames or Series automatically align on the index, which is powerful (joining by label is one line) and dangerous (a mismatched or duplicated index silently produces `NaN`s or duplicated rows instead of an error). A MultiIndex over `(station_id, timestamp)` is the natural structure for panel data like PeMS readings, because it lets you group, slice, and shift within one station's time series without accidentally crossing into another station's rows — `df.groupby(level='station_id')` and `.shift()` within groups both rely on this. Index alignment has a real performance cost if the index is not sorted or not unique; pandas warns about this, and a common fix is `df.sort_index()` right after building a MultiIndex. `reset_index()` is often used right before merging with another table that expects plain columns, since `merge` operates on columns by default while `join` operates on the index. Getting index handling wrong — for example, resetting it and losing station boundaries — is a common, quiet source of the leakage bugs this course warns about.

Index-based alignment is one of pandas' most powerful and most misused features: arithmetic between two Series with different indexes reindexes both to their union and fills mismatches with `NaN` rather than raising an error, which means a subtle bug (an off-by-one in a shift, or a duplicate timestamp from a daylight-saving transition) can silently propagate `NaN`s through a computation instead of crashing where the bug was introduced. A duplicate index — two rows both labeled `(station_5, 08:00)`, for instance from a sensor that reported twice — turns a `.loc[]` lookup that expects one row into one that returns two, breaking code downstream in ways that are hard to trace back to the index. Performance-sensitive pipelines care about whether the index is a `RangeIndex` (cheap, implicit) versus an explicit label index (more expensive to construct and query, though `sort_index()` mitigates the cost with binary search); building and resetting large MultiIndexes repeatedly in a loop is a common, avoidable performance mistake. Practitioners moving from R or SQL sometimes fight the index model entirely and reset it everywhere, giving up its alignment guarantees along with its footguns — a defensible choice for correctness-first pipelines, at some cost in code compactness.

At the scale of distributed dataframes (Spark, Dask, Polars), the pandas notion of a mutable, label-based index mostly disappears — these systems favor explicit joins on columns and avoid implicit alignment altogether, precisely because the silent-`NaN`-on-mismatch behavior that is manageable on a single machine becomes a serious correctness risk when data is partitioned across a cluster and alignment can hide a partitioning bug. This is part of a broader trend in production data engineering: systems increasingly favor explicit, checked joins over implicit, index-based ones, treating pandas' convenience as something to be careful with rather than to lean on once a pipeline moves from a notebook to a scheduled job.

terms.def: A column of true/false, one per row, used to select rows: `df[df.speed < 35]`.
levels: A boolean mask is like putting a sticker on every row that says yes or no, and then you only keep the rows with a yes sticker.

A boolean mask is a column of True and False values, one for each row of a table, made by writing a comparison like `df.speed < 35`. Putting that mask inside square brackets, `df[df.speed < 35]`, keeps only the rows where the comparison was True. This is the main way to filter rows in pandas without writing a loop.

`df.speed < 35` compares every value in the `speed` column to 35 and returns a new column of booleans, the same length as `df`, one True or False per row. `df[mask]` then keeps only the rows where the mask is True, so `df[df.speed < 35]` returns every row where speed is below 35. Masks combine with `&` (and) and `|` (or), each side wrapped in parentheses: `df[(df.speed < 35) & (df.pct_obs > 50)]` keeps slow rows that are also well-observed.

A boolean mask works because pandas, and numpy underneath it, support elementwise comparison and indexing: the comparison produces an array of the same shape as the original, and indexing with that array is vectorized, evaluated in compiled C rather than a Python loop, which is why `df[mask]` is both idiomatic and fast on large tables. Masks compose with assignment too: `df.loc[mask, "speed"] = np.nan` sets a value only in the rows where the mask is True, which is exactly how this course's cleaning stage blanks impossible or low-confidence readings. A common failure mode is chained indexing, `df[mask]["speed"] = x`, which can silently write to a temporary copy instead of the original DataFrame; `df.loc[mask, "speed"] = x` avoids the ambiguity.

Boolean masking's elegance hides a real cost at scale: each mask allocates a new boolean array the size of the table, and chaining several conditions creates several intermediate arrays, which matters when a table has tens of millions of rows and memory, not compute, is the binding constraint, as it is on this project's 16 GB machine. NaN complicates masks in a way beginners miss: any comparison against NaN returns False, so `df.speed < 35` silently excludes already-missing rows rather than raising an error, which is usually the desired behavior but needs to be checked, not assumed. Practitioners sometimes reach for masks where `query()` or a database-style filter, in DuckDB or SQL, would be both faster and more memory-efficient at real scale, because those engines can push the filter down before materializing full columns rather than building an explicit mask array first.

At the scale where a single DataFrame no longer fits comfortably in memory, boolean masking's core idea, predicate-based row selection, survives but the implementation changes: columnar engines like DuckDB, Spark, or Arrow-backed pandas push predicates down into the storage layer, filtering during a scan rather than materializing a full mask over an already-loaded table. The recurring production lesson is that masking logic, which rows count as valid, out of range, or trustworthy, is itself part of the model and needs the same versioning and testing discipline as the model's weights, since a silently changed cleaning threshold can shift a metric as much as a real model change would.

terms.def: Select by label (`.loc[row, column]`) or by position (`.iloc[0]`). Assigning to `.loc[mask, col]` changes only the masked rows.
levels: Imagine a row of numbered mailboxes with names taped on them. `.iloc` finds a mailbox by counting boxes from the start, while `.loc` finds it by reading the name taped on it.

In pandas, `.loc` selects rows and columns of a DataFrame by their labels (the index value and column name), while `.iloc` selects by plain position, counting from 0, no matter what the labels say. `df.loc[5, "speed"]` gets the value in the row labeled 5 and the column named speed; `df.iloc[0, 1]` gets the value in the first row and second column, wherever it is. You can also use a true/false mask with `.loc`, like `df.loc[df["speed"] < 20, "is_slow"] = True`, which changes only the rows where the condition is true.

`.loc[row_label, col_label]` indexes by label and includes both endpoints when given a slice (`.loc[3:5]` returns rows labeled 3, 4 and 5); `.iloc[row_pos, col_pos]` indexes by integer position and excludes the end, like Python slicing (`.iloc[3:5]` returns two rows). The distinction matters most after filtering or sorting, when a DataFrame's index no longer matches row position 0, 1, 2, `.iloc[0]` after a sort gives the first row in the new order, while `.loc[0]` gives whatever row still carries the label 0, which may be somewhere else entirely. Assignment through `.loc` with a boolean mask, `df.loc[df["speed"] < 20, "is_slow"] = 1`, only touches the rows the mask selects and leaves the rest of the column untouched, which is the safe way to conditionally modify a DataFrame in place.

The label-versus-position distinction reflects a deeper design choice in pandas: the index is data, it can be a date, a station id, anything meaningful, that survives operations like filtering and sorting, so `.loc` lets code refer to 'this specific row' stably across transformations, while `.iloc` refers to 'whatever is currently in this position,' which is only stable if nothing has reordered the data since. Chained indexing, like `df[mask]["col"] = value`, is a common and dangerous anti-pattern that pandas warns about because it may operate on a copy rather than the original DataFrame; `df.loc[mask, "col"] = value` avoids the ambiguity by doing the selection and assignment in one call. `.loc` with a boolean mask is also how conditional feature engineering is usually written in this course, for example labeling a row 'slow' relative to a station's own historical median speed. Both accessors raise an error on an out-of-range label or position, rather than silently returning `None`, which is a deliberate fail-loud design.

Performance differs meaningfully at scale: `.iloc` on a default RangeIndex is effectively array indexing and very fast, while `.loc` on a non-unique or unsorted index can force pandas into a linear scan, so a DataFrame with a duplicated or unsorted datetime index used heavily with `.loc` can become a real bottleneck without any error to signal it, profiling, not intuition, is the way to catch this. A subtler correctness issue is that `.loc` with a slice on a sorted index is inclusive of both ends, but on an unsorted index the behavior of a slice is undefined and pandas will raise, which surprises people coming from plain Python slicing habits. Practitioners frequently reset the index after a groupby or filter specifically to get back to a clean integer index where `.iloc` and `.loc` coincide, trading away whatever meaning the previous index carried for positional simplicity. Multi-indexed DataFrames complicate `.loc` further, since a tuple of labels is required per level, and partial indexing silently returns a sub-frame rather than a scalar if not all levels are specified.

At production data-pipeline scale, `.loc`/`.iloc`-style row-and-label semantics generalize to distributed frameworks (Spark, Dask, Polars), each of which makes different tradeoffs about whether a stable row label even exists across a cluster of machines, Spark DataFrames, for instance, have no guaranteed row order or label at all, which is a real behavioral gap when porting research code written against pandas's `.loc` semantics to a production-scale system. Vectorized, label-aware indexing like this is also foundational to how time-series feature pipelines avoid subtle look-ahead bugs: selecting by a timestamp label rather than a row position is what lets code stay correct even as new data is appended in front of or behind existing rows. The open engineering concern is less about `.loc` itself than about teams building brittle pipelines around pandas's positional guarantees that silently stop holding once the same logic is scaled onto a distributed engine.

terms.def: Split a table into groups by a key, compute something per group, and combine. `groupby("station_id").size()` counts rows per station.
levels: Imagine sorting a big pile of toys into bins by color, then counting how many are in each bin. groupby is the computer doing that sorting-and-counting for you, but with rows of a table instead of toys.

groupby splits a table into smaller groups based on a column's value, does something to each group separately, and then puts the results back together. `df.groupby("station_id").size()` splits the table into one group per station and counts how many rows are in each group. This pattern, split, apply a computation, combine the results, is called split-apply-combine, and it is one of the most common things you do with a table.

The general form is `df.groupby(key).agg(function)`, where key is one or more columns and function is something like mean, sum, size, or a custom function. `df.groupby("station_id")["speed"].mean()` gives the average speed for each station, as a new smaller table indexed by station_id. You can group by more than one column at once, like `df.groupby(["station_id", "hour"])`, to compute something per station per hour. `describe()` chained after a groupby is a fast way to check every station has roughly the same number of rows.

Internally, groupby builds an index mapping each group key to the row positions belonging to it, then applies the aggregation function to each group's slice; for a built-in aggregation like mean or sum, pandas uses a fast, vectorized path, but a custom Python function passed via `.apply()` falls back to a slow per-group Python call. Grouping keys can include multiple columns, producing a MultiIndex on the result, which then needs `reset_index()` to turn back into flat columns for merging elsewhere. A frequent correctness bug is calling `shift` or `rolling` on the whole table when the intent was per-group; the fix is `df.groupby(key)[col].shift(n)`, which resets the window at every group boundary instead of sliding across them. It fails to produce a meaningful result silently, not with an error, when a NaN key value is dropped from the groups by default, quietly discarding those rows from the output.

`.transform()` versus `.apply()` versus `.agg()` are subtly different: agg returns one row per group, transform returns a result the same length as the input aligned back to the original rows, useful for something like each row's deviation from its station's mean, and apply is the general but slowest escape hatch that can return either shape depending on what the function does. A groupby-shift on a large table can be memory-expensive because pandas may hold the grouped index, the sorted intermediate, and the output simultaneously; sorting the DataFrame by the group key first and using a lower-level approach is a common optimization once this becomes a bottleneck. `observed=True` matters for categorical group keys: by default groupby can materialize every combination of categories, including ones that never occur in the data, wasting memory and confusing downstream code that did not expect empty groups. Practitioners commonly get burned by silently changed row order: a naive groupby-then-concat can reorder rows relative to the original table, which breaks code downstream that assumed positional alignment.

At scale, groupby-shaped computations are exactly what distributed engines reimplement with partitioning strategies designed to avoid shuffling all of one group's data onto a single machine, which single-machine pandas does not need to worry about but which becomes the dominant cost once data is sharded across a cluster. Feature stores in production ML systems are largely built around precomputing groupby aggregations, per-user, per-station, per-item, because computing them on the fly at prediction latency is too slow; the open engineering problem is keeping those precomputed aggregations correctly time-bounded, so a feature used to predict at time t never accidentally includes information from after t.

terms.def: A groupby method that returns a result the same length as the input, so it can be stored as a new column.
levels: Imagine every kid in class gets a sticker showing how they compare to their own table group, like you are the tallest at your table. transform is the computer's way of giving everyone their own personal sticker like that, one per row, without shrinking the list down. Nobody disappears, everyone still gets an answer.

transform is a pandas method used after groupby that gives back one value per original row, unlike a plain summary that gives back one value per group. For example, grouping traffic rows by `station_id` and calling `transform('mean')` on the speed column gives every row that station's average speed, right next to its own reading. Because the result is the same length as the input, you can save it straight into a new column, like `df['station_avg_speed'] = df.groupby('station_id')['speed'].transform('mean')`. This is different from `groupby(...).mean()`, which would collapse the data down to one row per station.

transform operates within each group defined by groupby and broadcasts a group-level result back to every row in that group, so `df.groupby('station_id')['speed'].transform('mean')` returns a Series exactly as long as `df`, aligned to its original index. It accepts a string name of a built-in aggregation, mean, std, rank, or a custom function, and unlike `.apply()`, transform requires the function to either return a scalar, broadcast to the group, or a same-length result. A typical use in Traffic1 is z-scoring speed within each station: subtracting the station's transformed mean and dividing by the station's transformed standard deviation. This differs from `.agg()`, which returns one row per group rather than one row per original row.

transform is the natural tool whenever a feature needs to compare a row to its group without losing the row-level granularity, which describes most within-entity normalization: station-relative speed, day-relative traffic volume, or user-relative rating in other domains. Under the hood, pandas computes the grouped result once per group and then maps it back onto every row belonging to that group via the group's index, which is efficient because the aggregation itself is vectorized even though the broadcast touches every row. A common mistake is using transform with a Python-level custom function when a built-in aggregation would do, a lambda passed to transform loses much of the C-level speed that a named aggregation like mean gets, which matters once station groups have millions of rows across years of PeMS data. transform versus apply versus agg is a frequent source of confusion precisely because all three accept similar function arguments but return outputs of different shapes, and getting this wrong produces either a shape mismatch error or, worse, a silently misaligned column.

The efficiency of transform depends heavily on whether the underlying operation has a fast, vectorized groupby implementation, mean, std, rank, cumsum, versus requiring a Python callback per group, and profiling a slow feature pipeline often reveals a transform call with a custom lambda as the bottleneck, fixable by rewriting it in terms of built-in aggregations or numpy operations. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is leakage through transform: computing a station's mean speed via transform over the entire dataset, including future rows relative to some prediction time, silently leaks future information into a feature meant to describe the past, the fix is either an expanding or rolling transform restricted to data available at prediction time, or explicitly computing the statistic only on the training window and merging it in. Group-wise transform also interacts awkwardly with time ordering: if the DataFrame is not sorted by timestamp within each station group before a rolling transform, the rolling window is computed over rows in whatever order they happen to be in, not chronological order, producing numbers that look plausible but are wrong.

At the scale of feature pipelines that must run identically in batch, training, and streaming, serving, a groupby-transform operation has to be reimplemented as a stateful streaming aggregate, a running mean per station updated incrementally as new PeMS rows arrive, which is a fundamentally different computational model from pandas's batch-oriented transform, and keeping the two mathematically equivalent, same window, same handling of missing data, is a recurring source of training-serving skew. Feature stores exist partly to solve this by letting engineers define a transform-like aggregation once and having the system compile it to both a batch job and a streaming job automatically. The open research and engineering problem is making that compilation general enough to cover the full range of transforms data scientists actually write, including custom ones, without falling back to batch and streaming being maintained by hand and hope they agree.

terms.def: Line two tables up on shared key columns and combine their other columns. `how="left"` keeps every row of the left table.
levels: Merging two tables is like putting two lists side by side and drawing lines between the rows that are about the same person. If your class has a list of names and another list of favorite colors, merging lines up each name with their color into one combined list. If someone's color is missing, a left merge still keeps them on the list, just with a blank where the color should be.

A merge (also called a join) combines two tables by matching rows that share the same value in a key column, like a station ID or a timestamp, and putting their other columns side by side in one new table. `pd.merge(left, right, on='station_id')` matches rows in both tables where `station_id` is equal. `how='left'` keeps every row from the left table even if there is no match in the right table, filling missing values with NaN, while `how='inner'` keeps only rows that matched in both. This course uses merges to attach the station registry (freeway, neighbors) onto raw sensor rows.

`pd.merge(sensor_df, registry_df, on='station_id', how='left')` keeps every row of `sensor_df` and adds the registry's columns wherever `station_id` matches, leaving NaN in those new columns for any sensor row whose station is not in the registry. The `how` parameter controls behavior on unmatched rows: `'inner'` drops rows with no match on either side, `'left'` keeps all left rows, `'right'` keeps all right rows, and `'outer'` keeps everything, filling gaps with NaN. Merging on a non-unique key can multiply rows, called a fan-out: if the right table has three rows per key and the left has one, the merged result has three rows for that key, which is a common source of an unexpectedly larger row count after a merge. Checking row counts before and after a merge, or using pandas's `validate='one_to_many'` argument, catches this kind of mistake early.

A relational join's cost and behavior depend on the cardinality of the key in each table: one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many joins behave very differently, and a many-to-many join on a key that is not actually meant to repeat almost always indicates a data problem rather than an intended fan-out. Merging on floating-point or timestamp columns is fragile because exact equality rarely holds after any transformation, so time-based joins typically use `pd.merge_asof`, which matches each row to the nearest earlier (or later) row in the other table within a tolerance, rather than an exact merge. Merge performance on large tables depends on whether the key columns are indexed and sorted; an unindexed merge on a ten-million-row table can be substantially slower than the same merge on a pre-sorted, indexed one. A left merge is the right default whenever the analysis's unit of observation is defined by the left table (every sensor reading, say) and the right table (station metadata) is auxiliary information that should never cause rows to disappear.

The subtlety practitioners miss most often is that a merge can silently introduce leakage if the right-hand table encodes information that was not actually available at the time represented by the left-hand row — joining in a station's 'typical speed profile' computed using the full dataset, including future dates relative to a given training row, leaks future information into a supposedly time-respecting feature. Merge semantics also interact badly with duplicate or near-duplicate keys from upstream data quality issues; a station ID that appears twice in the registry due to a data entry error silently fans out every sensor row for that station, inflating the training set without an obvious symptom besides a slightly larger table. `merge_asof` requires both frames to be sorted on the join key beforehand, and getting the `direction` argument wrong (matching to a future row instead of a past one) is a specific, easy-to-make leakage bug in exactly this kind of time-series feature engineering. At scale, an inner join that appears to work correctly on a sample can behave differently on the full data if the key's match rate is not actually representative of the sample, which is why validating merge assumptions against the full dataset, not just a development slice, matters.

In production data pipelines, joins of this kind run inside distributed query engines (Spark, BigQuery, or Apple's internal equivalents) rather than in a single pandas process, and the cardinality and leakage issues above become correctness and cost problems simultaneously: an accidental fan-out join can silently multiply a petabyte-scale table's size and blow through a job's memory or time budget. Feature stores are partly a response to exactly this class of bug: they formalize point-in-time-correct joins (joining each row only to information that existed as of that row's timestamp) as a first-class, tested operation rather than something every pipeline reimplements by hand and gets subtly wrong. An open engineering question is how to make these point-in-time joins both efficient and hard to misuse by default, since the naive, easiest-to-write join is almost always the leaky one, and the safe version requires either careful discipline or infrastructure that enforces it.

terms.def: Move a column down by k rows (a lag). A negative k moves it up, which looks into the future: allowed only for targets.
levels: Shift is like everyone in a line taking one step back and leaving an empty spot at the front. The number tells you how many steps to take.

`shift(k)` moves every value in a column down by k rows, leaving the first k rows empty, NaN, because nothing was above them to move into their place. `df.speed.shift(3)` creates a column showing what the speed was three rows earlier, exactly a lag feature: what the model knew fifteen minutes ago on a five-minute grid.

`df['speed_lag_3'] = df.speed.shift(3)` shifts values down by 3 rows; the value that used to sit at row 100 now sits at row 103, and rows 0 through 2 become NaN because there is nothing above them. A negative argument shifts up instead: `df.shift(-6)` moves row 106's value up to row 100, looking six rows into the future, so it is used only to build the target column, never a feature, or the model would train on information it cannot have at prediction time. `df.groupby('station_id').speed.shift(3)` shifts within each station separately so a lag never crosses from one station's data into another's.

A positive shift is always safe to use as a feature because it only reaches into the past, while a negative shift reaches into the future and defines the label the model is trying to predict, so mixing the two up, accidentally training on a negative-shifted column as a feature, is the single most common way to leak the answer into the inputs. Shift assumes rows are already sorted by time within each group; an unsorted DataFrame produces a shift that is nonsense but doesn't error, a silent-failure risk. At the boundaries of the data, start and end of each month's file, or a gap where a station went offline, shift produces NaN rows that must be dropped before training rather than imputed, since there is no honest value for 'the reading fifteen minutes ago' when fifteen minutes ago doesn't exist in the file.

`shift` is the atomic operation behind almost every classical time-series feature, lags, rolling statistics, differences, and its main pitfall in practice is scope: shifting on a DataFrame sorted globally by time but not grouped by station silently pulls in another station's last reading as this station's lag, a bug that will not raise an error and will look like real signal in a naive train and validation split, since it inflates apparent accuracy through a form of leakage. A related subtlety: at inference time in a streaming setting, `shift(3)` on a static DataFrame and 'the reading three steps ago from a growing buffer' are the same operation conceptually, but implementing the second one correctly, right buffer size, no off-by-one at the boundary, is where most production time-series bugs actually live, not in the training-time pandas code.

In production feature pipelines, `shift`-based lag computation moves from a single-machine pandas call to a window function in a distributed engine, `LAG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY ts)` in SQL, or a streaming state store keyed by station, and the two must be proven to produce identical results, a routine and easy-to-get-wrong reconciliation between offline training features and online serving features. Feature stores increasingly compute and cache these lag features once, shared across many models, rather than recomputing per model, since the same handful of lags, 3, 6, 12 steps, tend to recur across a whole traffic-prediction product line.

terms.def: A window of the last n rows; `.mean()`, `.std()`, `.sum()`, `.max()` summarize it. Rows must be in time order first.
levels: Imagine you only ever look at your last three days of homework grades and average them, and every new day you drop the oldest one and add the newest. That sliding little window of "the last few" is what rolling means.

`rolling(n)` in pandas creates a window that always covers the most recent n rows, and slides forward one row at a time as you move down the table. Calling `.mean()` on it gives you the average of the last n rows at every point, `.std()` gives the spread, and `.max()` gives the largest value. It only makes sense if your rows are already sorted in time order, since a rolling average of scrambled rows is meaningless.

`df['speed'].rolling(6).mean()` computes, for each row, the average of that row and the 5 rows before it, six 5-minute slots, or 30 minutes, in this course's data. By default the window is right-aligned, meaning it only looks backward, which matters because a feature that peeks at future rows can't be used at prediction time; `rolling(6, center=True)` would look ahead and must never be used for a feature. `min_periods` controls how many rows are required before a window produces a value at all, so with `min_periods=1`, the first few rows compute an average over fewer than 6 rows instead of returning missing values.

Rolling windows can be defined by row count (`rolling(6)`) or by a fixed time offset (`rolling('30min')`), which differ meaningfully when rows are not perfectly evenly spaced, since a row-count window silently assumes uniform spacing, while a time-offset window is robust to a missing or duplicated row. `rolling` composes with `groupby`, so `df.groupby('station_id')['speed'].rolling(6).mean()` computes a separate rolling average per station without them leaking into each other, which is essential in this course since a citywide rolling average across mixed stations would be meaningless. Rolling features are the mechanism behind lag- and trend-based features, such as a 30-minute rolling mean of speed or a rolling standard deviation of occupancy as a volatility signal, and they fail specifically at the start of every group's time series, where `min_periods` and NaN-handling decisions directly affect how many usable rows a station contributes. A subtlety is that `rolling` operates on whatever order the DataFrame is currently in, not on a datetime index automatically, so an unsorted or re-indexed table silently produces a wrong rolling calculation with no error.

The choice between count-based and time-based rolling windows interacts with how you handle irregular sampling and detector dropouts: a count-based window over a station with several missing 5-minute slots quietly spans a longer wall-clock interval than intended, biasing a "last 30 minutes" feature toward being a "last 40 minutes" feature without any signal that this happened, whereas a time-based window handles the gap correctly but can include fewer real observations than expected. Rolling statistics are also autocorrelated by construction, since adjacent rows share most of the same underlying observations, which inflates apparent smoothness and is a common reason cross-validation on rolling-derived features overstates performance unless folds respect time order, rolling-origin evaluation, not random shuffling. Practitioners often forget that a rolling window computed before a train/test split can leak future information across the boundary if the split isn't strictly time-based, since a window near the split point reaches slightly into the other side. Choice of statistic matters too: `rolling().std()` on a short window is a noisy estimate with few degrees of freedom, and using it as a feature without accounting for that noise can make a model overreact to windows that happened to be short due to missing data.

At production scale, rolling features computed offline in pandas must be reproduced exactly at serving time from a streaming feed, which is a genuine engineering challenge, since a streaming rolling window has to handle late-arriving or out-of-order detector rows, decide how long to wait before finalizing a window's value, and guarantee the online computation matches the offline training computation bit-for-bit or close to it, or the model sees systematically different features live than it did in training. Feature stores generally solve this with a shared definition, the window logic specified once and compiled to both a batch job and a streaming operator, specifically to eliminate training-serving skew in exactly this class of feature. An open problem at scale is bounding staleness guarantees for rolling features under real network and sensor failure patterns, since a rolling window's value is only as trustworthy as the assumption that its constituent rows arrived roughly on time.

terms.def: Turn a long table (one row per station and time) into a wide one (one row per time, one column per station).
levels: Pivot means turning a table on its side, like taking a long list of who sat where at lunch and turning it into a seating chart with everyone's name in their own square. The same information, arranged differently.

A long table has one row per combination of things, like one row per station and time. Pivoting turns that into a wide table with one row per time and one column per station, so you can see all the stations side by side at each moment. In pandas this is `df.pivot(index='timestamp', columns='station_id', values='speed')`. It is useful for plotting or for models that expect one row per time step with every station as a feature.

`DataFrame.pivot(index=..., columns=..., values=...)` reshapes a long ('tidy') table, with one row per (station, time) pair, into a wide table with one row per time and one column per station, using the specified value column to fill the cells. Pivoting requires that each (index, columns) combination appear at most once — if a station has two rows for the same timestamp, `pivot` raises an error, and `pivot_table` (which aggregates duplicates, for example with `mean`) is used instead. The reverse operation is `melt`, which turns wide columns back into long rows. In this course, pivoting station speed to wide form is useful for visualizing all stations at once, while the model training pipeline mostly keeps data in long form because it groups and shifts per station.

Pivoting is a fundamental reshape between 'long' (tidy) and 'wide' formats, and the choice between them depends on what comes next: long format is natural for per-group operations (groupby, shift, rolling windows per station) and for storage, since it has a fixed, small set of columns regardless of how many stations exist, while wide format is natural for operations that treat all stations as parallel features at once, like a correlation matrix between stations or certain matrix-based models. `pivot` requires uniqueness of the (index, columns) pair and fails loudly if that is violated, which is a useful sanity check for catching duplicate rows; `pivot_table` instead aggregates duplicates, which can silently mask a data quality problem (two sensor readings for the same station and minute) if the aggregation function is not chosen deliberately. Pivoting to wide format scales poorly as the number of distinct column values (stations) grows, since it produces one column per station regardless of whether that station's data is used — for a metro area with thousands of stations, a fully wide table can become sparse and unwieldy. Graph-based models later in the course (which treat stations as nodes) effectively need a wide, matrix-shaped view of speed at each timestamp, which is exactly what a pivot-to-wide operation, or its matrix equivalent, produces.

The tidy-versus-wide distinction is not just a formatting convenience; it encodes an assumption about what varies together. A long table treats station id as just another column value, which is appropriate when a model is meant to generalize across stations (a single LightGBM model with station_id as a categorical feature), while a wide, pivoted table treats each station as a fixed, named dimension, which is appropriate when a model's structure is tied to a specific fixed set of stations (a graph neural network with a fixed adjacency matrix, or a VAR-style multivariate time series model). Practitioners sometimes pivot to wide format for convenience in an exploratory notebook and then unintentionally bake a fixed station set into a training pipeline, so that the model silently cannot handle a new station added later without retraining the whole pivot logic, an assumption that long-format, per-group pipelines avoid by construction. A performance subtlety: pivoting a very long table with many unique (index, columns) pairs is a memory-expensive operation, since the result's shape is the full cross product regardless of how sparse the actual observed combinations are, and a large-enough pivot can exhaust memory where the equivalent long-format table would fit comfortably.

At production scale, an explicit in-memory pivot is often replaced by a storage layout decision made earlier in the pipeline: a columnar store partitioned so that a wide-style query (all stations at one timestamp) is answered efficiently without materializing a full pivot in memory, for example via Parquet partitioning or a purpose-built time-series database. For graph and spatiotemporal models specifically, the open systems question is how to keep the 'wide, fixed-node' view that these models need in sync with a 'long, flexible' view that ingestion and monitoring pipelines need, as the underlying network of stations changes (new sensors installed, old ones decommissioned) — a mismatch here is a common source of production bugs when a model trained on one station ordering is served with a different one.

terms.def: Reading a file in pieces (`chunksize`) and keeping only what is needed from each, so memory stays small.
