levels: If a book is too heavy to carry all at once, you read it one page at a time instead, and chunking is the computer doing the same trick with a giant file.

Chunking means reading a big file in smaller pieces instead of loading the whole thing into memory at once. In pandas, `pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=200_000)` returns an iterator that gives you two hundred thousand rows at a time, and you process each piece and keep only what you need before moving to the next. This matters for a file too large for the computer's memory, like a full day of PeMS data.

A day's PeMS file is around 200 MB compressed but expands to several gigabytes as a DataFrame, more than a 16 GB Mac can comfortably hold alongside everything else running. `for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=200_000):` turns the read into a loop, where each `chunk` is its own small DataFrame; inside the loop you filter, clean, and keep only the rows you need, then discard the rest before the next chunk arrives. Streaming this way keeps peak memory bounded regardless of the file's total size, at the cost of processing rows in pieces rather than all at once.

Chunking trades memory for a constraint on the computation: any operation confined to one chunk, filtering, per-row transforms, simple aggregation, works cleanly, but operations that need to see the whole dataset at once, a global sort, a full groupby spanning chunk boundaries, need either a second pass or an accumulator carried across chunks. `chunksize` is the simplest form of this pattern; a Python generator using `yield` is the more general one, letting you write custom streaming logic, like line-by-line filtering of a gzipped file, rather than relying on pandas's built-in chunk iterator. Chunk size itself is a tuning knob: too small and per-chunk overhead dominates; too large and you are back to the original memory problem, so 200,000 rows here is chosen empirically for this project's row width and the machine's memory budget.

The general principle behind chunking is that of any streaming data pipeline: idempotence, rerunning gives the same result, bounded memory independent of input size, and careful handling of state that must persist across chunks, like a running mean, which otherwise silently reintroduces the memory-growth problem chunking was meant to solve. A subtlety practitioners often miss: chunk boundaries are arbitrary with respect to the data's own structure, so a computation needing all of one entity's rows together, all of one station's day, for example, can be split across two chunks unless the file is pre-sorted or chunks are read to respect entity boundaries, which is why some pipelines chunk by group rather than by fixed row count. Columnar formats like Parquet make a different, often better, tradeoff available: predicate and column pushdown reads only the needed columns and row groups directly from disk, avoiding chunking's per-chunk Python overhead entirely for many workloads.

At production scale, chunking generalizes into stream processing proper: systems like Spark or Flink face the same core tension between memory, latency, and correctness under out-of-order or late-arriving data, and the chunking pattern here, bounded memory, one pass, keep only what is needed, is the same idea a distributed stream processor implements with watermarks and windowing instead of a fixed `chunksize`. The open engineering question at scale is less about reading a single file in pieces and more about maintaining correctness, exactly-once processing, consistent state across restarts, when the file is actually an unbounded, continuously arriving stream, a substantially harder problem than the batch chunking used to clean one PeMS day.

terms.def: Number types that use 4 bytes and 1 byte instead of 8. Halving or quartering memory with no real loss for speeds and flags.
levels: Numbers can be written in a big fat notebook or a tiny pocket notebook. float32 and int8 are the small pocket notebooks; they hold plenty of room for a speed or a yes-or-no flag without needing the big one.

Computers usually store decimal numbers as float64 (8 bytes) by default, but float32 (4 bytes) holds almost as much precision using half the memory, which is plenty for something like a traffic speed measured to one decimal place. int8 (1 byte) stores small whole numbers, from -128 to 127, which is enough for a flag like 'is this slow: 0 or 1.' Using the smaller types when you can means a big table of traffic data takes up much less room in memory.

float64 gives about 15-17 significant decimal digits of precision; float32 gives about 7, which is far more than a speed measurement (accurate to maybe 1 mph) actually needs, so `df["speed"] = df["speed"].astype("float32")` halves that column's memory with no meaningful loss. int8 covers -128 to 127 and uint8 covers 0 to 255, both a good fit for a boolean-like flag column or a small category code; `df["is_slow"] = df["is_slow"].astype("int8")` quarters the memory of a column that pandas would otherwise store as a 64-bit integer or float by default. `df.memory_usage(deep=True)` shows exactly how much each column costs before and after the conversion.

Choosing a numeric dtype is a real engineering decision, not a formality: with roughly 100 stations times 288 five-minute steps times 365 days, a year of data is about 10.5 million rows, and even five float64 columns would cost around 420 MB in memory, versus 210 MB at float32, a difference that determines whether a full year fits comfortably in memory on a laptop or forces chunked processing. The risk with narrower types is overflow and precision loss: int8 silently wraps around outside its range in some numeric libraries rather than raising, and float32 accumulates more rounding error over long chains of arithmetic, many additions in a rolling sum, for instance, which matters more for training stability than for storing a single sensor reading. GPUs and Apple's Neural Engine are also simply faster at float32, and increasingly float16, than float64, since consumer hardware allocates far more silicon to lower-precision throughput, so the memory savings come with a real speed benefit during training too. Casting should happen deliberately and early, and the resulting dtype should be checked, since an accidental upcast back to float64 during a computation, like a plain Python `+` with a float64 constant, silently undoes the savings.

Mixed-precision training exploits the same idea deliberately at model-training time: keeping master weights in float32 for numerical stability while running the forward and backward pass in float16 or bfloat16 for speed, with a loss-scaling trick to prevent small gradients from underflowing to zero in the lower-precision format, a technique responsible for a large share of the real-world speedups in modern deep learning training. int8 quantization for inference goes further, mapping a trained float model's weights and activations onto 8-bit integers via a learned or calibrated scale factor, trading a small, carefully bounded accuracy loss for large gains in memory and latency, especially on device. Practitioners commonly get float32-versus-float16 numerical stability backwards, assuming any precision loss is negligible; certain operations, softmax over near-equal logits, or a poorly conditioned loss landscape, are precision-sensitive in ways that show up as training divergence rather than a gentle accuracy drop, which is why frameworks keep certain ops in float32 even inside a nominally float16 training run. bfloat16 versus float16 is itself a real tradeoff, bfloat16 keeps float32's exponent range, avoiding overflow, at the cost of fewer mantissa bits, which is why it dominates on TPUs and increasingly on other accelerators for training specifically.

On-device deployment is where dtype choice stops being an optimization and becomes the product constraint: Apple's Neural Engine and Core ML pipeline are built around float16 and int8 execution, and a model that only runs well in float32 may simply not fit an on-device latency or battery budget, which is why quantization-aware training, simulating low-precision arithmetic during training itself rather than quantizing only after the fact, has become standard practice for models shipping to phones. Research on even lower precision, int4, mixed 4-and-8-bit schemes, and structured sparsity combined with quantization, is active because every further bit removed compounds across billions of inferences a day at Apple's scale. The open problem is automating the precision-assignment decision per layer or per tensor, some layers tolerate int8 fine, others need float16 or better, rather than relying on the current mix of hand-tuning and heuristics.

terms.def: Text with values filled in: `f"speed_lag_{k}"`.
levels: An f-string is a fill-in-the-blank sentence. You write "My name is ___" and the computer drops your actual name into the blank for you, every time, automatically.

An f-string is a way to build text in Python by putting a value inside curly braces, and Python fills it in automatically. Writing `name = "Sam"` and then `f"Hello, {name}!"` produces the text "Hello, Sam!". It is called an f-string because you write a lowercase f right before the opening quote, which tells Python to look inside the braces for things to fill in.

An f-string is written as `f"..."` with any Python expression inside curly braces, not just a variable name: `f"speed_lag_{k}"` with k equal to 3 produces the text speed_lag_3, and `f"{3.14159:.2f}"` produces 3.14 using a format spec to control decimal places. They are commonly used to build column names in a loop, like generating speed_lag_0 through speed_lag_3 by looping k from 0 to 3 and writing `f"speed_lag_{k}"` each time. Without the f, the same text would print the literal characters {k} instead of the value of k.

f-strings, added in Python 3.6, are evaluated at run time each time the line executes, and the expression inside the braces can be arbitrarily complex, a function call, an attribute access, even another f-string, not just a bare variable, which is more general than the older percent-style or `.format()` string formatting it mostly replaced. The format spec after a colon controls things like decimal places, alignment, and thousands separators, following the same mini-language as `str.format()`. They fail, or rather misbehave, in one common way: forgetting the f prefix silently produces the literal template text with unfilled braces rather than raising an error, which is a frustrating class of bug to spot by eye.

f-strings are effectively syntactic sugar over `str.format()`, compiled directly into bytecode that evaluates the embedded expressions at the point the string literal appears, which makes them faster than `.format()` or string concatenation for building repeated column names or log messages in a hot loop. Python 3.12 relaxed the grammar further, allowing nested quotes of the same type and multi-line expressions inside the braces, which earlier versions rejected. A subtle correctness issue in ML code specifically is using an f-string to build a column name from a loop variable and then, elsewhere, hardcoding that name as a literal string; the two can drift out of sync if the loop range changes, producing a KeyError far from where the mismatch was introduced. Using f-strings for anything security-sensitive, like building a SQL query from user input, is a known anti-pattern, since it invites injection; parameterized queries exist for exactly this reason.

In production code, f-strings used to name generated features, as in `f"speed_lag_{k}"`, are convenient but implicit: the set of expected column names exists only as whatever the loop happened to produce, with nothing enforcing that training and serving code generate the identical set, a real and recurring source of train and serve skew in feature pipelines. Mature feature pipelines address this by making the naming scheme an explicit, tested contract, a schema or a shared feature-definition module, rather than trusting that two independent f-string loops elsewhere in the codebase stay in sync. This is a small instance of a broader production pattern: string-based conventions are cheap during prototyping and a recurring source of subtle bugs once a pipeline has more than one place that needs to agree on a name.

terms.def: A one-line loop that builds a list: `[c for c in cols if c != "y"]`.
levels: A list comprehension is a fast way to make a whole new pile of things by doing the same little job to each item in an old pile, all in one breath. It is like saying put a sticker on every apple in the basket instead of picking up each apple one at a time and saying it separately. You get a whole new basket, all stickered, in one go.

A list comprehension is a compact way to write a loop that builds a new list, all on one line. `[c for c in cols if c != "y"]` means make a new list of every column name c from cols, except the one called y. It does the same job as a for loop that appends to an empty list, but in fewer lines and, once you're used to reading them, more clearly.

The general form is `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`, where the condition is optional. `[c for c in cols if c != "y"]` filters out the target column name from a list of all column names, leaving the feature columns. List comprehensions can also transform each item, like `[c.upper() for c in cols]`, or nest, like `[x for row in matrix for x in row]` to flatten a list of lists. They are generally faster than an equivalent for loop with `.append()` because the list's final size can be anticipated internally, avoiding repeated resizing.

List comprehensions are Python's syntax for a common functional pattern, map combined with filter, compiled to bytecode that is more efficient than the equivalent explicit loop, because the interpreter can optimize the comprehension's specialized bytecode more than a generic loop-append pattern. There are also dict and set comprehension variants, and generator expressions, dropping the brackets, which produce a lazy iterator instead of a materialized list, useful when the sequence is large and you only need to iterate once. Overly complex comprehensions, deeply nested, with multiple conditions, trade the readability comprehensions are meant to buy for cleverness, and style guides generally recommend falling back to an explicit loop once a comprehension needs more than one or two clauses to stay readable. In Traffic1, the pattern `[c for c in cols if c != "y"]` recurs constantly for building the feature list handed to scikit-learn or LightGBM, since the target column must always be excluded from the inputs.

The performance advantage of comprehensions over explicit loops is real but usually secondary to their expressiveness advantage, and practitioners overestimate the former while underestimating how much comprehensions can obscure control flow when a reviewer needs to understand what a codebase actually does with an edge case, an empty input, a None value that should be filtered but silently is not. A subtlety is that comprehensions create their own scope in Python 3, a variable used only inside a comprehension does not leak into the enclosing scope the way it would in a plain for loop, which is generally desirable but occasionally surprises someone debugging why a loop variable is not accessible after the fact. Comprehensions with side effects are considered bad style precisely because a comprehension reads as a pure expression, and hiding a side effect inside one makes code harder to reason about. In numerically heavy code, a comprehension building a Python list of floats is typically much slower than the equivalent vectorized numpy or pandas operation, so their proper place in a data pipeline like Traffic1 is metadata manipulation, column names, file paths, rather than per-row numerical computation.

At scale, the pattern a list comprehension expresses, map, filter, or both, applied elementwise, is exactly what gets compiled down to vectorized or distributed execution in a production feature pipeline, so understanding comprehensions well is a stepping stone to understanding why the equivalent numpy, pandas, or Spark operation is faster: the comprehension is the correct semantics running through the slow, general-purpose Python interpreter, while the vectorized version is the same semantics running through specialized, typed, often compiled code. There is no deep open research question specific to list comprehensions themselves; their relevance at the frontier is mainly as a readability and correctness baseline against which a generated or optimized version of the same logic can be checked for equivalence.

terms.def: A small unnamed function written inline: `lambda s: s.rolling(3).sum()`.
levels: A lambda is a tiny nameless helper you write right where you need it, like a sticky note with one instruction instead of writing a whole recipe book page. If you just need to say 'add one to this number', you can scribble it in one breath instead of giving it a name and a whole page. `lambda x: x + 1` means exactly that: take x, and give back x plus one.

A lambda is a small, unnamed function written on one line, used when you need a quick function but do not want to give it a name with `def`. `lambda x: x + 1` is a function that takes `x` and returns `x + 1`, equivalent to writing `def add_one(x): return x + 1` but without a name. Lambdas are most often used as a short argument passed into another function, like `df['col'].apply(lambda x: x * 2)`, which doubles every value in a column. They can only contain a single expression, not multiple statements, which keeps them intentionally simple.

The syntax `lambda arguments: expression` creates a function object with no name; `lambda s: s.rolling(3).sum()` takes a pandas Series `s` and returns its 3-row rolling sum, and is typically passed straight into something like `df.groupby('station').apply(lambda s: s.rolling(3).sum())`. A lambda can take multiple arguments (`lambda x, y: x + y`) but its body must be exactly one expression, so it cannot contain a loop, an assignment statement, or multiple lines; anything needing those must be a regular `def` function instead. Lambdas are commonly used with `sorted(data, key=lambda row: row['speed'])` to sort by a specific field without writing a separate named function. They are ordinary Python function objects otherwise: they can be stored in a variable, passed around, and called with `()`.

A lambda expression is syntactic sugar over a normal function definition; both produce the same kind of function object, and the only real differences are that a lambda is anonymous and restricted to a single expression, with no statements, no docstring, and no annotations. This restriction is a deliberate design choice in Python (unlike some languages, where anonymous functions can be arbitrarily complex), meant to discourage burying nontrivial logic in an unreadable one-liner; the idiomatic Python style is to use a lambda only for something trivial and switch to a named `def` function the moment the logic needs a second line or a comment to explain it. Lambdas close over variables from their enclosing scope the same way nested functions do, which creates the classic late-binding bug: a lambda created inside a loop that references the loop variable captures the variable itself, not its value at creation time, so a list of lambdas built in a loop all end up referring to the loop's final value unless the variable is explicitly bound as a default argument. Performance-wise, a lambda is exactly as fast as an equivalent named function; there is no interpreter-level penalty for anonymity, so the choice between `lambda` and `def` is purely about readability, not speed.

The closure-capture bug is a real, well-known trap: `[lambda: i for i in range(5)]` produces five functions that all return 4, not 0 through 4, because each lambda looks up `i` in the enclosing scope at call time, and by the time any of them is called the loop has finished with `i` equal to 4; the fix, `lambda i=i: i`, binds the current value as a default argument, evaluated once at lambda-creation time. In data pipelines, overusing lambdas inside `apply` calls, especially on pandas or PySpark, can silently disable vectorization: pandas's `apply(lambda x: ...)` falls back to a slow, row-by-row Python loop under the hood even though the surface syntax looks like a single vectorized call, whereas the equivalent vectorized expression (`s.rolling(3).sum()` directly, without wrapping it in `apply`) runs in compiled code and can be orders of magnitude faster on large data. A lambda cannot be pickled the way a module-level named function can in most Python versions, which becomes a real limitation the moment a function needs to be sent to a separate worker process for parallel computation, a subtlety that has caused real production bugs when someone parallelizes an `apply(lambda ...)` call and it fails or silently falls back to serial execution. Practitioners sometimes reach for a lambda out of habit even where a plain column-wise numpy or pandas operation would be both clearer and faster, which is worth noticing as an anti-pattern rather than a style preference.

At production scale, whether a per-row transformation is written as a lambda, a vectorized array operation, or a compiled user-defined function matters directly for cost and latency: a lambda-wrapped `apply` over billions of rows in a distributed engine like Spark serializes the Python function and ships it to every worker, and interpreting it row by row is dramatically slower than pushing the equivalent logic down into the engine's native vectorized or compiled operators (Spark's pandas UDFs with Arrow, or native SQL expressions). Apple-scale data pipelines generally treat a lambda inside a hot path as a code-review flag prompting the question 'can this be a native vectorized operation instead', because the performance gap compounds across enough data to change infrastructure cost meaningfully. An ongoing tension in tooling for large-scale data processing is making the fast, vectorized path just as easy to write as the slow, per-row lambda path, since the lambda's simplicity is exactly what makes it the path of least resistance even when it is the wrong choice.

terms.def: A check that must be true or the program stops with an error. The cheapest safety net; put one before every write.
levels: assert is like a grown-up double-checking your shoes are tied before you run outside. If they aren't, everything stops right there instead of letting you trip later.

`assert` checks that something is true, and if it isn't, the program stops immediately with an error message instead of continuing with bad data. `assert df.speed.between(0, 100).all()` stops the program if any speed value is outside a sane range. It is the cheapest safety net in the whole toolkit, one line, no library needed.

`assert condition, 'message'` raises an `AssertionError` with that message if `condition` is falsy, and does nothing at all if it is true. `assert not df.duplicated(['station_id','timestamp']).any(), 'duplicate rows found'` is a good check to run right after loading raw data and right before writing processed data, since it catches a whole class of silent corruption. Python can strip out all asserts when run with `python -O`, which is why asserts should check invariants that are cheap to verify, not substitute for real input validation on untrusted data.

The convention this course follows, an assert before every write, treats data pipelines the way software engineering treats unit tests: cheap, local checks that fail loudly and immediately rather than letting a bad value propagate silently three stages downstream where it is much harder to trace back. Assertions check invariants the programmer believes must hold, row counts match after a join, no NaN in a column that should be complete, a probability stays within 0 and 1, which is different from `try/except`, which handles conditions the programmer expects might legitimately happen, like a network timeout. The `-O` flag stripping asserts means code that depends on side effects inside an assert statement, a rare but real bug pattern, breaks silently in optimized mode.

There is a real design tension between asserting broadly, catches more bugs but can make a pipeline brittle, halting a nightly job over a borderline case a human would have shrugged off, and asserting narrowly, which misses real corruption. Practitioners often get the granularity wrong in both directions: too few asserts, and a labeling bug from an earlier stage ships silently into a model that trains and evaluates 'fine' because nothing crashed; too many rigid asserts, and a legitimate seasonal shift trips an alarm that should have been a warning, not a halt. A more mature pattern at scale is a data-quality framework that runs the same checks as configuration rather than code, distinguishing hard failures from soft warnings and logging both.

In production ML systems, the descendants of a scattered `assert` statement are schema validation at ingestion, data contracts between teams that produce and consume a dataset, and automated data-quality monitoring that runs the equivalent of hundreds of assertions continuously and alerts rather than crashing a running service. The open problem is less whether to assert and more how to keep the set of assertions in sync with an evolving pipeline, stale assertions that no longer reflect the data's real invariants are a common source of alert fatigue, and some teams now generate expected-range assertions automatically from historical data rather than hand-writing every threshold.

terms.def: A fixed starting point for random numbers, so a run can be repeated exactly.
levels: When you shuffle a deck of cards, if you start the same special way every time, you get the same shuffle every time. A seed is that special starting point for a computer's "random" numbers, so the shuffle can be repeated exactly.

Computers don't generate truly random numbers; they use a formula that produces numbers that look random, starting from a starting value called a seed. If you set `random_state=0` or use `numpy.random.default_rng(0)`, you get the exact same sequence of "random" numbers every time you run the code. This matters because it lets you rerun an experiment, splitting the same data the same way or shuffling rows the same way, and get identical results to compare against.

In scikit-learn, passing `random_state=0` to something like `train_test_split` or a model fixes every random choice it makes internally, so re-running the same code produces the same split or the same trained weights. In numpy's newer API, `rng = numpy.random.default_rng(0)` creates a dedicated random number generator object seeded at 0, and calls like `rng.choice(...)` draw from it, which is preferred over the older global `numpy.random.seed(0)` because it doesn't affect unrelated code that also uses randomness. For example, `df.sample(1, random_state=0)` always draws the exact same row, which is useful for writing a repeatable spot-check.

A seed initializes a pseudo-random number generator's internal state, and everything the generator produces afterward is a deterministic function of that state, random only in the sense of passing statistical tests for randomness, not in being unpredictable if you know the seed and algorithm. Reproducibility with a seed requires controlling every source of randomness in a pipeline, not just one: numpy, Python's own `random` module, a model library's internal generator, and, for anything on a GPU, a separate CUDA-level random state and sometimes non-determinism from parallel reduction order that a seed alone cannot fix. Different generator algorithms (numpy's legacy `RandomState` versus the newer `Generator` from `default_rng`) can produce different sequences from the same seed number, so "seed 0" is not portable across libraries or even across numpy versions without care. Seeding does not make an experiment's conclusion more valid, only its individual run more reproducible, which is why a single seeded run can still be an unrepresentative draw, and serious evaluation reports results across multiple seeds rather than one.

The distinction between reproducibility and robustness is where practitioners most often go wrong: a model's headline metric under one fixed seed can look stable while actually depending heavily on which seed you happened to pick, so any comparison between two models or configurations should really report variance across several seeds, not a single seeded run that could favor one side by chance. Seeding a train/test split additionally interacts with time-ordered data in a way that plain seeded shuffling gets wrong, since a fixed seed guarantees the same random split, but a random split is the wrong split entirely for a time series problem like this course's, where evaluation should be rolling-origin, not randomly shuffled, no matter how carefully seeded. On parallel and GPU hardware, true bit-for-bit determinism from a seed often requires disabling certain fast, non-deterministic parallel algorithms, which is a real accuracy-versus-speed-versus-reproducibility tradeoff that teams have to decide on deliberately. A subtler mistake is seeding once at the top of a long pipeline and assuming every downstream random draw is now controlled, when a library update, a new randomness source, or code reordering silently changes what each seeded call actually produces.

At production and research scale, exact reproducibility from a seed becomes probabilistic rather than guaranteed, because distributed training introduces non-determinism from asynchronous gradient aggregation, floating-point summation order, and hardware-specific kernel implementations that a software-level seed does not control. Research organizations increasingly report results as a distribution over seeds, mean and spread across five or ten runs, precisely because single-seed comparisons have contributed to false claims of improvement in the literature, since an effect smaller than seed-to-seed variance is not a real effect. An open infrastructure problem is that full bit-for-bit reproducibility and maximum hardware throughput are often in tension, so teams have to explicitly choose, run by run, whether they need one or the other.

terms.def: Python's plotting library. `plt.plot`, `plt.scatter`, `plt.show`.
levels: matplotlib is the crayon box a computer uses to draw pictures of numbers, like turning a list of how tall you grew each year into a line you can see going up. `plt.plot` draws the line, and `plt.show` shows you the picture.

matplotlib is Python's main tool for drawing charts: line plots, scatter plots, bar charts, and more. `plt.plot(x, y)` draws a line through points, `plt.scatter(x, y)` draws individual dots, and `plt.show()` opens the picture on screen. In this course, plotting a station's speed over a day is one of the first things you do, because looking at the shape of the data catches problems a table of numbers would hide.

matplotlib is built around a `Figure` (the whole image) containing one or more `Axes` (an individual plot), and the `pyplot` interface (`import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`) provides shortcuts like `plt.plot()`, `plt.scatter()`, `plt.xlabel()`, and `plt.show()` that operate on a current figure implicitly. `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` is the more explicit, more controllable form used once a plot needs more than one panel or careful customization, calling `ax.plot(...)` instead of `plt.plot(...)`. A basic pattern in this course is `plt.plot(df['timestamp'], df['speed']); plt.xlabel('time'); plt.ylabel('speed (mph)'); plt.show()` to see one station's day at a glance, which reveals whether a slowdown pattern looks like real congestion or a sensor glitch.

matplotlib exposes two layers: the stateful `pyplot` interface, convenient for quick, one-off plots, and the object-oriented `Figure`/`Axes` interface, which is more verbose but composes reliably — the recommended default once a script produces more than a single quick plot, since `pyplot`'s implicit 'current axes' state becomes a source of bugs in anything beyond a linear script. Reading a plot correctly before trusting a number is emphasized in this course because visual defaults can mislead: an autoscaled y-axis can make a small, meaningless wobble look dramatic, and a plot with too many overlapping points can hide the actual density of data. matplotlib is the low-level engine underneath higher-level libraries like seaborn and pandas' own `.plot()` method, so understanding its object model (figure, axes, artist) pays off even when using those wrappers, because customizing anything beyond their defaults eventually drops back down to matplotlib calls. Saving a figure (`plt.savefig(...)`) at sufficient resolution and in a vector format (PDF or SVG) rather than a low-resolution PNG matters once a plot leaves a notebook and goes into a report.

matplotlib's design predates modern interactive and grammar-of-graphics libraries (plotly, altair, ggplot-style APIs), and its imperative, artist-by-artist model is powerful but verbose for anything beyond the standard chart types, which is why higher-level wrappers exist and why many practitioners default to seaborn or pandas plotting for exploratory work and drop to raw matplotlib only for final, publication-quality figures. A subtlety that trips people up: matplotlib's default rendering can silently downsample or alias very dense time series (millions of points plotted as a continuous line), producing a plot that looks smooth when the underlying data has sharp, important spikes — for high-frequency sensor data like PeMS readings, checking a zoomed-in window against the full-range plot is a useful habit. Choosing a colormap thoughtlessly (a rainbow colormap for continuous data, in particular) is a common and avoidable way to mislead a reader, since perceptually non-uniform colormaps can visually exaggerate or hide gradients that are not actually where the color intensity implies they are — matplotlib's default, viridis, was specifically chosen to fix this.

At production and research scale, static matplotlib figures are usually the last step of a much larger visualization stack: interactive dashboards (built on plotly, bokeh, or a web front end) are used for live monitoring where an analyst needs to zoom, filter, and drill down, while matplotlib remains the tool of choice for the precise, reproducible, publication-quality figure that goes in a paper or a postmortem, because its rendering is deterministic and fully scriptable. An open craft question, not really a research one, is how visualization choices themselves can mislead at scale: a dashboard aggregating millions of sensor readings into a single line can hide the exact kind of rare, high-impact event (a sudden severe slowdown at one station) that the whole system exists to catch, so production monitoring increasingly pairs aggregate plots with anomaly-triggered drill-downs rather than relying on a human noticing a dip in an averaged chart.

terms.def: The thing a row describes: one station at one timestamp.
levels: The unit is just what one little card in your card pile is about; here, each card is about one road-watcher at one moment in time.

The unit of a prediction problem is what one row of data represents. In this project, the unit is one station at one five-minute timestamp: every row is this detector, at this moment. Getting the unit clear first is what lets you decide what the inputs and the target should be.

A prediction problem has four parts, and the unit is the first: what one row describes, here station and timestamp, meaning one detector's reading at one five-minute mark. The other three parts build on it: the inputs are everything known about that unit at or before its timestamp, the target is a yes-or-no fact about its future, and the metric scores how good the guesses were. Written formally, the unit indexes a panel: feature vector x_{s,t} and target y_{s,t} both belong to the pair of station s and time t.

Fixing the unit as station and time is a modeling decision, not a fact about the world, and it determines what one training example means: every row in the training table is one station's state at one moment, and the model learns a function from that unit's inputs to that unit's target, treating different station-time pairs as separate examples even though nearby ones are strongly correlated. This choice has direct consequences for evaluation: because units at the same station and nearby times are not independent, a random train and validation split across units leaks information in a way a naive reading of more training rows is always better would miss, which is why this course splits by time instead. Choosing a coarser or finer unit changes the whole problem: a unit of freeway segment and hour would need different features and give a different, smoother prediction task than station and five-minute mark does.

The unit interacts with almost every other modeling choice in ways that are easy to get backwards: it sets the granularity of leakage checks, you must ask was this known for this exact unit at this exact time, not just was this known, the granularity of the metric, average precision computed per unit pools together very different traffic regimes unless slicing by station or time of day is done separately, and the granularity of the model's own assumptions, logistic regression per row assumes units are conditionally independent given their features, an assumption graph and sequence models exist specifically to relax. Practitioners sometimes redefine the unit implicitly and inconsistently across a pipeline, for instance aggregating to station and hour for one feature but leaving the target at station and five minutes, which silently misaligns training rows without raising an error.

At larger scale, the choice of unit is often the single design decision with the biggest downstream effect on what a system can and cannot do: a unit too coarse cannot express a fast-moving three-minute stall, a unit too fine multiplies the number of predictions a serving system must produce and calibrate, so production spatio-temporal systems often support multiple resolutions and reconcile them, rather than committing to one fixed unit the way this course does for pedagogical clarity. An open research question is how to let the unit itself be learned or adapted, dynamically choosing coarser units where traffic is stable and finer ones where it is volatile, rather than fixing station and five minutes uniformly across a whole freeway network.

terms.def: The columns a model reads. Every one must be known at the row's moment.
levels: Inputs are the clues you give a guessing game before someone guesses the answer, like telling a friend the sky is gray and windy before they guess if it will rain.

Inputs, also called features, are the columns of data a model actually looks at to make a prediction, like a station's recent speeds or the time of day. Every input has to be something you would actually know at the moment you want the prediction; you can't use a speed reading from five minutes in the future as an input for predicting right now, because you would not have it yet. Choosing good inputs is a big part of building a model that works.

In scikit-learn code, the inputs are conventionally called `X`, a table where each column is one feature and each row is one example; the target being predicted is `y`. For the Fremont traffic project, typical inputs include a station's own recent speed lags (`speed_lag_0` through `speed_lag_3`), the time-of-day slot, and the day of week, all values available at the moment the prediction is made, 30 minutes before the label's time. Using a value that would not actually be available yet, like a future speed reading, is called leakage, and it makes a model look far better in testing than it will in real use.

The defining constraint on a valid input is temporal: every feature must be computable using only information available at or before the prediction timestamp, which is a stricter requirement than merely 'the column exists in the training table,' since a table built after the fact can easily contain columns that encode future information without it being obvious from the column name. Feature selection trades off two failure modes: too few inputs and the model cannot express the true relationship (underfitting), too many redundant or noisy inputs and the model can fit spurious patterns in the training set that do not generalize (overfitting), especially with a small amount of training data relative to the number of features. Inputs also need consistent preprocessing between training and prediction time; if speed is standardized using the training set's mean and standard deviation, the exact same values must be used at prediction time, not values recomputed from whatever data happens to be available then. Categorical inputs like station id need an explicit encoding, one-hot, embedding, or a numeric code, before most models can use them at all.

Feature leakage is subtler than 'don't use the future': target leakage occurs when a feature is a proxy for the label computed slightly differently, for example, a rolling average of speed that happens to include the label window's own timestamp due to an off-by-one in the window boundary, and it is dangerous precisely because it inflates validation performance without any obvious code smell, the model looks great until deployment. A second subtlety is that inputs available in a research pipeline are not always available in production at the same latency; a feature that depends on a batch job that runs once a day cannot be an input to a model that needs to predict every five minutes, unless the feature is explicitly allowed to be stale. Practitioners often treat feature engineering as separate from model choice, but the right feature set genuinely depends on the model, a linear model needs explicit interaction terms and nonlinear transforms that a tree-based model or neural network can learn on its own from raw inputs. Feature importance, once computed, is also frequently over-interpreted: a feature can look unimportant only because a correlated feature already carries its signal, not because it carries no information at all.

At production scale, feature availability becomes an infrastructure problem as much as a modeling one: a feature store exists specifically to guarantee that the exact computation used to build a training feature is also used, with matching latency guarantees, to serve that feature at prediction time, since training-serving skew, subtly different feature computation between the two, is one of the most common causes of a model that validates well but underperforms in production. Feature engineering research increasingly moves toward learned representations that reduce reliance on hand-designed features, though for well-understood structured problems like traffic, hand-designed lag and time features still tend to outperform learned ones given realistic data volumes. The open frontier is automating leakage detection itself, static and dynamic analysis tools that can flag a feature computed with information not actually available at serving time, since human review alone reliably misses this class of bug at scale.

terms.def: The column the model tries to predict. Here 1 if the station is inside a slow episode h minutes later, else 0.
levels: The target is the answer the model is trying to guess, like when you play a guessing game and someone checks your answer against the real one. Here, the game is guessing whether the road will be slow in half an hour.

The target, also called the label, is the column in your data that holds the correct answer for each row, the thing you are trying to predict, not something you feed into the model as a clue. In this course, the target is 1 if a station is inside a slow-traffic episode h minutes in the future, and 0 if it is not. Everything else in the row, past speed, time of day, and so on, is a feature, a clue, not the answer.

The target column is built by looking ahead: for a row at time t, the label is 1 if the station's speed h minutes later, say 30, falls below the slow threshold, and 0 otherwise, which in pandas means shifting a was-it-slow indicator backward in time relative to the features, effectively `df["target"] = df["is_slow"].shift(-6)` at 5-minute steps for a 30-minute horizon. This makes the target a genuinely future value relative to the row's other columns, so building it correctly requires care not to accidentally include information from the target's own time or later in the features. A model is trained to predict this column from the other columns, and evaluated by how well its predictions on held-out rows match the true target values.

The target here is a relative label, meaning slow is defined relative to that station's own typical speed rather than an absolute speed cutoff, because a state highway's normal speed and a local arterial's normal speed differ enough that one fixed threshold would mislabel one or the other. Choosing the target this way is a modeling decision as consequential as the choice of algorithm: too strict a threshold makes slow episodes rare and the problem heavily imbalanced, and too loose a threshold makes slow nearly meaningless. Constructing the target requires shifting label information into the past relative to features, and getting the sign or shift amount wrong is a common and serious bug, since it can silently create a target that either leaks future information into the features or predicts the wrong horizon entirely. The target's exact definition, the threshold, the horizon, whether it is a point-in-time label or an any-time-within-the-next-h-minutes label, determines what question the whole downstream model actually answers.

A binary in-a-slow-episode-or-not target discards information a regression on raw future speed would keep, a genuine tradeoff: classification gives interpretable probabilities and handles the imbalance-fighting toolkit well, but a continuous speed target could support a richer notion of severity. Label leakage around target construction is the most consequential mistake in this kind of project: any feature computed with a window that reaches even slightly past the label's own time horizon, a centered rolling average, for instance, will make an offline model look far better than it can perform in real deployment, because at serving time those future values do not exist yet. The horizon, 30 minutes here, is itself a hyperparameter with real consequences; shorter horizons are easier to predict but less actionable, longer horizons are more actionable but harder to predict, and multi-task models that predict several horizons at once are one way to avoid committing to just one. Class imbalance in the target, slow episodes are the minority class, means accuracy is a misleading headline metric, and the target's rarity should drive the choice of loss weighting or resampling, not be treated as a detail to handle after the fact.

In production forecasting systems, the target definition is rarely fixed once and left alone; it evolves as stakeholders discover that slow or the chosen horizon does not match what they actually need to act on, which means the labeling logic itself needs the same versioning and review as the model code, since a silent change in how the target is computed invalidates comparisons against past model versions. Multi-horizon, multi-definition targets, several thresholds, several horizons, sometimes a continuous severity score alongside the binary label, are common in mature systems specifically so that different downstream consumers of the prediction do not have to negotiate over a single label. The open research question connecting to the target's definition is causal: today's target only captures whether traffic will be slow, not why, and a target or auxiliary task tied to identifiable causes, an incident, an event, weather, is more useful for a system meant to inform action rather than just alert.

terms.def: How far ahead the prediction looks: 15, 30 or 60 minutes, one model each.
levels: A horizon is how far into the future you are trying to guess, like guessing whether it will be raining by the time you finish your snack, versus by bedtime. A short horizon is an easy, close-up guess; a long horizon is a harder, farther-away guess. Traffic1 guesses about the next half hour.

The horizon is how far ahead a prediction looks, measured in minutes here: 15, 30, or 60 minutes from now. Traffic1 trains a separate model for each horizon, since predicting 15 minutes ahead is a different, usually easier, problem than predicting 60 minutes ahead. A short horizon has less time for conditions to change, so it is generally easier to get right than a long horizon.

The horizon h defines the target: for a station s at time t, the label is whether that station is slow at time t plus h, so a 30-minute horizon means the model at time t is trained to predict the state at t plus 30 minutes using only information available up to t. Traffic1 trains one model per horizon, 15, 30, 60 minutes, rather than one model that outputs all three, because the right features and even the right model complexity can differ by horizon, a 60-minute prediction leans more on typical time-of-day patterns and less on the last five minutes of speed than a 15-minute prediction does. Choosing the horizon is a product decision as much as a modeling one: a navigation app warning about traffic needs enough horizon to be useful but not so much that accuracy collapses.

As the horizon grows, the mutual information between current conditions and the future state generally decreases, so predictive accuracy typically degrades with horizon length, this is a structural property of the problem, not a modeling failure, and it means horizon-specific evaluation, not one blended accuracy number, is necessary to understand a model honestly. Feature importance often shifts with horizon: short-horizon models lean heavily on the most recent lag features, autocorrelation is strongest at short lags, while long-horizon models lean more on calendar features because recent speed has decayed in predictive value by then. Training one model per horizon avoids forcing a single model to learn a shared representation across fundamentally different amounts of predictive signal, at the cost of more models to maintain, tune, and monitor. An alternative, a single sequence model that outputs a full horizon curve at once, trades this simplicity for potential efficiency and consistency across horizons, at the cost of more complex training.

Multi-horizon forecasting architectures can share representations across horizons and enforce coherence, a 60-minute prediction should not wildly contradict a 45-minute prediction for the same target time, but they introduce their own failure mode: a shared representation can let noisy long-horizon labels drag down short-horizon accuracy through shared parameters, an effect separate single-horizon models avoid entirely. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating horizon length as purely a modeling parameter when it also interacts with label construction, if slow is defined relative to a rolling historical profile, a longer horizon means the profile itself may have shifted between t and t plus h, a holiday, a schedule change, which the label does not account for. Evaluating horizon-specific calibration matters more than it might seem: a model can have similar accuracy across horizons while being systematically overconfident at long horizons, because uncertainty genuinely grows with horizon length in a way accuracy alone does not reveal.

Production forecasting systems increasingly move toward models that output a full predictive distribution over a continuous range of horizons rather than a fixed set of discrete ones, both for efficiency and because downstream consumers, routing, ETA, alerting, often want an arbitrary horizon, not exactly 15, 30, or 60 minutes. At Apple's scale, Maps traffic and ETA prediction across a global road network, the open problem is maintaining calibrated uncertainty across a wide range of horizons and geographies simultaneously, since a single global model's horizon-dependent error structure can vary enormously between a dense urban grid and a rural highway, and collecting enough labeled data to characterize that per-region, per-horizon behavior is itself a hard data-engineering problem.

terms.def: Three consecutive five-minute rows with speed below 60 percent of the station's typical speed for that slot and day type.
levels: A slow episode is when the cars on the freeway near a sensor crawl instead of zoom, for a good long while, not just for a second. Imagine cars usually run like they are racing, but suddenly they are moving like they are wading through mud, and they stay muddy for at least fifteen minutes. That muddy stretch, not just one slow moment, is what counts as a slow episode.

A slow episode is a stretch of time, at least fifteen minutes long, where a freeway station's traffic speed drops well below what is normal for that time of day and day of the week. Specifically, it needs three consecutive five-minute readings, each below 60 percent of the station's typical speed for that slot. A single slow reading does not count, because that could just be noise; three in a row is a more reliable sign of a real slowdown. This is the event the whole prediction project is trying to see coming.

A slow episode requires three consecutive 5-minute rows where `speed < 0.6 * typical_speed`, where `typical_speed` is the historical average speed for that station, at that time of day, on that type of day (weekday versus weekend). The 60 percent threshold and the three-row (15-minute) minimum duration are both chosen thresholds, not laws of physics, and the course's code versions them in the output filename so a later change to the threshold does not silently change what an old result means. The first row of the three is the episode's onset. Because 'typical' is computed per station and time slot, the same raw speed (say, 45 mph) can count as a slow episode at a station whose normal speed is 75 mph but not at one whose normal speed is 50 mph.

Defining 'slow' relative to each station's own typical speed, rather than a single absolute threshold across all stations, is a deliberate modeling choice: it accounts for the fact that free-flow speed itself varies by location (a station on a curve or near an interchange may never reach highway speed even in ideal conditions), so a relative threshold targets genuine congestion rather than a station's inherent geometry. The three-consecutive-row requirement is a smoothing choice that trades detection latency for reliability: it filters out single noisy readings but means the true onset of a slowdown is only confirmed 15 minutes after it starts, which sets a floor on how early any model built on this label could, in principle, detect an episode from data alone. Because the label depends on a historical 'typical speed' baseline computed over some window of past data, that baseline itself needs to be computed without leaking future information (using only data available up to the point of prediction), or the label used in training will not match what would be computable in a live system. The choice of day type (weekday versus weekend, and whether holidays are treated separately) materially changes which slowdowns qualify, since a holiday's typical traffic pattern looks like a weekend even on a weekday.

The 60 percent-of-typical, three-consecutive-row definition is one point in a design space, and the course's plan explicitly flags alternatives that keep more information: regressing the raw speed ratio with a quantile (pinball) loss and thresholding afterward preserves the ordinal severity of a slowdown instead of collapsing it to a binary label, and modeling episode onset as a hazard (time-to-event) problem directly targets the lead-time question rather than a fixed horizon's yes-or-no label. A binary threshold-based label is also sensitive to exactly where 60 percent falls relative to the natural distribution of speed ratios at a station; a threshold near a density mode makes the label's boundary noisy in a way that inflates apparent label disagreement between similar traffic states. Practitioners commonly under-appreciate how much a labeling threshold like this shapes every downstream metric: the same underlying traffic data can look like a well-calibrated, useful classifier or a poorly-calibrated one purely as an artifact of where the 60 percent line falls, which is why the course insists on baselines and ablations across nearby threshold values rather than trusting one fixed choice as ground truth. The 'typical speed' baseline itself has an implicit assumption of stationarity within a day-of-week and time-of-day bucket that road construction, a permanent lane closure, or a long-term demand shift can violate, silently drifting the definition of 'slow' over the months a model is deployed.

In a real traffic operations system, a fixed relative threshold like 60 percent is a starting point that gets replaced or supplemented with adaptive, multi-signal definitions of congestion — combining speed with occupancy, flow, and sometimes probe (GPS) data to distinguish a genuine capacity-limited slowdown from a sensor fault or a temporary event like a stopped vehicle — because a single-sensor speed threshold has real false-positive and false-negative modes at scale. Production traffic-management deployments also have to handle label drift explicitly: as road geometry, speed limits, or demand patterns change over years, a 'typical speed' baseline computed once at deployment time becomes stale, so operational systems retrain or recompute baselines on a rolling schedule and monitor for exactly the kind of threshold sensitivity described above. The open research and engineering question behind this kind of event label is how to define 'the event a stakeholder actually cares about' (drivers care about delay and reliability, not a specific speed ratio) in a way that is both operationally computable from noisy sensor data and faithfully connected to that real-world outcome, and most deployed systems are an imperfect, continuously-revisited answer to that question rather than a solved one.

terms.def: The typical speed per station, day type and slot, computed as the median over training rows only.
levels: The profile is what's normal for a road at a certain time, like knowing your friend is usually happy in the morning, so you can tell when something's off.

The profile is the typical speed at a station for a given day type, weekday or weekend, and time slot, computed as the median speed over the training data only. It is the 'normal' the model compares each new reading against: 40 mph might be perfectly normal at 2 a.m. but slow for 8 a.m. rush hour, and the profile is what lets the model tell the difference.

The profile is built with `train.groupby(['station_id','daytype','slot']).speed.median()`, computing one typical speed per station, per weekday-or-weekend, per five-minute slot of the day, using only the training rows so no information from validation or test leaks in. A cell with too few samples, fewer than about 20 training days, falls back to a coarser aggregation rather than trusting a noisy median. The label is then defined relative to this profile, speed dropping to some ratio below it, rather than against one fixed threshold for every station.

Using a relative profile rather than an absolute speed threshold is a deliberate modeling choice: a freeway station with a free-flow speed of 65 behaves very differently from an on-ramp with a free-flow speed of 40, and an absolute threshold would call the ramp slow constantly. The assumption underneath the profile is that a station's own typical speed by day-type and slot is a stable, meaningful baseline, which holds well in the medium term but degrades slowly as roadwork, seasonal patterns or detector replacement shift what typical actually means. The median, rather than the mean, is used specifically for robustness: a handful of incident days should not drag the profile down and make ordinary slow traffic look extra slow by comparison.

Because the label is defined relative to an estimator, the profile, rather than a fixed rule, label noise inherits the profile estimator's own error, and that error's structure changes with the split: computing the profile on training data only and comparing test rows against it means the test-period positive rate is not pinned at a fixed value by construction, which is correct, but if the profile were instead computed on the test period too, the positive rate would be artificially pinned near a fixed quantile, hiding any real change in typical traffic. A subtlety practitioners get wrong: the median's standard error scales like σ divided by the square root of n, so with roughly forty weekday samples per station-slot cell, smoothing across neighboring time slots trades a little bias for a real reduction in profile noise, and skipping that smoothing makes the label noisier than the underlying traffic actually is.

In production, a profile like this must be versioned and monitored as a first-class artifact, not recomputed ad hoc, because the model's label definition, and therefore its entire meaning, depends on it; retraining with a silently different profile changes what 'slow' means without changing any code that looks like a bug. Open questions include how to update the profile online as roadwork and seasonal patterns shift without either lagging real change or overfitting to recent noise, and whether a smoothed, hierarchical estimate, borrowing strength across nearby stations, not just nearby time slots, improves on the simple per-station median used here.

terms.def: The share of rows that are positive. Small here, which is why accuracy is useless and average precision is used.
levels: If you have a big jar of one hundred jellybeans and only three are the yucky flavor, prevalence is how many out of the hundred are yucky. In this course, "slow traffic" rows are the rare, yucky-flavor ones.

Prevalence is the fraction of all your data rows that are the thing you're trying to predict, the positive class. If out of 100,000 rows only 3,000 are labeled "slow traffic," the prevalence is 3%. Low prevalence matters a lot for how you judge a model: a model that always guesses "not slow" would already be right 97% of the time, so plain accuracy is a bad way to tell whether it's actually useful.

Prevalence is computed as (number of positive rows) / (total rows); in this course it's a few percent, since slow-traffic events are rare relative to all 5-minute station readings. Because prevalence is low, accuracy is a misleading metric, since always predicting the majority class scores high accuracy while being useless, so the course uses average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve, instead, since it directly measures how well the model ranks true positives near the top. Prevalence also isn't fixed: `df['label'].mean()` computed separately by season or by time of day can shift noticeably, since slow traffic is more common at rush hour and during storms.

Low prevalence changes which metrics are informative and which are not: ROC-AUC can look deceptively good under class imbalance because it's dominated by the much larger number of true negatives, while average precision, the area under precision-recall, focuses on how well the model ranks the rare positives, which matches the actual operational question of whether the top of the ranked list is mostly real slow-traffic events. Prevalence also determines the achievable precision at any given recall, since a rarer positive class makes high precision fundamentally harder to reach at the same recall, independent of model quality, so precision-recall curves for problems with different prevalence are not directly comparable without normalizing for that. A model trained naively on low-prevalence data can also learn a poorly calibrated probability output, since the raw score from a tree ensemble in particular tends to be biased toward the majority class, which is a separate problem from ranking quality and is why this course treats calibration, via isotonic regression, as a distinct step from choosing a threshold. Techniques like class weighting or resampling address training-time imbalance but change what the model's raw probability output means, so they interact with calibration and threshold choice rather than being free fixes.

Prevalence is not a fixed property of the problem but a property of the sampling window, and treating it as constant is a common mistake: seasonal effects, roadwork and weather shift the true rate of slow-traffic events, so a model calibrated and thresholded on one period's prevalence will systematically over- or under-alarm when deployed into a period with different prevalence, even if the model's discrimination ability, its ranking quality, hasn't degraded at all. This is why monitoring prevalence itself, alongside metric values, is part of a serious deployment, since a drop in average precision could mean the model got worse, or it could mean prevalence dropped and the ranking task got intrinsically harder, and those call for different responses. A related subtlety is that average precision itself is sensitive to prevalence in a way practitioners sometimes forget when comparing across time windows or across stations with very different base rates, and a fair comparison sometimes requires reporting metrics conditional on prevalence, or using a prevalence-independent measure of ranking quality. Threshold choice downstream of prevalence is itself a decision under a cost model, not a statistical fact, since the "right" threshold moves as the cost of a false alarm versus a missed jam changes, and that tradeoff is a business decision the model's raw output does not make for you.

At production scale, prevalence drift is one of the most common causes of a model quietly going stale without an obvious code or data bug, since a real change in the world, a new highway interchange opening or a shift in commute patterns, changes the base rate the model was calibrated against, and monitoring systems have to distinguish that from actual model degradation using metrics like the population stability index alongside recomputed average precision. Extremely low-prevalence problems more broadly (fraud, rare medical events, safety-critical anomalies) push practitioners toward specialized techniques, anomaly-detection framings, extreme value theory, or active learning to enrich rare positive examples, when the positive rate becomes too small for standard supervised metrics to be statistically stable over a practical evaluation window. An open question in these systems is how to set alerting thresholds that remain well-calibrated automatically as prevalence drifts, rather than requiring a human to notice and manually recalibrate.

terms.def: Any information from after a row's moment getting into its inputs, or test data influencing training choices. The mistake that makes models look great and then fail.
levels: Leakage is like peeking at the answer key before a test and then feeling like you're a genius, when really you just cheated. A model that peeked at the future while learning looks amazing during practice but then fails for real, because in real life it cannot peek.

Leakage happens when information that would not actually be available at prediction time sneaks into the training data, making a model look much better than it really is during testing. For example, if a feature accidentally includes something that happened after the moment being predicted, the model 'cheats' by seeing a bit of the future. The danger is that leakage does not show up as an error — it shows up as a great-looking score that falls apart once the model is used for real, on data it truly has not seen.

Leakage is any pathway by which information from outside the legitimate training scope reaches the model — most commonly, information from after the timestamp being predicted (using `speed` at time t+5 to help predict a label defined using time t+5), or information from the test set influencing decisions made before testing (like scaling a feature using statistics computed on the full dataset, test rows included). The tell is a model that performs implausibly well, far better than a sensible baseline, especially if performance seems to defy how hard the underlying problem should be. The fix is discipline in pipeline order: compute lag features and labels strictly from data available at or before the prediction time, and fit any transformation (scalers, encoders) on the training split only, then apply it unchanged to validation and test.

Leakage comes in several recognizable forms: target leakage (a feature that is itself derived from or correlated with the label in a way that would not hold at prediction time — for instance, a feature computed using the same future window the label uses), train-test contamination (fitting any statistic, from a mean used for scaling to a feature-selection decision, on data that includes the test set), and temporal leakage specific to time series (shuffling rows before splitting, so a model trains on data from after the point it is tested on). In this course's traffic project, the risk is concrete: a naive random train/test split would let the model train on data five minutes after a test row's own five-minute window, effectively letting it see the near future when the whole point is to predict it. The standard defense is a strictly time-ordered split (train on earlier weeks, test on later weeks) plus a careful audit of every feature's computation for any dependency on data at or after the label's timestamp. Cross-validation for time series uses forward-chaining folds (train on an expanding or sliding window, always test on the period right after it) rather than the random k-fold splits appropriate for i.i.d. data, precisely to avoid this leakage.

Leakage is often subtler than 'used a future column' — group leakage is a common, easy-to-miss variant, where rows from the same entity (the same station, on nearby timestamps) end up in both train and test, so the model partly memorizes station-specific quirks rather than learning generalizable patterns, inflating test performance even with a perfectly time-ordered split, if station-level grouping is not also respected. Feature engineering pipelines that compute a rolling statistic (a station's typical speed at this time of day, used to define the relative 'slow' label itself) can leak if that baseline is computed using the full dataset rather than only data available up to the prediction time, since the label's own definition then implicitly depends on the future it is trying to be blind to. A related and often-missed case is leakage through hyperparameter tuning or early stopping: if a validation set used to pick a stopping point or a hyperparameter is reused as the final test set, the reported test score is optimistic, because information from that set influenced model selection even though no feature literally leaked. Practitioners often only catch leakage retrospectively, after a model that looked excellent offline performs at baseline level once deployed — building the habit of asking, for every feature, 'would this value have actually existed at prediction time, computed only from past data' catches most cases before deployment.

At production scale, leakage detection becomes partly an engineering and organizational problem rather than a purely statistical one: feature stores are built specifically to guarantee point-in-time correctness, serving a feature's value 'as it was known' at any historical timestamp so that training and serving pipelines cannot drift into using different, leakage-prone definitions of the same feature. A subtler, ongoing research and engineering concern is online feedback leakage in deployed systems: once a model's predictions influence real-world outcomes (routing decisions, alerts that change driver behavior), future training data reflects a world already shaped by the model's own past predictions, which is a form of leakage that a static train/test split cannot even in principle catch, and which pushes serious deployed systems toward causal or counterfactual evaluation instead of naive retraining on live outcomes.

terms.def: Deciding and computing the input columns: lags, rolling statistics, time-of-day circle, holidays, neighbor readings.
levels: Feature engineering is picking which clues to write down before you guess, like noticing the sky is grey and the wind picked up before guessing it will rain.

Feature engineering means deciding which input columns to compute from the raw data and then actually computing them. For the traffic project this includes lag features, the speed 5 or 15 minutes ago, rolling statistics, the average speed over the last half hour, and neighbor readings, what the upstream and downstream stations are seeing right now. Good features often matter more than which algorithm you use afterward.

A feature is one input column, and feature engineering is the process of turning raw signals into a table the model can use, following one strict rule: every feature must be computable only from rows at or before the current timestamp. `g = df.groupby("station_id")` groups the data so features stay inside one station, and from there `g.speed.shift(3)` makes a lag feature, speed 15 minutes ago, while `g.speed.rolling(6).mean()` makes a rolling average over the last half hour. Time of day is usually encoded as a circle, sine and cosine of the time, rather than a raw hour number, so that 23:59 and 00:01 read as close together instead of far apart.

Feature engineering is best thought of as hypothesis-making: each feature encodes a specific belief about what predicts the target, momentum, spatial propagation, or periodicity, and a feature's usefulness is really a test of that hypothesis once the model is trained. The one invariant across every feature in this course is the leakage rule, computed only from information available at or before the prediction timestamp, because a single feature that peeks even five minutes into the future can make an offline metric look excellent while the same feature is undefined or wrong at serving time. Correlation with the target is a cheap first check, `speed_lag_0` correlates less with `y_60` than with `y_15`, for example, because momentum decays with horizon, but it does not replace fitting a model, since features can matter jointly, or after interacting with each other, in ways a single correlation coefficient cannot show.

The subtlety practitioners get wrong most often is not computing a leaky feature outright but computing a feature correctly in training and differently at serving time, point-in-time correctness, since a rolling mean computed once over a whole historical table and a rolling mean computed incrementally as new rows arrive in production can differ subtly at the edges, especially around missing data or station gaps. Feature engineering also interacts with model choice in ways easy to underweight: gradient-boosted trees can find some nonlinear interactions and thresholds on their own, reducing the need for hand-crafted interaction features that a linear model like logistic regression requires explicitly. A well-designed feature set is also a form of documentation: a feature importance ranking that surprises a domain expert is often a sign of leakage or a data bug, not a genuine discovery, so surprising importances deserve suspicion before celebration.

At production scale, feature engineering becomes a systems problem as much as a modeling one: the same feature logic must run identically in a batch training pipeline and a low-latency serving path, exactly the point-in-time correctness problem that feature stores with time-travel joins exist to solve, and this course's small-scale answer, one shared feature module used by both paths plus a golden-file test comparing them bit for bit, is a miniature of that same discipline. The open research direction is reducing how much of this work is manual at all: learned feature representations increasingly substitute for hand-built lags and rolling statistics, though in practice teams still keep interpretable hand-engineered features alongside learned ones, because the hand-built features are what a human can audit when a prediction goes wrong.

terms.def: A value from k steps earlier in the same station's series.
levels: A lag is like remembering what you had for lunch yesterday to help guess what you might want to eat today; it's a peek backward in time at the same thing.

A lag feature takes a value from some number of steps earlier in the same time series and uses it as an input right now. `speed_lag_1` at a given time is just that station's speed reading from one five-minute step before; `speed_lag_2` is two steps before, and so on. Lags are useful because traffic right now is usually a lot like traffic a few minutes ago.

In pandas, a lag is built with `.shift(k)`: `df["speed_lag_1"] = df.groupby("station")["speed"].shift(1)` shifts each station's speed series forward by one row, so every row's `speed_lag_1` holds the previous row's speed for that same station. Grouping by station before shifting matters; without it, the last row of one station's data would leak into the first row of the next station's lag. The course typically builds several lags, `speed_lag_0` through `speed_lag_3`, to give the model a short recent history rather than just the single most recent reading.

Lag features are the simplest and often most effective way to give a model access to a time series' own recent history, working for the same reason autoregressive models like ARIMA have worked for decades: traffic speed is highly autocorrelated at short lags, so recent values carry most of the predictive signal for what comes next. A key correctness property is that lag features are stationary by construction, a lag is always relative to 'now,' so it does not drift in absolute value the way a raw calendar feature or a static station attribute might as roadwork or detector recalibration changes conditions over months. The number of lags to include is a real hyperparameter: too few loses information about trend and acceleration, is speed dropping or recovering, too many adds redundant, highly correlated columns that mostly just add noise and computation. `.shift()` introduces `NaN` values at the start of each group's series, which must be dropped or imputed before training, and forgetting to group by station before shifting is one of the most common leakage bugs in this exact project.

Lag features implicitly assume the process is Markovian at the chosen lag depth, that the last k values summarize everything relevant about the recent past, which is a strong and sometimes wrong assumption; a model that also needs to know whether there was an incident 40 minutes ago outside the lag window will not get that from lags alone and needs either more lags or a genuinely different feature, an event indicator.
