There's a real tension between engineering explicit lag features for a linear model or LightGBM and letting a recurrent or attention-based model learn its own implicit representation of recent history from a raw windowed sequence; the explicit-feature approach is more interpretable and often more sample-efficient with limited data, while the learned approach scales better with more data and can capture longer or more irregular dependencies. Practitioners frequently compute lags per station correctly but then forget the same discipline when they add lags of a different signal, nearby stations' speeds, say, producing subtle cross-station leakage that is much harder to spot than the single-station case. A related trap is defining a lag relative to a resampled or reindexed series that has silently introduced gaps, which shifts every subsequent lag by an unnoticed amount.

Production time-series systems generally move beyond a small fixed set of hand-picked lags toward automated windowing, a model or search procedure that selects which lags and window statistics actually help, since at scale, thousands of series, changing over time, manually re-tuning lag depth per series does not survive. Sequence models (RNNs, temporal convolutions, transformers) subsume explicit lag features in principle, learning arbitrary functions of the recent window, but in practice production systems often keep a handful of engineered lags as auxiliary inputs even alongside a sequence model, because they are cheap, robust, and provide a useful inductive bias when training data is limited for a given series. An open question, especially for spatial-temporal problems like traffic, is how to combine per-station lag structure with cross-station graph structure in one architecture without one drowning out the other's signal.

terms.def: Placing a time on a circle with sine and cosine so 23:55 and 00:05 are close.
levels: Think of a clock face. 11:55 at night and 12:05 just after midnight are right next to each other on the clock, even though as plain numbers 2355 and 5 look nothing alike. Cyclic encoding is a trick that makes the computer see time the way a clock does, as a circle, not a straight line of numbers.

If you just wrote time of day as a number of minutes since midnight, 23:55, minute 1435, and 00:05, minute 5, would look almost as far apart as two numbers can be, even though only 10 minutes separate them in real life. Cyclic encoding fixes this by turning the time into a point on a circle using sine and cosine, so that times close together on a clock stay close together as numbers, no matter where midnight falls.

Given a value that repeats, like hour-of-day, first convert it to an angle: angle equals 2π times hour divided by 24. Then create two features: sin(angle) and cos(angle). Midnight, hour 0, and just before midnight, hour 23.9, now land at nearly the same sin-cos point on the unit circle, instead of at opposite ends of a 0-to-23 number line. The same trick applies to day-of-week, period 7, or day-of-year, period 365.

Cyclic encoding turns a periodic variable into a pair of coordinates on the unit circle, which preserves the true circular distance between any two times as ordinary Euclidean distance between their sin-cos points, something a raw integer encoding or even one-hot encoding of hour does not give a model for free. It requires knowing the period in advance, 24 for hour, 7 for day-of-week, and using the wrong period silently produces a broken, non-cyclic mapping. It matters most for models that treat features as ordered or distance-based in a naive way, linear models and neural networks benefit clearly, while tree-based models like LightGBM can partly recover cyclic structure on their own by learning a threshold-based split near midnight, so the encoding helps them less, though it rarely hurts.

Using sin and cos together, rather than either alone, is necessary because a single sine value is not invertible; sin of 30 degrees and sin of 150 degrees are equal, so one feature alone cannot distinguish those two times, while the pair sin-cos is a bijection onto the circle and resolves the ambiguity. A subtlety practitioners often miss is that cyclic encoding assumes the underlying relationship really is smoothly periodic, a reasonable assumption for hour-of-day traffic patterns but a poor one for something like day-of-week, where weekday and weekend behavior can differ sharply rather than blend smoothly across the boundary; in that case, a categorical encoding of day-type may serve better than treating it as continuous and cyclic. Tree models split on a single feature's threshold at a time, so sin and cos features interact only through multiple sequential splits, which can make trees slower to discover cyclic structure than a linear or neural model would, even though trees do not strictly need the encoding to eventually get there.

At production scale, cyclic encoding is a small piece of a larger feature-engineering pattern, Fourier or spectral encodings of time, used more elaborately in industrial forecasting systems, sometimes with multiple harmonics to capture non-sinusoidal periodic shapes like a sharp morning commute spike that a single sine wave fits poorly. An open question in more modern forecasting architectures, transformers, temporal models, is whether learned time embeddings, trained end-to-end rather than hand-specified as sine and cosine, capture this structure better in practice; empirically the answer often depends on how much data is available to learn the embedding from scratch versus how well the hand-built cyclic prior generalizes with limited data.

terms.def: Dividing the data by date. The model learns from training, choices are made on validation, and test is scored once at the end.
levels: Splitting is like sorting your Halloween candy into three piles: one pile to practice trading with your sibling, one pile to check if your trading rules actually work, and one special pile you only open once, at the very end, to see how you really did. You are not allowed to peek at that last pile early, or it does not count. Traffic1 splits its data by day the same way.

A split divides the dataset into three parts by date: training data the model learns from, validation data used to make choices like which settings work best, and test data, which is looked at only once, at the very end, to report a final score. Splitting by date, rather than randomly mixing rows, matters for time series because you want to test whether the model can predict the future, not just fill in gaps in the past. In Traffic1, an early chunk of days is training, a middle chunk is validation, and the most recent chunk is test.

The standard time-series split puts entirely disjoint, chronologically ordered date ranges into train, validation, and test, for example, six months for training, one month for validation, and one month of the most recent data for test, so that no test-period information, even indirectly, through a feature computed from the whole dataset, leaks backward into training. Using `train_test_split` with `shuffle=True`, the default for i.i.d. data, is a common and serious mistake for time series, because it puts future rows into training and past rows into test, letting the model implicitly see the future during training. A validation set exists specifically so you can tune hyperparameters or compare models without touching the test set, preserving test as an honest, unbiased final check. Traffic1's split is date-based: training on earlier months, validating on a middle month, testing on the most recent month, matching how the model will actually be used, trained on the past, evaluated on data it has never seen chronologically.

A time-series split must guard against two distinct forms of leakage: temporal leakage, where a feature computed using future information crosses into training, and information leakage through the label construction itself, such as a slow threshold computed from a rolling historical window that inadvertently includes test-period data. A single fixed split can also be unlucky, validation performance on one particular month might not represent typical performance, so time-series cross-validation, rolling-origin or expanding-window splits, is preferred when compute allows, giving a distribution of validation scores rather than one number. The test set should be touched exactly once, and re-running model selection after seeing test performance turns test into a second validation set and invalidates its role as an honest estimate. Splitting by station versus by date matters too: for Traffic1's setup, splitting by date but keeping the same set of stations across all three splits tests temporal generalization, while a held-out set of stations would test spatial generalization, a different, also important question the standard split does not answer.

The theoretically clean approach, nested cross-validation with proper rolling-origin evaluation, is expensive enough that most practitioners default to a single validation split, accepting a somewhat noisier estimate of generalization in exchange for tractable compute, and understanding when that shortcut is acceptable, stable, high-volume data like PeMS, versus dangerous, a small, non-stationary dataset, is itself a modeling judgment. A subtlety practitioners consistently get wrong is treating the validation set as reusable indefinitely; every model comparison and hyperparameter choice made by looking at validation performance leaks a small amount of information from validation into the final model, and after enough iterations validation performance becomes an optimistic estimate too, which is exactly why the test set exists as a separate, disciplined final check. Group-aware splitting is another subtlety: if two rows from the same station five minutes apart end up on opposite sides of the split boundary, they are so highly correlated that the split boundary itself creates a slightly leaky handoff, and a gap is a common mitigation. Distributional shift between splits, traffic patterns genuinely changing between the training months and the test month, means a split can be leak-free and still misleading if the underlying process is nonstationary in a way the split does not surface.

In production systems, the split evolves from a one-time offline decision into an ongoing evaluation protocol: backtesting across many historical windows to estimate how a model would have performed if deployed at various past points, combined with shadow deployment before any traffic split decision is trusted for a real launch. At scale, the open engineering problem is maintaining split discipline automatically across a large number of models and pipelines, since manual discipline does not scale to hundreds of models retrained on a schedule, this is typically solved by infrastructure that enforces temporal boundaries and logs exactly what data each training run could see. A deeper open question, especially relevant to a global system like Apple Maps, is how to define a meaningful split at all when the underlying world is continuously changing, which pushes toward continual or online evaluation rather than a single static train, validation, test partition.

terms.def: The simplest forecast without a model: persistence (the future equals now) and the profile rate (the historical average). Every model must beat them.
levels: A baseline is the simplest possible guess you could make, without doing anything clever at all, like guessing tomorrow's weather will be exactly like today's. If your fancy weather machine cannot beat that simple guess, the machine is not actually helping. So before trusting any clever answer, you always check it against the easy, lazy answer first.

A baseline is the simplest reasonable prediction you can make without a trained model, used as a minimum bar that any real model has to clear. Persistence is one baseline: guess that the future will look exactly like right now. The profile rate is another: guess the historical average for this time of day and day of week, ignoring today's actual conditions. If a fancy model cannot beat these simple guesses, it is not adding real value, no matter how sophisticated it looks.

Persistence predicts the value 30 minutes from now equals the value right now (`y_pred = y_t`), which works well when conditions change slowly but fails badly right when something is starting to shift, exactly the moment a prediction matters most. The profile baseline predicts the historical average speed for that station, that time of day, and that day type, computed from past data and ignoring today's live reading entirely; it captures regular daily patterns (like rush hour) but misses today's unusual event, like an accident. A real model is judged by how much it beats both: if a model's average precision is barely above the profile baseline's, most of its apparent skill is really just re-deriving the daily pattern the baseline already captures for free. Reporting a metric (like AP or MAE) without also reporting the same metric for these baselines makes the number impossible to interpret.

Baselines exist because a raw metric number has no inherent scale of goodness; 92 percent accuracy sounds impressive until you learn that always predicting 'not slow' also gets 92 percent accuracy on an imbalanced dataset, which is exactly why this course insists a baseline accompany every reported number rather than trusting the number alone. Persistence and the historical-profile baseline probe two different, complementary kinds of information: persistence tests whether a model is adding anything beyond 'nothing changed since the last reading', while the profile baseline tests whether a model is adding anything beyond 'this is a typical Tuesday at 5pm'. A model that beats persistence but not the profile is capturing daily seasonality it did not need machine learning to capture; a model that beats the profile but not persistence is arguably just interpolating recent conditions. The strongest possible baseline for a given problem is not always obvious in advance, and a well-run project deliberately searches for stronger baselines (a combination of persistence and profile, say) before declaring a learned model a genuine improvement.

The subtlety experienced practitioners watch for is baseline sandbagging: choosing a weak baseline (or one computed with a subtle leakage advantage removed, unlike the real model) to make a proposed model look better than it is, which is a well-documented problem in published machine learning research and one reason serious evaluation protocols require baselines to be tuned and evaluated under exactly the same data-leakage constraints as the main model. A second subtlety is that different baselines dominate in different regimes: persistence is nearly unbeatable at very short horizons (seconds to a couple of minutes) because almost nothing changes that fast, while the profile baseline becomes relatively stronger at longer horizons where today's specific conditions have had time to diverge from now but a learned model that only uses very recent history has little signal left to exploit. A baseline can also fail silently if it is computed with a look-ahead bug (for instance, a 'historical profile' accidentally including the very day being predicted), inflating its apparent strength and making a real model look weaker by comparison than it actually is, so baselines deserve exactly as much leakage scrutiny as the primary model, not less because they seem too simple to get wrong.

In production forecasting systems, baselines are not a one-time evaluation step but a permanent, continuously computed comparison that ships alongside the live model, because a monitoring dashboard that only shows the model's own metric over time cannot distinguish 'the model got worse' from 'the underlying prediction problem got easier or harder', whereas a model-minus-baseline gap isolates the model's actual contribution and is far more stable to watch for regressions. Large forecasting systems, including Apple's internal ones for things like demand or capacity prediction, often maintain a small portfolio of baselines rather than one, because different baselines are sensitive to different failure modes (a sudden regime change breaks the profile baseline first; a fast-changing signal breaks persistence first), and a model that only beats the weakest of them is a warning sign worth investigating before shipping. An open practical question in forecasting is how to keep baselines honest and up to date automatically as the underlying data distribution shifts, since a baseline computed once at project start and never revisited becomes exactly the kind of stale, uninformative comparison the whole practice exists to avoid.

terms.def: How guesses are scored. Average precision, precision, recall, Brier score, lead time and false-alarm rate are the course's metrics.
levels: A metric is the number that tells you how good a guess was, like counting how many stars you get for cleaning your room.

A metric is a rule for turning a model's predictions into one number that says how good they were. This course uses several: average precision, how well the model ranks likely-slow moments above others, precision and recall, the Brier score, how close predicted probabilities are to the truth, lead time, how early an alert fires, and the false-alarm rate.

Average precision is the area under the precision-recall curve, computed with `sklearn.metrics.average_precision_score(y_true, y_score)`; because only a few percent of rows are truly slow, accuracy is a useless metric here, a model that always predicts not-slow is right most of the time, and average precision, which focuses on ranking true positives near the top, is the right one. The Brier score, the mean of (p - y) squared, checks calibration, whether a predicted 0.3 really corresponds to a 30 percent chance. Lead time and false-alarm rate are computed per episode rather than per row, since what matters operationally is how early and how reliably an alert fires, not the score on any single five-minute slot.

The right metric follows from the decision the model supports, not from convention: because positives are rare, a threshold-free ranking metric like average precision is preferred during development, while a threshold-dependent metric like precision at a fixed recall matters once a specific alerting threshold is chosen for deployment. Average precision assumes the ranking, not the raw probability value, is what's being evaluated, so a model can have excellent average precision and terrible calibration at the same time, exactly why the Brier score and a reliability diagram are reported separately. A model's metric can look great on random validation rows and still fail operationally if episode-level metrics tell a different story, because a per-row metric treats every five-minute slot inside one long slowdown as an independent success, double-counting.

Metrics interact with the label's own definition in ways practitioners commonly miss: because the label is relative to an estimated profile, and prevalence drifts across seasons and roadwork, a single held-out test window is one draw from a moving distribution, so one number is not a reliable comparison between two models, rolling-origin evaluation across multiple folds is needed to see whether an apparent improvement is real or noise. There is a real tradeoff between metrics optimized for ranking and metrics that reward calibrated, decision-useful probabilities, and optimizing purely for the first can produce a model that ranks well but whose raw probabilities are unusable for setting a principled alert threshold. A subtle failure: reporting a metric only in aggregate across all stations hides that a model can be excellent on high-traffic stations and near-useless on low-traffic ones, since the aggregate is dominated by the stations with the most rows.

Production systems typically track a portfolio of metrics rather than one, an offline ranking metric for model comparison, a live calibration check against delayed ground truth for monitoring, and business metrics that the offline metrics are only a proxy for, because no single number captures everything a deployed model needs to get right, and optimizing tightly against just one invites Goodhart's law. An open and genuinely unresolved problem across the industry is metric drift under a moving population: as a model's own alerts change driver behavior, an alerted driver takes a different route, the very traffic pattern the metric is evaluated against changes, breaking the usual assumption that evaluation data reflects the world the model will act in.

terms.def: Precision is the share of alarms that were right; recall is the share of real jams that were alarmed. Raising one usually lowers the other.
levels: If you have a smoke alarm, precision is how often it goes off only when there's really a fire, and recall is how many real fires it actually catches. A jumpy alarm that goes off for burnt toast has bad precision; a lazy alarm that misses real fires has bad recall.

Precision answers "of the times the model said 'slow traffic,' how often was it right?" Recall answers "of all the times traffic really was slow, how many did the model catch?" If the model raises 100 alarms and 80 were real jams, precision is 80%; if there were 200 real jams total and it caught those 80, recall is 40%. You usually can't max out both at once, since being pickier about alarms, raising precision, tends to mean you miss more real jams, lowering recall.

Precision = true positives / (true positives + false positives); recall = true positives / (true positives + false negatives). Both come from the same confusion matrix, and moving the decision threshold on the model's score trades one against the other: a lower threshold catches more real jams (higher recall) but raises more false alarms (lower precision), and a higher threshold does the reverse. A precision-recall curve plots this tradeoff across every possible threshold, and the area under it, average precision, summarizes overall ranking quality independent of any one threshold choice.

Precision and recall are computed from a binary decision at a chosen threshold on the model's continuous score, so they describe an operating point, not the model itself, since the same model can be reported at very different precision-recall pairs depending purely on where the threshold is set, which is why comparing two models' precision at arbitrary, unmatched thresholds is not meaningful. The F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, collapses the tradeoff to one number under an implicit assumption that false positives and false negatives cost the same, which is rarely true operationally, since for a traffic alert system, missing a real jam and crying wolf plausibly have very different real-world costs, so F1 is often the wrong single number to optimize. Precision and recall both depend on prevalence: at very low prevalence, achieving high precision is intrinsically harder even for a strong model, since a small false-positive rate among a huge number of negatives still produces many false alarms in absolute terms. They fail as useful metrics on their own when reported at a single, unstated threshold, since a reader can't tell whether a reported precision reflects a genuinely better model or simply a more conservative threshold.

The precision-recall curve's shape, not just the area under it, carries information a single average-precision number discards, since a curve that holds high precision until very high recall and then collapses sharply behaves very differently in deployment than one that degrades gradually, even at matched average precision, and the right operating threshold depends on which shape you have. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is optimizing average precision in development and then choosing a deployment threshold based on a different, later criterion, say a fixed alert budget per day, without re-checking that the model's precision-recall behavior near that specific operating point is actually good, since average precision integrates over the whole curve and can look fine while the one region you actually operate in is weak. Precision and recall computed on a held-out test set are themselves estimates with sampling variance, particularly at low prevalence where the number of positive examples in any given test window can be small, so a single-window precision-recall comparison between models can be noise rather than signal without confidence intervals or multiple evaluation windows. In a real alerting system, precision and recall interact with the cost structure asymmetrically over time, since a run of false alarms erodes operator trust in a way that a matched number of one-off missed alarms might not, which is a dynamic that the static metrics don't capture at all.

At production scale, precision and recall are tracked as continuously monitored, prevalence-adjusted metrics rather than one-off evaluation numbers, since deployment prevalence drifts and a model's precision at a fixed threshold moves with it even when the model itself hasn't changed or degraded. Multi-stakeholder systems often need multiple simultaneous operating points, such as a high-precision threshold for an automated action and a high-recall threshold for flagging items to a human reviewer, which means precision and recall have to be reported and monitored as a family of thresholds, not a single pair. An open research question in imbalanced, high-stakes settings is how to design objective functions and evaluation protocols that better reflect asymmetric real-world costs than precision, recall or their averages do on their own, since none of the standard metrics are actually the loss function decision-makers care about.

terms.def: The area under the precision-recall curve: the prevalence for random guessing, 1.0 for perfect. Not fooled by rare positives.
levels: Imagine you are guessing which of many toy boxes has a prize inside, and you get to guess in order, best guess first. Average precision checks whether your first guesses were actually the ones with the prize, not the last ones. A perfect guesser gets a perfect score.

Average precision (AP) is a score for how well a model ranks things, used when what you care about is rare, like a slowdown that only happens a small percent of the time. It looks at the precision-recall curve — precision is how many of your guesses were right, recall is how many of the real cases you found — and AP is the area under that curve. A score of 1.0 means perfect ranking; a model guessing at random scores around the rate at which the rare thing actually happens, which for a slowdown might be just a few percent.

Average precision is the area under the precision-recall curve, which plots precision (true positives divided by all predicted positives) against recall (true positives divided by all actual positives) as the decision threshold is swept from strict to lenient. It ranges from the prevalence rate (what a random guesser achieves) up to 1.0 for a perfect ranker. It is preferred over metrics like plain accuracy or ROC-AUC when the positive class is rare — a slowdown might be only 3% of five-minute windows — because a model can score well on accuracy or even ROC-AUC by mostly ignoring the rare class, while AP specifically rewards putting the true positives near the top of a ranked list of predictions.

Average precision summarizes the precision-recall tradeoff into one number by computing the area under the PR curve, typically via a step-function approximation over the sorted predicted scores: AP = Σₙ (Rₙ − Rₙ₋₁) Pₙ, summing precision at each recall level as the threshold moves through each positive example in ranked order. Unlike ROC-AUC, which averages over all thresholds including the many where the classifier is confidently correct on the (usually huge) negative class, AP is dominated by behavior near the top of the ranking, which matches the operational question in this course's traffic project — 'if I can only act on the top few percent of predicted slowdowns, how many are real.' A model that scores well on AP concentrates its highest scores on true slowdowns rather than spreading confidence evenly; a random guesser's expected AP equals the prevalence rate, which for a rare positive class can look deceptively low even for models that are doing something useful, so AP scores should always be read next to that baseline. AP is threshold-independent — it does not require picking a single decision cutoff — which makes it well suited to comparing models before an operational threshold has been chosen.

AP's dominant weighting of the top of the ranking is both its strength and its main pitfall: because it heavily weights the region of high precision and low recall, a model can post an impressive AP while performing poorly at the recall levels that actually matter operationally, if for instance an application needs to catch most slowdowns (high recall) rather than just be confident about the easiest few. Comparing AP across problems or datasets with different class prevalence is a common mistake, since AP is not baseline-corrected the way, say, a normalized score would be — an AP of 0.3 might be excellent on a dataset where positives are 2% of rows and mediocre on one where positives are 15%, so AP is meaningful mainly against its own random-guess baseline, not as an absolute number compared across settings. There are multiple slightly different implementations of the PR-curve interpolation (the interpolated 11-point average precision used historically in information retrieval versus the exact step-function version scikit-learn's `average_precision_score` computes), and mixing them up when comparing to a paper's reported numbers is a subtle, common error. AP also does not distinguish between errors that are 'close calls near the threshold' and ones that are badly wrong, so two models with identical AP can behave very differently in the region an operator actually cares about, which is why AP is usually reported alongside a precision-recall curve plot and a specific operating point, not as a single number in isolation.

In production systems handling rare, high-stakes events at scale, AP remains a standard offline model-selection metric, but the metric that actually governs deployment is usually precision and recall at a small number of chosen, business-relevant operating points (for example, 'top 1% of alerts must be at least 80% precise'), because AP averages over threshold regions that will never actually be used in practice. An open, recurring challenge is that AP computed offline on historical data can diverge from a model's effective real-world 'AP' once deployed, both because the positive rate itself can drift over time (traffic patterns change) and because, as with any deployed predictor, the act of acting on predictions changes the distribution being measured — which is why production systems track live precision-recall behavior continuously rather than trusting a single offline evaluation to hold indefinitely.

terms.def: The score above which an alert fires. Chosen on validation to meet a required precision.
levels: A threshold is a line in the sand: if your worry-o-meter goes above it, you ring the bell; if it stays below, you stay quiet.

A threshold, written τ (tau), is the score above which the model's alert fires. The model outputs a number between 0 and 1 for each row, and if that number is above τ, the system says slow traffic is coming; otherwise it stays silent. The threshold is chosen after training, on a separate validation set, not decided in advance.

A model gives each row a probability-like score, for example `p_30`, between 0 and 1, and an alert fires when that score exceeds τ. Choosing τ is a business decision translated into a precision requirement, for instance at least half of all alarms must be correct, and `precision_recall_curve` gives the tool: it returns precision and recall at every possible threshold, so you scan for the lowest threshold meeting the precision bar, `thr[ok[0]]`, since scikit-learn orders thresholds increasing and the lowest one meeting the bar keeps the most recall. Save τ per horizon into `models/calibration.json` so it can be re-tuned later without retraining the underlying model.

The threshold is deliberately kept separate from model training because it encodes a cost tradeoff, false alarms versus missed jams, that belongs to the product, not to the loss function the model was fit with: logistic regression and LightGBM here are both trained to produce a well-ranked score, and only afterward is a single operating point chosen on that score. This separation lets the required precision change, say from 50% to 70%, by re-running only the threshold search on the validation split, not retraining, since the underlying ranking is unaffected. It also means threshold choice is only as good as the calibration of the underlying scores; if the model's probabilities are systematically too high or too low, a fixed precision target picked on validation may not transfer to a differently-distributed period, like a holiday week, without recalibration.

A subtlety many practitioners miss is that a threshold picked once on a single validation window is a point estimate with sampling variance, and it can shift meaningfully if re-derived on a different slice of time, since traffic is non-stationary; bootstrap resampling across validation days, as this course does, gives a distribution of plausible thresholds, not just one number, and reporting that range is more honest than reporting τ to three decimal places. There is also a subtle asymmetry in the optimal-decision derivation: writing expected cost as a function of the decision shows that alerting is worth it exactly when the predicted probability exceeds the false-alarm cost divided by the sum of false-alarm and miss costs, which means the right precision target is not a fixed universal number but depends on how costly a missed jam is relative to a false alert, a business input the threshold search can only reflect, not derive.

In production, a single global threshold rarely survives contact with a large, heterogeneous deployment: different stations, times of day, or user segments can have different cost structures or different score distributions, so systems at scale often move to per-segment or continuously recalibrated thresholds, sometimes chosen automatically to hold precision constant as the underlying score distribution drifts, a harder and more fragile problem than the one-time offline threshold search this course teaches. An open production question is how to detect threshold staleness, a τ that once met its precision target but silently no longer does because the world changed, before it shows up as a spike in complaints about false or missed alerts.

terms.def: Whether a score of 0.3 really means a 30 percent chance. Checked with a reliability diagram; fixed with isotonic regression.
levels: If a weather app says there's a 30 percent chance of rain, calibration is asking: out of all the times it said that, did it actually rain about 3 times out of 10? A calibrated app tells the truth about its guesses.

A calibrated model's probability outputs mean what they say: among all the times it predicted a 30 percent chance of something, that thing should actually happen about 30 percent of the time. You check this by grouping predictions into bins, all the times the model said 'around 30 percent', and comparing the predicted probability to how often the event actually happened in that bin; that comparison is a reliability diagram. If a model is overconfident or underconfident, a fix like isotonic regression can adjust its raw scores into better-calibrated probabilities.

A reliability diagram bins predictions by predicted probability (0-10 percent, 10-20 percent, and so on) and plots the actual observed frequency of the positive class in each bin against the bin's midpoint; a perfectly calibrated model traces the diagonal line. Many models, especially ones optimized purely for ranking or accuracy, like gradient-boosted trees, produce scores that are useful for ordering examples but are systematically over- or under-confident as literal probabilities. Isotonic regression fits a non-decreasing step function mapping raw scores to calibrated probabilities using a held-out calibration set, and Platt scaling, fitting a logistic regression on top of the raw score, is a simpler, parametric alternative that works better with less calibration data.

Calibration and discrimination, the model's ability to separate positive from negative examples, measured by ROC-AUC or average precision, are different properties, and a model can be excellent at one and poor at the other; a model that perfectly ranks examples but always outputs either 0.05 or 0.95 has fine discrimination and poor calibration if the true rate in a given bin is actually 30 percent. This matters operationally whenever a probability is used for a downstream decision that depends on its literal value, setting an alert threshold, combining scores from multiple models, or estimating expected cost, rather than just for ranking or picking the single most likely class. Logistic regression, trained by minimizing log loss, is calibrated 'for free' on data similar to its training distribution because log loss is a proper scoring rule that rewards honest probabilities; tree ensembles and neural networks trained with the same loss can still end up miscalibrated in practice due to overfitting or class imbalance. Calibration must be fit and evaluated on a held-out set distinct from both training and final test data, or the calibration mapping itself will overfit and the reported calibration will be optimistic.

Proper scoring rules give calibration a rigorous foundation: a scoring rule, log loss, Brier score, is proper if the expected score is uniquely minimized by reporting one's true belief, which is why minimizing log loss during training pushes a model toward calibration as a side effect of pursuing accuracy, not as a separate objective, but this guarantee is asymptotic and in-distribution, and it says nothing about calibration under distribution shift or with a misspecified model class. Isotonic regression, being nonparametric, can fit any monotonic miscalibration pattern but needs more calibration data to avoid overfitting the calibration curve itself, especially in low-probability regions where events are rare by definition; Platt scaling's parametric form is more data-efficient but cannot correct a non-sigmoidal miscalibration shape. A common practitioner mistake is calibrating on a random train-test split when the deployment distribution has temporal or spatial shift, a model calibrated on last month's traffic data is not guaranteed calibrated for next month's, especially across a regime change like a new detector coming online. Multi-class and multi-label calibration are considerably harder than the binary case, since fixing marginal calibration per class does not guarantee the joint distribution of predictions is calibrated.

In production ML systems, calibration is often the difference between a model that is merely accurate and one that is safe to act on automatically, a fraud or safety system that fires an automated action at a threshold needs its probabilities to mean what they say, consistently, as the underlying population drifts, which is why production pipelines monitor calibration continuously, not just at launch, and recalibrate on a rolling window. Deep learning models are known to be poorly calibrated by default, especially large, overparameterized networks trained with cross-entropy for many epochs past the point of minimum validation loss, which is why techniques like temperature scaling, a single learned scalar that softens overconfident softmax outputs, are near-universal in production deep learning pipelines. An open research question is calibration under distribution shift and for rare, high-stakes events specifically, where there is not enough data in the tail to verify calibration empirically at all, forcing a choice between trusting an extrapolated calibration curve or falling back to a more conservative, uncalibrated decision rule.

terms.def: Mean squared difference between predicted probability and outcome; lower is better.
levels: Imagine guessing how likely it is to rain, like a 70 percent chance of rain, and then checking how close your guess was to what actually happened. The Brier score is a way to grade those percentage guesses; the closer your guesses are to reality, the lower, and better, your score.

The Brier score measures how good a probability prediction is, by squaring the difference between the predicted probability and the actual outcome, 1 if it happened, 0 if it did not, and averaging that over every prediction. If you predict 90 percent and it happens, your error for that prediction is small, 0.1 squared; if you predict 90 percent and it does not happen, your error is large, 0.9 squared. A perfect predictor has a Brier score of 0; a model that is confidently wrong a lot has a high Brier score.

The formula for one prediction is (p minus y) squared, where p is the predicted probability and y is the actual outcome, 0 or 1; the Brier score is the average of this over all predictions. It ranges from 0, perfect, to 1, perfectly wrong every time, and always predicting the base rate gives a baseline score to compare against. Unlike accuracy, it rewards a model for saying I am not sure, predicting near 0.5, when it genuinely is not sure, rather than forcing an overconfident guess.

The Brier score decomposes into calibration, how close predicted probabilities match observed frequencies, and refinement or resolution, how much the predictions vary and separate the classes, which is why two models can have similar Brier scores for very different reasons, one well-calibrated but not very discriminating, another sharp but poorly calibrated. It is a strictly proper scoring rule, meaning a forecaster who truly believes the outcome has probability p minimizes their expected Brier score by reporting p honestly, rather than by hedging toward 0.5 or rounding toward 0 or 1, a real mathematical property, not just a convenient interpretation. It generalizes log loss's goal of penalizing confident wrong answers, but with a bounded, squared penalty rather than log loss's unbounded one, which makes it less sensitive to a single very confident wrong prediction. It fails to be very informative on its own when class imbalance is severe, since a trivial always-predict-the-base-rate model can already achieve a fairly low Brier score, so it should be compared to that baseline, not read as an absolute number.

The calibration-refinement decomposition, sometimes called the Murphy decomposition, lets you diagnose why a model's Brier score is what it is: a reliability diagram visualizes the calibration component directly, and a model with excellent AUC but poor calibration can still have a mediocre Brier score, surprising practitioners who expected the two metrics to agree. Brier score and log loss usually rank models similarly but not always identically, because log loss's unbounded penalty for confident wrong predictions makes it far more sensitive to rare, badly miscalibrated extreme predictions than the bounded, squared Brier penalty is. A common practitioner mistake is comparing Brier scores across datasets or across different class balances as if the number were an absolute quality measure, when it should always be compared against the Brier score of the trivial base-rate predictor on that same dataset. Post-hoc calibration methods, Platt scaling, isotonic regression, are typically evaluated by how much they improve Brier score or log loss on a held-out set without hurting AUC, which is the standard way to check that recalibration is fixing probabilities rather than distorting them.

In production systems where a probability is shown to a person or feeds into a downstream decision, routing, alerting, resource allocation, Brier score is often tracked in production monitoring, not just at training time, because calibration can drift after deployment even when discrimination, AUC, stays stable, and Brier score is sensitive to exactly that kind of drift. Multi-class and multi-label generalizations of Brier score exist and are used when a system outputs a full distribution over more than two outcomes, not just a single slow or not-slow probability. An open practical problem is that Brier score treats all miscalibration equally regardless of the cost of being wrong at different operating points, so production systems often complement it with cost-weighted or threshold-specific metrics tied to the actual downstream decision the probability feeds into.

terms.def: Estimating uncertainty by resampling the data many times and recomputing the score. Resample whole days for time series.
levels: Imagine you have a jar of marbles and you want to know how sure you are about their average color. You reach in, grab a handful, write down what you got, put them back, and do it again and again. Doing that many times shows you how much your answer might wobble from one handful to the next.

The bootstrap is a way to estimate how uncertain a number is by resampling the data many times and recomputing the number each time. If you have 100 days of traffic data and you resample 100 days with replacement, some days picked more than once, some not picked at all, a thousand times, and compute the accuracy each time, the spread of those thousand accuracies tells you how much to trust the original number. For time series, you resample whole days at once, not individual five-minute rows, so you do not break up the patterns within a day.

The bootstrap procedure: from a dataset of size n, draw a new sample of size n with replacement, compute the statistic of interest on that resample, and repeat this hundreds or thousands of times to build a distribution of the statistic. The spread of that distribution, often summarized as a 95 percent interval by taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles, approximates the sampling uncertainty of the original estimate without requiring a closed-form formula. For time-series data like PeMS traffic, resampling individual rows would break the autocorrelation structure, so the block bootstrap resamples whole contiguous chunks, a full day, in Traffic1, instead of individual five-minute readings. `scipy.stats.bootstrap` or a short custom loop implements this directly in Python.

The bootstrap works because the empirical distribution of the data is itself a consistent estimator of the true underlying distribution, so resampling from the data approximates resampling from the true distribution, and the variability across resamples approximates the true sampling variability of the statistic, this holds asymptotically for i.i.d. data under fairly general conditions, but the approximation quality depends on sample size and how smooth the statistic is as a function of the data. For dependent data like a time series, the ordinary row-level bootstrap underestimates true uncertainty because it discards the correlation between nearby observations, which is why the block bootstrap is the standard fix, trading some bias for a more honest variance estimate. Bootstrap confidence intervals come in several flavors, percentile, basic, bias-corrected-and-accelerated, and the naive percentile method, while simplest, can be biased for skewed statistics. In Traffic1, the bootstrap is naturally used to put an uncertainty band around a metric like AUC or accuracy: resample days with replacement, recompute the metric on each resample, and report the spread alongside the point estimate.

Choosing block length for a block bootstrap is itself a bias-variance tradeoff with no universally correct answer, too short and dependence structure is lost, too long and there are too few effectively independent blocks to resample from, and methods like the stationary bootstrap exist specifically to reduce sensitivity to this choice. A common mistake practitioners make is bootstrapping a statistic that is itself computed across the full dependent structure of the data, like an AUC that implicitly compares many pairs of points, without recognizing that resampling days changes which pairs of positive and negative examples get compared. The bootstrap is not a universal fix for small-sample problems: with genuinely little data, especially few slow event days, the bootstrap's own sampling distribution is itself poorly estimated, since it can only ever resample from the handful of unique days actually observed, never generate genuinely new information. Bootstrapping model predictions to get prediction intervals is a related but distinct use, it requires resampling and refitting the model itself many times, which is far more expensive and raises questions about whether refitting captures model uncertainty correctly or just adds noise from an unstable fitting procedure.

At production scale, bootstrapping every metric for every model retrain is often too expensive to do naively, so production systems approximate it, analytic variance formulas where available, or a reduced number of bootstrap resamples combined with monitoring the metric's variance over time as an empirical alternative to a fresh bootstrap each run. A genuinely open question in applied uncertainty quantification is how to combine bootstrap-style resampling uncertainty with model uncertainty and true aleatoric uncertainty into one interpretable number that an engineer or a downstream system can act on, since conflating these three is a common source of both overconfident and needlessly conservative production systems.

terms.def: An onset is the first row of an episode; lead time is minutes from the first alert to the onset; a false alarm is an alert with no episode in the next hour.
levels: The onset is the exact moment traffic starts getting slow, like the very first raindrop before a whole rainstorm. Lead time is how much warning you got, like hearing thunder five minutes before the rain actually starts. A false alarm is like someone yelling 'it's raining!' when really the sky stays dry the whole time.

The onset of a slow episode is its very first five-minute row, the moment the slowdown officially begins. Lead time is how many minutes passed between when a warning was first raised and when the onset actually happened; more lead time means more useful advance warning. A false alarm is a warning that was raised but no slow episode actually followed within the next hour, which wastes the warning's credibility. A good early-warning system wants long lead times and few false alarms, and there is usually a tradeoff between the two.

Given a slow episode's onset time (the first of its three defining rows), lead time is computed as `onset_time - first_alert_time` for whichever alert preceded that onset, measured in minutes; a model that only ever fires exactly at onset has zero lead time, while one that fires reliably 20 minutes early is far more operationally useful even at the same raw accuracy. A false alarm is counted when an alert fires but no slow episode's onset occurs within some following window, typically the next hour in this course's setup; the false alarm rate is the fraction of alerts that were false alarms, not the fraction of all time periods that were false alarms, which is an important distinction when the underlying event is rare. Reporting lead time and false alarm rate together, rather than a single aggregate metric like accuracy, is standard practice for any early-warning system, from weather to traffic to seismic alerts, because those two numbers directly describe the tradeoff an operator actually experiences.

Lead time and false alarm rate are two coordinates of the same underlying tradeoff a model's decision threshold controls: lowering the alert threshold raises average lead time (the model fires earlier, more often, catching onsets sooner) but also raises the false alarm rate, and raising the threshold does the reverse, so there is no single 'best' operating point without a stated preference between the two costs. Because onset is itself defined by a labeling rule (three consecutive rows below a relative speed threshold) that has its own detection latency, a model's theoretical maximum lead time is bounded by how far in advance the true underlying slowdown, as opposed to the label's confirmed onset, actually begins, which is a ceiling no amount of modeling can push past. Aggregating lead time across many alerts requires care: reporting only the mean can be misleading if the distribution is bimodal (many alerts fire right at onset with zero lead time, some fire much earlier), so reporting a distribution or percentiles of lead time is more honest than a single average. A false alarm 'within the next hour' window is itself a modeling choice with the same sensitivity issues as any other threshold: a longer window makes false alarms rarer by construction, not because the model actually improved.

The precision-recall framing that underlies false alarm rate has a well-known asymmetry practitioners often mishandle: minimizing false alarms alone drives a system toward never alerting, and maximizing lead time alone drives it toward always alerting far in advance, so any single operating point implicitly encodes an assumed cost ratio between a missed slowdown and a false alarm that should be stated explicitly, ideally set by whoever actually acts on the alerts rather than defaulted to a metric-optimal but operationally meaningless threshold. A subtler issue is that lead time, computed only for correctly detected onsets, silently ignores missed onsets (recall failures), so a system can show an impressively long average lead time purely by only ever alerting on the easiest, most gradual slowdowns and missing the sudden ones entirely; lead time should always be read alongside recall, not in isolation. In practice, false alarms are rarely uniform in cost — a false alarm during an already-known incident, or one that clusters right after a true alarm as the model 'chatters' near the threshold, is less costly to an operator than an isolated, surprising false alarm, and raw false alarm counts do not distinguish these, which is a common gap between an evaluation metric and what actually erodes operator trust.

Production early-warning systems, whether for traffic, network outages, or hardware failures, generally do not ship a single fixed alert threshold at all; they tune per-context operating points (different lead time and false-alarm tradeoffs for a highway known for sudden incidents versus one with mostly predictable rush-hour congestion) and continuously monitor whether the deployed threshold's realized false alarm rate matches what was validated offline, since data drift silently moves that rate over time. At Apple's scale, alerting systems for operational metrics generally add alert suppression and deduplication logic on top of the raw model output specifically to address the false-alarm-clustering problem, because operators who receive many correlated alerts for what is really one event learn to ignore the alerting channel entirely, which defeats the system's purpose regardless of what the offline lead time and false alarm numbers say. An open problem in this space is jointly optimizing lead time and false alarm rate against the real, and usually asymmetric and context-dependent, cost of a miss versus a false alarm, rather than against a fixed, symmetric proxy metric chosen mostly because it is easy to compute offline.

terms.def: The data slowly changing after training. Measured with the population stability index; confirmed by delayed scoring.
levels: Drift is when the world slowly changes without telling you, like your shoes fitting fine in September and feeling tight by spring because your feet grew.

Drift is when the data a model sees in production slowly stops looking like the data it was trained on. New roadwork changes typical speeds at a station, a detector gets replaced and reports slightly differently, or driving patterns shift over the seasons, and the model's assumptions quietly become out of date. Drift is measured with the population stability index, comparing a feature's distribution now against its distribution at training time, and confirmed by checking the model's actual accuracy once true outcomes catch up.

The population stability index buckets a feature into bins, compares the share of current data in each bin against the share at training time, and sums a weighted log-ratio across bins; a value above roughly 0.2 is a common rule-of-thumb threshold for meaningful drift. Lag features like `speed_lag_3` are stationary by construction, since they are differences and ratios relative to recent history, while calendar and static features, like a station's typical top speed, drift as roadwork or detector replacement changes what free flow actually looks like there. The index flags a distributional change immediately; confirming it actually hurt the model requires waiting for delayed scoring, matching predictions against ground truth once it arrives.

Drift comes in two flavors that call for different responses: covariate drift, where the input distribution shifts but the relationship between inputs and the label stays the same, and concept drift, where the relationship itself changes, the more dangerous case because retraining on more of the same kind of data does not fix it. The population stability index detects that something changed but not which kind, so it is a trigger for investigation, not a diagnosis. A model can show zero drift on every monitored feature and still be silently wrong if the world changed along a dimension nobody thought to monitor, which is why drift monitoring is complementary to, never a replacement for, tracking real accuracy against delayed ground truth.

A specific subtlety here: lag and rolling-window features are stationary by construction, so a stability index on them will look deceptively calm even while the calendar and static features paired with them are drifting hard, and a monitoring system that only checks the stable-looking features misses the real signal. Practitioners commonly set a drift threshold once and never revisit it, even though the right sensitivity depends on how costly a missed drift event is versus how costly a false alarm that triggers an unnecessary retrain is, the same cost-asymmetry reasoning used to pick the model's own alert threshold, one level up. Retraining blindly in response to detected drift, without checking whether it is concept drift, in which case more historical data does not help, or a genuine permanent shift versus a temporary anomaly, can make a model worse, not better.

In production ML at scale, drift detection runs continuously across thousands of features for many models, and the practical problem shifts from detecting drift, solved, to deciding which of the daily drift alerts deserve a human's attention, since these statistics fire constantly on any system with real-world variability, mostly on features that don't actually matter for the label. Automated retraining pipelines increasingly gate on drift signals combined with a live calibration check, retraining only when both a distributional shift and an actual accuracy drop are observed together, which reduces false-alarm retrains but adds the latency of waiting for ground truth. An open research question is causal drift attribution: given a drifted metric, automatically identifying which upstream feature or data-source change caused it, rather than a human tracing it by hand across a large feature pipeline.

terms.def: One number comparing a feature's distribution now with training. Below 0.1 stable, above 0.25 moved.
levels: Imagine you counted your friends' favorite ice cream flavors on the first day of school, and you count again in the winter to see if everyone changed their mind. PSI is one number that says how much the count changed.

The population stability index, or PSI, compares a feature's distribution today against its distribution back when the model was trained, and gives you a single number summarizing how different they are. It works by splitting the feature into bins, say, ranges of speed, checking what fraction of rows fell into each bin during training versus what fraction falls into each bin now, and combining the differences. A small PSI, below about 0.1, means the feature looks about the same as before; a PSI above about 0.25 means it has shifted enough to worry about.

PSI is computed as the sum, over bins, of (current % − training %) × ln(current % / training %), where the feature is bucketed into the same fixed bins both times, typically deciles from the training distribution. In this course, PSI is computed per feature, average speed, occupancy, hour of day, comparing the last week's values against the training window, as part of routine monitoring. A rule of thumb treats PSI < 0.1 as stable, 0.1–0.25 as a moderate shift worth watching, and > 0.25 as a real distribution change that likely means the model's assumptions no longer hold.

PSI is a discretized, symmetrized measure related to the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two distributions binned the same way; unlike a raw statistical distance, it's designed to be interpretable at fixed thresholds (0.1, 0.25) that practitioners have converged on as rough conventions rather than anything derived from theory. It's computed per feature independently, which means it can miss a shift that only shows up jointly, such as two features whose individual marginal distributions look stable while their correlation has changed entirely, a real limitation for a spatially and temporally correlated problem like traffic. PSI also depends heavily on the binning choice: too few bins hides a real shift, too many makes the statistic noisy on any bin with few observations, and it's undefined, or requires a small-count adjustment, if a bin that had training-time mass has exactly zero current observations. It fails specifically for features with heavy-tailed or highly seasonal distributions, like traffic speed at different hours, where a "shift" it flags might just be the ordinary daily cycle rather than genuine drift, unless it's computed conditional on time of day.

PSI is a useful triage signal, not a diagnosis: a high PSI tells you a feature's distribution moved, but not whether that movement matters for the model's actual predictions, since a feature can drift substantially in a region the model barely relies on, or drift only slightly in exactly the region that drives its decisions, which is why serious monitoring pairs PSI with a direct check of prediction or performance drift, not PSI alone. A mistake practitioners make is computing PSI against a fixed, aging training-time reference forever, when a rolling or periodically refreshed reference window is usually more appropriate for a naturally seasonal quantity like traffic, or every winter will trip every summer-trained threshold. PSI's additive, per-bin structure also means a large positive shift in one bin can be partly canceled by a large negative shift in another when they're of similar magnitude but different sign contribution, though this is less of an issue than with a naive difference-of-means statistic because PSI sums absolute-value-like contributions, not signed ones. Choosing PSI over other divergence measures, population-level KL, Jensen-Shannon, or a two-sample statistical test like Kolmogorov-Smirnov, is mostly a practical decision, since PSI is cheap, well-understood by non-statisticians on a team, and has established thresholds, rather than a claim that it's the most statistically powerful choice.

At production scale, PSI, or a family of PSI-like statistics, one per feature, is usually just the front layer of a larger drift-detection system that also monitors label distribution, prediction distribution, and joint feature correlations, since per-feature marginal drift alone catches only a subset of the ways a deployed model's world can change under it. Automated systems increasingly try to move beyond fixed thresholds (0.1, 0.25) toward statistically calibrated alerting that accounts for the natural sampling variance of PSI at a given window size and feature cardinality, since a rigid threshold either fires too often on noise at small sample sizes or too rarely to be useful at very large ones. An open problem is closing the loop from a PSI alert to an actual decision automatically, since flagging drift is comparatively easy, but deciding whether to retrain, roll back, or simply widen a confidence interval in response is still mostly a human judgment call layered on top of the statistic.

terms.def: A function from inputs to a score, with parameters set by training.
levels: A model is like a recipe that takes some ingredients — numbers about the road — and turns them into a guess, like 'traffic will be slow soon.' You teach the recipe to be good at guessing by showing it lots of examples of what actually happened.

A model is a function: you give it inputs (like a station's recent speeds) and it gives you back a score or a prediction, like the chance traffic will be slow in 30 minutes. What makes a model useful is training — showing it many past examples so it can adjust its internal numbers, called parameters, to make good guesses. Different kinds of models (logistic regression, decision trees, neural networks) are different shapes of that same idea: inputs in, a score out.

Formally, a model is a function f(x; θ) that maps an input vector x (the features, like recent speed and time of day) to an output (a score or class probability), where θ are the parameters — numbers learned from data rather than set by hand. Training is the process of choosing θ to make the model's outputs match known labels as closely as possible, usually by minimizing a loss function with an algorithm like gradient descent. Logistic regression's model is `sigmoid(w · x + b)`, with weights `w` and intercept `b` as its parameters; a decision tree's 'parameters' are instead the sequence of splits it learned. In this course, the same input features feed logistic regression, LightGBM, and neural network models in turn, each a different function shape learned from the same training table.

A model is defined by three things: its functional form (the hypothesis class — linear, tree-based, neural, and so on, which determines what relationships it can represent at all), its parameters θ (the specific numbers within that form, set by training), and the training procedure that sets them, typically by minimizing a loss function over a training set via an optimization algorithm like gradient descent or a tree-building heuristic like gradient boosting. A model's capacity — roughly, how flexible its functional form is — determines the bias-variance tradeoff it sits at: too little capacity underfits (misses real patterns), too much overfits (memorizes noise in the training data rather than the underlying signal), which is why model complexity and regularization are chosen alongside, not independently of, the amount of training data available. Model comparison should always happen through held-out evaluation, never training performance, since a sufficiently flexible model can fit training data near-perfectly without learning anything that generalizes. In this course's traffic project, the same features are deliberately fed to a spectrum of models (logistic regression to LightGBM to neural networks to graph networks) to make the capacity-versus-data tradeoff concrete: a simple model can match a complex one when data and signal are limited, and only clearly loses once there is enough structured signal (the graph among freeway stations) that a plain tabular model literally cannot represent.

The choice of model class is itself a strong inductive bias — logistic regression assumes a linear decision boundary in feature space (or in a transformed feature space, if you engineer nonlinear features by hand), tree ensembles assume the target is well-approximated by axis-aligned splits and their combinations, and graph neural networks assume the label depends on a specific relational structure among inputs (which stations are physically adjacent) — and a model can only be as good as the match between this bias and the real structure in the data, which is a large part of why feature engineering and model choice interact rather than being independent decisions. A subtlety practitioners often get wrong is treating a model comparison as fair when the models were not tuned with comparable effort or comparable access to the same information — a heavily-tuned LightGBM beating an out-of-the-box neural network says more about tuning effort than about which model class is actually better suited to the problem. Model parameters and hyperparameters are frequently conflated informally but are a meaningfully different kind of object: parameters (θ) are learned by the training algorithm from data, hyperparameters (learning rate, tree depth, network architecture) are chosen by the practitioner, usually via a separate validation procedure, and set the conditions under which parameter learning happens. As models scale in parameter count, the classical picture of overfitting (more parameters than data means memorization) breaks down in ways that are still not fully theoretically understood — very large neural networks can have far more parameters than training examples and still generalize well, a phenomenon (double descent, benign overfitting) that remains an active area of theoretical research.

In production, 'the model' is rarely just the parameters — it is the parameters plus a frozen specification of preprocessing, feature computation, and postprocessing, all of which must be versioned and deployed together, since a model trained against one feature computation and served against a subtly different one (a classic training-serving skew bug) fails silently rather than with an error. At scale, model selection also has to weigh inference cost and latency alongside accuracy — a marginally more accurate model that is ten times slower or larger can be a net loss if it cannot serve within a latency budget or fit an edge deployment — which is why production model comparisons routinely report cost-accuracy tradeoff curves rather than a single best number. An open, largely unsolved problem is model behavior under genuine distribution shift after deployment: offline evaluation measures how well a model fits the data it was trained and tested on, but says little about how gracefully it degrades, or fails to, once the world changes in ways the training data never showed it — which is exactly why retraining cadence, monitoring, and rollback plans are treated as part of the model, not an afterthought.

terms.def: Parameters are learned from data; hyperparameters (learning rate, number of leaves) are chosen before training.
levels: Parameters are the numbers a robot slowly figures out by practicing, like how hard to push a swing; hyperparameters are the rules you set for the robot's practice before it even starts, like how many times it gets to try.

Parameters, also called weights, are the numbers a model learns from the training data, adjusted a little bit at a time to make its guesses better. Hyperparameters, like the learning rate or the number of leaves in a tree, are settings you choose before training even begins, and they are not learned. In logistic regression, `w` and `b` are the parameters; how big a step gradient descent takes each round is a hyperparameter.

A parameter is a number the training algorithm updates, like the weight vector `w` and bias `b` in logistic regression, which start random or zero and are nudged every epoch by `w -= eta * gw`. A hyperparameter is chosen up front and held fixed during that training run, for example `learning_rate=0.05` and `num_leaves=63` in LightGBM, or `eta` in the hand-written gradient descent loop. You cannot fit hyperparameters the same way you fit parameters; instead you try several values and keep whichever gives the best validation score.

Parameters live inside the model's functional form and are optimized by minimizing a loss function on training data, gradient descent for logistic regression, leaf-splitting for LightGBM, so the number of parameters is fixed by the model's architecture, one weight per feature plus a bias for logistic regression, and their values are entirely determined by the data and the optimizer. Hyperparameters, by contrast, control the model's capacity and the optimization process itself, and they cannot be chosen by minimizing training loss, since more capacity, deeper trees, smaller `min_data_in_leaf`, always fits training data at least as well and often overfits; hyperparameters are instead selected using a held-out validation score. This distinction generalizes past logistic regression and trees: in a neural network the weight matrices are parameters, while the number of layers, hidden width, and learning rate are hyperparameters, and the same overfitting risk applies to searching over hyperparameters as to fitting parameters.

A subtlety many practitioners skip is that hyperparameter search is itself a form of fitting, and choosing among many configurations on a single validation split is optimistic in exactly the way choosing parameters on the training split is; nested or rolling-origin validation, where an outer split evaluates the whole selection process, is the honest but more expensive answer, and skipping it quietly inflates a reported metric. Another common confusion is treating more hyperparameters tuned as strictly better: heavy hyperparameter search on a small or noisy validation set can overfit to that split's particular noise, which is why this course emphasizes checking whether reported gains hold up across rolling folds, not just one split. There is also a real cost asymmetry: gradient-based parameters update cheaply via backpropagation on millions of examples at once, while most hyperparameter search methods treat each configuration as an expensive black-box evaluation requiring a full retrain, which is why hyperparameter tuning is often the more compute-expensive half of a modeling project despite touching far fewer numbers.

At the scale of large neural networks, the parameter and hyperparameter line has started to blur: scaling laws let researchers predict good hyperparameters, learning rate, batch size, for a large model from experiments on much smaller ones, effectively treating hyperparameter choice itself as something learnable across scale rather than something re-searched from scratch for every model size. Hyperparameter importance analysis, understanding which dials actually matter for a given architecture and dataset, is itself now a research tool, and the reproducibility concern this raises is real: many reported gains in the literature turn out to be within the noise of the tuning budget used, meaning the tuning process, not just the parameters found, deserves to be reported and scrutinized.

terms.def: Weighted sum of features plus bias, squashed by the sigmoid into a probability. The simplest model that outputs a probability.
levels: Logistic regression is like a scale that weighs different clues about whether it will rain, adds them up, and then squishes the total into a number between 'definitely not' and 'definitely yes.'

Logistic regression takes each input feature, multiplies it by a learned weight, adds them all up along with one extra number called the bias, and then passes that total through a squashing function called the sigmoid, which turns any number into something between 0 and 1, a probability. It's the simplest model that outputs a real probability instead of just a raw score, which is why it's usually the first model tried on a new problem. Training means finding the weights that make its probabilities match the real outcomes as closely as possible.

The formula is p = sigmoid(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + b), where the sigmoid function is σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), squashing any real number z into the range (0, 1). In scikit-learn, `LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)` finds the weights w and bias b that minimize log loss (also called binary cross-entropy) on the training data, and `.predict_proba(X)` returns the resulting probabilities. For the traffic project, the features might be recent speed lags and time-of-day, and the output is the probability that a station will be slow 30 minutes from now; a threshold, often 0.5, turns that probability into a yes-or-no prediction.

Logistic regression assumes the log-odds of the outcome are a linear function of the features, which is a strong assumption; it cannot represent interactions or nonlinear relationships unless they are added explicitly as extra features, products of existing features, polynomial terms, and it will underfit data with genuinely nonlinear structure. It is trained by maximum likelihood, equivalent to minimizing the cross-entropy loss, using an iterative optimizer, gradient descent or a quasi-Newton method like L-BFGS, since there is no closed-form solution the way there is for plain linear regression. Its main strengths are calibration, its probabilities tend to be honest, since it is optimizing a proper scoring rule directly, and interpretability, each weight says how log-odds change per unit of a standardized feature, holding others fixed, which is why it remains the standard first baseline even in a course that goes on to LightGBM and neural networks. It fails when features are highly correlated (weights become unstable and hard to interpret, though predictions are still reasonable), when the true relationship is strongly nonlinear, or when classes are severely imbalanced without any adjustment to the loss or threshold.

Regularization (L2 by default in scikit-learn, sometimes L1 for sparsity) is not optional in practice; without it, on separable or near-separable data, the unregularized maximum-likelihood weights diverge toward infinity, since the model can always reduce the loss further by pushing decision-boundary-crossing points further into certainty, which is a real numerical failure mode, not just a theoretical curiosity. The decision boundary is linear in feature space, but with sufficient hand-engineered nonlinear features it can approximate more complex boundaries, a fact often used to argue logistic regression is 'inside' every neural network's output layer, since the final layer of a classification network is exactly a logistic or softmax regression on the learned representation beneath it. Practitioners commonly misread the coefficients as measuring 'importance' in an absolute sense, but a coefficient's magnitude is only meaningful after standardizing features to a common scale, and correlated features split their shared signal arbitrarily between their coefficients, which can make a genuinely important feature look weak. Convergence warnings from an iterative solver are frequently ignored, but an unconverged fit gives weights that depend on the optimizer's stopping point rather than a true minimum, which quietly undermines any claims about the fitted coefficients.
