An MLP has no structural assumptions about its input, no notion of position, order, or locality, so unlike a convolutional network built for images or a recurrent network built for sequences, it must learn everything about a problem's structure from data alone, which makes it a reasonable default for the traffic project's flat, tabular lag-and-time features but a weak choice for genuinely sequential or spatial structure. Overfitting is a constant risk given enough hidden units and few training examples, addressed with weight decay, dropout, and early stopping on a validation set.

Optimization landscape theory partly explains why heavily overparameterized networks, far more weights than training examples, tend to train reliably despite the loss surface being highly non-convex: results connecting overparameterization to a loss landscape with mostly benign saddle points rather than bad local minima, and the neural tangent kernel perspective viewing very wide networks as approximately linear (kernel) models in weight space, both offer partial explanations, though a full theory of why deep learning generalizes as well as it does empirically is still incomplete. Initialization scheme (Xavier or He initialization, chosen to match ReLU's asymmetry) and learning rate interact nontrivially with depth; too naive an initialization compounds through many layers into vanishing or exploding activations before training even starts, which is why deep MLPs were historically hard to train before these initialization schemes and normalization layers became standard. Practitioners commonly under-tune an MLP baseline, default hidden sizes, no learning-rate schedule, and conclude neural networks 'don't work' on their tabular problem, when in practice a well-tuned gradient-boosted tree often does genuinely outperform a naively-trained MLP on small-to-medium tabular data like PeMS traffic tables, which is a real, empirically-documented finding, not just poor tuning, though the gap narrows with enough data and with modern tabular-specific architectures.

At production and research scale, plain MLPs mostly persist as a component inside larger architectures, the feedforward block in a transformer is an MLP, and the final classification head of nearly every deep vision or graph model is one, rather than as standalone models for anything but genuinely unstructured tabular problems, where gradient-boosted trees still frequently compete with or beat them given realistic data sizes. On device, an MLP's simplicity, dense matrix multiplies, no exotic ops, makes it easy to run efficiently on the Neural Engine, which matters when the alternative is a more exotic architecture with ops that are poorly supported or slow on mobile silicon. An active research question is when and why depth generalizes better than width holding parameter count fixed, and how that tradeoff shifts as available data and compute both scale up, since the empirical answer keeps changing as larger, better-regularized models are tried.

terms.def: max(z, 0): zeroes negatives. The nonlinearity that lets a network bend.
levels: Imagine a wall with a ramp: if you're already above the ground, you keep going up exactly as much as you pushed, but if you try to go below the ground, the wall just stops you flat at zero. ReLU does that to numbers; positive numbers pass right through, and any negative number becomes zero.

ReLU stands for rectified linear unit, and it is a simple rule: if the number is positive, keep it exactly as it is; if the number is negative, turn it into zero. A neural network computes a weighted sum of its inputs, and then ReLU decides which of those sums turn on, stay positive, and which get shut off to zero. This small bend is what lets a network learn shapes more complicated than a straight line.

The formula is ReLU(z) equals max(z, 0): if z is 5, ReLU(z) is 5; if z is negative 3, ReLU(z) is 0. In a neural network layer, you first compute z, a weighted sum of the inputs plus a bias, then apply ReLU to get the layer's output, which becomes the next layer's input. Without a nonlinear function like ReLU between layers, stacking multiple layers would mathematically collapse into one single linear layer, no matter how many layers you stacked, because a linear function of a linear function is still linear.

ReLU's derivative is 1 for z greater than 0 and 0 for z less than 0, undefined exactly at z equals 0, conventionally set to 0 or 1 in practice, which is much cheaper to compute than sigmoid's derivative and, crucially, does not shrink toward zero for large positive z, which is why ReLU networks train faster and avoid much of the vanishing-gradient problem that plagued deep sigmoid networks. Its main failure mode is the dying ReLU problem: if a unit's weights update such that its input is always negative across the training data, its output and gradient are permanently zero, and that unit stops learning entirely for the rest of training. Variants like Leaky ReLU, a small nonzero slope for negative z, and ELU exist specifically to address this by letting a small gradient flow even for negative inputs. ReLU networks are not differentiable everywhere, the kink at zero, but in practice this almost never matters for optimization, since landing exactly on zero has probability essentially zero during real training.

The dying ReLU problem interacts with initialization and learning rate: a learning rate that is too high can push many units into the permanently-negative regime in the first few steps of training, part of why initialization schemes tuned for ReLU networks and careful learning-rate warmup matter more for ReLU networks than the activation function's simplicity might suggest. GELU and Swish, smooth approximations to ReLU used in transformers and other modern architectures, trade ReLU's cheap computation and hard zero for a small but empirically consistent improvement in performance on large models, though the underlying reason is still not fully settled beyond smoother gradients seem to help optimization at scale. A common misconception is that ReLU's nonlinearity is what makes deep learning powerful in some deep theoretical sense; in fact almost any nonlinearity between layers restores the network's ability to represent nonlinear functions, and ReLU's popularity is mostly about optimization behavior, fast, sparse, well-behaved gradients, rather than representational power specifically. ReLU also induces sparsity, roughly half of a randomly initialized network's ReLU units are inactive for a typical input, which some researchers view as a useful inductive bias and others view as wasted capacity, and the tradeoff is still debated.

At production scale, the choice of activation function is one of the more thoroughly explored architecture hyperparameters, and different families of models have settled on different defaults for reasons that are partly empirical and partly about matching hardware; GELU-family activations dominate in transformers, while ReLU and its cheap variants remain common in latency-sensitive on-device models, in part because ReLU is trivial to implement efficiently in low-precision, quantized inference on mobile or embedded hardware. An open research question is why smooth activations consistently edge out ReLU on large-scale pretraining tasks despite ReLU's clean theoretical simplicity, since the standard vanishing and dying-unit explanations do not fully account for the gap. On-device and hardware-constrained deployment often specifically favors ReLU precisely because it composes well with quantization, its output range and sparsity are cheap to represent in low bit-widths, even when a smoother activation would train to marginally better accuracy, making activation choice one of the places accuracy and deployment cost trade off directly.

terms.def: The chain rule applied layer by layer, backward from the loss, to get every gradient.
levels: Imagine you and four friends stand in a line passing a ball, and someone at the end tells the last person exactly how to fix their throw. That person tells the next person how they should have thrown it differently to help, and it passes backward all the way to you. Backpropagation is the computer doing that, passing blame backward through its layers so everyone knows how to improve.

Backpropagation is how a neural network figures out how to improve. After the network makes a prediction and it is compared to the right answer, backpropagation works backward through the network's layers, figuring out exactly how much each connection contributed to the mistake. Each connection's weight then gets nudged a little to reduce future mistakes. It uses a math rule called the chain rule, applied one layer at a time, going from the last layer back to the first.

Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight in the network by applying the chain rule layer by layer, starting from the output layer and working backward to the input layer. For a network with several stacked layers, the gradient at an early layer depends on multiplying together the local gradients of every layer after it, which is why it is computed backward, each layer's contribution reuses work already done for the layers after it, rather than recomputing everything from scratch. Once every weight's gradient is known, an optimizer like gradient descent updates each weight by subtracting a small step in the gradient's direction, scaled by a learning rate. Frameworks like PyTorch compute backpropagation automatically via `loss.backward()`, using a computation graph built during the forward pass.

Formally, backpropagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to a computation graph: the chain rule for a composition of functions expresses each parameter's gradient as a product of Jacobians, and reverse-mode evaluates that product right-to-left, from the loss backward to the parameters, which is far cheaper than forward-mode when there are many parameters and one scalar loss, exactly the situation in deep learning. Each layer needs to cache values from its forward pass because computing its local gradient during the backward pass depends on them, which is why memory usage during training scales with network depth and batch size, not just parameter count. Vanishing and exploding gradients are a direct consequence of the chain rule's repeated multiplication: if each layer's local gradient is consistently below 1 in magnitude, the product shrinks exponentially with depth, and if consistently above 1, it grows exponentially, which is the core motivation behind architectural fixes like residual connections and careful weight initialization. Backpropagation computes exact gradients, up to floating-point precision, not approximations, which distinguishes it from gradient-free optimization methods that must estimate gradients through sampling.

Backpropagation's memory cost, needing to retain every layer's activations from the forward pass until the corresponding backward computation, becomes a real constraint at the scale of large models, and gradient checkpointing, recomputing some activations during the backward pass instead of storing them, is a standard tradeoff of extra compute for reduced memory. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating backpropagation as inherently biologically plausible or as the mechanism of learning in any general sense, it requires a differentiable computation graph and, in its standard form, symmetric forward and backward weight use that has no clear biological analog, which is an active area of debate in computational neuroscience, separate from its role as the dominant practical algorithm for training artificial networks. Higher-order derivatives require differentiating through the backpropagation computation itself, which is supported by modern autodiff frameworks but is substantially more expensive and numerically delicate than first-order gradients. Mixed-precision training interacts with backpropagation in a way that requires care: gradients computed in low precision can underflow to zero for small values, which is why loss scaling, multiplying the loss by a constant before the backward pass and dividing gradients by the same constant after, is a standard technique to keep small gradients representable.

At the scale of training very large models, backpropagation itself is not the bottleneck so much as the systems problem of distributing it, splitting the computation graph, and therefore the backward pass, across many devices while keeping gradients synchronized correctly and communication overhead manageable, which is a major focus of large-scale training infrastructure. On-device and low-power settings sometimes avoid full backpropagation entirely for fine-tuning or personalization, using approximations or restricting which parameters receive gradients, because the memory cost of caching activations for a full backward pass can exceed what a phone or watch can afford. An open research question is whether backpropagation-free training methods can match backpropagation's sample efficiency and final performance at scale, so far none reliably do for large networks, which is part of why backpropagation, despite its costs, remains the default nearly everywhere.

terms.def: The deep-learning library; autograd derives gradients automatically; MPS is how it reaches the Mac's GPU.
levels: PyTorch is a toolbox for building brain-like computer programs called neural networks. Autograd is like a magic helper who watches every math step you make and automatically figures out how to fix your mistakes afterward, without you doing that math by hand. MPS is a special fast lane that lets these programs run on the graphics chip inside a Mac, which is much quicker than the regular chip for this kind of work.

PyTorch is a library for building and training neural networks, the models used for the later, harder parts of this course after logistic regression and LightGBM. Its key feature, autograd, automatically computes gradients (the direction to adjust each weight to reduce the loss) by tracking every operation done on a tensor, so you never have to derive and code calculus by hand for a complicated model. MPS stands for Metal Performance Shaders, Apple's way of letting PyTorch run computations on a Mac's GPU instead of just its CPU, which is much faster for the large matrix operations neural networks need. `model.to('mps')` moves a model's computation onto the GPU on a Mac with Apple silicon.

In PyTorch, a `Tensor` is like a numpy array but with an extra ability: setting `requires_grad=True` makes it track every operation performed on it, building a computation graph, and calling `.backward()` on a final loss walks that graph backward, computing the gradient of the loss with respect to every tracked tensor using the chain rule, automatically. A typical training step is: `optimizer.zero_grad()`, `loss = criterion(model(x), y)`, `loss.backward()`, `optimizer.step()`, which computes gradients and then updates every weight in the direction that reduces loss. `torch.device('mps')` selects the GPU on Apple silicon Macs, analogous to `'cuda'` on machines with an NVIDIA GPU, and moving both the model and the data to the same device (with `.to(device)`) is required before running anything on it. `nn.Module` is the base class for defining a model's layers and its forward pass.

Autograd's computation graph is built dynamically, operation by operation, as Python code executes (this is PyTorch's 'define-by-run' design, as opposed to older frameworks that required a static graph defined in advance), which makes debugging with ordinary Python tools and control flow (loops, conditionals depending on tensor values) far easier, at some cost in ahead-of-time optimization compared to a static-graph approach. Gradients accumulate by default in PyTorch, meaning each `.backward()` call adds to existing `.grad` values rather than replacing them, which is why `optimizer.zero_grad()` must be called before each step; forgetting it is one of the most common PyTorch bugs, silently corrupting training with stale gradients from previous steps. MPS support, while functional for most common operations, has historically lagged CUDA in operator coverage and numerical parity, so a small number of operations may fall back to the CPU silently or produce slightly different floating-point results than the same code run on CUDA, which matters for exact reproducibility across hardware. Training on MPS versus CPU produces the same expected result asymptotically but can differ in exact floating-point values, since GPU reductions (like summing a large tensor) do not sum in the same order as a CPU implementation.

Autograd computes exact gradients (up to floating-point precision) via reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which is efficient specifically because the number of outputs (one scalar loss) is small compared to the number of inputs (many weights); this asymmetry is why backpropagation, not forward-mode differentiation, is the standard for training neural networks, and understanding that asymmetry is what lets you reason about when a custom autograd function would actually be faster to write by hand. Memory is the usual constraint in practice, not compute: `.backward()` requires the entire forward computation graph to be kept in memory until backward pass completes (unless gradient checkpointing trades recomputation for memory), and on a Mac's unified memory architecture, MPS shares memory with the CPU rather than having dedicated VRAM, which changes the practical memory budget and failure modes (system-wide slowdown rather than a clean out-of-memory error) compared to a discrete GPU. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is detaching tensors from the graph incorrectly: calling `.item()` or `.numpy()` on a tensor that still requires grad, inside a loop that is supposed to remain differentiable, silently breaks the gradient chain for anything downstream, and PyTorch will not always raise an obvious error, just silently different (usually much worse) training behavior. Mixed-precision training (using 16-bit floats for most operations, with select operations kept at 32-bit for numerical stability) speeds up training substantially on hardware that supports it, but MPS's mixed-precision support and behavior differs meaningfully from CUDA's, so code tuned for one is not guaranteed to behave identically on the other.

In production ML at scale, PyTorch models are rarely deployed as-is; they are typically exported to a more constrained, optimized runtime (TorchScript, ONNX, or Apple's own Core ML for on-device inference) that trades away Python's dynamic flexibility for predictable latency and a smaller footprint, and PyTorch's role there is training and research, with a separate, carefully validated conversion step before anything reaches a device. Apple's on-device deployment story specifically routes trained models through Core ML tools, which convert and quantize PyTorch models to run efficiently on the Neural Engine, a specialized chip distinct from both the CPU and the GPU that MPS targets, so 'runs fast on Mac via MPS during training' and 'runs fast on an iPhone via Core ML in production' are genuinely different engineering problems with different toolchains. An open and actively worked-on problem is closing numerical and operator-coverage gaps between backends (CUDA, MPS, and the eventual on-device runtime) well enough that a model validated on one produces reliably equivalent behavior on another, since today a model can pass every test on a CUDA training cluster and behave subtly differently once quantized and run through the on-device pipeline, and diagnosing exactly where that divergence entered remains a genuinely hard debugging problem.

terms.def: The rule that turns gradients into parameter updates; AdamW adapts the step per parameter and adds weight decay.
levels: An optimizer is the coach that tells the model which way to nudge itself after every practice guess, so next time it guesses a little better.

The optimizer turns the gradient, which direction makes the error bigger or smaller, into an actual change to the model's numbers. Plain gradient descent just takes a step opposite the gradient; Adam is a fancier optimizer that adjusts how big a step to take for each parameter separately, based on how that parameter's gradient has behaved recently. AdamW is Adam with weight decay added, which gently shrinks the model's weights toward zero to keep them from growing too large.

Plain gradient descent updates each parameter as w ← w − η∇L, where η is the learning rate; Adam instead keeps a running average of the gradient itself, call it m, and of the squared gradient, call it v, for every parameter, and updates using both: θ_t = θ_{t−1} − α·m̂_t/(√v̂_t + ε), where θ_t is the parameter after step t, α is the learning rate (the same idea as η above, just a different letter), m̂_t and v̂_t are those two running averages with a small correction for the fact that they both start at zero, and ε is a tiny number added only so the division never blows up if v̂_t happens to be zero. This gives each parameter effectively its own adaptive step size, parameters with noisy, small gradients get relatively bigger steps than under plain gradient descent. AdamW adds weight decay as a separate term subtracted directly from the weights each step, rather than folding it into the gradient the way old-style L2 regularization did, which matters for how well the regularization actually works.

Adam combines two older ideas, momentum, which smooths the gradient by averaging over recent steps so the optimizer doesn't zigzag on a noisy loss surface, and per-parameter adaptive scaling, which divides each parameter's step by the square root of its recent squared-gradient average, with bias correction terms that fix the fact that both running averages start at zero and are biased low early in training. The key insight behind AdamW, versus plain Adam with L2 regularization added to the loss, is that Adam's adaptive scaling interacts badly with L2 added inside the gradient, it gets divided by the same per-parameter scale as everything else, weakening regularization exactly where needed most, so AdamW decouples weight decay from the gradient-based update entirely. Adam converges fast and is forgiving of a poorly chosen learning rate compared to plain SGD, but can generalize slightly worse than well-tuned SGD with momentum on some problems, which is why some vision models still use SGD despite Adam's convenience.

The theory behind Adam's convergence guarantees turned out to have gaps, the original paper's proof was later shown flawed for certain sequences, and AMSGrad was proposed as a fix, though in practice plain Adam or AdamW remains what almost everyone uses because the theoretical counterexamples rarely bite on real problems. A subtlety practitioners get wrong constantly: Adam's adaptive per-parameter learning rate means the effective step size for a nominal learning rate isn't comparable across models with different parameter scales, so a rate tuned for one model rarely transfers cleanly to another. Bias-correction terms matter disproportionately in the first few hundred steps and their effect washes out later, which is why warmup schedules, starting the learning rate very low and ramping up, are often paired with Adam-family optimizers specifically to avoid instability during that early, high-variance phase.

At the scale of large model training, the optimizer's memory footprint becomes a real engineering constraint: Adam and AdamW store two additional full-size buffers per parameter, roughly tripling memory needed for optimizer state beyond the model weights, which is why 8-bit Adam, factored second-moment estimates, and optimizer state sharding across devices exist specifically to make Adam-family training feasible at billions of parameters. An open research question is whether Adam-style adaptive optimizers remain necessary as scale grows, since some recent large-scale training recipes have found simpler optimizers competitive when paired with careful learning-rate schedules and normalization, suggesting some of Adam's advantage may be about forgiving hyperparameter tuning more than a fundamentally better trajectory.

terms.def: A model that reads a sequence step by step, keeping a hidden state; the GRU uses gates to decide what to remember.
levels: Imagine reading a story one word at a time, and after every word you update a little note to yourself about what's happened so far, so you don't have to remember every single word. A recurrent network reads data the same way, one step at a time, keeping a running note called its hidden state.

A recurrent network reads a sequence, like a station's speed readings over the last hour, one 5-minute reading at a time, and after each step it updates an internal "memory," called the hidden state, that summarizes everything it's seen so far. A GRU (gated recurrent unit) is a specific, popular kind of recurrent network that has small gates deciding how much of the old memory to keep and how much of the new information to let in. This lets it handle sequences where recent events usually matter more, but something from a while ago can still matter too.

A basic recurrent network updates its hidden state at each time step as a function of the current input and the previous hidden state: ht = f(Wx·xt + Wh·ht-1 + b), and its final hidden state, or its state at each step, can be fed to an output layer to make a prediction. A plain recurrent network struggles to remember information from many steps back, because the same weight matrix is applied repeatedly and gradients tend to vanish over long sequences; a GRU fixes this with an update gate and a reset gate, learned functions that control how much of the previous state to keep versus overwrite at each step. In code, PyTorch's `nn.GRU(input_size, hidden_size)` takes a sequence of shape `(batch, time, features)` and returns a hidden state sequence you can use to predict, for example, whether a station will be slow 30 minutes from now.

Understanding ARIMA-style time series models first clarifies why lag features work in the simpler logistic regression and LightGBM models in this course, and what a recurrent network adds beyond them: nonlinearity in how past values combine, the ability to take exogenous inputs, like occupancy and flow alongside speed, naturally within the same sequence, and parameters shared across every time step and, if trained that way, across every station, rather than a fixed, hand-chosen set of lag features. A GRU's gates are themselves small learned neural network layers, a sigmoid over a linear combination of the current input and previous hidden state, which is why a GRU has more parameters and requires more data to train well than a plain recurrent unit, but converges more reliably because the gating mitigates the vanishing gradient problem that plain RNNs suffer over long sequences. Recurrent networks fail, or need care, when sequences are very long, since gates alone don't fully solve vanishing gradients at hundreds or thousands of steps, which is part of why attention-based architectures largely replaced RNNs for very long sequences, when data is irregularly sampled, since recurrent networks implicitly assume a fixed step size, or when there's too little training data relative to the model's parameter count, which favors the simpler logistic regression or LightGBM baselines in this course instead. Training is done via backpropagation through time, unrolling the recurrence across all time steps and applying the chain rule backward through the whole unrolled graph, which is more expensive and more prone to instability than training a non-sequential model.

The GRU versus LSTM choice is a real but often overstated tradeoff in practice: GRUs have fewer parameters, since they merge the LSTM's separate forget and input gates and drop its distinct cell state, train slightly faster, and empirically perform comparably to LSTMs on most tasks, so the choice is usually more about engineering convenience than a principled difference in modeling power for a given problem. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming a recurrent network will automatically discover the right lag structure without help, since in practice feeding it well-chosen engineered features, rolling means, lags, alongside raw values often still improves performance over raw sequences alone, because gradient-based training doesn't always find every useful nonlinear combination on its own within a practical training budget. Recurrent architectures for spatiotemporal data like PeMS also face a genuine architectural choice about how to handle multiple correlated stations: running one shared GRU per station independently ignores spatial correlation entirely, while naively concatenating all stations into one input vector treats the network's fixed topology as arbitrary feature order, which is exactly the gap that graph-based architectures (DCRNN, STGCN, Graph WaveNet) exist to fill by combining a recurrent or convolutional temporal component with an explicit graph structure over stations. Vanishing and exploding gradients, gradient clipping, and the choice of sequence length to backpropagate through, truncated versus full backpropagation through time, remain real, hands-on tuning decisions rather than settled defaults, especially as sequence length grows.

At production scale, plain recurrent networks including GRUs have been substantially displaced in much of the sequence-modeling literature by attention-based and transformer architectures, which parallelize across the sequence dimension far better on modern accelerator hardware and handle long-range dependencies more directly, though GRUs remain attractive in latency- and memory-constrained settings, on-device or low-power inference, precisely because their step-by-step, constant-memory computation is cheap compared to attention's full-sequence cost. For spatiotemporal traffic forecasting specifically, the state of the art has moved toward graph neural networks that combine a recurrent or convolutional temporal component with learned or physical graph structure over the road network (Graph WaveNet, DCRNN, and their successors), treating a plain per-station GRU as a reasonable, well-understood baseline rather than a frontier method. An open research question is how to combine the efficiency and simplicity of gated recurrence with the long-range and multi-entity reasoning that attention and graph structure provide, without paying the full computational cost of either at inference time.

terms.def: The vector a recurrent network carries from step to step: its summary of what it has read.
levels: Imagine reading a story one word at a time, and after each word you keep a little summary in your head of what has happened so far, like 'a dog ran to the park.' A hidden state is a computer's version of that little summary, updated after every new bit of information.

A hidden state is a list of numbers that a recurrent neural network keeps and updates as it reads through a sequence, step by step, like a running summary of everything it has seen so far. After reading the last five-minute speed reading in a sequence, the final hidden state is meant to capture what matters about that station's recent history. The network uses this summary, not the raw sequence, to make its next prediction.

In a recurrent network (like an RNN, LSTM, or GRU), the hidden state hₜ is a vector updated at each time step from the current input xₜ and the previous hidden state hₜ₋₁: hₜ = f(xₜ, hₜ₋₁), where f is the network's learned update function. This lets the network process a sequence of any length while carrying forward a fixed-size summary of everything seen so far, rather than needing the whole sequence at once. In code, `self.gru(seq)[1][0]` extracts the final hidden state after reading a whole sequence, which is then used as the input to a prediction layer — one number capturing 'what this station's recent speed history implies about the next 30 minutes.'

The hidden state is the mechanism that gives recurrent networks their sequence-modeling ability: rather than a fixed window of past values like a lag feature, hₜ is a learned, compressed summary whose content the network itself decides during training, in principle capturing long-range dependencies that a fixed set of lag features would miss. In practice, plain RNNs struggle to carry information across many time steps because of vanishing gradients during backpropagation through time, which is why gated architectures (LSTM, GRU) were introduced: they add learned gates that control how much of the previous hidden state to keep versus overwrite at each step, making it easier to preserve relevant information over longer sequences. The hidden state's dimensionality is a hyperparameter and a real capacity tradeoff: too small and it cannot represent everything relevant about the sequence so far, too large and the model has more parameters to overfit with, especially with limited training sequences. For the traffic project's spatiotemporal models, a hidden state is computed per station (each station's speed sequence is read independently by the recurrent unit), and the reshape step (`reshape(B, N, -1)`) puts each station's hidden state back into its place in the full network of stations before any graph-based mixing across stations happens.

Even with gating, hidden states in practice tend to be dominated by recent time steps rather than genuinely capturing arbitrary long-range dependencies, an empirical limitation that motivated attention mechanisms and transformers, which let a model look back directly at any past step rather than relying on everything relevant being compressed into a single fixed-size vector passed forward. A subtlety often missed: the hidden state's meaning is entirely learned and not directly interpretable — there is no guarantee that any individual dimension corresponds to something a person would recognize (like 'is this rush hour'), which makes debugging a poorly-performing recurrent model harder than debugging a tree model with named, interpretable features. Initialization of the hidden state at the start of a sequence (usually zeros, sometimes learned) is a small design choice with a real effect, particularly for short sequences where the model has little chance to 'warm up' before the initial state's influence fades. In the graph-recurrent hybrid used later in this course (DCGRU), the hidden state update itself is modified to mix information from a station's own history and its graph neighbors' hidden states at each step, via diffusion convolutions rather than a plain dense matrix multiply — which is a meaningfully different inductive bias than a standard GRU, since it builds spatial structure directly into the recurrence rather than leaving the network to discover it from data alone.

At production scale, maintaining and updating hidden state for many entities (thousands of stations, each with their own recurrent state) in a low-latency serving system is a real infrastructure problem, not just a modeling one — stateful serving (keeping each station's hidden state warm between requests) trades memory and complexity for avoiding a full sequence recompute on every prediction, and getting this wrong is a common source of production latency or staleness bugs. The broader research trajectory has moved away from recurrent hidden states toward attention-based architectures for exactly the long-range-dependency limitation described above, though recurrent and state-space models (a newer line of work, including S4 and Mamba) have seen a research resurgence specifically because they can process very long sequences with better computational efficiency than full attention, while still keeping some of the sequential hidden-state idea — an active, unresolved area of debate is which inductive bias wins for which class of problems, spatiotemporal forecasting included.

terms.def: An N × N table of 0/1 saying which stations are neighbors. `A @ h` sums each station's neighbors' vectors.
levels: An adjacency matrix is a big chart where every road-watcher gets a row and a column, and you put a 1 wherever two watchers are next-door neighbors, and a 0 everywhere else.

An adjacency matrix is a grid with one row and one column for every station, N rows by N columns for N stations. Entry (i, j) is 1 if station j is station i's neighbor and 0 otherwise. If each station also has a summary vector `h` of its recent traffic, then `A @ h` adds up each station's neighbors' vectors, one sum per station.

For N stations, the adjacency matrix A is N × N, with A[i, j] = 1 exactly when station j is a neighbor of station i, and 0 otherwise. If `h` is a matrix with one row per station holding that station's hidden summary vector, `A @ h` computes, for every station at once, the sum of its neighbors' vectors, a single matrix multiplication doing what would otherwise be a loop over every station and its neighbors. On a directed road, upstream and downstream are different relationships, so this course actually uses two matrices, `A_up` and `A_down`, rather than one symmetric one.

The adjacency matrix is what turns a road network into something linear algebra can operate on: multiplying by A is a form of message passing, where each station's next representation incorporates a sum of its neighbors' current representations, and stacking this operation K times lets information propagate K hops across the graph. For a directed graph like a freeway, A is not symmetric, and using separate `A_up` and `A_down` matrices, as this course does, lets a station's representation update differently depending on whether information is flowing with or against the direction of traffic, which matters because a slowdown that starts downstream propagates upstream, not the other way around. Dense adjacency matrices are wasteful for sparse, realistic road graphs, where most station pairs are not neighbors, so real implementations typically store A as a sparse matrix or an edge list once N is large.

A subtlety that trips up newcomers to graph neural networks is that raw adjacency, unnormalized 0/1 entries, can make message-passing outputs grow with a station's number of neighbors, so most practical formulations normalize A, for instance dividing each row by its degree, or using a symmetric normalization involving the degree matrix, which is closer to a true averaging operation and keeps values from exploding as layers stack. The adjacency matrix also encodes a modeling assumption about what neighbor means, geographic adjacency, direct road connectivity, or a learned, adaptive adjacency, as in Graph WaveNet, that the model fits from data rather than assumes from geometry, and this choice matters enormously: a fixed geographic adjacency cannot represent that a distant on-ramp sometimes affects a station more than its immediate physical neighbor during unusual traffic patterns. Any graph representation must also respect permutation invariance, the result should not depend on the arbitrary order stations happen to be listed in, which rules out simply treating the adjacency matrix as an image.

At the scale of a full metro or state-wide road network, a full N × N dense adjacency matrix stops being practical, both because most of it is zero and because the memory to store and multiply by it grows quadratically, so production systems store sparse adjacency and use sparse matrix multiplication or explicit neighbor-sampling schemes rather than dense `A @ h`. An open research direction is learning the adjacency itself rather than fixing it from road geometry, since the true functional relationship between stations does not always match physical adjacency, and letting a model learn or adapt this structure from data can outperform a fixed geographic graph, at the cost of losing the physical interpretability a hand-built adjacency matrix provides.

terms.def: A model that lets each station read transformed summaries of its neighbors, using the adjacency matrices.
levels: Imagine every traffic sensor is a kid at a big table who can only whisper to the kids sitting right next to them. After a few rounds of whispering, everyone knows a little bit about what's happening further down the table too.

A graph neural network treats the freeway's stations as nodes in a graph, connected to their physically nearby neighbors by edges, and lets each node update its own representation by combining information from its connected neighbors, this is called neighbor mixing or message passing. Which stations count as neighbors is recorded in an adjacency matrix, a grid of 1s and 0s (or distances) saying which pairs of stations are connected. Doing this once lets a station 'see' its direct neighbors; doing it twice lets it indirectly see its neighbors' neighbors too.

One graph-convolution layer computes something like H' = σ(A · H · W), where A is the (often normalized) adjacency matrix describing which stations connect to which, H is the current matrix of per-station feature vectors, W is a learned weight matrix shared across every station, and σ is a nonlinearity like ReLU, so every station's new representation is a learned, weighted mixture of its own and its neighbors' current representations, the essence of neighbor mixing. Stacking this operation twice lets information reach two hops away, a station's neighbors' neighbors, which for a freeway graph might mean information from a couple of stations up or down the corridor. In the traffic project, this lets a model use the fact that slowdowns tend to propagate upstream from one station to the next, information that a model looking at each station in isolation cannot see.

The adjacency matrix encodes an inductive bias, which relationships the model is told matter before it sees any data, and for road networks it is usually built from physical proximity or direct connectivity, adjacent mainline stations, or stations linked by the same road segment, rather than learned from scratch, since a well-chosen fixed structure both regularizes the model and makes it more sample-efficient than requiring it to discover which stations relate to which. Normalizing the adjacency matrix, row-normalizing, or the symmetric normalization used in the original graph convolutional network paper, prevents high-degree nodes from dominating the aggregation simply by having more neighbors to sum over. A GNN differs from applying the same MLP to every station independently specifically in this neighbor-mixing step; without it, a graph neural network collapses to per-station models that cannot see anything happening a few stations away, no matter how deep the network is. Depth, the number of message-passing layers, trades off receptive field against oversmoothing, too many layers and every node's representation converges toward the same average value across the whole graph, losing the local distinctions that made the graph structure useful in the first place.

Oversmoothing is a well-documented and somewhat surprising failure mode: unlike a plain MLP or CNN, where more layers usually help or at worst plateau, a GNN's performance can degrade past a fairly small number of layers, often just 2 to 4, because repeated neighbor averaging is a low-pass filter on the graph signal, and enough applications of it erase the very local structure the model was meant to exploit, this is a real theoretical result connecting GNN depth to graph Laplacian eigenvalues, not just an empirical curiosity. Static, hand-built adjacency (physical proximity) is a strong prior but misses dynamic relationships, an incident can effectively 'connect' distant stations that share no direct edge by rerouting traffic between them, which motivates attention-based graph models, graph attention networks, that learn edge weights rather than fixing them, at the cost of needing more data and being harder to interpret. Practitioners commonly build the adjacency matrix once from static road geometry and never revisit it, but detector outages, lane closures and construction change which stations are actually informative neighbors of which, a form of structural nonstationarity that a fixed graph cannot represent. For spatio-temporal traffic forecasting specifically, architectures like DCRNN and STGCN interleave graph-convolution layers, spatial mixing, with recurrent or temporal-convolution layers, temporal mixing, and getting the order and balance of the two right is itself an open design question, not a solved recipe.

At the scale of a full metropolitan road network, adjacency structure itself becomes a research and engineering problem: whether to use physical road topology, historical correlation between stations, or a learned graph structure entirely, graph structure learning, inferring edges from data rather than assuming them, and how to keep that structure current as road infrastructure changes without retraining from scratch. Production traffic and mapping systems at Apple's scale combine graph-structured fixed-sensor models with far denser probe data from phones, which effectively supplies a much richer, continuously updated graph signal than any fixed sensor network alone, changing which parts of the GNN framework, fixed adjacency, sparse nodes, still make sense once far more granular position data is available. An open research direction is scaling message passing efficiently to graphs with millions of nodes, a full national road network, without either prohibitive compute cost or the oversmoothing and information-bottleneck problems that plague naive deep GNNs at that scale.

terms.def: One model with several outputs, here the three horizons.
levels: Imagine one friend who can answer three of your questions at once instead of you asking three different friends. A multi-task model is like that: one model that gives you several answers, will it be slow in 15, 30, and 60 minutes, all from the same brain.

Multi-task means training a single model to predict more than one thing at the same time, instead of training a separate model for each prediction. In this course, one model predicts whether a station will be slow in 15 minutes, in 30 minutes, and in 60 minutes, all at once, rather than needing three completely separate models. The model shares most of its internal computation across the three predictions and only splits into separate outputs at the very end.

A multi-task neural network shares hidden layers, the parts that learn general patterns from the input, across all tasks, then has a separate small output layer, or head, for each task. For three horizons, the final layer might be `nn.Linear(hidden_size, 3)`, turning one shared internal representation into three separate numbers, logits, one per horizon, each then passed through sigmoid to get a probability. The training loss is usually the sum, or a weighted sum, of the loss for each task, so a single backward pass updates the shared layers using information from all three predictions at once.

Multi-task learning works when the tasks are related enough that learning one helps the others; here, the three horizons share almost all of the same underlying physics, how traffic at a station evolves, so a representation useful for predicting 30 minutes ahead is largely useful for 15 and 60 minutes too. This acts as an implicit regularizer: a shared representation trained on three related signals is less likely to overfit to noise specific to any one horizon than three separate models trained independently would be, especially when data for any single horizon is limited. It fails, or at least stops helping, when tasks are not actually related, or when one task's gradient signal is much larger than another's and dominates the shared layers during training, effectively starving the smaller task of useful updates unless the loss is reweighted. Choosing how to weight each task's loss in the sum is itself a real design decision, not an afterthought, since an unweighted sum implicitly favors whichever task has a naturally larger loss scale.

Task weighting is a genuinely hard subproblem; fixed weights chosen by hand are brittle across datasets, and more principled approaches, uncertainty-weighted losses, gradient normalization schemes, or dynamically adjusting weights during training, exist specifically because naive equal weighting often lets an easy task dominate a shared representation at a harder task's expense. Negative transfer is the central risk: when tasks are less related than assumed, forcing a shared representation can make every task's performance worse than training separate single-task models would, the opposite of the intended benefit and genuinely hard to predict in advance without trying both. Architecture choice matters too; how much of the network is shared versus task-specific is a spectrum, from almost everything shared with tiny per-task heads, as in this course's 3-horizon setup, to mostly separate networks that share only early layers, and the right point on that spectrum depends on how similar the tasks really are. A subtlety practitioners often get wrong is evaluating a multi-task model only on its combined loss rather than checking each task's individual metric separately, which can hide a case where two tasks improved and one quietly got worse than its single-task baseline.

In production systems, multi-task models are attractive beyond pure accuracy because they reduce serving cost; one forward pass produces several predictions instead of running several separate models, which matters a great deal at scale where inference cost is a real budget line, not just an accuracy metric. Large multi-task and multi-domain models are an active area where the central open problem is the same negative-transfer question from the research literature, just at much larger scale and with much higher cost to diagnosing it, since retraining a huge shared model to test whether one task is hurting another is expensive. Mixture-of-experts architectures are a modern industrial answer to this tension, letting different tasks or inputs route to different subsets of a large shared network's parameters instead of forcing every task through exactly the same shared layers, which softens the sharing-versus-specialization tradeoff instead of resolving it by hand-picked architecture.

terms.def: Adding a layer's input to its output (`h + f(h)`), so the layer learns a correction.
levels: Imagine you're building a tower and instead of tearing down what you built to try something new, you just add a little extra piece on top while keeping the original tower exactly as it was. A residual connection lets a layer keep everything it already had and just add a small improvement, instead of risking losing what it already knew.

A residual connection is a shortcut in a neural network that adds a layer's input straight to its output, written as `h + f(h)`, where f is whatever the layer computes. Instead of forcing the layer to learn the entire new value from scratch, it only has to learn the correction needed on top of what it already had. This makes deep networks, ones with many stacked layers, much easier to train, because information can flow through the shortcut even if a particular layer's learned correction is small or unhelpful early in training.

A residual block computes output equals h plus f(h), where h is the input to the block and f(h) is a small sub-network, often a couple of layers. Without the h plus shortcut, a deep stack of layers must learn the entire identity mapping from scratch if that is what is needed, which turns out to be surprisingly hard for plain deep networks; with the shortcut, learning f(h) close to zero trivially recovers the identity, making it much easier for gradients to flow all the way back through many layers during training. Residual connections were introduced in ResNet for image classification and are now standard in most deep architectures, including transformers, where every attention and feed-forward sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection. In a graph neural network over traffic stations, h plus f(h) lets a station keep its own summary while adding in what it learned from its neighbors, rather than replacing its own information entirely.

Residual connections directly address the vanishing gradient problem described by the chain rule: without a shortcut, the gradient flowing back through n stacked layers is a product of n Jacobians, which can shrink or blow up exponentially with depth; the identity shortcut in h plus f(h) means the gradient with respect to h always has an identity term added to whatever f(h)'s gradient contributes, so gradients have a guaranteed path back through every layer regardless of how poorly f is behaving early in training. This is why residual connections enabled meaningfully deeper networks to train successfully where plain stacked layers plateaued or degraded in accuracy well before that depth. In practice, residual connections are usually paired with normalization, and the exact placement, before or after the residual addition, has a real, empirically observed effect on training stability, especially at greater depth. In a spatial graph model over traffic stations, the residual term lets the model default toward trust this station's own recent history and only deviate when the neighbor information genuinely helps, which is a useful inductive bias when neighbor data is sometimes missing or unreliable.

Residual connections can be understood theoretically as making a deep network behave like an ensemble of shallower networks of varying effective depth, since each residual block can be skipped, contribute approximately zero, without breaking the overall computation, unlike a plain stacked network where every layer is a mandatory link in a single chain, this reframing explains empirically observed robustness of ResNets to removing individual layers post-training, which plain deep networks do not share. A related theoretical view treats a stack of residual blocks as an Euler discretization of an ordinary differential equation, where h plus f(h) is one discrete step of continuous-depth dynamics, which has motivated both new architectures and new analyses of why residual networks train more stably. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming residual connections alone solve all deep-network optimization difficulties; at sufficient depth or width, without careful initialization and normalization, gradients can still explode or vanish even with residual shortcuts present, because the shortcut guarantees a path for gradient flow but not that the path's magnitude stays well-scaled. In graph neural networks specifically, over-reliance on the residual term can indicate the graph structure itself is not being learned from, which is worth checking explicitly rather than assuming the architecture is using its neighbor information just because it is present.

At the scale of very deep production models, residual connections are load-bearing for optimization stability, and variations on the basic idea, scaled residuals, learnable per-layer residual weights, different normalization placements, are an active area of architecture research aimed at training even deeper or more efficient networks reliably. On-device deployment adds a different concern: residual connections increase the number of intermediate activations that must be kept in memory or written to and read from memory during inference, so efficient on-device architectures sometimes deliberately trade off some of the depth residual connections enable for a shallower, faster network that fits power and latency budgets. An open research question is understanding more precisely which residual and normalization design choices matter for a given architecture family and scale, since much of current practice is empirically validated rather than derived from a complete theory of deep network optimization.

terms.def: Correlation of a series with itself at a lag; how long the past stays informative.
levels: Autocorrelation is a fancy way of asking 'does knowing what happened a little while ago help you guess what is happening right now?' If it is raining right now, it was probably also raining five minutes ago, so rain has strong autocorrelation. If you flip a coin, knowing the last flip tells you nothing about the next one, so coin flips have no autocorrelation at all.

Autocorrelation measures how related a series of numbers is to itself at an earlier point in time, called a lag. Traffic speed has strong autocorrelation: the speed five minutes ago is a very good clue about the speed right now, because traffic does not change instantly. A completely random series, like the result of dice rolls, has essentially zero autocorrelation, because each new value has nothing to do with the ones before it. Autocorrelation is why lag features (like 'speed 5 minutes ago', 'speed 10 minutes ago') are useful inputs for a model predicting traffic.

Autocorrelation at lag k is the correlation between a series `x_t` and its shifted version `x_{t-k}`, computed the same way as any correlation coefficient, ranging from -1 to 1. In pandas, `series.autocorr(lag=1)` computes the lag-1 autocorrelation directly. An autocorrelation function (ACF) plot shows this value across many lags at once, and for traffic speed it typically starts near 1 at lag 0 and decays gradually as lag increases, meaning the current speed stays predictive of speed several time steps into the future, though less and less so. This decay pattern is directly why the course builds lag and rolling-window features (`df.shift(3)`, `df.rolling(6).mean()`) as model inputs: they are explicitly encoding the autocorrelation structure the raw timestamp alone does not expose to a model.

Autocorrelation is central to understanding a time series's dependence structure, and it directly determines a series's effective sample size: highly autocorrelated data, like five-minute traffic readings, contains far less independent information than its raw row count suggests, because consecutive rows are largely redundant with each other. A stationary process (one whose statistical properties do not change over time) has an autocorrelation function that depends only on the lag, not on the absolute time, which is the assumption behind most simple time-series tools, and traffic data violates this assumption at daily and weekly scales (rush hour is not stationary within a day), which is why the course conditions its 'typical speed' baseline on time-of-day and day-type rather than treating traffic as a single stationary process. Partial autocorrelation, distinct from ordinary autocorrelation, measures the relationship between `x_t` and `x_{t-k}` after removing the influence of the lags in between, and is what actually determines how many lag features are worth including as separate model inputs versus being redundant with each other. High autocorrelation is also exactly why a naive random train-test split leaks: a row from 2:35pm and a row from 2:30pm at the same station are so similar that putting one in training and the neighboring one in testing lets the model 'cheat' by essentially memorizing a near-duplicate, which is why this course insists on a chronological split instead.

The interaction between autocorrelation and evaluation is subtler than 'use a chronological split': even a properly chronological train-test split can still overstate performance if the test set's early rows are autocorrelated with the training set's final rows, since a short gap between train and test periods, not just their temporal order, is what actually breaks residual dependence, which is why serious time-series evaluation protocols include an explicit embargo period between training and test windows. Effective sample size under strong autocorrelation can be dramatically smaller than the row count, and using the naive row count to compute standard errors or confidence intervals on a metric systematically understates uncertainty, sometimes by orders of magnitude for data as densely autocorrelated as five-minute traffic readings, which is a mistake even experienced practitioners make by defaulting to formulas that assume independent observations. A related, easy-to-miss issue is that spatial correlation (nearby stations moving together) compounds with temporal autocorrelation in exactly the kind of panel data this course's PeMS dataset is, so neither the 's' dimension (stations) nor the 't' dimension (time) can be treated as independent, and the true effective sample size is the product of two separate discounting factors, not just one. Long-memory processes, where autocorrelation decays slowly (as a power law) rather than exponentially, require different modeling tools (fractional differencing, long-range dependence models) than the exponentially-decaying case most introductory time-series material assumes, and distinguishing the two from a finite, noisy sample is itself a nontrivial statistical problem.

In production forecasting and monitoring systems, autocorrelation structure is not just an academic concern; it directly determines how often a system needs fresh data to stay accurate (a highly autocorrelated signal tolerates more staleness before predictions degrade) and how confidence intervals on any live metric should be constructed, since treating autocorrelated production telemetry as independent observations is a very common and consequential statistical error in operational dashboards. At Apple's and similar companies' scale, systems that monitor a metric over time for anomalies explicitly model its autocorrelation structure (through methods like ARIMA-family models or learned sequence models) specifically so that an alerting threshold accounts for expected short-term dependence rather than firing false alarms every time two adjacent, naturally correlated readings both look unusual. An open research question in this space is how to build models that automatically adapt their effective use of history as autocorrelation structure itself shifts over time (say, before and after a road construction event permanently changes traffic dynamics), rather than relying on a fixed set of lag features chosen once and never revisited as the underlying process's memory changes.

terms.def: Flow against occupancy: rising while the road is free, falling once it is saturated. Congestion is the falling branch.
levels: Picture a hallway. A few kids can run through fast. Pack the hallway full of kids, and now nobody can move, that's the fundamental diagram, cars instead of kids.

The fundamental diagram is a plot of traffic flow, how many cars pass per minute, against how packed the road is, density or occupancy. At first, more cars means more flow, since traffic is still moving. Past a point, though, the road gets so packed that cars slow down and flow actually starts falling, that's a traffic jam.

The fundamental diagram plots flow on the vertical axis against density, or occupancy, its close proxy, on the horizontal axis: flow rises roughly linearly as density increases from empty, peaks at the road's capacity, then falls as density keeps rising and speed collapses. The falling branch, high density, low speed, low flow, is exactly what this project's slow label is trying to catch before it fully happens. Flow is approximately density times speed, so at any point on the diagram you can read off the implied average speed as the slope of a line from the origin.

The fundamental diagram assumes traffic is roughly in a steady state, a reasonable approximation over a five-minute detector interval but not instantaneously, and its exact shape, parabolic, triangular, or a more complex fitted curve, varies by road type, lane count, and weather. Its practical use in this project is diagnostic and for feature engineering, not as the model itself: since the falling branch is where flow and speed decouple from their free-flow relationship, a feature like the ratio of current speed to a station's typical high-occupancy speed carries some of the same information. The diagram breaks down at a detector level when the station itself misbehaves, a stuck loop reporting near-100 percent occupancy, or when the relationship is confounded by an incident that changes the road's actual capacity, not just its current load.

A subtlety the two-branch diagram hides: the same flow-density pair can correspond to either the free-flow branch or the congested branch, so flow and density alone are ambiguous without also knowing speed or which regime the road is in, which is why flow by itself is a weaker feature than the combination of flow, occupancy and speed together, and why practitioners who feature-engineer only on flow miss the branch information that speed makes explicit. Hysteresis is a real, well-documented deviation from the simple diagram: the flow-density relationship during the transition into congestion measurably differs from the relationship during recovery out of it, at the same density, because driver behavior differs going in versus coming out, exactly the kind of regime-dependent structure that motivates change-point models for detecting breakdown rather than a fixed threshold. Capacity itself is not a fixed number for a road segment; it drops measurably once congestion has set in, a capacity drop, part of why a jam clears more slowly than the buildup that caused it.

Production traffic systems increasingly move beyond the classical single-point fundamental diagram toward network-level and macroscopic models, cell transmission models and their learned neural analogues, that capture how a breakdown at one point propagates spatially to upstream detectors, exactly the graph-based extension this project's later lessons build toward. Open research questions include how to fuse the classical, physically grounded fundamental-diagram relationship with a purely learned model, as a prior, a feature, or a constraint on outputs, so the model respects known traffic-flow physics, flow cannot exceed capacity, speed cannot exceed free flow, rather than learning it purely from data that may not cover every regime well.

terms.def: A step function that only goes up, fitted to map raw scores to observed frequencies. The calibration method used.
levels: Imagine you sort your test scores from lowest to highest and draw a staircase that only ever goes up, never down, to match how often you actually got things right. Isotonic regression is a computer doing exactly that staircase-fitting trick.

Tree-based models like LightGBM produce scores that rank things correctly, since higher score really does mean more likely, but the actual numbers aren't trustworthy as real probabilities. Isotonic regression fixes this: it fits a step function, one that's only allowed to go up (or stay flat) as the raw score increases, so that within each step the model's stated probability actually matches how often things were true in that group. It's the calibration method this course uses to turn a raw LightGBM score into a number you can genuinely read as "this is a 73% chance of slow traffic."

Isotonic regression fits a non-decreasing step function g(score) → probability by minimizing squared error subject to the constraint that the function never decreases as the raw score increases; in scikit-learn this is `IsotonicRegression().fit(raw_scores, true_labels)` on a held-out calibration set, separate from the data used to train the original model. The result is applied after the model: `calibrated_prob = iso.predict(model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1])`. A reliability diagram, predicted probability on one axis, observed frequency on the other, shows the fix directly: before calibration the points often sit off the diagonal, and after fitting isotonic regression, they should sit close to it.

Isotonic regression solves a constrained least-squares problem (via the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm) to find the best-fitting monotonic step function mapping raw scores to calibrated probabilities, and because it makes no assumption about the shape of the miscalibration beyond monotonicity, it can fix arbitrarily shaped calibration curves that a simpler parametric method like Platt scaling, which fits a sigmoid, cannot. This flexibility is also its weakness: with limited calibration data, isotonic regression can overfit, producing a jagged step function that memorizes noise in the calibration set rather than a smooth true relationship, which is why Platt scaling is often preferred with small calibration sets and isotonic regression with larger ones. Calibration must be fit on data the original model never trained on, since using the training set itself for calibration would just reproduce the model's own overconfidence rather than correct it, so this course reserves a separate calibration split distinct from both the training and final test data. Isotonic regression only reorders and remaps scores monotonically; it cannot fix a model whose ranking is wrong to begin with, since a monotonic transformation preserves rank order exactly, so calibration is strictly a probability-accuracy fix, not a discrimination-quality fix.

A subtlety practitioners routinely miss is that calibration is dataset- and time-window-specific: a calibration map fit on one period's data assumes the relationship between raw score and true frequency is stable, and under prevalence drift, which this course expects, given seasonal traffic patterns, that assumption breaks, so a calibration map needs periodic refitting, not a one-time fix. Isotonic regression's flexibility becomes a real liability with small calibration sets or with scores that have many ties, common with tree ensembles, which produce a limited number of distinct leaf-combination scores, since the fitted step function can end up with very wide, coarse steps that lose most of the score's resolution; some practitioners smooth or bin the isotonic fit as a compromise. The choice of calibration metric to evaluate afterward matters too, since expected calibration error, binned average gap between predicted and observed frequency, and the Brier score capture different aspects of calibration quality, and a model can look well-calibrated on one while being poorly calibrated on the other, particularly in the sparse, low-prevalence tail this course's slow-traffic problem lives in. Calibration is also not free with respect to ranking-sensitive metrics: isotonic regression preserves rank exactly by construction, so it never changes average precision, but downstream systems that threshold on the calibrated probability rather than the raw score are implicitly relying on both the ranking and the calibration being good simultaneously.

At production scale, calibration has to be monitored and refreshed continuously rather than fit once, since prevalence and score distributions drift, and a stale calibration map can silently make a model's probabilities misleading even while its underlying ranking quality, average precision, stays perfectly fine, which is exactly the kind of failure that a metric dashboard tracking only ranking metrics would miss entirely. Multi-model and multi-population systems raise a further calibration question: whether to fit one global calibration map or many population-specific ones, per station, per time-of-day regime, trading statistical efficiency, more data per map, against fidelity to genuinely different subpopulations whose true score-to-frequency relationship may differ. An open research question is how to calibrate scores from models that themselves change frequently, since a model retrained weekly needs its calibration map refit in lockstep, and doing that reliably and automatically, without a human in the loop each time, is still mostly solved by careful pipeline engineering rather than a general algorithmic answer.

terms.def: Write to a temporary file, then rename it over the real one, so a reader never sees a half-written file.
levels: If you are erasing and rewriting a sign, someone could walk by and see it half-erased and get confused. An atomic write is like writing the new sign somewhere else first, finished and correct, and only then swapping it in for the old one all at once, so no one ever sees a half-finished sign.

An atomic write is a way of saving a file so that anyone reading it never sees a half-written, broken version. Instead of writing directly over the real file, the program writes a whole new temporary file first, then renames it on top of the real one in a single, instant step. If a program crashes partway through, the temporary file might be broken, but the real file is untouched until the very last, instant step.

An atomic write pattern writes new content to a temporary file (often named with a `.tmp` suffix in the same folder), then calls a rename operation (`os.replace(tmp_path, real_path)` in Python) to swap it in for the real file. On most filesystems, rename is an atomic operation at the OS level — it either fully happens or fully does not, with no in-between state visible to another process — which is what guarantees a reader never observes a partially-written file. This matters for any file another process might read while it is being updated, like a JSON status file a monitoring script polls, or a checkpoint file a training job writes periodically. Writing directly to the destination path with `open(path, 'w')` does not have this guarantee, since a crash or a concurrent read partway through leaves a truncated or corrupted file.

The atomicity guarantee of rename comes from the filesystem, not the application: `os.replace` (or `rename` at the OS level) updates a directory entry to point to the new file's data in one indivisible step, so any process opening the path either gets the fully old version or the fully new version, never a mix, as long as the temporary and destination files are on the same filesystem — rename across filesystems is not atomic and typically falls back to a copy-then-delete, which reintroduces the very race condition this pattern exists to avoid. This is standard practice for any file that is updated in place and read concurrently: checkpoint files during long-running training jobs, cached intermediate results, or a status file a dashboard polls, all benefit from atomic writes so a reader never sees a truncated JSON or a half-written pickle. It does not, by itself, protect against multiple writers racing to update the same file simultaneously — two processes both writing a temp file and renaming it will each succeed, with whichever rename happens last simply winning, silently overwriting the other's update without any error, so atomic writes solve torn reads but not write-write races, which need a separate locking mechanism. A further detail: the temp file should live in the same directory as the destination (not a system-wide temp folder), both because it guarantees the same-filesystem requirement for atomicity and because it avoids leaving orphaned temp files scattered elsewhere if a job is interrupted before the rename.

The 'same filesystem' requirement is a genuine, sometimes non-obvious gotcha in real deployments: a container or a mounted volume can straddle multiple filesystems in ways that are not visible from the application code, and an atomic-write pattern that silently degrades to non-atomic copy-then-rename under those conditions is a subtle production bug that only manifests as an occasional corrupted read under load, hard to reproduce and diagnose after the fact. Durability is a separate, often-conflated guarantee from atomicity: a rename can be atomic with respect to concurrent readers while the underlying data is still only in the OS page cache, not yet flushed to physical storage, so a power loss immediately after a rename can still lose or corrupt data unless an explicit `fsync` is called on the file and, in the strictest implementations, on the containing directory as well, before the rename — a detail most simple 'atomic write' code (this course's included) skips because the failure mode it protects against is rare enough not to be worth the added complexity for most pipeline uses. Cleanup of orphaned `.tmp` files after a crash is a loose end this pattern does not handle automatically; production systems typically add a periodic sweep for stale temp files as a companion to the atomic-write pattern itself. On networked or distributed filesystems (NFS, some cloud storage mounts), rename semantics can differ from local POSIX guarantees in ways that quietly break the atomicity assumption, which is a recurring source of confusion when code that works reliably on a local disk is deployed against network storage.

At the scale of a distributed system, the single-machine atomic-rename pattern generalizes to compare-and-swap or conditional-write operations offered by distributed storage and coordination systems (object stores with conditional PUTs, or a coordination service like etcd or ZooKeeper), because 'atomic' now has to mean atomic with respect to many concurrent writers across many machines, not just one process versus its own crash. Model checkpointing at scale is a direct, high-stakes application of this idea: a checkpoint write that is interrupted partway through (a preemption, a hardware failure mid-write during a multi-hour training run) must never leave a corrupted checkpoint that a resumed job would silently load and continue training from, which is why production training frameworks build atomic, verified checkpoint writes (often with an explicit integrity check after the rename, not just the rename itself) as a first-class piece of infrastructure rather than an afterthought.

terms.def: The RAM a process is actually using, logged per stage so a 16 GB machine never swaps.
levels: Resident memory is how much of the computer's thinking-space a program is actually using right now, like how much room your toys actually take up on the floor versus how much floor there is.

Resident memory, or RSS (resident set size), is the amount of RAM a running program is actually using at a given moment, measured in bytes and usually reported in gigabytes. In this project, every pipeline stage prints its own RSS at the end, using Python's `psutil` library, so you can see which stage uses the most memory. This matters because a 16 GB Mac mini will slow to a crawl, swapping, if any one stage grows too large.

`psutil.Process(os.getpid())` gets a handle on the currently running program, and `.memory_info().rss` returns its resident set size in bytes, the memory currently held in RAM rather than paged out or never allocated; dividing by 1e9 converts that to gigabytes. This course has every stage print one structured line at the end, like a name, an input, a runtime, and a peak memory figure, easy to search across a log. Watching RSS across stages catches a stage quietly growing toward the machine's 16 GB limit before it starts swapping and slowing everything down.

RSS differs from a process's virtual memory size, which can be much larger, including memory reserved but not yet touched, and from its total allocated memory, which can include pages later reclaimed by the operating system, which is why RSS specifically, memory actually resident in physical RAM, is the number that predicts whether a machine will start swapping.
