Gradient boosted trees, XGBoost included, remain the default choice for structured, tabular production problems specifically because they train and serve efficiently, handle mixed feature types robustly, and provide feature-importance and tree-structure interpretability that deep models generally lack, factors that matter as much operationally as raw predictive accuracy. An open research question, revisited by the field regularly, is why architectures built for tabular data, including deep-learning-based tabular models explicitly designed to compete with XGBoost and LightGBM, still struggle to reliably beat well-tuned gradient boosted trees on most real-world tabular benchmarks, despite deep learning's dominance on unstructured data like images, audio and text.

terms.def: The knobs that control how big and how careful LightGBM's trees are: num_leaves, max_depth, min_data_in_leaf, max_bin, feature_fraction, bagging_fraction, and learning_rate.
levels: Building a LightGBM model is a bit like growing a bunch of small decision trees, and these are the dials that control how big and how careful each tree grows, and how big a step the whole team of trees takes each time it learns something new.

LightGBM is a model made of many small decision trees added one after another, and several settings control how each tree grows and how carefully the whole model learns. `num_leaves` limits how many end-points (leaves) one tree can have — more leaves means a more complex tree. `min_data_in_leaf` says a leaf must contain at least that many examples, so it cannot form around a tiny handful of rows that might just be noise. `learning_rate` controls how big a step each new tree contributes to the overall prediction; `feature_fraction` and `bagging_fraction` add randomness by using only part of the columns or rows for each tree, which helps prevent overfitting.

`num_leaves` (default 31, often tuned around 31 to 127) sets the maximum number of leaves per tree and is LightGBM's primary complexity control, since it grows trees leaf-wise rather than level-by-level, so `num_leaves` matters more directly than `max_depth`, which is a secondary cap that prevents any single branch from growing implausibly deep. `min_data_in_leaf` (for example 200) requires a minimum number of training rows in every leaf, preventing the tree from creating leaves that fit noise in just a handful of examples. `max_bin` controls how many buckets a continuous feature is discretized into before splitting, trading off split precision against speed and memory. `feature_fraction` and `bagging_fraction` randomly subsample columns and rows respectively for each tree, adding randomness that reduces overfitting the way random forests do, and `learning_rate` (for example 0.05) shrinks each tree's contribution to the overall prediction, usually paired with early stopping on a validation metric to decide how many trees are actually needed.

These hyperparameters jointly control the bias-variance tradeoff of a gradient-boosted ensemble, and they interact rather than acting independently: a large `num_leaves` with a small `min_data_in_leaf` can badly overfit by carving out leaves around individual noisy rows, while a small `num_leaves` with a large `min_data_in_leaf` may underfit by being unable to represent real, finer-grained patterns in the data. `learning_rate` and the number of boosting rounds trade off directly — a smaller learning rate needs more trees to reach the same fit but tends to generalize better, which is why 'small learning rate, many trees, with early stopping on validation loss' is a standard, robust default recipe rather than a large learning rate with few trees. `feature_fraction` and `bagging_fraction` are LightGBM's version of the randomness that makes random forests robust, applied within a boosting framework instead: subsampling rows and columns per tree decorrelates the trees somewhat and reduces variance, at some cost to per-tree fit quality. `max_bin` is mostly a speed and memory setting rather than a regularization one, though very coarse binning (a small `max_bin`) can blur genuinely important fine-grained thresholds in a feature, which matters for a feature like speed where a difference of a few miles per hour can be meaningful.

LightGBM's leaf-wise growth strategy (always splitting the leaf that most reduces loss next, regardless of tree depth or shape) makes it more sample-efficient per split than the level-wise growth XGBoost historically defaulted to, but also more prone to overfitting on small datasets if `num_leaves` and `min_data_in_leaf` are not tuned together, which is why LightGBM's own documentation recommends keeping `num_leaves` below 2^max_depth as a rough sanity constraint even when using leaf-wise growth. A subtlety practitioners often get wrong is tuning `num_leaves`, `min_data_in_leaf` and `learning_rate` independently in separate hyperparameter sweeps, when they meaningfully trade off against each other — the same effective model complexity can be reached through different combinations, so a systematic joint search (or at minimum, fixing a small learning rate with many trees plus early stopping, then tuning the tree-shape parameters) tends to be more reliable than tuning one knob at a time. Categorical feature handling interacts with these settings too: LightGBM's native categorical split search effectively considers a different, larger space of possible splits than numeric threshold search does, so a categorical column with very high cardinality (thousands of station ids) can disproportionately dominate `num_leaves` budget if not watched, sometimes warranting a smaller `num_leaves` or explicit per-feature constraints. `bagging_fraction` requires setting `bagging_freq` to a nonzero value to actually take effect at each iteration, a specific, easy-to-miss LightGBM API detail that silently makes bagging inert if forgotten.

At production scale, these hyperparameters are usually tuned automatically (Bayesian optimization, or successive-halving-based search) against a validation objective directly tied to the deployment metric rather than by hand, because the interaction effects described above make grid search over each parameter independently both expensive and misleading. Beyond raw accuracy, `num_leaves` and tree count directly determine inference latency and model size, which matters when a model must serve within a strict latency budget at high query volume; production teams often deliberately choose a smaller, faster model over a marginally more accurate but slower one, treating these hyperparameters as a joint accuracy-versus-cost optimization rather than an accuracy-only one. Retraining pipelines at scale also have to handle these settings staying stable across retraining cycles as the underlying data distribution shifts — a hyperparameter configuration tuned once on historical data can quietly become miscalibrated for the tree-complexity-versus-data-size tradeoff months later as the training set grows or the underlying traffic patterns change, which is a reason some production systems periodically re-tune rather than freezing hyperparameters indefinitely.

terms.def: A classifier that finds the widest possible margin between classes, using kernels to draw curved boundaries; strong on small data, slow on millions of rows.
levels: Imagine drawing a line between red and blue marbles so that the fattest possible gap separates them. An SVM is a computer that finds exactly that widest gap.

A support vector machine, or SVM, is a classifier that draws a boundary between two groups of points, choosing the boundary that leaves the biggest possible margin, or gap, on either side. Only the points closest to the boundary, called support vectors, actually determine where the line goes. SVMs can also use kernels to draw curved boundaries instead of straight lines, when a straight line cannot separate the groups well.

An SVM finds the line, or with more features a hyperplane, that maximizes the margin, the distance to the nearest point of either class, rather than just any line that separates them, which tends to generalize better than the first separating line found. The soft margin version allows some points to sit inside the margin or even on the wrong side, controlled by a penalty parameter, so the SVM works even when the classes are not perfectly separable. A kernel, like the RBF kernel, lets the SVM effectively draw curved decision boundaries by measuring similarity in a higher-dimensional space without ever computing that space directly.

The SVM is formulated as a convex optimization problem, maximize the margin subject to correctly classifying, or softly penalizing errors on, every training point, and its dual formulation reveals that the resulting decision boundary depends only on the support vectors, with every other training point's coefficient equal to zero at the optimum. The kernel trick exploits the fact that the dual problem only needs inner products between data points, not the points themselves, so replacing the ordinary dot product with a kernel function implicitly computes an inner product in a much higher-dimensional feature space, letting the SVM separate classes that are not linearly separable in the original space, without ever constructing that space explicitly. SVMs use hinge loss rather than logistic regression's cross-entropy, which produces a maximum-margin rather than a maximum-likelihood boundary, and they need feature scaling to work well, since the margin's geometry is distorted by features on very different numeric scales.

The Bayes-optimal-classification view situates the SVM among its competitors: it is a large-margin discriminative model, unlike naive Bayes, a generative model with a factorized likelihood assumption, or k-nearest neighbors, which estimates the posterior locally and is consistent as k grows with n but suffers the curse of dimensionality; the SVM's margin-based generalization theory connects it to boosting's own margin arguments in a way that is theoretically elegant but does not fully explain either method's practical success. The dominant practical limitation practitioners run into is scale: standard SVM training is roughly quadratic to cubic in the number of training examples because the dual optimization involves an n×n kernel matrix, which makes SVMs strong on small, clean datasets, a few thousand to tens of thousands of rows, but impractical on the millions of rows a project like this one's traffic data has, where gradient-boosted trees train comparably well in a fraction of the time. Kernel choice and its hyperparameters, like the RBF kernel's bandwidth, matter enormously and are not learned from data the way SVM's own weights are, requiring the same held-out-validation hyperparameter search as any other model family.

SVMs remain genuinely useful in small-sample scientific settings, bioinformatics, some scientific measurement tasks, where data is expensive and clean and the classical margin-maximization theory's generalization guarantees are worth the computational cost, but they have been largely superseded by gradient-boosted trees and deep networks for the large, messy, tabular or unstructured datasets that dominate industrial machine learning, including this project's traffic data. Their lasting contribution is conceptual rather than a still-dominant production tool: the kernel trick they popularized underlies Gaussian processes and other kernel methods still actively used for small-data, uncertainty-aware modeling, and margin theory remains a live research thread connecting classical statistical learning theory to why certain deep learning training procedures generalize as well as they empirically do.

terms.def: A technique that finds new axes, ranked by how much variance they capture, to compress correlated features into fewer numbers.
levels: Imagine taking a messy pile of photos taken from every angle and finding the one best angle that shows the most about the scene; PCA finds that best angle, and then the next best one, and so on.

Principal component analysis finds new directions, called principal components, through a dataset that capture as much of the spread (variance) in the data as possible, with the first component capturing the most, the second capturing the next most while being unrelated to the first, and so on. If several features are correlated, like a station's speed and flow both dropping together during congestion, PCA can often summarize them with just a couple of these new components instead of all the original columns. It's mainly used to compress data or to visualize high-dimensional data in two or three dimensions.

PCA works by computing the covariance matrix of the (usually standardized) features and finding its eigenvectors and eigenvalues; the eigenvectors are the principal components (the new directions), and their eigenvalues say how much variance each direction captures. In scikit-learn, `pca = PCA(n_components=2); X_reduced = pca.fit_transform(X)` projects the data onto the top two components, and `pca.explained_variance_ratio_` reports what fraction of the total variance each kept component accounts for. For traffic data, PCA might reveal that most of the variation across many correlated speed-lag features actually lives along just one or two dominant directions, roughly 'how congested is this station overall.'

PCA is an unsupervised technique, it looks only at the feature matrix X, never at the labels y, so the directions it finds capture variance in the inputs, which is not guaranteed to align with what is actually useful for predicting the target; a feature with huge but label-irrelevant variance can dominate the first principal component while a subtly predictive feature with small variance gets discarded. The components are linear combinations of the original features and orthogonal to each other by construction, which follows directly from the fact that eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, the covariance matrix always is, are orthogonal. Because it depends on variance, standardizing features before PCA is essential unless all features are already on comparable scales, or a feature with a naturally larger numeric range dominates the components purely as an artifact of units, not genuine importance. PCA assumes linear relationships among features; when the true structure is nonlinear, kernel PCA or nonlinear methods like t-SNE or UMAP, typically used for visualization rather than as model inputs, capture structure that plain PCA misses entirely.

PCA is one view of the singular value decomposition, and the SVD is the more general, more numerically stable way to compute it in practice, decomposing the data matrix directly as X = UΣVᵀ avoids explicitly forming the covariance matrix, which is important because squaring the data to get the covariance matrix squares its condition number too, amplifying numerical error for ill-conditioned data. Choosing how many components to keep involves a real tradeoff, commonly guided by a scree plot, a sharp elbow suggesting where additional components stop adding much, or by keeping enough components to explain some target fraction of total variance, 90 or 95 percent, say, but this choice is somewhat arbitrary and should be validated against actual downstream task performance, not just variance explained. A frequent practitioner mistake is fitting PCA on the full dataset, including validation and test data, before splitting, since PCA's fitted components are themselves derived from data statistics, this is a leakage bug structurally identical to fitting a StandardScaler on data it shouldn't see, and it should be fit only on the training set. PCA components are also not inherently interpretable; the first component being a mix of speed, flow and occupancy with certain loadings does not by itself explain what that mix 'means' physically, and assigning it a story, like 'overall congestion,' requires separate domain reasoning, not something PCA proves on its own.

At scale, PCA and its variants, randomized SVD, incremental PCA for data too large to fit in memory at once, remain a standard tool for dimensionality reduction as a preprocessing step, for whitening features before certain algorithms, and for diagnosing dataset structure and redundancy, even in an era dominated by learned representations. It is also foundational to techniques well beyond visualization; PCA underlies whitening transformations used in some normalization schemes, and the same eigendecomposition machinery reappears in spectral clustering and in analyzing the geometry of learned neural network representations, where researchers use PCA on a network's internal activations to understand what structure the model has learned. An open research question is how classical linear techniques like PCA compare to and complement learned, nonlinear dimensionality reduction, autoencoders, contrastive embeddings, for structured, moderate-dimensional data like traffic sensor readings, where the interpretability and stability of PCA are real practical advantages a learned embedding does not automatically share.

terms.def: Stochastic gradient descent: updating a model's weights using the gradient from a small batch of examples at a time, not the whole dataset.
levels: Imagine you're trying to find the lowest point in a hilly park, but instead of walking around with your eyes closed feeling for the slope everywhere at once, you take one step at a time downhill, checking just a little bit of ground each step. SGD walks downhill toward a better model the same way, one small step at a time.

Gradient descent is how a model learns: it looks at how wrong its current guesses are, figures out which direction to adjust its numbers, weights, to be less wrong, and takes a small step in that direction, over and over. Stochastic means it does this using just a small random batch of examples at a time instead of the entire dataset every single step, which makes each step much faster, even though it is a little noisier and less precise than using everything at once.

The update rule is w, a weight, becomes w minus eta times the gradient, where eta is the learning rate, how big a step to take, and the gradient is computed from a small batch of training examples rather than the full dataset, which is what stochastic refers to. A batch size of, say, 32 or 64 examples is common; using the full dataset every step is called batch gradient descent, and using exactly one example per step is the extreme, noisiest version of SGD. Too large a learning rate causes the loss to bounce around or diverge instead of decreasing; too small a learning rate makes training painfully slow.

SGD's core tradeoff is noise for speed: computing a gradient from a small batch is a noisy, unbiased estimate of the true full-dataset gradient, but it is far cheaper per step, which lets a model take many more, smaller steps in the same amount of time; in practice this usually reaches a good solution faster than fewer, more precise full-batch steps would. For a convex problem like logistic regression, SGD is guaranteed to converge to the global optimum under a properly decaying learning rate schedule, though in practice a well-tuned constant or simple decay schedule is used instead of the theoretically ideal one. Momentum, accumulating a moving average of past gradients before applying the update, and adaptive methods like Adam, which additionally adapt the learning rate per parameter based on recent gradient magnitudes, are refinements of plain SGD meant to speed convergence and reduce sensitivity to the learning rate choice. It fails, or trains poorly, when the learning rate is badly mismatched to the problem, too high diverges, too low stalls, when batches are too small to give a useful gradient estimate for a very noisy loss surface, or when features are on very different numeric scales, which distorts the effective step size differently across parameters.

For a convex loss like logistic regression's, SGD provably reaches the global optimum because the loss surface has no local minima to get stuck in, but for the highly non-convex loss surfaces of deep networks, SGD's noise is itself believed to be part of why it generalizes well; it tends to avoid sharp, narrow minima that fit the training data too exactly, settling instead into flatter minima that are argued, though not fully proven, to generalize better. Adam and other adaptive optimizers converge faster in early training and are less sensitive to learning-rate tuning, but plain SGD with momentum, tuned carefully, often generalizes at least as well or better on the final model for many vision and tabular tasks, a real, somewhat counterintuitive tradeoff practitioners have to weigh rather than always reaching for the fanciest optimizer. Learning-rate schedules, warmup, then decay, cosine annealing, one-cycle policies, matter as much as the choice of optimizer itself, and a fixed learning rate is rarely optimal across an entire training run, since the ideal step size early in training is typically larger than the ideal step size near convergence. Batch size and learning rate are coupled, not independent choices: scaling up batch size without also scaling the learning rate, roughly linearly, up to a point, tends to produce worse generalization even though the gradient estimate itself is less noisy, which surprises practitioners who assume more data per step is strictly better.

At production training scale, SGD's per-step compute cost and its interaction with distributed training, splitting a batch across many GPUs or accelerators, then synchronizing gradients, becomes as important as its statistical convergence properties, and much of large-scale training engineering is about keeping large-batch distributed SGD both fast, well utilized hardware, and stable, not diverging as batch size and learning rate both scale up. Modern large-model training almost universally uses Adam or a close variant rather than plain SGD, largely for optimization speed and robustness on the huge, irregular loss surfaces of transformer models, even though the theoretical understanding of why Adam works so well at that scale remains incomplete. An open research question, directly relevant to why SGD's noise seems to help generalization, is developing a rigorous theory connecting optimizer choice, batch size, and learning rate to the generalization of the specific solution SGD or Adam converges to; the empirical practice at scale has run well ahead of a full theoretical explanation.

terms.def: Momentum smooths gradient steps using past updates; Adam adapts each parameter's step size using that history; weight decay shrinks weights toward zero to fight overfitting.
levels: Momentum is like rolling a ball down a hill, once it's moving, it keeps going the same way instead of stopping and starting over each time. Adam is a smart helper that uses that rolling trick plus a bit more cleverness to help the computer learn faster. Weight decay is like gently reminding the computer not to hold onto ideas too tightly, so it stays open to being a little bit wrong.

When a model learns, it takes many small steps to get better, and momentum means each step remembers a bit of the direction from the step before, so learning does not zigzag around as much. Adam is a popular way of taking those steps that also keeps track of how bumpy each direction has been recently, taking bigger steps where things are steady and smaller steps where things are shaky. Weight decay is a small extra rule added during training that nudges every number in the model a little bit toward zero on each step, which helps stop the model from memorizing the training data too exactly. Traffic1's neural network models typically use Adam with a bit of weight decay by default.

Plain gradient descent updates a weight by subtracting the learning rate times the gradient at each step; momentum instead keeps a running average of past gradients and steps in that averaged direction, which smooths out noisy updates and speeds up progress along consistent directions. Adam combines momentum with a second running average that tracks the squared gradient, then divides the step by roughly the square root of that average, so each parameter effectively gets its own adaptive learning rate, parameters with small, consistent gradients get larger relative steps than parameters with large, erratic gradients. Weight decay adds a term to the update that shrinks each weight by a small fixed fraction every step, which discourages any single weight from growing too large and is a form of regularization against overfitting. In PyTorch, `torch.optim.AdamW` implements Adam with weight decay applied correctly, decoupled from the gradient-based update, which is now generally preferred over the original Adam's slightly different, less clean interaction between the two.

Momentum can be derived as an approximation to Nesterov's accelerated gradient method or simply understood as exponential smoothing of the gradient signal, which reduces the variance of noisy stochastic gradients and helps navigate loss surfaces with narrow ravines, where plain gradient descent oscillates across the narrow direction while making slow progress along the long one. Adam's per-parameter adaptive scaling, dividing by the square root of a running average of squared gradients, makes it much less sensitive to learning-rate choice than plain SGD, which is a major reason for its popularity as a default optimizer, though this same adaptivity can sometimes converge to sharper minima that generalize slightly worse than well-tuned SGD with momentum. Weight decay, in its classical form, is mathematically equivalent to L2 regularization only for plain SGD; for Adam, applying weight decay through the loss function interacts badly with Adam's adaptive per-parameter scaling, which motivated AdamW's decoupled weight decay, applying the shrinkage directly to the weights outside the gradient computation, as the now-standard fix. Mini-batch SGD without momentum is often adequate and even preferred for convex or near-convex problems, like a small logistic regression, where Adam's added machinery is unnecessary though generally harmless; its real advantages show up on non-convex, ill-conditioned problems like training a deep network.

The choice between SGD-with-momentum and Adam is not settled by theory alone, Adam tends to converge faster and more robustly in early training, especially on architectures like transformers where gradient scales vary enormously across layers, but well-tuned SGD with momentum sometimes reaches a better final generalization performance on some tasks, a gap that is not fully explained and is an active area of empirical and theoretical study. Adam's adaptive denominator can cause instability early in training when the second-moment estimate is still poorly calibrated from few samples, which is why bias correction terms are built into the standard Adam update, and why warmup, starting with a small learning rate and increasing it, is common practice alongside Adam for training large models. Weight decay's effective strength interacts with the learning rate and with Adam's per-parameter scaling in ways that make a single global weight decay value behave inconsistently across parameters of different typical magnitude, which is part of the motivation behind more recent optimizers that try to decouple these interactions more cleanly. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating momentum, Adam's adaptivity, and weight decay as independent, freely tunable knobs, when in practice their effective interaction means they should be tuned together, often starting from well-established defaults rather than searched independently from scratch.

At the scale of training very large models, the specific optimizer and its hyperparameters are tuned as part of a broader training recipe that has become almost as important as architecture itself, since a suboptimal optimizer configuration can waste enormous compute on a run that trains a large model poorly or unstably, and getting it right is often the difference between a training run succeeding and diverging partway through. Newer optimizers trade off Adam's per-parameter memory overhead, it must store two running averages per parameter, against speed or memory footprint, which matters enormously when training models with billions of parameters where optimizer state itself can be a dominant memory cost. On-device fine-tuning and personalization often cannot afford Adam's full memory overhead at all, pushing toward optimizers or approximations designed specifically for memory-constrained settings, an open and active area, since the theoretical understanding of why Adam-style adaptive methods work as well as they do, and exactly when a cheaper alternative is safe to substitute, remains incomplete.

terms.def: Randomly turning off some neural-network neurons during training, so the network cannot rely on any one of them too heavily.
levels: Dropout is a training trick where a neural network randomly closes its eyes to some of its own inner parts while it is learning, so it cannot lean too hard on any one part. It is a bit like practicing a relay race sometimes with one runner missing, so the whole team learns to work well no matter who shows up. That way, when it is time for the real race, the team does not fall apart if one runner has an off day.

Dropout is a training technique for neural networks where, during each training step, a random fraction of neurons are temporarily turned off (set to zero) and ignored, forcing the rest of the network to not rely too heavily on any single neuron. A typical dropout rate might be 0.2, meaning 20 percent of neurons are randomly dropped at each step. This helps prevent overfitting, because the network cannot memorize the training data by depending on one very specific pathway through it; it has to learn patterns that work even when parts of it are missing. Dropout is only applied during training; at prediction time, the full network is used, usually with its outputs scaled to account for the fact that more neurons are now active.

In PyTorch, `nn.Dropout(p=0.5)` added as a layer randomly zeroes out each input to it with probability p during training, and during evaluation (`model.eval()`), dropout does nothing and passes every value through unchanged, which is why toggling between `model.train()` and `model.eval()` mode matters and is a common source of bugs when forgotten. The remaining active neurons' outputs are scaled up by 1/(1−p) during training (inverted dropout), so the expected total signal stays roughly consistent between training and evaluation without needing any adjustment at inference time. Dropout rates commonly range from 0.1 to 0.5 depending on the layer and how prone the network is to overfitting; higher dropout means stronger regularization but slower, noisier training. Dropout is typically applied to fully connected layers and less often, or with smaller rates, to convolutional layers, where the redundancy between neighboring pixels already provides some natural regularization.

Dropout can be understood as an efficient approximation to training an enormous ensemble of thinner sub-networks (one for each possible pattern of dropped neurons) and then, at test time, approximately averaging their predictions in a single forward pass through the full network, which is why it produces an effect similar to model averaging without literally needing to train or store many separate models. It works particularly well in large, overparameterized networks where individual neurons or small groups of neurons can otherwise co-adapt to detect very specific, narrow patterns in the training data that do not generalize; dropout breaks up this co-adaptation by making any single neuron's presence unreliable during training. Dropout interacts with batch normalization in ways that are not always beneficial: applying both together, especially in certain orderings, can sometimes hurt rather than help performance, because batch normalization's own statistics (computed per mini-batch) get disrupted by dropout's added randomness, which is why many modern architectures use one or the other in a given block rather than stacking them by default. Dropout adds real training-time noise to the optimization process, effectively acting as a form of stochastic regularization on top of whatever noise mini-batch gradient descent itself already introduces, which is why dropout networks sometimes need more training epochs to converge to their best validation performance than an equivalent non-dropout network.

Whether dropout helps or hurts depends heavily on the amount of available training data relative to model capacity: on small datasets with a large network, dropout is often essential to avoid catastrophic overfitting, but on very large datasets, where the network barely has time to overfit before training ends, dropout can slow convergence and slightly hurt final performance relative to other regularizers, which is a large part of why very large modern language and vision models trained on massive datasets frequently use little or no dropout, relying instead on the sheer scale of data and other regularization (weight decay, data augmentation) for generalization. Monte Carlo dropout, a technique that keeps dropout active at inference time and runs multiple stochastic forward passes, repurposes dropout's randomness as an approximate Bayesian uncertainty estimate, giving a cheap way to get a predictive distribution rather than a single point estimate, though the theoretical justification for treating this as a proper Bayesian posterior approximation is debated and its calibration quality varies considerably across architectures and tasks. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is applying dropout inconsistently between where it was used during training and how the model is deployed, especially with model export or quantization tooling that does not always handle dropout layers correctly by default, silently leaving dropout active (or with mismatched scaling) in a supposedly deterministic deployed model. The specific dropout rate and which layers it is applied to interact nontrivially with other hyperparameters (learning rate, weight decay strength, network depth), so tuning dropout in isolation from the rest of the training recipe often gives misleading conclusions about whether it is actually helping.

In large-scale production model training, dropout has become less universally applied than in the 2014-era literature that popularized it, replaced or supplemented by other regularization and generalization strategies (large-scale data augmentation, weight decay, label smoothing, and simply training on enough data that overfitting is less of a concern) that better suit the very large models and datasets common in modern deployed systems, though dropout remains standard in smaller or more overfitting-prone components of larger systems, like classification heads fine-tuned on limited labeled data. Apple's on-device and server models, when fine-tuned on relatively small task-specific datasets after large-scale pretraining, do commonly reintroduce dropout specifically at that fine-tuning stage, since a small fine-tuning dataset relative to a large pretrained model reintroduces exactly the overfitting risk dropout was originally designed to address. An open research question is understanding dropout's interaction with the double-descent and scaling-law phenomena observed in very large models, where the classical bias-variance intuition dropout was designed around does not always hold cleanly, and current large-model training recipes are as much the product of extensive empirical search as they are of a settled theoretical account of when and how much dropout actually helps.

terms.def: A layer that rescales its inputs to have roughly zero mean and unit variance across each mini-batch, with a learned scale and shift, so training is faster and more forgiving.
levels: Batch normalization is like a teacher making sure everyone in the class is standing at about the same height before a group photo, so nobody's tiny voice or giant shout throws off the whole picture.

When training a neural network, the numbers flowing through each layer can grow too large or shrink too small as training goes on, which makes learning slow or unstable. Batch normalization fixes this by rescaling each layer's inputs, for every mini-batch of training examples, so they have roughly zero average and a standard spread, then lets the network learn its own small adjustment, a scale and a shift, on top of that if it needs one.

For a mini-batch of activations x, batch normalization computes y = γ·(x − μ_B)/√(σ_B² + ε) + β, where μ_B and σ_B² are the batch's mean and variance, ε is a tiny constant avoiding division by zero, and γ and β are learned parameters the network can use to undo the normalization if that helps. It's typically inserted between a layer's linear transformation and its nonlinearity, like a ReLU. At test time, since there's no batch to compute statistics from a single example, a running average of μ_B and σ_B² collected during training is used instead.

Batch normalization's practical benefit, faster, more stable training that tolerates a higher learning rate and is less sensitive to initialization, is well established empirically, though the original explanation, reducing internal covariate shift, has been challenged; later work argued its main effect is smoothing the loss landscape, making gradients more predictable step to step, a different and more defensible theoretical story. A key assumption is a large-enough, representative mini-batch: with very small batches, batch statistics become noisy estimates of the true population statistics, which can hurt rather than help, motivating alternatives like layer normalization that don't depend on batch size at all. It interacts subtly with other regularization: because batch statistics add a form of noise, each example's normalized value depends on which other examples share its batch, batch normalization has a mild regularizing effect similar to, and sometimes redundant with, dropout.

The train and test discrepancy, computing statistics from the current batch during training but using a fixed running average at test time, is a genuine source of bugs when the deployment distribution differs from training, since the running average no longer reflects what the model is actually seeing, one reason batch normalization can silently degrade under real-world drift in a way easy to miss if only training-time metrics are checked. Practitioners commonly get bitten by its interaction with distributed training: statistics computed only within one device's local mini-batch, rather than synchronized across devices, can differ meaningfully from the intended global-batch statistics at large batch sizes, which is why sync batch norm exists specifically for multi-GPU training. Modern architectures, transformers especially, largely moved to layer normalization or RMSNorm instead, partly because sequence models often have variable-length, small-batch settings where batch statistics are unreliable, so treating batch normalization as universally the normalization choice, rather than one architecture-specific tool among several, is a dated assumption.

On-device and low-latency inference settings fold batch normalization's learned scale and shift directly into the preceding linear layer's weights at deployment time, since at inference the running statistics are fixed constants, a standard batch-norm-folding optimization that removes the normalization as a separate runtime operation entirely with no change in output. Research continues on normalization schemes that combine the training benefits of batch normalization with robustness to small or variable batch sizes and to distribution shift at inference, since production traffic-prediction and other streaming systems often score one example, or a handful, at a time, exactly the regime where the classical batch-statistics assumption is weakest.

terms.def: The number of training examples a model looks at before updating its weights once.
levels: Imagine grading a small stack of homework papers at a time, then adjusting how you teach, instead of waiting to grade all thousand papers before changing anything. Batch size is how big that stack is.

When training a model, instead of updating its weights after looking at just one example, or waiting to look at the entire dataset, you usually update after looking at a small group of examples at once, and that group's size is the batch size. A batch size of 32 means the model computes its average error over 32 examples, then adjusts its weights once, and moves on to the next 32. A bigger batch gives a smoother, more reliable estimate of the error each time, but takes more memory and computer power per update.

Batch size is a hyperparameter you set before training, like `batch_size=32` in a PyTorch `DataLoader` or a Keras `model.fit(X, y, batch_size=64)` call. An epoch is one full pass through the training data, so with 10,000 rows and a batch size of 100, one epoch takes 100 update steps. Smaller batches make more, noisier updates per epoch, which can help escape a bad local minimum but slows convergence per step, while larger batches make fewer, smoother updates that use hardware more efficiently but sometimes generalize slightly worse in practice.

Batch size interacts directly with the learning rate: because a larger batch produces a lower-variance gradient estimate, using the same learning rate at a larger batch size typically means fewer, larger effective steps toward convergence, which is why practitioners commonly scale the learning rate up, roughly linearly, within limits, when increasing batch size, rather than leaving it fixed. Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent is a middle ground between full-batch gradient descent, which computes the exact gradient every step but is memory-heavy and slow per step, and single-example stochastic gradient descent, which is cheap per step but extremely noisy; the mini-batch's noise is not purely a cost, since it acts as an implicit regularizer that can help escape sharp, poorly generalizing minima in a non-convex loss landscape. Batch size also directly affects batch normalization, if used, since batch norm's statistics, mean and variance, are computed over the current batch, and a very small batch size gives batch norm noisy, unreliable statistics, which is one reason batch norm behaves poorly with tiny batch sizes and is often replaced by layer normalization in architectures, like sequence models, that use small or variable batch dimensions. Choosing batch size fails to be a free lunch in either direction: too small wastes hardware parallelism and trains slowly in wall-clock time; too large can both hurt generalization and simply run out of GPU memory.

The empirical finding that very large batch training tends to converge to sharper minima that generalize somewhat worse than smaller-batch training, at a matched number of epochs, is a genuine and still not fully settled area of research, since some of the effect is explainable by the reduced number of gradient updates at large batch size rather than batch size itself, and results depend on how carefully the learning rate schedule and warmup are tuned to compensate, which is a subtlety many practitioners skip by just scaling up batch size without correspondingly adjusting the schedule. Linear learning rate scaling with batch size, plus a warmup period at the start of training, is the standard practical fix used at scale to keep large-batch training competitive with small-batch training's generalization, but it's an empirical recipe more than a rule with tight theoretical guarantees. Batch size choice is frequently constrained by hardware, available GPU or accelerator memory, rather than chosen purely for statistical reasons, and gradient accumulation, computing gradients over several small "micro-batches" and summing them before one update, is the standard workaround for training with an effectively larger batch size than fits in memory at once. A related and often overlooked subtlety is that a fixed batch size interacts with dataset size and class imbalance: with a rare positive class, as in this course's slow-traffic label, a small batch can easily contain zero positive examples, producing a noisy and sometimes uninformative gradient for the minority class on that step, which is a real, practical reason to consider larger batches or stratified batch sampling for imbalanced problems specifically.

At the scale of large distributed training runs, batch size becomes a systems-level lever as much as a statistical one: very large global batch sizes, achieved by splitting a batch across many accelerators and synchronizing gradients, are used specifically to maximize hardware utilization and shorten wall-clock training time, and a large body of scaling-law research studies the relationship between batch size, learning rate, model size, and compute budget to find efficient joint settings rather than tuning batch size in isolation. Beyond some critical batch size, adding more data per step yields diminishing returns in training-step efficiency, and identifying that critical point for a given model and dataset is itself an active area of empirical research relevant to allocating compute efficiently at scale. An open engineering question is how to preserve small-batch-style generalization behavior while still getting large-batch-style hardware efficiency, since the two currently trade against each other in ways that scheduling tricks, warmup, learning-rate scaling, and various adaptive schemes, only partially resolve.

terms.def: The gap between an actual and predicted value in regression; in deep learning, a residual (skip) connection adds a layer's input to its output, enabling very deep networks (ResNets).
levels: In a guessing game, a residual is just how far off your guess was from the real answer — too high or too low, and by how much. In building tall towers of connected boxes (a deep network), a residual connection is a shortcut that lets information skip past a box, so tall towers can still work well instead of getting confused.

In statistics, a residual is the difference between what actually happened and what a model predicted — actual minus predicted. Looking at a plot of residuals is a way to check whether a model is missing something, since a good model's residuals should look like random scatter with no leftover pattern. In deep learning, a 'residual connection' is a different but related idea: it's a shortcut wire that adds a layer's original input straight to its output, which turns out to make it much easier to train very deep stacks of layers, called ResNets, without them getting worse as more layers are added.

A residual in regression is rᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ, actual minus predicted, and residual plots (residuals against predicted values or against a feature) are a standard diagnostic: a random scatter around zero suggests the model captures the pattern well, while a visible curve or trend in the residuals suggests the model is missing structure it should be capturing. In a ResNet, a residual (or skip) connection computes output = F(x) + x for a block of layers F, rather than just output = F(x); the network learns the residual — the difference the block needs to add — instead of learning the whole transformation from scratch at every layer. This small architectural change made it practical to train networks with over a hundred layers, which plain (non-residual) deep networks of that depth could not be trained effectively before residual connections were introduced.

Residual plots in regression diagnose specific violated assumptions: a curved pattern in residuals versus a predictor suggests a missing nonlinear term, a funnel shape (widening or narrowing spread) indicates heteroscedasticity that can invalidate standard error estimates, and residuals correlated with an omitted variable point to a coefficient that is confounded rather than causal. The stationarity condition on the intercept in logistic and linear regression's optimum — that the mean residual is exactly zero at the fitted solution — is a consequence of the normal equations or the gradient of the loss with respect to the intercept being set to zero during fitting, and it can be derived directly from the calculus of the loss function. In deep learning, the residual connection's real benefit is on the gradient, not just the forward computation: because output = F(x) + x, the gradient flowing backward through a residual block always has a direct 'plus the incoming gradient unchanged' path in addition to whatever F contributes, which substantially mitigates the vanishing-gradient problem that made very deep plain networks hard to train. This reframing — learning a residual correction to an identity mapping, rather than learning an arbitrary transformation — also makes optimization easier in practice, since a residual block can, in the worst case, learn to contribute nothing (F(x) ≈ 0) and simply pass its input through, which is a much easier function to approximate than learning an exact identity mapping from scratch through ordinary layers.

The theoretical account of why residual connections help is still debated beyond the gradient-flow explanation: an influential line of work frames a ResNet's stack of residual blocks as an ensemble of many paths of different effective depths (since skip connections create exponentially many paths through the network of varying length), which behaves more like a shallow ensemble than a single very deep function, offering a different explanation for their robustness than pure gradient-flow arguments alone. In regression diagnostics, a subtlety practitioners often get wrong is checking residuals only against the fitted values, missing patterns that only appear against a specific omitted or mismeasured predictor — a systematic check against every candidate feature, not just the overall fit, catches more model misspecification. Residual connections also interact with normalization layers (batch norm, layer norm) in ways that are architecture-specific and not fully settled — the ordering of normalization relative to the residual addition (pre-norm versus post-norm) has a measurable, sometimes large effect on training stability at depth, which is why different influential architectures (the original ResNet versus later transformer variants) made different, deliberate choices here. A quiet failure practitioners should watch for: near-zero residuals in a regression model can mean either a genuinely excellent fit or overfitting on the very data used to compute them, so residual diagnostics on training data alone, without a held-out check, can be misleadingly reassuring.

Residual connections are now a nearly universal architectural default well beyond ResNets — transformers use them around every attention and feed-forward sublayer, and they are considered close to a prerequisite for training very deep or very large networks stably, to the point that architecture research treats their absence as the exception needing justification rather than the default. At production scale, the ensemble-of-paths view of residual networks has practical consequences for techniques like stochastic depth (randomly dropping some residual blocks during training as a regularization method, cheap because the network tolerates missing individual paths) and for model compression, where pruning entire residual blocks post-training is a viable strategy precisely because the network was implicitly trained to be robust to some paths being weak or absent. An open research question is how far this identity-shortcut principle generalizes to fundamentally different architectures (state-space models, mixture-of-experts routing) that are increasingly displacing plain transformer stacks in some large-scale systems, where the analogous 'let gradients and information flow with minimal obstruction' design principle still applies but the mechanics of implementing it differ substantially.

terms.def: Sliding a small filter across data to compute a local weighted sum at every position, reused for images, time, and graphs.
levels: A convolution is like sliding a little stamp across a coloring page, and everywhere the stamp lands it checks whether this little patch looks like a cat's ear, and writes down the answer.

A convolution slides a small filter, a little grid of numbers, across a bigger grid, like an image, and, at every position, multiplies the overlapping numbers together and adds them up. That single filter can then spot the same pattern, an edge, a curve, anywhere it appears in the image. Stacking many filters and layers lets a network build up from simple patterns to complicated ones, like a whole face.

A 2-D convolution slides, say, a 3×3 filter across every position of an image, computing one weighted sum per position, so a single filter with the right weights finds one pattern, like a vertical edge, wherever it occurs, instead of needing a separate detector for every location. A 1-D convolution does the same thing over time instead of over two spatial dimensions, sliding a filter across a sequence of readings, which is how temporal convolutions look for short-term patterns in a time series like a station's speed history. Key knobs are stride, how far the filter moves each step, and padding, whether the edges are filled in so the output stays the same size; stacking convolution layers with pooling in between, which shrinks the image, is the core recipe of a convolutional neural network.

Convolution's two big advantages, weight sharing, the same filter's weights are reused at every position, and locality, each output value depends only on a small neighborhood of the input, make it far more data-efficient than a fully connected layer for grid-structured data, and give it translation equivariance: shifting the input shifts the output the same way, so the network does not need to relearn a pattern separately at every image location. The idea generalizes past images and plain 1-D sequences in this course's own domain: spectral graph convolution, used in STGCN, generalizes convolution to a graph by working in the eigenbasis of the graph Laplacian, approximated efficiently with Chebyshev polynomial filters, while diffusion convolution, used in DCRNN, instead directly applies powers of a random-walk transition matrix, treating message-passing on the road graph as a form of convolution defined by graph structure rather than a Euclidean grid. Both graph variants inherit convolution's core motivation, share weights, exploit local or K-hop structure, but adapt it because a road network has no natural fixed grid the way an image does.

A subtlety that separates naive from sophisticated use of convolution is understanding it as a specific linear operator with structure, mathematically a Toeplitz matrix multiplication, which is why depthwise separable convolutions, factoring a full convolution into a cheaper per-channel step plus a 1×1 mixing step, can approximate a full convolution's expressiveness at a fraction of the compute, a tradeoff that matters enormously for on-device deployment. On graphs specifically, practitioners often assume spectral graph convolution and diffusion convolution are interchangeable graph convolution, but they encode different structural assumptions, spectral methods implicitly assume an undirected graph, while diffusion convolution naturally handles the directed structure of a road network, which is a real reason to prefer one over the other for a directed freeway graph rather than a purely stylistic choice. Residual, or skip, connections, now standard alongside convolutional stacks in both vision and graph networks, exist specifically to fix an optimization pathology, very deep stacks of convolutions become hard to train without them, not to add representational power the plain stack lacked.

At production and research scale, plain 2-D convolution's dominance in vision has been increasingly challenged by attention-based architectures, though convolutions remain the efficient default for on-device and latency-constrained deployment because of their strong inductive bias and comparatively cheap compute per parameter, a real consideration for anything running locally rather than in a data center. In the spatio-temporal domain this course's project touches, the open research question is less convolution versus not and more which structural assumption, a fixed geographic graph convolution, a learned diffusion process, or a fully adaptive, learned adjacency, generalizes best to road networks and traffic patterns the model was not trained on, since a filter's usefulness for images has a much less settled analogue for what a good local pattern means on an arbitrary road graph.

terms.def: A recurrent neural network (RNN) that processes a sequence step by step, carrying a hidden state forward; an LSTM is a gated version built to remember longer.
levels: An RNN, short for recurrent neural network, reads a story one word at a time, like you do, and keeps a little notebook in its head of what happened so far, updating that notebook after every word. An LSTM is the same idea with a smarter notebook that's better at remembering the important parts and forgetting the rest.

A recurrent neural network, or RNN, processes a sequence one step at a time, one five-minute reading after another, say, and keeps a hidden state, a running summary of everything it has seen so far, updating that summary at each step. A plain RNN tends to forget older information as the sequence gets long, which is the problem an LSTM (long short-term memory network) was designed to fix, using extra gates that let it decide what to keep, what to forget, and what to output at each step. Both are recurrent architectures built for data where order matters, like a time series of traffic speeds, rather than a flat table of independent rows.

A recurrent neural network computes, at each time step t, hₜ = tanh(Wₓxₜ + Wₕhₜ₋₁ + b), combining the current input xₜ with the previous hidden state hₜ₋₁ through learned weight matrices, so hₜ carries forward a compressed memory of everything before it. An LSTM replaces this single update with a cell state and three gates, input, forget and output, each a small sigmoid-based network deciding how much old information to keep, how much new information to add, and what to expose as the current output, which is specifically designed to let gradients flow back through many time steps without vanishing. In PyTorch, `nn.LSTM(input_size, hidden_size)` implements this, and feeding it a sequence of a station's past speed readings, one per five-minute step, produces a final hidden state usable as input to a prediction layer for the next 30 minutes.

RNN-family models, networks with this recurrent, step-by-step structure, struggle with long sequences because of the vanishing gradient problem: backpropagation through time multiplies gradients repeatedly through the recurrence, and if those factors are consistently less than 1, the gradient shrinks toward zero over many steps, meaning the network effectively cannot learn dependencies spanning more than a modest number of time steps. LSTMs, and the related, simpler GRU, address this with an additive, gated update to the cell state instead of a repeated multiplicative transformation, which lets gradients propagate much further back through time relatively unimpeded when the forget gate is near 1, giving the network a genuine mechanism for long-range memory rather than just more capacity. This family of models processes a sequence strictly in order, which makes it naturally suited to streaming, online prediction, updating a forecast as new five-minute readings arrive, but also means it cannot be parallelized across time steps during training the way a transformer's attention mechanism can, making it slower to train on long sequences. For traffic forecasting specifically, an RNN or LSTM can, in principle, learn temporal patterns, daily cycles, how quickly congestion builds and dissipates, directly from a raw sequence of readings without hand-engineered lag features, though in practice this requires more data than explicit feature engineering does to reach comparable performance.

Despite the reputation of vanishing gradients as the central problem for recurrent networks (RNNs), in practice exploding gradients are just as common a training obstacle and are usually handled with gradient clipping, a blunt but effective fix that caps the gradient norm rather than addressing the underlying dynamics; a deeper theoretical account connects the issue to the spectral radius of the recurrent weight matrix crossing certain thresholds. The bidirectional variant, running two RNNs, one forward and one backward through the sequence, and combining their hidden states, captures context from both directions but is only usable when the full sequence is available upfront, which rules it out for genuinely online, real-time forecasting where future readings are not yet observed at prediction time, a distinction practitioners sometimes miss when adapting architectures from offline benchmark papers to a production streaming setting. Attention mechanisms and transformers have largely displaced RNNs for sequence modeling where enough data and compute are available, since attention lets every position directly access every other position's information without the sequential bottleneck, but recurrent architectures retain real advantages for streaming inference, updating a hidden state incrementally, in constant memory, one new reading at a time, that a full-sequence transformer does not share without additional engineering. A frequent modeling mistake specific to spatio-temporal traffic data is applying a plain, per-station RNN and expecting it to implicitly learn cross-station spatial relationships it was never given any structural way to represent, which is exactly the gap that combining RNNs with graph neural networks, DCRNN, STGCN, is meant to close.

In current production and research settings, transformers and their variants have largely replaced RNNs and LSTMs, recurrent architectures, for large-scale sequence modeling given sufficient compute, but they remain genuinely competitive, and often preferred, for latency- and memory-constrained on-device inference, where their constant-memory, strictly sequential processing suits streaming input far better than an attention mechanism whose cost grows with sequence length. State-space models (S4, Mamba and related architectures) represent an active research direction explicitly reviving RNN-like sequential, linear-time processing while trying to match or exceed transformer-level modeling quality, motivated by exactly this efficiency gap. For real-time forecasting systems processing continuous sensor streams, an open engineering question is how to combine the streaming efficiency of recurrent state updates with the longer-range, more flexible relational modeling that attention or graph structure provides, without paying either architecture's full computational cost.

terms.def: A dense vector of numbers, learned from data, that represents a category so similar categories end up close together in that vector space.
levels: Imagine giving every animal a secret set of coordinates on a map, so that cats and lions end up near each other because they're both a bit alike, while cats and fish end up far apart. An embedding is a set of numbers like that for a category, learned so that similar things land close together.

An embedding turns a category, like a station ID or a word, into a list of numbers, a vector, that a model can actually do math with. Instead of just labeling each station with an arbitrary ID number that has no real meaning, station 5 is not more than station 3 in any real sense, an embedding learns numbers for each station such that stations that behave similarly end up with similar number lists. The model learns these numbers itself during training, rather than someone writing them by hand.

An embedding is typically a short vector, say 8 or 16 numbers, one per category, like one vector per station_id, stored in a lookup table that starts out random and gets updated during training just like any other weight in the model. In PyTorch, `nn.Embedding(num_stations, embedding_dim)` creates this lookup table; feeding in a station's ID returns its current embedding vector, which then flows into the rest of the network like any other feature. Stations with genuinely similar traffic behavior tend to end up with similar embedding vectors after training, even though nothing explicitly told the model which stations were alike, that structure is discovered from the data.

Embeddings are the standard way to handle a categorical feature with many possible values in a neural network, replacing one-hot encoding, a huge, mostly-zero vector with one 1 per category, with a compact, dense, learned representation that scales far better as the number of categories grows and lets the model share statistical strength across related categories instead of treating each one as entirely independent. Nearby points in the resulting embedding space tend to reflect meaningful similarity, for station embeddings this might mean stations on the same freeway segment or with similar typical congestion patterns cluster together, which is a byproduct of training on the actual prediction task, not a separately imposed goal. It requires enough data per category to learn a good embedding; a station seen only a handful of times in training gets a poorly estimated, essentially near-random embedding, a real limitation for rare categories, the cold-start problem. It fails to generalize to entirely new categories unseen during training, a brand-new station added after deployment has no learned embedding at all, which typically requires falling back to some default or average embedding until enough new data accumulates.

Embedding dimension is a real hyperparameter with a tradeoff: too small and the embedding cannot capture the true diversity of station behavior, too large and the model has more parameters to overfit with, especially for categories with limited data per category, a rough rule of thumb some practitioners use is scaling embedding dimension with the log or fourth root of the number of categories, though this is a heuristic, not a theorem. Pretrained or transfer-learned embeddings, learning them on a large related task, then reusing or fine-tuning them on a smaller target task, can substantially help the cold-start and limited-data problems, an idea borrowed directly from word embeddings in NLP and widely reused across recommender systems and tabular deep learning. A frequent practitioner mistake is comparing embedding-based neural models against tree-based models using native categorical support and concluding embeddings are unnecessary, when in fact the two approaches handle categorical information via genuinely different mechanisms, trees split on category subsets directly, embeddings learn continuous geometry, and which wins depends heavily on how much data exists per category and how smoothly categories relate to each other. The geometry of a learned embedding space is not automatically interpretable; nearby points suggest similarity but the individual coordinate directions rarely have a clean, nameable meaning on their own, a genuine limitation when someone asks a model to explain why two stations were treated similarly.

At production scale, embedding tables for systems with millions of categories, users, items, locations, become the single largest source of model parameters and memory footprint, which drives specialized infrastructure, parameter servers, embedding sharding across many machines, and quantized or hashed embedding tables, purpose-built to store and update them efficiently, well beyond what a single-machine PyTorch embedding layer handles. Cold-start remains a genuinely unsolved production problem at scale: systems typically fall back to hierarchical embeddings, embed a broader category, like freeway segment, when the specific one, station, has too little data, or hybrid approaches that blend a learned embedding with hand-built features until enough data accumulates. An active research and engineering question is how embeddings learned for one task transfer to related but distinct tasks and domains without full retraining, which matters enormously for cost at scale but remains only partially solved, with transfer sometimes working well and sometimes silently degrading performance in ways that are hard to predict ahead of time.

terms.def: A mechanism letting a model weigh how much each input element should influence a given output, computed from learned similarity between them.
levels: Imagine you're in a noisy room and you can somehow turn up the volume on the one friend talking to you while everyone else gets quieter, without covering your ears. Attention lets a computer do that with information, it turns up the volume on the pieces that matter most for what it's trying to figure out right now, and turns down the rest.

Attention is a way for a model to decide, for each piece of information it is looking at, how much to focus on every other piece. Instead of treating every input the same, it computes a weight for each pair, how relevant is this word, or this station, to that one, and then blends information according to those weights. In a traffic model, attention could let a station look at all its neighbors and decide on its own how much each neighbor's data matters right now, rather than always using a fixed, hand-picked set of neighbors.

Attention computes, for a given query, a weighted sum of values, where the weights come from comparing the query against a set of keys, typically weight equals softmax of the query dot the key divided by the square root of the key dimension, which turns raw similarity scores into probabilities that sum to 1 across all the keys being attended to. Self-attention applies this within a single sequence or set, letting every element attend to every other element, which is the core operation inside a transformer. In a graph attention network applied to Traffic1's station graph, each station computes attention weights over its neighbors based on their current feature vectors, so a station with an unusually informative neighbor can weight that neighbor's information more heavily than a quiet, uninformative one. The division by the square root of the key dimension keeps the dot products from growing too large as dimension increases, which would otherwise push softmax into an overly peaked, hard-to-train regime.

Multi-head attention runs several attention computations in parallel, each with its own learned query, key, and value projections, which lets the model attend to different kinds of relationships simultaneously, one head might learn to attend to immediate temporal neighbors, another to spatially nearby stations, and then concatenates the results before a final linear projection. Because self-attention computes a weight between every pair of elements in a sequence of length n, its cost scales quadratically in both time and memory, which is the central scalability bottleneck of transformer-style attention and motivates sparse or linear attention variants for long sequences. Attention weights are sometimes interpreted as a form of built-in explainability, but this interpretation is contested, since high attention weight does not always correspond to high causal importance for the output, and studies have shown attention patterns can be manipulated or made uninformative while the model's predictions stay unchanged. In a graph neural network context specifically, attention generalizes a fixed-weight neighbor aggregation, like a simple average over upstream and downstream neighbors, by letting the model learn which neighbors matter more, at the cost of more parameters and a somewhat harder optimization problem than a fixed aggregation scheme.

The quadratic cost of full self-attention has driven substantial research into efficient variants, sparse attention patterns, low-rank approximations, kernel-based linear attention, each trading some modeling flexibility for better scaling, and none has fully displaced standard full attention for tasks where sequence length is manageable, because the approximations tend to lose a bit of accuracy or require careful tuning to match full attention's performance. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming attention mechanisms are strictly necessary for good performance on any sequential or relational problem; for many tabular or moderately sized structured problems, including much of traffic forecasting at the scale of a single freeway corridor, simpler architectures like gradient-boosted trees or even a fixed-neighbor aggregation can match or beat attention-based models, and attention's real advantages show up more clearly with larger datasets and more complex, less hand-engineerable relational structure. Attention's interaction with positional or structural information is a genuine design choice, not automatic: a transformer needs explicit positional encodings to know sequence order, and a graph attention network needs the graph's edges to define which pairs are even eligible to attend to each other, since attention alone has no inherent notion of order or adjacency without that information being provided. The theoretical understanding of why attention-based models transfer and scale so well compared to earlier recurrent architectures remains partly empirical, and connecting attention's inductive biases precisely to its observed scaling behavior is an active research area.

At production and research scale, attention is the core primitive behind essentially all large sequence and multimodal models, and a large fraction of current systems and hardware co-design work is about making attention's quadratic cost tractable for very long contexts, IO-aware implementations, which restructure the computation to reduce memory movement rather than changing the mathematical operation, have been as impactful in practice as any purely algorithmic sparse-attention variant. On-device deployment makes attention's memory and compute cost a hard constraint rather than a performance nicety, driving work on more efficient attention variants, quantized attention computation, and hybrid architectures that mix attention with cheaper operations to hit strict latency and power budgets on a phone or watch. An open research question is finding architectures that retain attention's flexible, content-based routing of information without its quadratic cost at very long context lengths, since the tradeoffs among current efficient-attention approaches are still not fully resolved, and each new approach tends to win on some tasks and lose on others in ways not yet well predicted by theory.

terms.def: A neural network architecture built on attention, letting every position in a sequence weigh and combine information from every other position.
levels: A transformer is a kind of computer brain that is really good at reading a whole sentence at once and figuring out which words matter most to which other words. It is like reading a mystery story and being able to instantly remember every clue from every page at the same time, instead of only remembering the page right before. That way it can notice that a word way back at the beginning of the story actually explains something happening at the very end.

A transformer is a type of neural network especially good at working with sequences, like sentences or time series, because of a mechanism called attention, which lets every position look at and weigh information from every other position, not just the ones right next to it. Unlike older sequence models that read one step at a time in order, a transformer can consider the whole sequence at once, which makes it both faster to train and better at catching relationships between distant parts of a sequence. Transformers are the architecture behind most modern language models. In this course, they appear in the later phases, after simpler models like logistic regression and LightGBM, as one of the more advanced tools in the modeling toolbox.

The core operation in a transformer is attention: for each position in a sequence, it computes a weighted average of every other position's information, where the weights (how much attention to pay to each other position) are themselves computed from the data, not fixed in advance. A transformer layer combines this attention mechanism with a simple feedforward network applied to each position, plus normalization and residual (skip) connections that help gradients flow through many stacked layers during training. `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` in PyTorch implements one such layer directly. Attention's weights are computed from three learned projections of the input, called queries, keys and values, whose interaction determines how much each position attends to each other position.

Formally, attention computes a weighted sum where the weight between a query at one position and a key at another is their scaled dot product passed through a softmax, so every position ends up as a data-dependent combination of every other position's value vector; this is the mechanism, and the rest of a transformer layer (feedforward sublayers, layer normalization, residual connections) is comparatively simple plumbing around it. Because attention considers every pair of positions, it has quadratic time and memory cost in sequence length, which is the central scaling bottleneck of transformers and the reason a great deal of transformer research targets making attention cheaper for long sequences. Transformers have no inherent notion of order (unlike a recurrent model that processes a sequence step by step), so positional information has to be injected explicitly, typically through positional encodings added to the input embeddings, and getting this encoding wrong or omitting it degrades the model's ability to use sequence order at all. Training a transformer from scratch typically requires substantially more data than a comparably-sized model with stronger built-in structural assumptions (like a convolutional network for images), because a transformer's flexibility (it makes fewer assumptions about the data's structure) is a double-edged property: powerful when there is enough data to learn the right structure, but prone to underperforming smaller, more structured models on small datasets.

Attention's expressiveness comes precisely from having no fixed structural bias about which positions should interact, which is a strength on large, diverse data and a real weakness on small data, where a more structured inductive bias (convolution's locality assumption, or a recurrent model's inherent sequential ordering) can generalize better from fewer examples, a tradeoff still actively debated depending on the domain and data scale.
