The quadratic attention cost has motivated an entire research subfield of efficient attention variants (sparse attention, linear attention approximations, sliding-window attention), each trading some modeling flexibility or exactness for better scaling, and none has fully displaced standard full attention for tasks where quality matters most, suggesting the tradeoff is genuinely difficult rather than simply unsolved due to insufficient effort. A common misconception, even among practitioners, is that attention weights are directly interpretable as 'what the model is paying attention to' in a causally meaningful sense; empirically, attention weights often do not align cleanly with feature importance measures like Shapley values computed on the same model, and treating raw attention weights as a full explanation of model behavior is considered unreliable by much of the interpretability research community. Training stability is a genuine engineering challenge specific to transformers at depth: without careful initialization, learning-rate warmup, and normalization placement, deep transformer training can diverge or plateau in ways shallower or more structurally-constrained networks typically do not, which is why transformer training recipes are unusually sensitive to these specific hyperparameters compared to other architectures.

At production and research scale, transformers underlie essentially every state-of-the-art large language and multimodal model, and the practical engineering challenges have shifted from 'does attention work' to how to serve extremely large transformer models efficiently: key-value caching to avoid recomputing attention over the whole sequence at every generation step, quantization to shrink memory footprint, and architectural variants (mixture-of-experts, grouped-query attention) that reduce the effective compute and memory cost per token without proportionally sacrificing quality. Apple's on-device deployment of transformer-based models faces the quadratic attention cost especially acutely given tight memory and power budgets, which is why on-device transformer variants typically use aggressive compression, smaller context windows, and specialized attention approximations relative to their server-side counterparts. Open research questions include finding attention variants that scale sub-quadratically without meaningful quality loss, understanding why transformers exhibit emergent capabilities at scale that smaller versions of the same architecture do not show at all, and building genuinely reliable interpretability tools for a mechanism (attention) whose weights, despite their apparent transparency, do not straightforwardly explain the model's actual decision process.

terms.def: A large language model: a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word, useful for writing, summarizing and answering questions.
levels: Imagine a very well-read robot that has read almost every book and website there is, and got so good at guessing "what word comes next" that it can write whole sentences and answer questions. That's what people mean by an LLM, or large language model.

An LLM, or large language model, is a computer program trained on enormous amounts of text, books, websites, articles, to get very good at one simple task: guessing the next word in a sentence. GPT (short for "generative pre-trained transformer") is a well-known family of these models. By getting extremely good at that one prediction task across billions of examples, the model ends up able to write essays, answer questions, summarize text, and even write code, even though "predict the next word" was the only thing it was directly trained to do.

An LLM like GPT is built from a transformer architecture, trained first on a "next word prediction" task over a huge text corpus (pre-training), then further adjusted with human feedback to be more helpful and safe (fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback). You interact with one through a prompt, the text you give it, and it generates a response one word (or word-piece, called a token) at a time, each new token chosen based on everything before it. For this course's traffic project, an LLM isn't part of the prediction model itself, but it could reasonably help with adjacent tasks: parsing free-text incident reports, or drafting a plain-English weekly summary of the monitoring dashboard.

An LLM's core architecture is the transformer, which processes an entire input sequence in parallel using self-attention, every token's representation is updated based on a learned, weighted combination of every other token's representation, rather than reading step by step the way a recurrent network does, which is what allows LLMs to be trained efficiently at massive scale on modern accelerator hardware. Pre-training on next-token prediction over huge, diverse text turns out to be a surprisingly general-purpose objective: it forces the model to implicitly learn grammar, facts, and reasoning patterns as a side effect of getting good at prediction, and this pre-trained model is then adapted, via supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, into a model that follows instructions and holds conversations. LLMs fail in specific, well-documented ways: they hallucinate confident-sounding but false statements, especially about facts outside their training data or requiring precise calculation; they can be sensitive to how a prompt is worded; and their knowledge is frozen as of their training data's cutoff unless given external tools or retrieval. Using one for a task like this course's project means being deliberate about the boundary, since an LLM parsing an incident report's free text is a reasonable, bounded use, while trusting an LLM's raw judgment for a safety-relevant alerting decision is not, precisely because its errors aren't well-characterized statistically the way a calibrated classifier's are.

Evaluating LLMs rigorously is itself a hard, unsettled problem: benchmark contamination, test data leaking into training data, benchmark saturation, models scoring near-ceiling on older benchmarks without necessarily improving on the underlying capability, and "LLM-as-judge" evaluation, using one LLM to grade another's output, all carry known biases, since an LLM judge tends to favor longer, more confident-sounding answers regardless of correctness, which is why task-specific evaluation sets built for your actual use case generally beat leaderboard rankings for deciding whether a model is good enough for a particular job. A subtlety many miss is that an LLM's fluency is not evidence of its calibration or reliability: unlike a properly calibrated classifier's probability output, an LLM's confident tone carries no formal guarantee about its actual correctness rate, and treating fluent output as trustworthy output is a common and consequential mistake. Retrieval-augmented generation, grounding an LLM's answer in retrieved documents rather than relying purely on its trained-in knowledge, and tool use, letting the model call external functions, like a calculator or a database query, are the standard mitigations for hallucination and stale knowledge, each introducing its own new failure modes around retrieval quality and tool-call correctness. For a project like this one, the disciplined position is to keep an LLM firmly out of any decision loop that needs calibrated, auditable probabilities, alerting thresholds, safety-relevant automation, while allowing it into loops that are naturally human-reviewed, like report drafting or summarization.

At the frontier, scaling laws relating model size, data size and compute budget to performance have guided most of the field's progress, though there's active debate about where returns from simply scaling further begin to flatten relative to gains from better data curation, better post-training, alignment and reasoning-focused fine-tuning, and architectural changes like mixture-of-experts that decouple total parameter count from per-token compute cost. Production deployment of LLMs raises engineering concerns largely orthogonal to research benchmarks, inference latency and cost at scale, prompt injection and other security surfaces when a model has tool access, and the challenge of keeping behavior consistent and monitorable across frequent model updates. Open research questions include how to make LLM reasoning verifiably reliable rather than merely fluent, how to evaluate genuinely novel capabilities without contaminated benchmarks, and how much of what looks like reasoning in these models is a distinct capability versus a sophisticated form of pattern completion over their training data, a question without full scientific consensus as of now.

terms.def: Generative models that learn to produce realistic data — a GAN pits a generator against a discriminator; a VAE compresses data into a latent code it can decode or sample from.
levels: A GAN is like a game between a forger who tries to paint fake pictures and a detective who tries to catch the fakes; they both get better and better until the fakes look real. A VAE and an autoencoder are more like a machine that learns to squish a picture down into a tiny description and then unsquish it back into (almost) the same picture.

An autoencoder is a network trained to compress its input down into a small code and then rebuild the original input from just that code, learning what matters most about the data in the process. A VAE (variational autoencoder) is a version of this that also learns a smooth, probability-based code space, so you can pick a random point in that space and decode something new and plausible from it, not just reconstruct known inputs. A GAN (generative adversarial network) takes a different approach: a generator tries to create fake examples realistic enough to fool a second network, the discriminator, which is simultaneously trying to tell real from fake, and both improve by competing against each other.

An autoencoder has an encoder that compresses input x into a smaller latent code z, and a decoder that reconstructs x̂ from z, trained by minimizing reconstruction error, ‖x − x̂‖². A VAE adds a probabilistic constraint: instead of encoding to one fixed point, it encodes to a distribution (typically Gaussian, parameterized by a mean and variance), and its loss combines reconstruction error with a term (KL divergence) that pushes the latent distribution toward a standard normal, which is what makes the latent space smooth enough to sample new, plausible outputs from. A GAN instead trains two networks against each other in a minimax game: the generator G tries to produce fake samples from random noise that fool the discriminator D, while D tries to correctly classify real versus generated samples, and training alternates updating each network to improve against the current version of the other.

GANs and VAEs represent two different theoretical approaches to generative modeling: a VAE explicitly optimizes a lower bound on the data's log-likelihood (the evidence lower bound, ELBO), which gives it a principled probabilistic training objective at the cost of generated samples that are often noticeably blurrier than a GAN's, a known artifact of the reconstruction loss and the Gaussian assumption on the decoder's output. A GAN has no explicit likelihood objective at all — it is trained adversarially, which can produce sharper, more realistic samples, but the minimax game is notoriously unstable to train: mode collapse (the generator learns to produce only a narrow subset of plausible outputs, having found a few examples that reliably fool the discriminator) and vanishing gradients (if the discriminator becomes too good too fast, the generator gets almost no useful learning signal) are well-known, common failure modes. A plain autoencoder without the VAE's probabilistic structure is good at compression and denoising but has an unstructured, often discontinuous latent space, so interpolating between two points in its latent space, or sampling a random point, tends to produce unrealistic outputs — the VAE's KL term is specifically what fixes this for generative sampling purposes. Evaluating generative models quantitatively is itself nontrivial; there is no single agreed-upon metric analogous to accuracy, which is why generative work typically combines a quantitative proxy (like FID, comparing statistics of real and generated image features) with human judgment.

The VAE's ELBO objective is a genuine approximation, not the true likelihood, and the gap between the two (controlled by how well the variational posterior approximates the true posterior) is a real source of the blurriness commonly attributed loosely to 'the VAE's Gaussian assumption' — more expressive posterior approximations (normalizing flows composed with the VAE's encoder) close some of this gap at real added complexity. GAN training instability has motivated an entire subfield of alternative formulations and regularizations — Wasserstein GANs replace the original Jensen-Shannon-divergence-based objective with the Wasserstein distance, which provides more informative gradients even when the generator and true data distributions barely overlap (the exact regime the original formulation handles poorly), and gradient penalty and spectral normalization techniques stabilize training by constraining the discriminator's Lipschitz behavior. A subtlety often missed by practitioners moving between these model families: a VAE's latent space has an explicit, checkable structure (you can compute a likelihood lower bound, inspect the KL term, and verify the prior is roughly matched), while a GAN's latent space has no such explicit guarantee — it is whatever the generator happens to have learned, evaluated only indirectly through the discriminator's judgment or downstream sample quality, which makes GANs harder to debug systematically when they misbehave. Diffusion models, which now dominate high-fidelity image generation, can be understood as addressing both families' weaknesses at once — they retain an explicit, tractable training objective closer to the VAE's likelihood-based approach while achieving GAN-level or better sample fidelity, at the cost of much slower sampling (many sequential denoising steps versus a GAN's single forward pass).

At production and research scale, pure GANs have been largely displaced by diffusion models for high-fidelity generation because diffusion training is dramatically more stable (no adversarial minimax game to balance) and scales more predictably with data and compute, even though GANs retain an edge in sampling speed (a single forward pass versus many diffusion steps), which still matters for latency-sensitive, on-device generation. VAEs, meanwhile, persist as a core architectural component rather than a standalone generative model in their own right — they are the compression stage inside latent diffusion models (compressing images to a smaller latent space before the expensive diffusion process operates there), which is a large part of why modern large-scale image generation systems are computationally feasible at all. An open research area is combining the stability and likelihood-based grounding of VAE- and diffusion-style training with GAN-level sampling speed, alongside the harder, still-unresolved problem of rigorously evaluating generative model quality and safety (bias, memorization of training data, and misuse) at the scale these systems are now deployed.

terms.def: Graph neural networks for traffic: GCN mixes each station with its neighbors, STGCN adds temporal convolutions, DCRNN adds directional diffusion and a sequence model.
levels: These are computer brains that let each road-watcher on a map whisper to its next-door neighbors, share what they are seeing, and pass the news along the road.

A GCN, graph convolutional network, is a neural network built for data that lives on a graph, like stations connected to their neighbors on a freeway, where each station updates its own summary by mixing in its neighbors' summaries. STGCN and DCRNN are two specific designs built for traffic: STGCN alternates looking at time patterns and looking at neighbor patterns, while DCRNN combines a GRU, good at sequences, with a version of neighbor-mixing that respects the one-way direction of traffic flow.

A GCN updates each node's, or station's, representation using its neighbors, via something like `A @ h`, mixing in neighbor information, then a learned weight matrix and nonlinearity, stacked in layers so information can reach further neighbors with each added layer. STGCN alternates gated temporal convolutions, which look for patterns across recent time steps, with Chebyshev graph convolutions, a spectral form of graph convolution, so it captures both when and where patterns. DCRNN instead uses diffusion convolution, applying forward and backward random-walk matrices on the directed road graph, wrapped inside an encoder-decoder GRU that reads a sequence of past readings and predicts a sequence of future ones, with scheduled sampling to make training match how it is actually used at prediction time.

All three are ways of combining two things a plain sequence model or a plain per-station model lacks together: spatial structure, what affects what given the road graph, and temporal structure, how a station's own history predicts its near future. GCN alone provides only the spatial half, mixing each node with its graph neighbors through learned weight matrices, typically requiring full-batch access to the whole graph during training, which is what makes it hard to scale to very large graphs without neighbor-sampling extensions like GraphSAGE. STGCN and DCRNN each combine spatial and temporal modeling but with different design choices, reflecting different assumptions about the road network: STGCN's spectral graph convolution implicitly assumes something close to an undirected graph, while DCRNN's diffusion convolution explicitly models forward and backward random walks on a directed graph, arguably a better structural match for one-way traffic flow, at the cost of a more complex encoder-decoder training procedure with scheduled sampling to bridge the gap between training and inference.

A subtlety practitioners often get wrong when reading this literature is treating graph neural network for traffic as one interchangeable technique, when the design choices, symmetric versus directed adjacency, spectral versus spatial convolution, joint sequence prediction versus per-horizon classification, are not incidental implementation details but encode different, sometimes incompatible, assumptions about how traffic actually propagates. This course's own challenger model, a shared GRU plus two rounds of neighbor mixing with directed A_up and A_down matrices, is explicitly described as a stripped-down DCRNN, illustrating that the real architectures in the literature are often elaborations of a much simpler core idea, sequence model plus K-hop directed message passing, rather than something categorically different. Benchmarks report MAE, RMSE, and MAPE at 15, 30, and 60 minutes on standard datasets, METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, and comparing a reproduction's numbers against a paper's published table, as this course's reading-and-reproducing phase does, routinely surfaces both implementation subtleties and genuine gaps between what a paper reports and what a careful from-scratch reproduction actually achieves.

At the scale of a full metro or state highway network rather than one corridor, full-batch GCN-style training becomes infeasible, and production and research systems adopt neighbor sampling, GraphSAGE, subgraph sampling, Cluster-GCN, or precomputed propagation, SGC, to make training tractable on graphs with tens of thousands of nodes. Open questions this course flags as thesis-chapter-worthy remain genuinely open in the field: multi-horizon coherence, making sure a model's 15, 30, and 60-minute predictions relate sensibly to each other, handling non-stationarity, whether the model adapts online or gets periodically retrained, and performative prediction, the fact that drivers who see and react to a traffic alert change the very future the model was trying to predict, a feedback loop that graph-based traffic forecasting research has only recently started to treat seriously.

terms.def: A reinforcement-learning method that learns the expected future reward of taking an action in a state, to guide which action to pick.
levels: Q-learning is a way for a video game character to slowly learn, by trial and error, which button to press in each room to get the most points later, not just right away. Learning like this, by trying things and getting rewards, is called reinforcement learning.

Q-learning is a method from reinforcement learning, the general idea of an agent learning through trial and error how good each possible action is in each situation, measured as the total future reward it expects from taking that action and then acting well afterward. It keeps a table (or, for bigger problems, a function) called Q that maps a state and an action to an expected value, and after every action it updates that value based on the reward it actually got plus its current best guess about what comes next. Over many tries, the agent learns to pick whichever action has the highest Q-value in each state, which becomes its strategy, or policy.

The Q-learning update rule, one of the foundational algorithms in reinforcement learning, is Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ·max Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)], where s and a are the current state and action, r is the reward received, s' is the next state, α is the learning rate, and γ (gamma) is a discount factor between 0 and 1 that weighs future rewards against immediate ones. This is a Bellman-equation-based update: it nudges the current estimate of Q(s,a) toward the reward just received plus the best value achievable from the next state, discounted. It's model-free, it never builds an explicit model of how the environment works, just learns values directly from experience, and it's typically explored with an epsilon-greedy strategy, choosing the best-known action most of the time but a random one with small probability epsilon, to keep discovering potentially better options.

Q-learning is an off-policy reinforcement-learning algorithm, meaning it can learn the optimal policy's values even while the agent is actually behaving differently, exploring randomly some of the time via epsilon-greedy, because its update always bootstraps toward the max over next-state actions rather than toward whatever action was actually taken next, this distinguishes it from on-policy methods like SARSA, which update toward the value of the action actually chosen. Convergence to the true optimal Q-values is guaranteed under fairly mild conditions, every state-action pair visited infinitely often, a suitably decaying learning rate, for tabular Q-learning with a finite state and action space, but this guarantee evaporates once a neural network replaces the table, since function approximation introduces its own error and correlation between updates that can cause divergence in practice. The exploration-exploitation tradeoff, controlled by epsilon, is fundamental: too little exploration and the agent settles on a suboptimal policy having never tried better actions, too much and it wastes experience acting close to randomly even once it has learned enough to do better. Reward design is a subtle and consequential part of applying Q-learning to a real problem; a poorly shaped reward can lead an agent to learn a policy that technically maximizes the specified reward while completely failing the intended goal, a phenomenon often called reward hacking.

Deep Q-networks (DQN) replace the tabular Q-function with a neural network to handle large or continuous state spaces, extending reinforcement learning to problems no lookup table could cover, but this combination is famously unstable without specific stabilizing tricks: experience replay, storing and randomly resampling past transitions to break the strong correlation between consecutive updates, and a separate, periodically-updated target network, to prevent the bootstrapped target from chasing a rapidly-shifting estimate of itself. Q-learning is also known to systematically overestimate action values, because the max operator in the update is a biased estimator when Q-values themselves are noisy estimates; Double Q-learning addresses this by decoupling action selection from value estimation using two separate value estimates, a fix that meaningfully improves performance in practice, not just in theory. Compared to policy-gradient methods, which directly optimize a parameterized policy rather than deriving one from learned values, Q-learning tends to be more sample-efficient in discrete-action settings but does not naturally extend to continuous action spaces, where taking a max over an infinite action set is not directly tractable, motivating actor-critic hybrids. Practitioners applying Q-learning-style methods to real operational problems, like deciding ramp-metering rates based on predicted traffic state, frequently underestimate how much reward shaping and careful state representation matter relative to the choice of learning algorithm itself.

Production use of Q-learning and its descendants is comparatively rare compared to supervised learning, largely because most real deployment settings lack a cheap, safe, high-throughput way to let an agent actually try actions and observe rewards, this has pushed reinforcement learning research toward offline RL, learning a policy from a fixed, previously logged dataset of experience, without further live interaction, as the more practically deployable framing for problems like traffic control, ad ranking, or recommendation, where live exploration carries real cost or risk. When reinforcement learning is used in production, it is much more often for tuning a system's operating policy, adaptive resource allocation, adaptive ramp metering, on top of a solid predictive model like the one this course builds, rather than replacing prediction with control end to end. An open research area is safe and sample-efficient reinforcement learning under realistic constraints, limited or costly interaction, non-stationary environments, and the need for guarantees against catastrophic actions during learning, none of which the clean tabular Q-learning setting has to contend with.

terms.def: A model that predicts not just one number but a whole range of likely curves, giving wider uncertainty where it has seen less data.
levels: Imagine drawing a squiggly line through some dots, but around your line you also draw a fuzzy cloud showing how sure you are, a thin cloud where you have lots of dots nearby, and a big fat cloud where you are just guessing. A Gaussian process draws that line and that cloud together.

A Gaussian process is a way for a model to predict not just a single guess, but a range of reasonable guesses, along with how confident it is. Where it has seen a lot of similar examples, its guess is confident and the range is narrow; where it has seen very little data, it admits it is unsure and gives a wide range. This is different from most models, which just give one number and no sense of how trustworthy that number is.

A Gaussian process defines a probability distribution over entire functions, not just over individual values, using a kernel, a similarity function, that says how strongly two points' predictions should influence each other based on how close together they are. Given some observed points, it produces a predicted mean curve plus a confidence band, the variance, around it at every point, and that band widens automatically in regions with no nearby observed data. Fitting one usually means choosing a kernel, like a periodic kernel for a daily traffic pattern, and tuning its hyperparameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the observed data.

Formally, a Gaussian process is a collection of random variables, any finite subset of which has a joint Gaussian, normal, distribution, fully specified by a mean function and a covariance, kernel, function; the kernel encodes prior assumptions about smoothness, periodicity, or other structure the modeler expects the true function to have. Predicting at a new point is a closed-form Bayesian update: conditioning the joint Gaussian on the observed points gives an exact posterior mean and variance at any new input, which is what produces both the predicted curve and its uncertainty band without needing iterative optimization for prediction itself, only for fitting kernel hyperparameters. It fails to scale well: exact inference requires inverting an n by n matrix of pairwise similarities between all observed points, which costs cubic time in the number of points and becomes impractical past a few thousand data points, a serious limitation for anything approaching typical dataset sizes in this course's traffic data. The choice of kernel matters enormously and is itself a modeling decision with real consequences; a smooth kernel assumes a smooth underlying function, and using the wrong kernel family produces systematically overconfident or underconfident uncertainty bands.

The kernel is where all of a Gaussian process's assumptions live, and composing kernels, adding a periodic kernel for daily cycles to a smooth kernel for slower trends, for instance, is a principled and common way to encode structured prior knowledge about a signal like a station's daily traffic profile, though choosing and validating a kernel composition is closer to craft than an automated procedure. Sparse and approximate Gaussian process methods, inducing points, variational approximations, exist specifically to address the cubic-time scaling wall, trading some predictive accuracy for tractability on datasets of realistic size, and are what makes Gaussian processes usable at all beyond toy or small-data problems. A common misconception is treating a Gaussian process's uncertainty band as automatically well-calibrated in any absolute sense; it is well-calibrated only relative to the assumed kernel and prior, so a badly chosen kernel produces a confidence band that looks principled but is quietly wrong. Gaussian processes are prized specifically for problems with limited data where honest uncertainty matters more than raw predictive accuracy, a real and different tradeoff from this course's main models, logistic regression, LightGBM, neural nets, which are chosen instead for scalability to a large dataset.

In production settings, Gaussian processes are mostly reserved for problems where data is genuinely scarce and calibrated uncertainty is worth the computational cost; Bayesian optimization for tuning expensive hyperparameters or physical experiments is the most common production use, precisely because each evaluation is costly and a Gaussian process's uncertainty estimate directly guides which point to try next. Deep kernel learning and neural process methods are active research attempts to combine a Gaussian process's calibrated uncertainty with a neural network's ability to scale to large, high-dimensional data, an open problem because the two approaches' strengths, uncertainty quantification versus raw scale, have historically traded off against each other rather than combining cleanly. For a large sensor network like this course's, a full Gaussian process over every station is impractical, but the underlying idea, a model that tells you not just its prediction but how much to trust it, wider where data is thin, remains a genuinely valuable property that cheaper production models try to approximate without paying the Gaussian process's computational cost.

terms.def: A method for building prediction intervals or sets with a guaranteed coverage rate, using held-out data to calibrate how wrong the model usually is.
levels: Imagine you're guessing how many jellybeans are in a jar, and instead of giving one number, you give a range, like somewhere between 80 and 120, because you've checked before how far off your guesses usually are. Conformal prediction is a way for a computer to make ranges like that, and to make sure the true answer really does land inside the range most of the time, not just sometimes.

Conformal prediction is a way to turn a single guess into a range you can trust. It works by checking, on data the model has not used for training, how far off the model's predictions usually are, and then building a range around new predictions wide enough to cover the true answer a chosen percentage of the time, like 90 percent. Unlike some other ways of making ranges, conformal prediction does not assume the errors follow any particular pattern, it just measures them directly and uses that.

Conformal prediction produces a prediction set, for classification, or interval, for regression, with a guaranteed coverage rate, meaning that across many predictions, the true answer falls inside the interval at least as often as the target rate, say, 90 percent, under fairly weak assumptions. The standard split-conformal procedure: hold out a calibration set separate from training data, compute a nonconformity score for each calibration example, take the appropriate quantile of those scores, and use that quantile to widen any new prediction into an interval. For Traffic1, this could mean checking on held-out days how wrong the model's slow-traffic probability usually is, and widening a new prediction into a range guaranteed to cover the true outcome 90 percent of the time. The guarantee holds regardless of the underlying model's correctness or the true data distribution's shape, which is what distinguishes conformal intervals from intervals derived from assuming errors are normally distributed.

Conformal prediction's coverage guarantee relies on exchangeability, the assumption that the calibration and test examples are drawn in a way where their order does not matter statistically, which holds for i.i.d. data but is a real concern for time series, where PeMS traffic data is temporally correlated and not exchangeable in the strict sense, requiring adapted methods to preserve the coverage guarantee honestly. The choice of nonconformity score matters for the resulting interval's usefulness even though it does not affect the coverage guarantee itself, a well-chosen score produces tighter, more informative intervals than a poorly chosen one, even though both are technically valid. Split conformal prediction is simple but wastes data by holding out a calibration set that could otherwise be used for training; full conformal prediction avoids this by conceptually retraining the model for every candidate label, which is far more computationally expensive and rarely practical outside small models. Coverage is a marginal guarantee, averaged over all test examples, rather than a conditional one, correct for every subgroup or every individual example, so a conformal method can have exactly 90 percent coverage overall while systematically undercovering on, say, one particular station or one time of day, a gap between marginal and conditional coverage that practitioners frequently misunderstand as a stronger guarantee than it actually is.

The gap between marginal and conditional coverage is the central practical limitation of conformal prediction, and much recent research works on getting closer to per-group or per-example coverage guarantees, generally at the cost of requiring more calibration data per group or accepting somewhat weaker theoretical guarantees than the clean marginal case. For non-exchangeable data like time series, weighted conformal prediction, down-weighting older calibration points, or explicit adaptation to distribution shift are active research directions, and applying standard split-conformal methods naively to genuinely nonstationary traffic data can silently produce intervals with worse-than-nominal coverage without any error message indicating the guarantee has broken. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating conformal prediction as making the underlying model better; it does not, it only wraps the existing model's predictions with a calibrated notion of uncertainty, so a systematically biased model produces conformal intervals that are honestly wide rather than pushing the model itself toward better accuracy. Conformal methods compose reasonably well with other uncertainty quantification techniques, but combining multiple layers of uncertainty estimation without care can produce intervals that are technically valid but so conservative they are not actionable, which is a real, if underappreciated, failure mode distinct from the interval simply being wrong.

In production systems, conformal prediction is attractive precisely because its coverage guarantee is distribution-free and model-agnostic, letting the same calibration wrapper sit on top of very different underlying models without needing model-specific uncertainty machinery, which matters when a system must swap or ensemble models over time without breaking its uncertainty guarantees. At scale, maintaining valid coverage under continuous distribution shift requires continuously refreshed calibration data and monitoring of realized coverage against the nominal target, since a coverage guarantee proven at calibration time silently decays as the live data distribution drifts away from the calibration set's distribution. An open research question relevant to real-time systems like traffic or ETA prediction is how to maintain valid, tight conformal guarantees online, incorporating new calibration data continuously without ever fully retraining, while still detecting and reacting quickly enough when a genuine distribution shift breaks the exchangeability assumption the whole guarantee depends on.

terms.def: A model too simple to capture real patterns in the data, so it performs poorly even on the data it trained on.
levels: Underfitting is what happens when your guess is too simple to actually match what is really going on, like trying to draw a whole dog using only one straight line. No matter how hard you try, that one line just cannot capture the dog's ears, tail and legs. A model that underfits is stuck making the same kind of too-simple mistake, even on the exact same examples it was shown.

Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the real patterns in the data, so it performs poorly not just on new data but even on the training data it already saw. A straight line trying to fit a curved relationship is a classic example: no matter how the line is positioned, it cannot bend to match the curve, so its errors stay large everywhere. This is the opposite problem from overfitting, where a model is too complex and memorizes noise instead of learning general patterns. The fix for underfitting is usually a more flexible model, more useful features, or training for longer, rather than adding regularization, which would make an already-too-simple model even simpler.

A model is underfitting when both its training error and validation error are high and close together, unlike overfitting, where training error is low but validation error is much higher. For example, fitting a straight-line logistic regression to a traffic pattern that genuinely depends on interactions between time of day and upstream congestion will underfit, since a linear model cannot represent that interaction without engineered interaction features added explicitly. Diagnosing underfitting typically means plotting training and validation performance (like AP) against a model-complexity control, such as LightGBM's number of leaves; in the underfitting region, both curves sit low and rise together as complexity increases. Fixing underfitting usually means increasing model capacity (more leaves, deeper trees, more features), not adding regularization, which would push an already too-simple model further in the wrong direction.

Underfitting is the high-bias end of the bias-variance tradeoff: a model with too little capacity relative to the true complexity of the underlying function cannot represent it well regardless of how much training data it sees, so unlike overfitting, more data alone does not fix underfitting, only a more expressive model or better features does. In the traffic project specifically, a model that only uses current speed and ignores lag features, neighboring stations, and time-of-day effects will underfit, because it structurally cannot represent the temporal and spatial dependencies that actually drive slow episodes, no matter how well its few parameters are tuned. Underfitting can also arise from optimization failure rather than genuinely insufficient model capacity: a sufficiently expressive model trained with too few epochs, too small a learning rate, or unconverged gradient descent can look underfit on both training and validation error even though the model class itself could, in principle, fit the data well if training were allowed to actually converge, which is a distinct root cause requiring a different fix (more training, a better optimizer) than adding model capacity. Feature scaling problems can also masquerade as underfitting in gradient-based models: if features have wildly different scales, gradient descent can converge extremely slowly toward a good fit, producing training-error behavior that looks like underfitting but is really an optimization pathology fixable by standardizing the features rather than changing the model.

The bias-variance framing of underfitting versus overfitting is a useful simplification but not the whole picture, particularly for very flexible model classes like deep neural networks, where the classical U-shaped 'more complexity eventually overfits' curve can be interrupted by double descent, in which validation error worsens and then improves again well past the point of apparent overfitting, complicating the naive advice to simply match capacity to apparent underfit or overfit. A model that appears to underfit on a naive random train-validation split can actually be reflecting a legitimate distribution shift rather than genuine underfitting; distinguishing 'the model is too simple for this data' from 'the validation set represents a genuinely different distribution than training' requires deliberately probing with a more expressive model or checking whether training error itself is also high, since only the former, not the latter, is diagnostic of true underfitting. In imbalanced classification, like slow-episode prediction, a model can show reasonable aggregate error while badly underfitting the minority class specifically, because aggregate error metrics are dominated by the majority class; this class-conditional underfitting is invisible unless metrics are broken out by class, which is a common and consequential oversight. Practitioners sometimes misdiagnose underfitting caused by a fundamentally mis-specified problem (labels that are inherently noisy or only weakly related to the available features, a ceiling no model complexity can push past) as if it were fixable by adding capacity, when in fact no amount of added flexibility helps once the irreducible noise floor of the labeling process itself is the real limiting factor.

In production ML systems, underfitting is a less common failure mode than overfitting once teams have access to large-scale data and modern flexible model architectures, but it still shows up in constrained deployment contexts, particularly on-device models deliberately kept small for latency, memory, or power reasons, where engineers must consciously accept some underfitting relative to what a larger server-side model could achieve, and the real engineering tradeoff becomes choosing where on that capacity-versus-cost curve to sit rather than eliminating underfitting outright. Apple's on-device ML work regularly confronts exactly this tradeoff: a compact model that must run within a strict latency and battery budget is deliberately underfit relative to an unconstrained server model, and techniques like knowledge distillation (training the small model to mimic a larger, better-fit teacher model) exist specifically to recover some of that lost capacity within the same size constraint. An open research and engineering question is how to detect underfitting automatically and early in a training pipeline, before a full, expensive hyperparameter sweep, since the standard diagnosis (comparing training and validation curves across a capacity sweep) is itself computationally costly at the scale of modern large-model training runs, and cheaper proxies for 'is this model fundamentally too small' remain an active area of practical research.

terms.def: Classical, purely time-based forecasting methods: ARIMA fits a linear model on a series' own lags and differences, and exponential smoothing forecasts as a weighted average that favors recent observations.
levels: ARIMA and exponential smoothing are ways to guess tomorrow's number by looking only at yesterday's numbers, like guessing how tall you'll be next year just from how tall you were the last few years, no other clues allowed.

Exponential smoothing forecasts the next value as a weighted average of past values, giving more weight to recent ones and less to older ones, the weights shrinking the further back you go. ARIMA is a family of models that predicts a series' next value from a linear combination of its own recent past values and recent forecast errors, sometimes after first differencing, today minus yesterday, to remove a trend. Both work on a single time series at a time, using nothing but that series' own history.

The ARIMA(p, d, q) model is written (1 − Σφᵢ·Bⁱ)(1 − B)^d·yₜ = c + (1 + Σθⱼ·Bʲ)·εₜ, where B is the backshift, or lag, operator, p is how many past values, autoregressive terms, it uses, d is how many times the series is differenced to remove trend, and q is how many past forecast errors, moving-average terms, it uses. `ARIMA(series, order=(p,d,q)).fit()` fits one such model to one station's speed series. Exponential smoothing's simplest form forecasts ŷₜ₊₁ = α·yₜ + (1−α)·ŷₜ, where α between 0 and 1 controls how much weight the newest observation gets versus the previous forecast.

Both methods assume the series is, or can be made via differencing, stationary, its statistical properties like mean and variance don't change over time, an assumption traffic speed genuinely violates across a full day, rush hour looks nothing like 3 a.m., which is why these classical models need seasonal terms, SARIMA or seasonal exponential smoothing, to handle daily and weekly cycles explicitly. ARIMA's parameters are chosen by examining autocorrelation plots or by automated search minimizing AIC across candidate orders, and the fitted model assumes a linear relationship between a value and its own past, a real limitation for traffic, where that relationship changes shape entirely depending on whether the road is approaching or leaving congestion. This project uses ARIMA mainly as an early, interpretable baseline to calibrate expectations before moving to trees and neural models that use many stations' data jointly and capture nonlinearity.

One ARIMA model per series does not scale to a corridor of a hundred stations with real spatial dependence between them, a slowdown at one station is not independent of its neighbors, exactly the gap that motivates moving from per-series classical models to a single global model, LightGBM trained across all stations at once, or later a graph model, that can share statistical strength and learn spatial structure ARIMA has no way to represent. A subtlety practitioners often get wrong: ARIMA's forecast intervals rely on the assumed error distribution being correct and on the series genuinely being described by a linear process, so its stated uncertainty can be badly miscalibrated exactly during the nonlinear regime changes, onset of congestion, that matter most operationally. Exponential smoothing methods generalize into the broader class of state-space, ETS, models, which express the same weighted-average intuition in a probabilistic framework that also yields proper forecast intervals, a strictly more principled version of the simple formula.

In production forecasting systems handling many series at once, thousands of stations, products, or sensors, the field has largely moved from fitting one ARIMA per series toward global models, trained jointly across all series, sharing parameters and pooling statistical strength, whether gradient-boosted trees on lag features, this project's approach, or neural sequence models, because per-series classical fitting doesn't scale operationally and ignores cross-series structure a global model can exploit for free. ARIMA and exponential smoothing remain valuable as fast, robust, well-understood baselines and as components of hierarchical forecasting systems where classical per-series methods are blended with, or used to sanity-check, more complex learned models, particularly because their simplicity makes it easy to explain exactly why a given forecast came out the way it did, a property most learned global models lack.

terms.def: Stationarity means a time series' statistical properties stay the same over time; seasonality is a regular repeating pattern, like a daily rush hour, that strict stationarity actually rules out.
levels: If a merry-go-round always spins the exact same way no matter what day it is, that's stationary, always the same. But if it goes faster every morning at 8am and slower at night, every single day, that repeating pattern is seasonality.

A time series is stationary if its average, its spread, and its overall pattern stay the same no matter which stretch of time you look at. Traffic speed is not stationary in that strict sense, because it has seasonality, a repeating daily pattern, slow during rush hour and fast late at night, that happens over and over on a predictable schedule. Seasonality is actually useful, not a problem, since because the pattern repeats, you can use "what usually happens at this time of day" as a strong, free prediction to compare any new reading against.

Formally, a series is (weakly) stationary if its mean and variance don't depend on time and its autocorrelation depends only on the lag between two points, not on when those points occur, a condition that traffic speed clearly violates, since its mean at 8am rush hour is very different from its mean at 3am. Seasonality is a specific, regular repeating component of a time series, and this course handles it by computing a time-of-day, and sometimes day-of-week, baseline speed per station, then working with speed relative to that baseline (`ratio_ff`, speed relative to free flow) rather than raw speed, which effectively removes the daily seasonal pattern and leaves a series closer to stationary for modeling. Statistical tests like the augmented Dickey-Fuller test can formally check a series for stationarity, and models like ARIMA explicitly require or model a stationary series, often achieved by differencing, before their assumptions hold.

Stationarity matters because most classical time series theory, autocorrelation structure, standard confidence intervals, ARIMA's own assumptions, is derived under it, and applying those tools to a genuinely non-stationary series without first removing trend and seasonality, through differencing, or through seasonal decomposition, can produce badly miscalibrated inference, even though the resulting point predictions might look reasonable by coincidence. Seasonality can be modeled in multiple ways: explicitly, with dummy variables or Fourier terms for time of day and day of week; implicitly, by using a station's own historical baseline, a time-of-day profile, as a normalizing reference the way this course does; or left to a flexible model like a recurrent or graph network to discover from raw timestamps and recent history, at the cost of needing more data and offering less interpretability about what pattern it actually learned. Traffic data specifically has both daily and weekly seasonality, weekday commute patterns differ substantially from weekend patterns, plus irregular, non-seasonal effects, weather, incidents, holidays, that seasonality models don't capture and that a good pipeline has to handle separately, often as a "detect the anomaly relative to the seasonal baseline" step rather than folding it into the seasonal model itself. A common failure is fitting a strong seasonal model on a limited history and then extrapolating it confidently through a holiday or an unusual event, where the learned seasonal pattern simply doesn't apply.

A more general and honest treatment moves from strict stationarity, which almost no real process satisfies exactly, to characterizing the series' dependence structure directly, autocorrelation, effective sample size given that structure, and how estimator variance behaves under dependent rather than independent data, since even a series that looks "stationary enough" by eye can have long-range dependence that standard error estimates and cross-validation schemes assuming independence badly understate. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating seasonality removal as a solved preprocessing step rather than something whose own estimation error propagates downstream, since a time-of-day baseline estimated from a limited or unrepresentative training window, say, a period without much roadwork, carries its own uncertainty that a model trained on the resulting "deseasonalized" ratio inherits, often silently. Traffic seasonality also isn't fixed forever, since it drifts slowly with changing commute patterns, remote work trends, or new infrastructure, which means a "stationary after removing seasonality" assumption itself has a shelf life, and this is one of the concrete reasons the course monitors feature and prediction distributions over time, via the population stability index, rather than assuming the seasonal correction, once fit, stays valid indefinitely. The interaction between seasonality and rare events is also easy to get backward, since because slow-traffic events cluster at predictable seasonal times, rush hour, a model can appear to perform well largely by having learned the seasonal baseline rather than genuinely predicting the excess, harder-to-forecast deviation from it; separating "predicting the known seasonal pattern" from "predicting the surprise on top of it" is where the real modeling difficulty, and the real value, actually lives.

At production scale, seasonality and its slow drift are treated as a first-class, continuously re-estimated component of the pipeline rather than a one-time preprocessing choice, since holidays, daylight saving transitions, school calendars and long-term commute-pattern shifts, like post-pandemic hybrid work, all change the seasonal baseline in ways that need to be tracked and periodically refit, not assumed fixed at training time. Modern spatiotemporal forecasting architectures, graph neural networks, temporal transformers, increasingly learn seasonal structure implicitly from raw timestamps and history rather than relying on hand-specified Fourier or dummy-variable seasonal terms, trading interpretability of the seasonal component for flexibility and reduced manual feature engineering. An open research question is how to build models that adapt smoothly to genuine, slow, non-seasonal drift in what looks like a seasonal pattern, distinguishing "this is an unusual Tuesday" from "Tuesdays have permanently changed," without either overreacting to every anomaly or underreacting to real, lasting shifts.

terms.def: The simplest forecast — predicting the next value equals the most recent one — and the baseline any real model must beat.
levels: A persistence forecast is like guessing that tomorrow's weather will be exactly like today's, because that's often a pretty good guess even without thinking hard about it. It's the simplest possible guess, and any smarter guess needs to beat it to be worth the trouble.

A persistence forecast just predicts that things will stay the same: the traffic speed 30 minutes from now will be whatever it is right now, or whatever it's been recently. It sounds too simple to be useful, but because traffic (and weather, and lots of things) tends to change slowly, this simple guess is often surprisingly hard to beat. It's used as a baseline: before trusting a fancier model, you check whether it actually does better than just assuming nothing changes.

A persistence forecast predicts ŷₜ₊ₕ = yₜ, using the most recently observed value as the prediction for h steps ahead, with no model fitting at all. For traffic prediction specifically, persistence is a strong baseline because traffic speed is highly autocorrelated over short horizons — the state 5 or 10 minutes from now is usually very close to the current state, so any model claiming skill has to demonstrably beat this trivial forecast, not just outperform random guessing. A model that only marginally beats persistence at a short horizon, or fails to beat it at all at a longer horizon, is telling you something important: either the problem is genuinely hard at that horizon, or the model has a bug. In this course, every predictive model's reported metric is compared directly against a persistence baseline computed the same way, on the same data, so the comparison is fair.

Persistence is the correct baseline for any time series prediction problem precisely because it captures a huge fraction of the predictable signal for free, through autocorrelation alone, without any actual modeling — a fancier model's value proposition is exactly the gap it opens up over persistence, not its absolute score. This matters especially for choosing a horizon: skill relative to persistence typically degrades as the prediction horizon grows, since autocorrelation weakens over longer time gaps, so persistence itself gets worse at longer horizons too, and a model's real contribution is best measured as the gap between the model's score and persistence's score at each horizon separately, not a single number averaged across horizons. A slightly stronger baseline variant, seasonal persistence (predicting the value from the same time of day last week, rather than the most recent value), controls for daily and weekly patterns and is a fairer comparison than plain persistence when the target itself has strong daily seasonality, as traffic speed does. Reporting a model's raw metric without a persistence baseline alongside it is a common presentation mistake, since a metric in isolation gives no sense of how much of the apparent 'skill' the model has actually earned versus how much is just the easy, autocorrelation-driven part any naive forecast would also capture.

Persistence baselines expose a subtlety in how forecast horizons should be evaluated: comparing a model's absolute error across different horizons is somewhat misleading, since longer horizons are intrinsically harder (persistence itself degrades), so the more meaningful comparison is skill relative to persistence at each horizon — a model with high absolute error at 60 minutes might still represent more genuine skill (more improvement over its much worse persistence baseline) than a model with low absolute error at 5 minutes, where persistence was already nearly optimal. A subtlety practitioners get wrong: persistence is not always the strongest trivial baseline — for strongly periodic signals, seasonal persistence or a simple moving average can beat plain persistence, and failing to check the strongest available naive baseline (not just the easiest one to implement) can make a real model look more impressive than it actually is. There is also a research-methodology point worth making: many published forecasting papers, across domains, have historically failed to include a persistence or seasonal-naive baseline at all, which has led to inflated claims of model skill that later, more careful benchmarking work walked back once naive baselines were properly included — this is a known, recurring pattern in the forecasting literature, not just a hypothetical risk.

In production traffic and forecasting systems, persistence (or a slightly more sophisticated seasonal-naive variant) is typically kept running permanently, not just as a development-time sanity check, as a fallback predictor for situations where the primary model's confidence is low, its inputs are stale or missing, or it is being rolled back — because a simple, well-understood baseline that degrades predictably is often preferable to a complex model failing unpredictably. An open, recurring engineering question at scale is exactly how to define the 'current' state that a persistence baseline conditions on when the real-time data feed itself is noisy, delayed, or partially missing, since a naive baseline computed on stale or wrong data no longer serves its purpose as a meaningful comparison point, and this quietly undermines confidence in the very metric it's meant to validate.

terms.def: A curve plotting true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the threshold moves; its area (AUC) summarizes ranking quality but looks flattering under imbalance.
levels: Imagine trying every possible worry-level for ringing an alarm bell, from always ring it to never ring it, and drawing a picture of how often you are right versus wrong at each setting. That picture is the ROC curve.

ROC stands for receiver operating characteristic, a curve that plots how many real positives you catch against how many false alarms you raise, as you slide the alert threshold from very cautious to very trigger-happy. AUC, area under the curve, is a single number, between 0.5, no better than guessing, and 1.0, perfect, summarizing that whole curve into one score. ROC-AUC is a common way to grade a classifier, alongside precision, recall, and F1.

The ROC curve plots the true positive rate, recall, on one axis against the false positive rate on the other, at every possible threshold, so it traces how the tradeoff between catching real positives and raising false alarms changes as the threshold moves. AUC, the area under that curve, is a single summary score between 0.5 and 1.0 that does not require picking any one threshold, and it has a clean interpretation: it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive example gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. In this course, scikit-learn's tools compute ROC-AUC alongside the precision-recall curve and average precision, but average precision, not ROC-AUC, is treated as the headline metric.

ROC-AUC's key mathematical property, that it depends only on the relative ranking of scores, not the actual predicted probabilities, and is computed from rates rather than counts, is exactly what makes it look deceptively good under severe class imbalance: because true negatives vastly outnumber positives in an imbalanced problem like slow-traffic prediction, with a five percent positive rate, the false positive rate stays low even when a model makes many false alarms in absolute count, since those false alarms are a small fraction of the huge negative population. The precision-recall curve and its area, average precision, instead directly track precision, what fraction of alarms are correct, which does not get inflated by a huge negative class the way the false positive rate does, which is why this course prefers average precision as the metric that actually reflects operational usefulness for a rare-event alerting problem. ROC-AUC remains useful and standard in balanced or moderately imbalanced problems, and as a ranking-quality check independent of any particular threshold, but reporting it alone on a severely imbalanced problem without also reporting precision-recall metrics risks a misleadingly rosy picture.

A subtlety practitioners frequently get wrong is treating ROC-AUC as a threshold-free, always-appropriate summary simply because it is standard, without asking whether the two error types it balances actually reflect the real operational cost structure; for an alerting system where false alarms directly cost trust while missed jams cost something different, a metric built around the actual decision, precision at a required recall, is more honest than a threshold-free ranking summary that never confronts the actual operating point that will be deployed. There is also a statistical subtlety: ROC-AUC has a known, elegant nonparametric interpretation, the Mann-Whitney U statistic, that makes it attractive for comparing models' ranking ability in a way that is somewhat robust to class balance shifts between training and deployment, a property average precision does not share as cleanly, since AP's absolute value is itself sensitive to the positive rate. Reporting both, ROC-AUC for a class-balance-robust ranking check and average precision for an operationally meaningful summary under the true imbalance, rather than picking one, is the practice more careful teams follow, even though this course deliberately emphasizes only average precision as its headline number.

In production systems facing severe class imbalance, fraud detection, rare medical events, rare traffic incidents, ROC-AUC is often reported alongside precision-recall metrics specifically because stakeholders unfamiliar with the imbalance pitfall default to asking for the AUC, and a model comparison based on ROC-AUC alone can rank two models in the opposite order from what precision-recall-based metrics would show, a discrepancy worth surfacing explicitly rather than silently picking whichever metric favors the preferred model. An open measurement question at scale is how to make ROC-AUC and precision-recall-based comparisons robust to positive-rate drift between training, validation, and live deployment, since a model's AUC can look stable while its live precision at a fixed threshold degrades sharply if the true prevalence of positives shifts after deployment, exactly the kind of silent metric-versus-reality gap a monitoring system built only around AUC would miss.

terms.def: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, a single number balancing both when neither alone tells the full story.
levels: F1 is a fairness score for guessing games: it checks both whether your 'yes' guesses were actually right, and whether you found most of the real yeses, and mixes those two report cards into one grade.

Precision measures, out of everything the model called 'slow,' how many actually were slow. Recall measures, out of everything that was actually slow, how many the model caught. F1 score combines both into one number using their harmonic mean, which only gives a high F1 if both precision and recall are reasonably good, a model that is great at one but terrible at the other still scores poorly. It's especially useful when the two classes, slow versus not slow, are imbalanced, since accuracy alone can be misleading in that case.

Precision = TP/(TP+FP), the fraction of predicted-slow rows that were truly slow; recall = TP/(TP+FN), the fraction of truly-slow rows the model caught, where TP, FP and FN are true positives, false positives and false negatives from the confusion matrix. F1 = 2 · (precision · recall)/(precision + recall), the harmonic mean rather than the plain average, which punishes a big imbalance between the two more severely than a simple average would, a model with precision 0.9 and recall 0.1 gets an F1 near 0.18, not 0.5. `sklearn.metrics.f1_score(y_true, y_pred)` computes it directly from predicted labels, and `classification_report` reports precision, recall and F1 together.

The harmonic mean is chosen over the arithmetic mean specifically because it is dominated by the smaller of the two values, which matches the intuition that a model doing very well on one metric and very poorly on the other should not get credit as if it were doing moderately well on both. F1 requires converting probabilistic predictions into hard labels via a threshold, so it inherits whatever threshold is chosen, the same model can have very different F1 scores at different thresholds, which means comparing F1 across models trained or thresholded differently can be misleading unless the threshold is chosen consistently or the comparison uses a threshold-free metric like average precision instead. The standard F1 weights precision and recall equally, but the F-beta score generalizes this with a parameter beta that weights recall beta times as much as precision, which matters in a domain like traffic alerting where missing a real slowdown, a false negative, might be considered worse than a false alarm, or the reverse, depending on what the alert triggers downstream. F1 says nothing about calibration or about the negative class's performance in isolation, so it should be reported alongside, not instead of, a fuller picture like the full confusion matrix or a precision-recall curve.

F1's threshold-dependence is a genuine limitation for model comparison during development, which is why average precision, the area under the precision-recall curve, summarizing performance across all thresholds at once, is often preferred for comparing models before a specific operating threshold has been chosen for deployment, with F1 computed only after that threshold is fixed for a final, concrete evaluation. Micro-averaged and macro-averaged F1 differ substantially in multi-class or multi-label settings: micro-averaging pools all true and false positives and negatives across classes before computing F1, effectively weighting by class frequency, while macro-averaging computes F1 per class and then averages unweighted, which can give a very different, and sometimes more informative, picture when classes are imbalanced, reporting only one without specifying which is a common and misleading omission in papers and reports. F1 treats false positives and false negatives as equally costly by construction, an assumption that is essentially never actually true in a real deployed system, where the operational cost of a missed slowdown alert and a false alarm are almost never symmetric, making F1 more of a convenient development-time proxy than a metric that should directly drive a production threshold decision. Optimizing a model or threshold directly for F1 on a validation set, rather than as a byproduct of optimizing calibration and then choosing a threshold from cost considerations, can produce a model that games the specific validation set's class balance rather than one that is robust to real-world shifts in that balance.

In production systems, teams increasingly move away from single scalar metrics like F1 as the primary target and instead define an explicit cost matrix, the real operational cost of each error type, from which an optimal threshold is derived analytically, using F1 mainly as a sanity check or a convenient number for dashboards and cross-team communication rather than the actual optimization target. F1 and related classification metrics also assume a static, known label definition, which becomes genuinely complicated at scale when the definition of the positive class itself evolves, what counts as 'slow' might be redefined as road geometry or typical speeds change over years, requiring careful metric versioning alongside model versioning. An open measurement challenge, especially for a rare-event problem like traffic slowdowns, is evaluating F1 or any threshold-based metric reliably when positive examples are scarce, since the metric's variance under resampling can be large enough that small reported differences between models are not actually statistically meaningful.

terms.def: A table showing how many predictions were correct or wrong, broken down by predicted class versus actual class.
levels: Imagine a chart with four boxes: times you correctly said yes, times you correctly said no, and the two kinds of times you got it wrong. A confusion matrix is exactly that chart, counting up how the model's guesses compared to what actually happened.

A confusion matrix is a small table that shows how a model's predictions compare to the real answers. For a yes or no prediction, it has four boxes: correct yes predictions, true positives, correct no predictions, true negatives, wrong yes predictions when it was actually no, false positives, and wrong no predictions when it was actually yes, false negatives. Looking at these four numbers together tells you a lot more about a model's mistakes than a single percent-correct score would.

For binary classification, the confusion matrix is a 2 by 2 table: true positives, predicted slow and actually slow, false positives, predicted slow but actually not, false negatives, predicted not slow but actually was, and true negatives, predicted not slow and actually not. In scikit-learn, `confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)` computes it directly from the true labels and the model's predicted labels. From these four counts you compute precision, true positives divided by true positives plus false positives, how often a slow prediction was right, and recall, true positives divided by true positives plus false negatives, how much of the real slow traffic the model actually caught.

The confusion matrix requires a classification threshold to exist at all; it is computed from hard predicted labels, 0 or 1, not raw probabilities, so it summarizes the model's behavior at one specific operating point, and a different threshold produces a different confusion matrix from the exact same underlying probabilities. Every standard classification metric, precision, recall, F1, specificity, false positive rate, is a simple ratio computed from the matrix's four cells, which is why the confusion matrix is often described as the source data behind nearly every other binary classification metric. It becomes especially informative, and especially necessary, under class imbalance: with rare slow episodes, a model that always predicts not slow achieves very high accuracy while its confusion matrix immediately reveals zero true positives and zero recall, exposing a failure that accuracy alone hides. It fails to summarize model quality across the full range of possible thresholds on its own, since it is a snapshot at one threshold; a precision-recall curve or ROC curve instead shows how the matrix's implied metrics change as the threshold varies.

Precision and recall trade off against each other as the threshold moves, and which one to prioritize is a decision about the real-world cost of each error type; for a slow-traffic alert system, missing a real slow episode, a false negative, may be far more costly than a false alarm, a false positive, which argues for choosing a lower threshold and accepting more false positives, a decision the confusion matrix alone cannot make but directly informs. Confusion matrices generalize to multi-class problems as an n by n table, where off-diagonal cells show specifically which classes get confused with which others, more diagnostically useful than a single accuracy number for understanding a multi-class model's specific failure modes. A common misconception is treating precision and recall as properties of the model itself, when they are really properties of the model at a chosen threshold; reporting them without stating the threshold, or comparing two models' precision and recall at different, unstated thresholds, is a subtle but real source of misleading comparisons. Normalized confusion matrices, showing rates rather than raw counts, per true class or per predicted class, are often more useful than raw counts for imbalanced data, since raw counts on the majority class can visually dwarf the minority class's counts even when the minority class's error rate is the one that actually matters.

In production monitoring, confusion matrices, and the metrics derived from them, are tracked continuously per-segment, per station, per time of day, per region, rather than as a single aggregate number, because a model with acceptable overall precision and recall can still perform badly for a specific slice of the population, and aggregate metrics hide that the way accuracy hides class imbalance. Threshold selection in production is typically not fixed once at training time but tuned or re-tuned against the confusion matrix computed on recent live data, since the right operating point can drift as the underlying distribution of traffic patterns shifts over time, seasonal changes, new construction, altered commute patterns. An open practical challenge is building monitoring systems that can detect a meaningful degradation in one cell of the confusion matrix, say, a rising false-negative rate for a specific corridor, quickly enough to act on it, without either drowning in noisy per-slice metrics or missing a real regression by only watching the aggregate numbers.

terms.def: A plot comparing a model's predicted probabilities against the actual observed frequency of the outcome, showing whether the model is well calibrated.
levels: Imagine you have a friend who says I'm 90 percent sure it'll rain a bunch of different days, and you check: did it actually rain about 9 times out of 10 when they said that? A reliability diagram is a picture that checks exactly that, for a computer's guesses instead of a friend's.

A reliability diagram is a chart that checks whether a model's probabilities can be trusted. You group all the times the model said something like 80 percent chance of slow traffic, and then check what fraction of those times traffic was actually slow. If the model is well calibrated, its 80 percent predictions should come true about 80 percent of the time, and the chart's dots should sit close to a diagonal line. Dots that stray far from that line show the model is overconfident or underconfident in that range.

A reliability diagram bins predicted probabilities, often into ten bins, 0 to 10 percent, 10 to 20 percent, and so on, and, for each bin, plots the average predicted probability against the observed frequency of the positive outcome within that bin. A perfectly calibrated model produces points lying exactly on the diagonal line; points below the diagonal at high predicted probability mean the model is overconfident, it says 90 percent but the true rate is lower, while points above the diagonal mean it is underconfident. For Traffic1's slow-traffic classifier, a reliability diagram checks whether the model saying 70 percent chance of slow traffic really does correspond to slow traffic about 70 percent of the time across all such predictions, which matters if the probability itself, not just the classification, is what a downstream system relies on. Reliability diagrams are typically drawn alongside a summary statistic like the expected calibration error, a single number averaging the gap between predicted and observed probability across bins.

A reliability diagram visualizes calibration, which is a distinct property from discrimination, how well the model separates positive from negative cases, as measured by AUC, a model can have excellent discrimination but poor calibration, or vice versa, so the two need to be checked separately rather than assuming a high AUC implies trustworthy probabilities.
