Bin choice matters and introduces a bias-variance tradeoff of its own: too many bins gives a noisy, hard-to-read diagram, while too few bins can hide genuine miscalibration within a bin that spans a wide probability range. Common fixes for a miscalibrated model include Platt scaling and temperature scaling, both fit on a held-out calibration set separate from training data, and both generally cheaper and simpler than retraining the underlying model. Reliability diagrams are especially important whenever a probability itself will be acted on downstream, rather than just a thresholded decision, for instance, if Traffic1's slow-traffic probability feeds into a routing system's expected-delay calculation, a miscalibrated probability biases that downstream calculation even if the classifier's accuracy or AUC looks fine.

Expected calibration error as a summary statistic has known weaknesses, it is sensitive to bin choice and boundary placement in ways that can make two genuinely different models appear similarly calibrated or vice versa, which has motivated alternative metrics that are less sensitive to these arbitrary choices. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is checking calibration only in aggregate and missing calibration failures specific to a subgroup, a model can be well calibrated overall while being systematically overconfident for one freeway or one time of day, which a single reliability diagram over all predictions would not reveal, calling for stratified reliability diagrams across meaningful subgroups. Calibration and class imbalance interact in a way that is easy to get wrong: with a rare positive class, calibration bins near the high-probability end can have very few examples, making the observed frequency in that bin a high-variance, unreliable estimate even when the model's true calibration is fine, bootstrap confidence bands on each bin's observed frequency help distinguish real miscalibration from bin-level noise. Calibration under distribution shift is a genuinely hard, unsolved-in-general problem: a model calibrated on validation data can become miscalibrated on live data purely because the underlying distribution shifted, even with no change to the model itself, and detecting this requires ongoing monitoring rather than a one-time reliability diagram check.

In production, reliability diagrams, or their summary statistics, are typically computed continuously on live traffic as part of a monitoring dashboard, because a model's calibration can degrade between retrains even while its discrimination stays roughly stable, and calibration drift is often a leading indicator of distribution shift before accuracy metrics move enough to trigger alarm. At Apple's scale, calibration matters especially for any system where a probability feeds a downstream decision with its own cost structure, since a systematically miscalibrated probability biases every decision built on it in a consistent direction, which is harder to notice than a random accuracy drop and can persist unnoticed for a long time if only discrimination metrics are monitored. An open research and engineering question is building calibration monitoring and correction that adapts automatically and safely to distribution shift in near-real time, without requiring a full recalibration pipeline to be manually triggered every time conditions change, while still being robust to short-term noise that should not trigger unnecessary recalibration.

terms.def: Three ways to score how wrong a numeric prediction is: mean absolute error, root mean squared error, and mean absolute percent error.
levels: MAE, RMSE and MAPE are three different ways of scoring how far off a guess was from the real answer, kind of like three different report cards for the same test. MAE just adds up how far off you were, on average, ignoring whether you guessed too high or too low. RMSE is a report card that is extra strict about really big mistakes. MAPE grades you as a percentage instead of a plain number, which makes it easier to compare very different kinds of guesses.

MAE, RMSE and MAPE are three ways to measure how wrong a model's numeric predictions are, on average, across many examples. MAE (mean absolute error) takes the average of how far off each prediction was, ignoring the direction of the error, and stays in the same units as the data, like mph. RMSE (root mean squared error) squares each error before averaging and then takes the square root, which makes big mistakes count much more than small ones. MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) expresses the average error as a percentage of the true value, which makes it easier to compare errors across very different scales, but it breaks down when the true value is zero, since you cannot divide by zero.

MAE = (1/n)·Σ|yᵢ − ŷᵢ|, the average absolute difference between predicted and true values, reported in the same units as the target, like mph for a speed prediction. RMSE = √[(1/n)·Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²], which squares errors before averaging, so a few large mistakes inflate RMSE more than they inflate MAE, making RMSE more sensitive to outliers. MAPE = (100/n)·Σ|((yᵢ − ŷᵢ)/yᵢ)|, expressed as a percentage, is useful for comparing prediction accuracy across stations with very different typical speeds, but is undefined (division by zero) whenever the true value yᵢ is exactly zero, which matters for a target like speed drop that can legitimately hit zero. `sklearn.metrics.mean_absolute_error` and `mean_squared_error` (with `squared=False` for RMSE) compute these directly in code, and this course's evaluation reports MAE against the persistence and profile baselines whenever it trains a model to predict a numeric target like speed 30 minutes out.

MAE corresponds to the loss whose minimizer is the conditional median of the target given the features, while RMSE (through its underlying squared error) corresponds to the loss minimized by the conditional mean, so choosing between them is implicitly choosing which central tendency the model is being optimized to predict, a distinction that matters when a target's distribution is skewed, like traffic delay durations with a long tail of unusually slow episodes. RMSE's extra sensitivity to large errors is a double-edged property: it correctly penalizes a model that makes occasional very bad predictions more than MAE does, but it also makes RMSE more sensitive to a small number of outlier or mislabeled data points that may not represent genuine model weakness, so RMSE and MAE reported together, rather than either alone, give a fuller picture of an error distribution's shape. MAPE's asymmetry is a real and often underappreciated flaw: because it divides by the true value, MAPE penalizes overprediction (predicting too high) less severely than underprediction (predicting too low) when the true value is small, systematically biasing a MAPE-optimized model toward overprediction in low-value regions, which is part of why symmetric variants (sMAPE) exist, though they introduce their own interpretability tradeoffs. R² (the fraction of variance in the target explained by the model, relative to always predicting the mean) is a fourth commonly reported metric alongside these three, and unlike MAE, RMSE and MAPE, which are all in either the target's units or a percentage, R² is unitless and therefore easier to compare across genuinely different prediction problems, at the cost of being harder to interpret in terms of the target's own real-world scale.

The choice between MAE and RMSE as an optimization target, not just an evaluation metric, has real consequences: training a model to minimize squared error (as most default regression losses do) optimizes for the conditional mean and is disproportionately influenced by rare, extreme values during training itself, not just at evaluation time, so a model trained with squared error can end up systematically biased if the extreme values are partly noise rather than genuine signal, whereas training with an absolute-error-based loss is more robust to exactly that kind of contamination but yields a less smooth optimization surface that some gradient-based methods handle less gracefully. Practitioners frequently misuse MAPE as a universal metric for comparing model quality across very different problems or datasets without checking how close to zero the target values get, silently producing wildly inflated or undefined MAPE values that get quietly excluded or clipped in ways that are rarely disclosed and can meaningfully distort a reported comparison. A subtler issue is that none of these three metrics accounts for whether errors are concentrated in operationally important regions of the target space; a model can have excellent MAE overall while being specifically bad at predicting the low-speed, congested regime that matters most for a traffic-slowdown application, which is why this course pairs regression metrics with the classification-style metrics (AP, lead time, false alarm rate) that speak directly to the slow-episode use case rather than trusting a single aggregate regression number. Reporting any of these metrics without a baseline (persistence, profile) alongside them makes the number essentially uninterpretable, since 'MAE of 4.2 mph' has no inherent meaning without knowing what MAE a trivial forecast would already achieve.

In production forecasting systems, MAE and RMSE (and their weighted or business-adjusted variants) are typically tracked continuously in monitoring dashboards rather than computed once at training time, specifically because a model's real-world error distribution can drift meaningfully after deployment even when nothing about the model itself has changed, so ongoing measurement, not a single offline evaluation, is what production teams actually rely on. Apple-scale forecasting and demand-prediction systems commonly use business-weighted variants of these metrics (weighting errors by their operational cost, rather than treating every unit of error identically) precisely because a raw MAE treats a 5 mph error during free-flow traffic the same as a 5 mph error right at the threshold of a slow episode, when the latter is far more consequential for anyone actually acting on the prediction. An open engineering practice, still inconsistently applied industry-wide, is designing evaluation metrics that are explicitly aligned with downstream decision costs from the start, rather than defaulting to MAE, RMSE or MAPE purely because they are standard and easy to compute, since the standard metrics' popularity reflects their mathematical convenience more than any guarantee that they measure what a given deployment actually needs.

terms.def: Pinball loss trains a model to predict one quantile, penalizing over- and under-prediction unevenly; Huber loss trains a robust regression, quadratic near zero and linear beyond a threshold.
levels: Pinball loss is like a game where guessing too high costs you a little and guessing too low costs you a little too, but by different amounts depending on which quantile you're aiming for. Huber loss is a referee who's gentle about a small mistake but only a little more upset, not a lot more, about a really big one.

The pinball loss trains a model to predict a specific quantile, like the 90th percentile of possible speeds, rather than just the average: it punishes an underestimate more than an overestimate when you're aiming for a high quantile, and the reverse for a low one. Huber loss is used for ordinary regression, and it acts like squared error for small mistakes, punishing them gently, but switches to acting like absolute-value error for large mistakes, so one huge outlier doesn't dominate training the way it would with pure squared error.

The pinball loss for quantile τ, a number between 0 and 1, is L_τ(y, ŷ) = τ·(y − ŷ) if y ≥ ŷ, and (1−τ)·(ŷ − y) if y < ŷ; setting τ = 0.9 means underpredicting costs 9 times more than overpredicting by the same amount, pushing the fitted value toward the 90th percentile rather than the mean. Huber loss is L(y, ŷ) = ½(y−ŷ)² if |y−ŷ| ≤ δ, and δ·(|y−ŷ| − ½δ) otherwise, where δ is a chosen threshold; it behaves like squared error for small errors and like absolute error, which grows more slowly, past that threshold. `objective='quantile', alpha=0.9` fits pinball loss at the 90th percentile in LightGBM; `objective='huber'` fits Huber loss.

Fitting several quantile models, say at 0.1, 0.5, 0.9, with the pinball loss gives a prediction interval without assuming any particular error distribution, more flexible than assuming Gaussian noise and computing an interval from a variance estimate, but it comes with a real failure mode called quantile crossing: because each quantile is fit as a separate model, nothing forces the 90th-percentile prediction to be above the 10th-percentile prediction for the same row, and on real data it sometimes isn't, needing post-hoc sorting or a joint model to fix. Huber loss's threshold δ is itself a hyperparameter controlling the tradeoff it embodies: a small δ behaves closer to purely robust absolute-error loss, barely influenced by outliers but less statistically efficient under Gaussian noise, while a large δ behaves closer to plain squared error, efficient under Gaussian noise but sensitive to outliers. Both losses assume the model underneath, a tree, a linear model, can flexibly enough approximate the true conditional quantile or robust mean; a badly misspecified model can't be fixed by choosing a better loss alone.

The pinball loss is a proper scoring rule for the quantile it targets, meaning its expected value is minimized exactly at the true conditional quantile, the formal justification for why minimizing it with enough data and a flexible-enough model recovers real quantiles rather than a biased approximation; this is the theoretical backbone for using gradient-boosted quantile regression as an alternative to a probability-output classifier here, regressing the speed ratio with pinball loss and deriving probabilities from the resulting quantiles avoids the label-definition brittleness of the fixed three-step-run label. Huber loss connects to M-estimation in classical robust statistics, where δ controls the estimator's breakdown point and efficiency tradeoff precisely; practitioners commonly pick δ by a rule of thumb, a multiple of the residual's median absolute deviation, rather than tuning it, which can leave real efficiency on the table if the actual noise distribution differs from what the default assumes. A subtlety often missed: fitting multiple separate quantile pinball-loss models is statistically less efficient than a joint model that shares information across quantiles, especially with limited data in the tails, since each separate model wastes information the other quantiles carry about the same conditional distribution.

In production systems that need calibrated uncertainty rather than a single point prediction, arrival-time estimates, capacity planning, or this project's own alternative framing of predicting a full speed distribution rather than a binary label, quantile and pinball-loss-based models are standard, and quantile crossing is handled either by architectures that guarantee monotonicity by construction or by treating it as a diagnostic signal that flags rows where the model's uncertainty estimate is unreliable. Huber loss and its variants remain the default robust-regression choice in production regression heads specifically because outlier-heavy real-world targets, a sensor glitch reporting an impossible travel time, are common enough that pure squared-error loss would let a small number of bad rows dominate training; an open research thread is adaptively setting δ per-batch or per-region of the input space rather than as one fixed global hyperparameter, since the right level of robustness genuinely differs across a large, heterogeneous production dataset.

terms.def: The speed traffic moves at when the road isn't congested, close to the speed limit with cars spaced out and unaffected by other traffic.
levels: Free flow is when the road is wide open and cars can just zoom along at their normal speed, nobody stuck behind anybody else.

Free flow is what traffic looks like when the road isn't crowded: cars driving at close to the speed limit, spaced comfortably apart, not slowed down by other vehicles. Each freeway station has its own typical free-flow speed, and this course uses that as a baseline: instead of just looking at a station's raw speed, it looks at how much slower than free flow the current speed is, which tells you much more directly whether traffic is actually congested.

A station's free-flow speed is best measured as its 85th percentile speed rather than its median or mean, because using the 85th percentile focuses on how fast traffic moves when it's genuinely uncongested, while a median can be pulled down by ordinary daily slowdowns that aren't full jams. This course computes `ratio_ff` by merging each row with its station's free-flow speed and dividing current speed by it, so a `ratio_ff` near 1.0 means traffic is moving normally and a `ratio_ff` well below 1.0 signals real congestion, in a way that's comparable across stations with very different speed limits.

Free-flow speed is a station-specific, roughly time-invariant physical quantity, bounded above by the road's design speed and speed limit, that serves as the natural reference point for defining congestion relatively rather than absolutely: a raw speed of 45 mph is a jam on a 65 mph freeway segment and completely normal on a 50 mph urban stretch, so any absolute-speed threshold for "slow" would need per-station tuning that a relative measure like `ratio_ff` avoids automatically. Estimating free-flow speed well requires care: using a simple average across all times of day underestimates it, since it's pulled down by routine peak-hour slowdowns, which is exactly why a high percentile, like the 85th, of the observed speed distribution is preferred, as it approximates the speed the road supports when genuinely unimpeded by other traffic. Free-flow speed can also drift slowly over time, construction, a new merge lane, a permanent capacity change, so a station's free-flow baseline estimated once during training can become stale and needs periodic re-estimation, similar to how time-of-day seasonal baselines need refreshing. The measure fails at stations with too little free-flow-condition data to begin with, since a chronically congested urban segment that's rarely genuinely free-flowing at any time of day makes the 85th-percentile estimate itself noisy and possibly not representative of true unimpeded capacity.

The fundamental diagram of traffic flow places free flow at the low-occupancy end of the flow-occupancy relationship, where speed is roughly constant and near the road's design speed as occupancy rises from very low levels, before crossing a critical occupancy point where flow peaks and speed begins dropping sharply as congestion sets in; free-flow speed is essentially the flat, high-speed segment of that curve, and estimating it well means correctly identifying which observations actually lie on that segment rather than already sliding down the congested side. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is treating `ratio_ff` as a clean, universal congestion measure without accounting for the fact that different road geometries, a merge area, a lane drop, a steep grade, have systematically different free-flow characteristics and different sensitivities to the same absolute drop in speed, so a `ratio_ff` of 0.7 doesn't necessarily mean the same operational severity at every station. Free-flow speed estimation also interacts with detector reliability, since a station with intermittent outages during exactly its free-flow periods, say, if certain sensor faults correlate with light traffic and off-peak hours, will have a free-flow estimate biased by whichever subset of readings happened to be reliable, which is a subtle form of selection bias that's easy to miss without explicitly checking for it. Because free-flow speed is estimated from historical data and then used as a fixed reference for a subsequent, evolving relative measure, there's a real question of how often to re-estimate it, since too rarely and it goes stale as road conditions change, too often and each re-estimate risks incorporating recent congestion into what should be an uncongested baseline.

At production scale, free-flow speed estimation is usually maintained as a continuously updated, per-segment reference rather than a fixed value computed once at training time, since infrastructure changes, new lanes, altered ramp metering, construction, shift true free-flow capacity in ways a stale baseline would misrepresent as a change in congestion rather than a change in the road itself. More sophisticated systems estimate free-flow conditions jointly across a network of correlated segments, using graph structure to borrow strength between a station with sparse genuinely-free-flow observations and its well-observed neighbors, rather than estimating each station's baseline in complete isolation. An open question in traffic modeling more broadly is how to define and estimate a meaningful "capacity" or "free-flow" reference for road segments whose behavior is increasingly shaped by non-stationary factors like autonomous or connected vehicles altering following behavior, where historical free-flow speed may no longer be the right target reference at all.

terms.def: Fitting a model again on newer data, on a schedule or when performance drops, so it keeps matching how the world is currently behaving.
levels: The world keeps changing, so a model that learned from old traffic patterns can go stale, like an old map that doesn't show a new road. Retraining is teaching the model again using newer information, so it stays up to date.

Retraining means running the training process again, usually on newer data, so a model keeps up with changes in the real world instead of getting stuck with what it learned once, months or years ago. Traffic patterns shift — new roads open, work habits change, seasons change driving patterns — so a traffic model trained once and never updated slowly gets less accurate. Retraining can happen on a schedule, like once a month, or be triggered when a model's accuracy is seen to be dropping.

Retraining re-runs the full model-fitting process on an updated training set, typically extending the historical window forward to include recent data, either on a fixed schedule (weekly, monthly) or triggered by detected performance degradation. A retraining pipeline needs the exact same feature computation, cleaning, and label definition used originally, run automatically and consistently, or the new model can end up trained on subtly different, incompatible data than the one it replaces. Retraining is distinct from fine-tuning, which starts from an existing model's parameters and updates them with new data rather than fitting from scratch; both are ways of keeping a model current, but they have different costs and different risks of forgetting older patterns. In this course's project, retraining a station-level traffic model on new months of PeMS data should not require redefining what 'slow' means or rebuilding the whole pipeline, which is why the label and feature definitions are designed to generalize across time and across stations rather than being retuned by hand each time.

Deciding when to retrain is a genuine tradeoff: retraining too rarely lets a model drift out of sync with a changing world (concept drift, where the relationship between features and the label itself changes, not just the input distribution), while retraining too often is expensive, adds operational risk (a newly retrained model can be worse, not better, if the new data window is anomalous or a bug crept into the pipeline), and can make model behavior less stable and harder to debug from one version to the next. A well-designed retraining pipeline validates a new model against the same held-out evaluation and against the previous production model before it is promoted, treating a retrain as a candidate to be tested, not an automatic replacement — this is the same discipline as any model deployment, just recurring on a schedule rather than a one-off event. Warm-starting (initializing training from the previous model's parameters rather than from scratch) can make retraining faster and sometimes more stable, particularly for gradient-boosted trees and neural networks, though it also risks anchoring the new model too close to old patterns if the underlying distribution has genuinely shifted and a fresh fit would serve better. Retraining frequency should generally be informed by evidence of actual drift (a monitored performance metric declining, or a statistical drift detector flagging the input distribution has changed) rather than an arbitrary calendar interval chosen without data.

The theoretically cleanest trigger for retraining is detected performance degradation on live outcomes, but this creates a circular practical problem: in many deployed settings, true labels for recent predictions are not available immediately, sometimes not for weeks (a slowdown's ground truth exists as soon as the window passes, but confirming a broader shift in accuracy needs enough recent labeled data to be statistically meaningful), so retraining triggers often rely on proxy signals — input distribution drift, prediction distribution drift — that correlate with but do not guarantee actual performance decline. A subtlety practitioners get wrong: retraining on a sliding window that always drops the oldest data can quietly erase a model's ability to handle rare but recurring conditions (a specific kind of severe congestion pattern that only shows up a few times a year), so retraining strategy interacts with how much historical diversity, not just recency, the training window is designed to preserve. Retraining at scale across many related models (one traffic model serving multiple regions or metrics) raises a further coordination question: retraining each model independently on its own schedule can leave a fleet of models at different effective 'ages' and calibrated against different historical windows, which complicates any comparison or aggregation across them, and argues for coordinated retraining schedules and shared validation infrastructure rather than each model's pipeline being retrained in isolation.

At production scale, retraining is usually one stage of a continuous, automated pipeline (sometimes called continuous training or CT, extending the CI/CD idea to models) with automated data validation, automated evaluation against holdout and shadow traffic, and staged rollout (canarying a newly retrained model against a small fraction of traffic before full promotion), because a bad retrain reaching all production traffic at once is a real, costly failure mode this infrastructure exists to prevent. An open, still largely unsolved problem is efficient continual learning at scale — updating a large model incrementally with new data without either forgetting older patterns (catastrophic forgetting) or paying the full cost of retraining from scratch on the whole accumulated history every cycle — which matters increasingly as models and their training data both grow large enough that full retraining becomes a genuine cost and latency bottleneck rather than a routine background job.

terms.def: Infrastructure that computes and serves the same feature values to both training and live prediction, keeping them consistent and correct as of each moment in time.
levels: A feature store is like a shared recipe box that both the kitchen practicing a dish and the kitchen actually serving dinner use, so the food tastes the same both times.

A feature store is a piece of infrastructure that computes input columns, features, once and serves them consistently to two different places: the pipeline that trains a model, and the live system that makes predictions. Without one, a team risks computing a feature slightly differently in each place, which can quietly break a model that worked fine in testing. Big companies build feature stores; this project's small-scale answer is simpler, one shared piece of code used by both paths.

A feature store solves point-in-time correctness: making sure a training example's features are computed exactly as they would have been known at that moment, no peeking at future data, while a live serving system also needs those same features computed instantly from current data. It typically has two backing stores, an offline data warehouse for building large historical training sets and an online key-value store for fast lookups at prediction time, and a time-travel join that can reconstruct what a feature's value was at any past moment. This project does not use a real feature store; instead, one feature module is imported by both the training script and the prediction script, plus a golden-file test comparing their outputs bit for bit, achieving the same consistency goal at a much smaller scale.

The central problem a feature store solves, offline and online skew, arises because training pipelines typically compute features in batch over historical data, fast, can look at a whole table at once, while serving pipelines compute or fetch features under tight latency constraints from live, incomplete data, and any difference between how a feature is defined or computed in the two paths, even a subtly different rolling-window boundary, produces a model that performs well offline and poorly once deployed. Time-travel joins are the mechanism a feature store uses to guarantee point-in-time correctness at training time: rather than joining a label to whatever the current feature value happens to be, the join reconstructs the feature's value as of the label's own timestamp, which requires storing feature history, not just the latest value, in the offline warehouse. This project's approach, one Python module computing features that both a batch training script and a live prediction script import, sidesteps most of this complexity because both paths run the same code rather than two independently maintained pipelines, a reasonable simplification at the scale of one Mac mini but one that does not remove the underlying correctness requirement, only makes it cheaper to satisfy by sharing code instead of building infrastructure.

A subtlety practitioners commonly get wrong even with a real feature store in place is assuming that using the same feature store automatically guarantees consistency, when the online and offline stores are still often separate systems that must be kept synchronized, and a lag or bug in that synchronization reintroduces exactly the skew the feature store was meant to prevent, just one layer further down. Feature stores also introduce governance and versioning obligations that are easy to underweight until they cause an incident: features change definition over time, and without careful versioning, a model trained against one feature definition can silently start receiving a different one in production, degrading performance in a way that looks like drift but is actually a feature-pipeline change. There is a real cost-benefit judgment to make about whether a feature store is worth building at all: for a small team or a single-machine project, the operational overhead of running and maintaining offline and online consistency infrastructure can exceed the value it provides, which is exactly the argument for this course's minimal shared-module approach over adopting a full feature-store framework prematurely.

At the scale where many models across a company share overlapping features, a feature store's value shifts from preventing training and serving skew for one model to preventing redundant, inconsistent feature computation across many teams, since without shared infrastructure, ten teams computing a rolling 7-day average ten slightly different ways is both wasteful and a source of silent inconsistency across a company's models. The open engineering problems at that scale are less about the basic online and offline consistency this course's small example already achieves and more about governance at organizational scale: lineage, which models depend on which feature, access control over sensitive features, and reconciling a warehouse that is constantly being backfilled or corrected with training sets built from an earlier, now-stale version of that same warehouse.

terms.def: Latency is how long one prediction takes to return; throughput is how many predictions a system can serve per second.
levels: Latency is how long you wait after asking a question before you get an answer. Throughput is how many questions a whole line of people can get answered in one minute.

Latency is the time between asking a model for a prediction and getting the answer back, for a single request, how long it takes. Throughput is different: it's how many predictions the whole system can produce per second when lots of requests come in at once. A system can have low latency for one request but low throughput overall if it can't handle many requests at the same time, and the two often trade off against each other depending on how the system is built.

Latency is usually measured in milliseconds for a single prediction, from request to response, and reported not just as an average but as percentiles like p50 (median) and p99 (the slowest 1 percent of requests), since a system with a low average but occasional very slow responses can still feel unreliable to users. Throughput is usually measured in requests or predictions per second, and increasing it often means batching multiple requests together to use hardware, a GPU or the Neural Engine, more efficiently, which tends to increase individual latency slightly in exchange for much higher overall throughput. On a 16 GB Mac mini, both are real constraints: a traffic prediction that needs to run every five minutes across 100 stations must fit comfortably within that interval, which is a throughput requirement, while a prediction that will be checked interactively by a person needs low per-request latency instead.

The tradeoff between latency and throughput is fundamental to how serving systems are designed: batching improves hardware utilization and thus throughput by amortizing fixed overhead, model loading, memory transfer, across many predictions at once, but it necessarily adds queuing delay, since a request has to wait for a batch to fill, or a timeout to expire, before it is processed, directly increasing that request's latency. A model's raw inference speed is only one contributor to end-to-end latency; feature computation, querying recent lag values, joining against a station's current state, network round-trips, and serialization overhead often dominate total latency for a small model, meaning a faster model does not automatically translate into a faster user-facing system. For a batch prediction job, predicting all stations' status once every five minutes on a schedule, throughput and total wall-clock time matter far more than the latency of any single station's prediction, whereas an interactive, on-demand prediction system needs the opposite optimization, this distinction should drive architecture choices from the start, not be discovered after building the wrong one. Percentile latency, p99, p99.9, matters disproportionately in systems serving many users, since even a rare slow outlier is experienced by someone on every large batch of requests, unlike a rare accuracy error, which mostly goes unnoticed.

Tail latency amplification is a subtle systems phenomenon: if a single user-facing request depends on several backend calls in sequence or in parallel, fetching features from a store, then running inference, then post-processing, the overall p99 latency can be considerably worse than any individual component's p99, because the probability that at least one of several independent calls hits its own tail grows with the number of calls, a well-known problem in distributed systems that applies directly to any ML serving pipeline with multiple stages. Latency-throughput tradeoffs also interact with model architecture choice in ways that are not obvious from accuracy alone: an architecture that is marginally more accurate but has much higher tail latency variance, due to dynamic computation graphs, for instance, can be a worse production choice than a slightly less accurate but far more predictable one, especially under a strict latency budget. Practitioners commonly benchmark latency on an unrealistically idle system or with a single request at a time, missing the throughput-under-load regime where contention for shared resources, GPU memory, CPU cores, I/O, causes latency to degrade nonlinearly as concurrent load increases, load testing at realistic concurrency is necessary to catch this before it surfaces in production. Caching predictions or intermediate features can dramatically improve both latency and throughput simultaneously when inputs repeat, but only if staleness, serving a cached prediction that no longer reflects current conditions, is an acceptable tradeoff for the specific use case.

On-device inference makes latency a hard constraint tied directly to product feasibility rather than a soft optimization target: Core ML and the Neural Engine exist specifically to hit millisecond-scale latency budgets locally, without a network round-trip at all, which changes the entire latency-throughput calculus compared to a data-center-served model, since there is effectively one 'request,' the device's own, and no batching opportunity across users to trade against latency. At data-center scale, throughput optimization increasingly relies on techniques like dynamic batching with request-level scheduling, speculative execution, and model cascades, a cheap model handling most traffic, escalating only uncertain cases to a more expensive one, to serve enormous request volumes within strict per-request latency budgets. An open engineering frontier is co-designing model architecture and serving infrastructure together, quantization, pruning and distillation chosen specifically for the latency profile of the target hardware, rather than as separate afterthoughts applied to a model already finalized for accuracy alone.

terms.def: Categorical data takes on a fixed set of named values, like freeway direction; one-hot and ordinal are two ways to turn it into numbers a model can use.
levels: Some things come as words, not numbers, like red, blue, or green, or north and south for which way a road goes. Categorical just means the answer is a word from a fixed list, not a number you could measure with a ruler.

A categorical feature is one that takes a value from a fixed set of categories, like the direction of a freeway, north, south, east, west, or a station's freeway number, rather than a number you can do arithmetic on directly. Since most models only understand numbers, categorical data has to be converted somehow: one-hot encoding makes a separate 0-or-1 column for each possible category, and ordinal encoding just assigns each category a number, 0, 1, 2, and so on, which only makes sense if the categories actually have a real order.

One-hot encoding turns a column with k categories into k separate columns of 0s and 1s, with exactly one 1 per row marking which category that row belongs to; in pandas, `pd.get_dummies(df["direction"])` does this. Ordinal encoding instead assigns each category an integer, like Monday equals 0 through Sunday equals 6, appropriate only when the categories have a genuine order; using ordinal encoding on something with no real order, like freeway direction, would falsely tell the model that east is somehow between north and south numerically. Some models, notably LightGBM, can take a categorical column natively, marked with a category dtype, without either encoding, and handle the splitting internally in a way that avoids the blown-up column count of one-hot encoding.

One-hot encoding is the safe general-purpose choice for models like linear and logistic regression that assume a linear relationship between a feature's numeric value and the outcome, since it makes no false assumption about ordering, but it has a real cost: a column with many categories, like station_id, with hundreds of unique values, produces hundreds of new sparse columns, which increases dimensionality and can hurt models sensitive to it. Ordinal encoding is more compact but only valid when categories genuinely have an order, day of week has one, freeway direction does not, and misapplying it to an unordered category introduces a false numeric structure that can seriously mislead a linear model, though tree-based models are somewhat more forgiving since they only ever use the ordering to define split thresholds, not to assume linear spacing. Native categorical support in tree-based libraries like LightGBM avoids both problems by finding an optimal grouping of categories directly during tree building, without expanding the column count or imposing a false order, generally the best option for high-cardinality categoricals when using a tree-based model. It fails, for one-hot encoding specifically, when a category seen at prediction time was never seen during training, a brand-new station added later, since there is no corresponding one-hot column for it, which needs to be handled explicitly, an unknown category, or falling back to some default.

High-cardinality categorical features, many unique categories, like station_id with hundreds of values, push practitioners toward target encoding or embeddings instead of one-hot, since both keep dimensionality low while still letting the model learn a numeric representation that reflects how the category actually relates to the target, but target encoding specifically introduces leakage risk if not computed carefully with proper cross-validation folds; encoding a category by its own target's average, without holding out the row itself, silently leaks the label into the feature. The choice between one-hot, ordinal, native categorical, and learned embeddings is not purely a matter of correctness but of what each model architecture can actually exploit: linear models benefit most from one-hot's lack of false structure, tree models benefit most from native categorical or well-chosen ordinal groupings, and neural networks benefit most from learned embeddings that can place similar categories near each other in a continuous space. A frequent practitioner mistake is one-hot encoding a feature with a natural but non-uniform order instead of a more informative ordinal or target encoding, discarding real ordering information the model could have used. Category drift between training and serving, new categories appearing, old ones disappearing, or their relative frequency shifting, needs to be actively monitored rather than assumed away, since most encoding schemes handle unseen categories poorly by default and fail silently rather than raising an obvious error.

At production scale, categorical feature handling is one of the most consequential and error-prone parts of a real feature pipeline, because encoding logic, the mapping from category to number, has to be computed once and then applied identically at both training and serving time; any mismatch, a category encoded differently, or an unseen category handled differently, is a classic and hard-to-debug source of train and serve skew. Large-scale recommendation and search systems, which deal with categorical features numbering in the millions, user IDs, item IDs, rely heavily on learned embeddings with hashing tricks to keep the representation size bounded regardless of how many distinct categories exist, accepting a small, controlled amount of hash collision in exchange for tractable memory use. An open engineering problem at scale is managing categorical feature schemas over time as a living, versioned artifact, tracking which categories existed when a given model was trained, so that a category's meaning and its encoding can be audited and reproduced long after the fact, not just handled correctly in the moment.

terms.def: The type of data stored in a column or array, such as integer, float, or string, which determines memory use and allowed operations.
levels: A dtype is like telling a box what kind of toy is allowed inside, a box for whole numbers, a box for numbers with decimals, or a box for words. If you try to put the wrong kind of toy in the wrong box, the computer gets confused. Knowing the right box for each toy keeps everything organized and fast.

dtype, short for data type, describes what kind of values a column or array holds, whole numbers, decimal numbers, text, or true or false values. In pandas, `df.dtypes` shows the dtype of every column, and mismatched or unexpected dtypes are a common cause of bugs, like a speed column accidentally stored as text instead of numbers, which would break any math you try to do on it. `astype` converts a column from one dtype to another, like `df['speed'].astype(float)`.

Common pandas and numpy dtypes include `int64`, `float64`, `bool`, `object`, usually text or mixed types, `category`, efficient storage for a column with few repeated values, like `station_id`, and `datetime64` for timestamps. Choosing a narrower dtype, `float32` instead of `float64`, or `int8` instead of `int64` for a column that only holds small numbers, uses less memory, which matters directly: memory is roughly rows times columns times bytes per value, and dtype choices decide whether a multi-year PeMS extract fits in 16 GB of RAM. `pd.isnull()` and dtype interact in an important way, integer columns in classic pandas cannot hold NaN, a missing value marker, which silently upcasts an integer column to float the moment any value is missing, unless you use pandas's nullable integer dtype instead. `replace`, `fillna`, and explicit `astype` calls are the usual tools for fixing a wrong or unwanted dtype after loading messy real-world data.

dtypes determine not just memory footprint but which operations are valid and how fast they run, vectorized numeric operations on a properly typed float or int column run in optimized, compiled code, while an object dtype column, even one that looks numeric but got parsed as text, falls back to slow, per-element Python-level operations, which is a frequent and easily overlooked performance bug in data pipelines. The classic-pandas limitation that integer columns cannot represent missing values has real downstream consequences: a station ID column, if it ever has a missing value and upcasts from int64 to float64, silently changes from an exact integer representation to a floating-point one, which can then cause subtle equality-comparison bugs, pandas's newer nullable dtypes and the Arrow-backed backend in pandas 2.x were introduced specifically to fix this class of problem. The category dtype is worth using deliberately for any column with a small, repeated set of values because it stores each unique value once and uses compact integer codes for the rest, both saving memory and speeding up groupby operations on that column substantially compared to leaving it as object. Type coercion during CSV loading is a frequent silent failure point: `pd.read_csv` infers dtypes column by column from a sample of the data, and a column that looks numeric in the first thousand rows but contains a stray text value later gets silently coerced to object dtype for the whole column, breaking downstream numeric operations without any error at load time.

dtype choice interacts with numerical precision in ways that matter for correctness, not just performance: float32 versus float64 affects the precision of accumulated sums, relevant for a large rolling aggregation over years of five-minute traffic readings, where float32 rounding error can accumulate to a visible bias, and this tradeoff between memory and numerical precision is a genuine engineering decision, not a default to accept blindly. The transition from numpy-backed to Arrow-backed dtypes in modern pandas is more than an implementation detail, Arrow's columnar memory format enables zero-copy interoperability with other tools, so a dtype decision made early in a pipeline can determine whether later stages can share memory efficiently or must pay a serialization cost converting between formats. A subtlety practitioners get wrong is assuming dtype consistency across a pipeline's stages is automatic; a script that writes a Parquet file with one dtype schema and a later script that reads it with slightly different type expectations is a common, hard-to-debug source of pipeline breakage precisely because it can pass silently for a long time before a genuinely missing value appears in production data. Mixed dtypes within a single object column defeat most of pandas's performance optimizations and vectorized operations, silently degrading a pipeline's performance without any explicit error, which is why validating dtypes right after data ingestion is standard practice in a well-engineered pipeline.

At production scale, dtype decisions are made as part of a schema, often enforced explicitly rather than left to runtime inference, because silent dtype drift between a training pipeline and a serving pipeline is a classic and costly source of training-serving skew, a feature computed as float64 during training but served as float32 in a low-latency inference path can produce numerically different, and occasionally meaningfully different, model outputs. Quantized dtypes are central to efficient on-device inference, trading numerical precision for a large reduction in memory and compute, and choosing which parts of a model or pipeline can tolerate that precision loss without meaningfully hurting accuracy is an active area of both research and careful empirical validation, particularly for models deployed on Apple's hardware with strict power and latency budgets. An open engineering question is building schema and dtype validation that is enforced automatically and consistently across every stage of a large, multi-team pipeline, since manual discipline about dtypes does not scale once dozens of engineers touch different stages of the same feature pipeline over years.

terms.def: Splitting data into separate groups, either physically on disk by a key (so queries skip irrelevant files) or logically within a query (like a running calculation restarted for each station).
levels: A partition is like sorting your toys into separate labeled bins instead of one giant pile, so when you want your cars, you only have to open the 'cars' bin instead of digging through everything.

Partitioning data means splitting it into separate chunks by some key, like storing each month's traffic data in its own file instead of one giant file. This makes reading faster: if you only need March's data, you can read just the March file and skip every other month entirely, instead of scanning a whole year's worth of rows.

Storing Parquet files partitioned by, say, station and month, one folder per station, one file per month inside it, lets a query engine perform partition pruning: `data/pems_processed/2026-03.parquet` can be read alone when a query only needs March, skipping every other file untouched. Inside SQL, a window function like `AVG(speed) OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN 5 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)` uses partition in a different but related sense: it restarts the rolling average separately for each station, so one station's rolling window never mixes in another station's readings.

Physical partitioning trades storage organization for query speed: choosing the right partition key means most real queries only touch a small fraction of total files, but partitioning by a high-cardinality key, exact timestamp instead of month, creates too many tiny files and slows things down instead, since file-open overhead starts to dominate. The `PARTITION BY` clause in a SQL window function is conceptually the same idea as `groupby` in pandas but computed in place alongside the original rows rather than collapsing them, exactly why a rolling lag written as a window function with `PARTITION BY station_id` gives the same result as `df.groupby('station_id').speed.shift(3)` in pandas, just expressed in SQL. Both senses of partition fail the same way when misapplied: forgetting to partition by station when computing a rolling statistic silently blends different stations' histories together, a bug that runs without error and produces plausible-looking but wrong numbers.

The physical partitioning scheme chosen for a dataset encodes an assumption about the query workload it will serve, and a scheme optimized for one access pattern, partition by month, good for last month's data, can be poor for another, partition by station, needed for one station's full history, which is why production systems sometimes maintain the same data in multiple partition layouts, or use a table format like Delta Lake or Iceberg that supports flexible, evolvable partitioning without a full rewrite. A subtlety with the SQL `PARTITION BY` sense: it does not reduce or reorder rows the way `GROUP BY` does, exactly why it can compute a per-station lag while keeping every original row intact for downstream joins, and practitioners who reach for `GROUP BY` when they need `PARTITION BY` lose row-level granularity they needed. Predicate pushdown and partition pruning together let an engine like DuckDB scan a multi-gigabyte Parquet dataset for one station-month in well under a second, but only when the query's filter conditions are written in a form the engine can push down.

At production scale, physical partitioning strategy is a first-class data-engineering design decision, often co-designed with the downstream compute engine and revisited as query patterns evolve; poorly chosen partitioning is one of the most common causes of surprising cost and latency blowups in a data warehouse, since a query that fails to prune partitions can silently scan orders of magnitude more data than intended with no error, only a large bill or a slow response. In streaming and feature-store systems, the `PARTITION BY`-style logical partitioning, per-entity state, like per-station rolling statistics, becomes a first-class abstraction in its own right, each entity's state maintained independently and often physically sharded across machines by that same key, exactly the mechanism that lets a production feature-serving system compute per-station lag features in real time at the scale of a whole freeway network.

terms.def: A public benchmark dataset of Bay Area freeway sensor readings, built from PeMS, used across the traffic-forecasting research literature.
levels: PEMS-BAY is a famous practice test that lots of researchers around the world use to see whose traffic-guessing program works best, built from the same Bay Area road sensors this course uses.

PEMS-BAY is a specific, publicly released dataset of freeway sensor readings from the San Francisco Bay Area, built from PeMS data and widely used by researchers to test new traffic-forecasting models. Because it's public, standardized, and reused by many research papers, it works like a shared practice test: if a new model does well on PEMS-BAY, other researchers can trust and compare that result against dozens of other models tested the same way. This course draws its own live data straight from PeMS, but PEMS-BAY is a fixed, published slice of that same kind of data from a specific set of Bay Area stations and time period.

PEMS-BAY covers 325 sensor stations in the Bay Area over about six months of 5-minute readings, and it's typically reported with speed forecasting error at 15, 30 and 60 minute horizons, using metrics like mean absolute error (MAE), root mean squared error (RMSE) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). It's one of two standard benchmarks, alongside METR-LA, from Los Angeles, that spatiotemporal forecasting papers report results on, which lets you directly compare, say, a graph neural network's 30-minute MAE on PEMS-BAY against a dozen other published models on the exact same data and horizon.

PEMS-BAY and METR-LA are the two dominant benchmarks in the spatio-temporal traffic forecasting literature, used to evaluate models like DCRNN, STGCN and Graph WaveNet, and their appeal is standardization: a fixed set of stations, a fixed adjacency structure derived from road-network distance between them, and a fixed train/validation/test split, which removes a lot of the variability that would otherwise make comparing published results across papers unreliable. Because both benchmarks are derived from the same kind of source data this course works with directly, techniques and architectures validated on PEMS-BAY transfer with unusual directness to a live PeMS-based project like this one, which is not true of most academic benchmarks relative to most real-world deployments. PEMS-BAY nonetheless has real limitations as a stand-in for a live production problem: it's a fixed historical snapshot, traffic patterns, road geometry and detector health from that specific period, so a model tuned to do well on it can be tuned to quirks of that particular six months rather than to traffic dynamics that generalize to a different city, era, or detector network. Reported benchmark numbers also assume relatively clean, complete data, which understates the real difficulty a live deployment faces from detector outages and imputation that PEMS-BAY's curated release has already mostly cleaned up.

A subtlety in interpreting PEMS-BAY results is that the benchmark's fixed sensor adjacency graph is usually built from simple road-network distance, not from actual measured traffic correlation between stations, so a model's reported gain from using "the graph structure" partly reflects how good that particular hand-built graph is as a proxy for true spatial dependency, and results don't necessarily generalize to a network where you'd have to build that graph yourself from noisier real data, as a live project does. Because PEMS-BAY has been used as the standard benchmark for years, there's a real risk of benchmark overfitting at the field level, since architectures and hyperparameters have been implicitly tuned across many published papers to do well specifically on this dataset's characteristics, which can inflate apparent progress relative to how well the same architectures would do on a genuinely new deployment. A related practitioner mistake is treating strong PEMS-BAY results as a green light to deploy a complex architecture directly on a new problem without validating that the same architectural choices, graph construction, horizon, feature set, still make sense given the new problem's own data quality, station count, and network topology, which can differ substantially from PEMS-BAY's specific setup. Comparing a project's own held-out results against PEMS-BAY-reported numbers directly is also methodologically shaky unless label definitions, horizons, and evaluation windows are matched exactly, which they rarely are between a relative "slow" classification label like this course's and PEMS-BAY's typical continuous speed-regression framing.

At the research frontier, PEMS-BAY and METR-LA are increasingly viewed as aging, comparatively small and static benchmarks relative to the scale and non-stationarity of real production traffic networks, prompting calls for larger, continuously updated, or synthetic benchmark suites that better reflect deployment conditions like sensor churn, network topology changes, and genuine distribution shift over years rather than a fixed six-month window. Because PeMS is the shared lineage behind both this course's live production-style data and the PEMS-BAY research benchmark, it's a rare case where a team can validate a new architecture on the well-understood public benchmark and then transfer it with real confidence to a live pipeline built on the same underlying data source, an alignment between research and production that's uncommon in most applied ML domains. An open question for the field is how to keep benchmark-driven progress in spatiotemporal forecasting honest as architectures increasingly specialize to PEMS-BAY and METR-LA's particular quirks, rather than to the more general and harder problem of forecasting traffic on an arbitrary, evolving road network.

terms.def: A platform for machine-learning competitions, datasets, and notebooks, and one of the most common places people first practice building models.
levels: Kaggle is like a big online playground where people practice building guessing machines using real puzzles other people share, and sometimes there are contests to see whose guessing machine works best.

Kaggle is a website where people share datasets, compete in machine-learning contests, and write and share code notebooks. Beginners often use it to practice: downloading a dataset, trying different models, and comparing scores on a public leaderboard against other people's attempts. It also hosts short courses that teach practical skills quickly, which is a common starting point for many people learning machine learning.

Kaggle hosts three main things: competitions, where participants submit predictions on a shared dataset and are ranked on a public leaderboard by a fixed metric; datasets, a large public library anyone can download and explore; and notebooks, an in-browser coding environment (with free GPU access) where people write and publish analysis. Its 'Learn' courses are short, practical, code-first tutorials aimed at getting a beginner writing working machine-learning code quickly, which makes Kaggle a common on-ramp into the field, though it teaches competition skills specifically rather than the full practice of building and shipping a production system. A Kaggle notebook is convenient for quick experimentation but is not, by itself, a substitute for a properly version-controlled, tested local or cloud development environment.

Kaggle competitions historically shaped a specific, influential style of applied machine learning practice — heavy feature engineering, careful cross-validation, ensembling many models, and squeezing out small metric gains — which is where much of tabular ML practice (gradient-boosted trees in particular, and disciplined validation and leakage-avoidance habits) was refined and popularized, largely predating and complementing academic deep learning research. That said, competition-optimized practice differs from production practice in real ways: Kaggle competitions have a fixed, clean, already-collected dataset and a single well-defined metric known in advance, while real projects (like this course's traffic model) involve building the dataset from scratch, choosing the metric and horizon, handling data that keeps arriving, and shipping something that keeps working after the competition-style optimization stops — skills Kaggle by itself does not teach or test. Kaggle notebooks are a fine scratchpad for exploration but a poor habit if they replace an actual local, version-controlled environment, since notebooks alone typically lack tests, reproducible dependency management, and the discipline of a proper git history that a real project needs. Kaggle's public leaderboard and code-sharing culture is also a good way to see how strong, working solutions to a given problem actually look, though blindly copying a leaderboard-topping approach without understanding why it works is a common beginner trap.

A recurring, documented critique of Kaggle-style competition practice is that its incentive structure — squeezing out marginal leaderboard gains on a fixed, already-clean dataset — over-trains a specific skill (careful validation and ensembling for a known, static metric) at the expense of skills that dominate real applied work: framing an ambiguous problem, building a data pipeline from messy raw sources, and deciding what to build and measure in the first place, none of which a competition format tests since those decisions are made for you before the competition starts. The Learn courses specifically function as a funnel into competitions, and while they lower the barrier to entry effectively, they also reflect and reinforce this same competition-shaped skill set rather than production-shaped skills, which is a reasonable critique to hold alongside their genuine value as a fast on-ramp. A subtler issue for anyone using Kaggle datasets for research or comparison: some popular, heavily-used Kaggle datasets have known quality issues (label noise, duplicated rows, subtle leakage baked into the data collection itself) that are easy to miss when a dataset is treated as ground truth just because it's popular and widely used, a lesson that generalizes to trusting any dataset, Kaggle-hosted or not, without independent scrutiny.

Kaggle's persistence as a common beginner platform, across many years and changes in the field, reflects something true about ML teams in practice: the bottleneck is often basic scripting and modeling fluency among people who understand a domain deeply but haven't yet built hands-on machine learning skill, and Kaggle is genuinely effective at closing that specific gap quickly. At the frontier, Kaggle-style competitions have expanded into large language model and agent evaluation benchmarks, applying the same leaderboard-and-fixed-metric structure to a very different kind of task, which raises the same critique at larger scale — a benchmark leaderboard optimizes exactly what it measures, and the open question, recurring across eras of the field, is how much leaderboard-optimized skill and even leaderboard-optimized model behavior transfers to the messier, less well-specified problems that make up most real deployed AI work.

terms.def: The language for asking a database questions: SELECT picks columns, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates by group, ORDER BY sorts, JOIN combines tables.
levels: SQL is how you ask a big filing cabinet of information a question out loud, like show me every red toy, biggest first, and it hands you back exactly that.

SQL is a language for asking questions of a database, a place that stores tables of rows and columns. `SELECT` picks which columns you want to see, `WHERE` filters which rows, `GROUP BY` groups rows together to count or average within each group, and `ORDER BY` sorts the results. For example, `SELECT road_names, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY road_names ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC` shows which roads had the most incidents, most first.

A basic SQL query has a fixed shape: `SELECT` names the columns, or an aggregate like `COUNT(*)`, `FROM` names the table, `WHERE` filters rows before any grouping happens, `GROUP BY` collapses rows sharing a value into one row per group so an aggregate can be computed per group, and `ORDER BY` sorts the final result; `JOIN` combines two tables that share a key, like incidents and stations. Running `SELECT road_names, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY road_names ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 5` against the incident log, in DuckDB or SQLite, answers which five roads had the most reported events without writing any pandas code. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, unlike `WHERE`, which filters rows before, and window functions like `LAG` or `AVG() OVER` compute a lag or rolling average inside the database, the same thing `.shift()` and `.rolling()` do in pandas.

SQL's declarative nature, you describe what result you want, not the step-by-step procedure to get it, means a query optimizer, not the programmer, decides how to execute a query: which table to scan first, whether to use an index, how to order a join, and understanding that separation, reading an `EXPLAIN` plan to see the chosen execution strategy, is what separates writing correct SQL from writing fast SQL. DuckDB specifically is built for analytical queries over columnar data and can query Parquet files directly without a separate load step, making it a strong fit for this project's cleaned traffic data, whereas SQLite, a single-file database with no server, suits smaller, transactional workloads better. A feature pipeline written entirely in SQL over Parquet, rather than in pandas, is often both faster, the query engine can push filters down before reading unnecessary data, and easier to audit, since the SQL itself is a readable specification of exactly what was computed, but SQL is comparatively awkward for anything requiring row-by-row Python logic or calling out to a machine learning library mid-computation.

A subtlety that separates competent from expert SQL use is understanding why some operations are cheap and others are not from a query plan: an index accelerates targeted lookups but does nothing for a full table scan or a `GROUP BY` over most of the table, and predicate pushdown, filtering before rather than after a join or aggregation, can change a query's runtime by orders of magnitude even though two differently-written queries return identical results. Window functions like `LAG` and `AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY timestamp)` deserve particular attention because they let you compute the same lag and rolling-mean features this course builds in pandas directly inside the database, in one query, which becomes the practical choice once data outgrows what comfortably fits in memory as a DataFrame. A common mistake even experienced practitioners make is treating `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` order as if they always commute freely with `WHERE` filtering; because SQL's declarative semantics guarantee the same result regardless of how a query is phrased, but not the same performance, restructuring a slow query to filter earlier or join smaller tables first is a real skill distinct from getting the right answer at all.

At production scale, the same core SQL, `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, window functions, runs largely unchanged across radically different execution engines, a single DuckDB process on one machine, a distributed engine like Spark or BigQuery spanning thousands of machines, which is precisely the argument for writing data transformations in SQL: the same logic scales from a laptop prototype to a production pipeline with mostly the same code, only the execution engine underneath changes. The remaining engineering complexity at that scale shifts from writing correct queries to query optimization under distribution, predicate pushdown, partition pruning, and join ordering across a cluster, all conceptually the same ideas a single-machine `EXPLAIN` plan already teaches, plus data platform concerns SQL alone does not address: streaming ingestion, table formats supporting time travel, and governance over who can query what, which is where feature stores and data platforms built on top of SQL engines actually earn their complexity.

terms.def: A SQL or pandas operation that computes a value per row from a set of neighboring rows, without collapsing them into one.
levels: A window function is like peeking at the few kids standing next to you in line to figure out something about your spot, like who's tallest nearby, without making everyone in line disappear into one big group.

A window function computes something for each row using a set of nearby or related rows, like the previous value, a running total, or a rolling average, without collapsing all those rows down into a single summary row the way GROUP BY does. In SQL, `LAG(speed) OVER (PARTITION BY station ORDER BY timestamp)` gets the previous row's speed for the same station, keeping every original row intact. In pandas, `.rolling()` and `.shift()` do similar things; they add new information to each row based on its neighbors, rather than merging rows together.

In SQL, a window function has the form `function() OVER (PARTITION BY column ORDER BY column)`, where PARTITION BY splits the data into groups, like each station separately, and ORDER BY defines the sequence within each group that functions like LAG, LEAD, or a moving AVG operate over. In DuckDB, `AVG(speed) OVER (PARTITION BY station ORDER BY timestamp ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS speed_ma3` computes a 3-row rolling average per station without any GROUP BY. The equivalent in pandas is `df.groupby("station")["speed"].transform(lambda s: s.rolling(3).mean())`, or more efficiently, `df.groupby("station")["speed"].rolling(3).mean()`; both keep one output row per input row, unlike a plain `.groupby().mean()`, which would collapse each station down to a single row.

The defining property of a window function, distinguishing it from a GROUP BY aggregate, is that it operates over a 'window' of related rows, defined by PARTITION BY and, for ordered windows, a frame like ROWS BETWEEN, but returns one value per original row rather than one value per group, which makes it the natural tool for feature engineering on time series, where you want to enrich every row with information about its neighbors without losing the row-level granularity a model needs. Correctness depends critically on getting PARTITION BY and ORDER BY right: partitioning by station is what prevents one station's window from leaking into another's, exactly analogous to the groupby-before-shift discipline for lag features in pandas, and an incorrect or missing ORDER BY makes a rolling computation nondeterministic, since 'the 3 preceding rows' is meaningless without a defined order. Window functions in a database engine like DuckDB can be computed far more efficiently than an equivalent pandas loop or naive groupby-apply, since the database can push the computation down into a single optimized pass over sorted, partitioned data rather than materializing intermediate group objects in Python. The frame specification, ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW versus RANGE-based alternatives, determines exactly which rows are included, and getting this boundary wrong by one row is a common, easy-to-miss source of leakage, especially when 'current row' is accidentally included in what should be a strictly-past-only lag feature.

Window functions in SQL engines are optimized quite differently depending on whether the engine can exploit a pre-sorted, partitioned physical layout, a table clustered or indexed by station and timestamp, versus needing to sort on the fly for every query, which can be the difference between a query that scales linearly and one that becomes a bottleneck as data volume grows, this is invisible from the SQL syntax itself and only shows up in query plans and execution time. The pandas equivalent, `groupby().rolling()` or `.transform()`, has real performance and correctness pitfalls at scale: `.apply()` with an arbitrary Python function inside a rolling window is often orders of magnitude slower than a vectorized rolling method, and chaining several window operations without careful index alignment can silently reorder or misalign results relative to the original DataFrame if the index is not unique and monotonic. A subtler correctness issue specific to time-series windows over irregular or gappy data is that ROWS-based framing, a fixed count of rows, and RANGE- or interval-based framing, a fixed time span, like 'the last 15 minutes,' give different answers whenever there are missing rows, a 3-row window silently spans more than 15 minutes of real time if a station has gaps, which is precisely the kind of bug that only surfaces on real, imperfect sensor data. Practitioners moving from single-machine pandas to a distributed engine need to relearn window function semantics, since exact ordering guarantees and partition-crossing behavior differ meaningfully between engines and can silently change results during a migration.

At production data-pipeline scale, window functions computed in a database or a distributed engine, Spark, Flink for streaming, are the standard way to build time-series features consistently between training and serving, precisely because expressing the computation declaratively, PARTITION BY, ORDER BY, frame, rather than as imperative pandas code makes it far easier to guarantee the exact same logic runs in both a batch training pipeline and a low-latency streaming feature-serving system, closing the training-serving skew gap discussed elsewhere in this course. Streaming window functions add real complexity absent from the batch case: out-of-order and late-arriving events force a choice between waiting, adding latency, and computing over an incomplete window, adding inaccuracy, governed by watermarking strategies that explicitly trade off completeness against timeliness. An open engineering challenge is keeping the semantics of a window-function feature provably identical across a batch backfill and a streaming implementation, since even a small unintentional difference in frame boundaries between the two silently reintroduces the exact skew this pattern was meant to eliminate.

terms.def: DuckDB is an embedded analytical database that runs SQL queries directly over files like Parquet or CSV, with no server to set up.
levels: Imagine a filing cabinet that can also do math for you, like counting how many red folders you have, just by asking it a question instead of counting yourself. DuckDB is like that: a database you can ask questions of, that lives right inside your project instead of needing its own separate computer.

DuckDB is a database, a tool for storing and asking questions about large tables of data, that runs entirely inside your own program without needing a separate server to set up or connect to. You can point it directly at a file, like a Parquet or CSV file of traffic readings, and ask it questions using SQL, a language designed for questions like how many rows have speed below 30. SQLite is a similar idea, a database that lives in a single file with no server, but DuckDB is built specifically to be fast at exactly this kind of ask-a-question-across-millions-of-rows analytical query.

A basic DuckDB query looks like `SELECT station_id, AVG(speed) FROM 'readings.parquet' GROUP BY station_id`, which DuckDB can run directly against a Parquet file on disk without first loading it all into a table. Its core SQL vocabulary includes `SELECT`, choose columns, `WHERE`, filter rows, `GROUP BY`, aggregate per group, like pandas's groupby, `JOIN`, combine two tables on a shared key, and window functions, compute something like a running total across ordered rows without collapsing them into groups. Unlike SQLite, which is designed for many small, quick read and write transactions, DuckDB is designed for scanning and aggregating large amounts of data quickly, exactly the kind of work a how-many-slow-episodes-happened-last-month question needs.

DuckDB is a columnar, vectorized query engine, meaning it stores and processes data column-by-column rather than row-by-row and operates on batches of values at once, which is why it can scan and aggregate a large Parquet file dramatically faster than an equivalent row-by-row Python loop, or often even faster than pandas for large aggregations, despite running on a single machine with no separate server process. It can query Parquet files directly without a separate load step, using Parquet's own columnar structure and metadata, min and max statistics per column chunk, to skip reading data it does not need for a given filter, a major reason it beats reading the whole file into memory first.
